4172-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-49-jan:
January 1666 to 1667 opens on a bitter, cold, frosty day, the frost grown old and the Thames covered with ice. Pepys lies long, then works at his desk all morning, and at noon walks the Change with Mr. James Houblon.

They speak of their ill condition in money matters, a winter talk of want amid war. The volume follows a frozen January, when ice on the river matched the freeze in Navy funds. Readers get Pepys in deep winter, counting cold, coin, and company together. Ice on the Thames and ice in the treasury make a bleak pair.
4173-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-50-feb:
February 1666 to 1667 opens with Pepys at his desk all morning, then home to dinner, then down by water on a thick, misty, rainy day. Pepys walks from Redriffe to Deptford, to Bagwell's by appointment, where a woman waits within expecting him.

The volume mixes Navy business with the diary's frank private life, mist and river journeys beside office routine. Pepys moves through winter London with his usual energy, from board room to riverside. Readers get a cold, wet slice of the diary, honest about work and desire alike. Mist over the river matches the murk of a winter of war debts.
4174-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-51-mar:
March 1666 to 1667 opens in very cold weather again, after warm summer-like days, and Pepys settles at the office to do much business. Soon he is sent for to Sir George Carteret, to discourse of Navy business, wants, and the best way to bestow the little money they have.

The volume follows a service stretching small funds across a great war, with Carteret and Pepys weighing every pound. Cold spring matches the cold treasury. Readers get the diary's money worries at their sharpest, when wants outran supply every week. Little money, honestly weighed, is the volume's constant theme.
4175-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-52-apr:
April 1667 sends Pepys with Sir John Minnes in his coach, setting him down at the Treasurer's Office in Broad Street, then on to Whitehall. There he walks with Sir William Coventry into the garden and reads their melancholy letter to the Duke of York, which Coventry likes.

The volume follows the Navy's money troubles toward the disaster at Chatham, with letters, gardens, and councils. Pepys's melancholy letter captures a service running out of funds and time. Readers get spring 1667 as a slow slide toward a famous humiliation. A garden walk with Coventry frames a letter full of gloom.
4176-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-53-may:
May 1667 opens on a fine day, with Pepys doing a little chamber business before his wife goes abroad with Hewer and his mother in a hackney coach, incognito, to the Park. Pepys himself goes to the Excise Office, meeting the Cofferer and Sir Stephen Fox about money matters.

The volume pairs a wife's disguised park ride with a husband's money meeting, a typical Pepys double day. Dutch war clouds gather, but parks and excise offices fill the foreground. Readers will enjoy the diary's domestic comedy beside its public cares. A park ride incognito and an excise meeting make a Pepys double day.
4177-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-54-jun:
June 1667 brings Mr. Commander, whom Pepys employs about hiring ground behind the office for a stable and coach house. Pepys finds it needful both for honor and for profit, since his expense in hackney coaches has grown so great.

The volume follows the Dutch raid summer, yet Pepys still plans stables and coaches amid national alarm. That mix of private building and public crisis is the diary in miniature. Readers will enjoy a Pepys who, even as the Dutch sail up the Medway, counts coach fares. Stables planned in a raid summer prove how stubborn daily life can be.
4178-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-55-jul:
July 1667 wakes Pepys betimes, about nine, with a damned noise between a sow gelder, a cow, and a dog, nobody able after rising to tell what it was. Ready, he takes coach and, very sleepy, dozes most of the way to Gravesend.

There he lights and goes down to the river, in a summer when the Dutch raid has shaken the nation. The volume mixes strange morning noises with wartime travel, Pepys drowsing through alarm. Readers get July 1667 as a tired, vivid journey, with comedy beside crisis. Sleepy coach rides and river air carry him through alarm.
4179-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-56-aug:
August 1667 gives Pepys a full morning of office work, then to dinner at Sir William Pen's with Mrs. Turner and her husband. The venison pasty, Pepys notes, stank like a devil, though he knew it not till dinner was done.

Nothing but the pasty, a leg of mutton, and a pullet made the meal, a poor show after a hard morning. The volume follows the summer after Chatham, when disgrace hung over the Navy and dinners disappointed. Readers will enjoy Pepys's frank food criticism amid public failure. Bad venison at a good house sums up a summer of letdowns.
4180-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-57-sep:
September 1667, a Lord's day, sends Pepys betimes by water from the Tower, calling at the Old Swan for a glass of strong water. He sends word for little Michell and his wife to dine with them that day, and takes in a gentleman and his lady who wanted a boat.

Setting them ashore, he goes on to Westminster, in the diary's familiar river rhythm. The volume follows autumn after Chatham, with hospitality and boat rides beside office blame. Readers get a Sunday of small kindnesses, strong water, and shared boats.
4181-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-58-oct:
October 1667 keeps Pepys busy with Navy papers all morning, pleased mightily with a new girl got to wait on his wife. At noon he dines with Sir George Carteret and fellow officers at Carteret's house in Broad Street, upon his accounts.

After dinner he takes coach to his wife, gone to sittings and company, in the diary's familiar round. The volume follows the Navy's reckoning after Chatham, with household pleasures beside official blame. Readers see Pepys rebuilding his standing one dinner and one account at a time. Accounts at Carteret's house anchor a month of rebuilding.
4182-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-59-nov:
November 1667 sends Pepys betimes down to the waterside, calling and drinking a dram at Michell's, though he does not see Betty. Thence to Whitehall and Sir William Coventry's lodging, where the two sit alone a good while.

Coventry gives Pepys the full of the Duke of Albemarle's and the Prince's narratives, accounts of the war at sea from its commanders. The volume follows inquiry season, when narratives were weapons and Pepys collected them. Readers see history gathered in private talk, dram by dram. Narratives from commanders become history in private talk.
4183-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-60-dec:
December 1667, a Lord's day, finds Pepys entering his journal for two or three days, then going to church. Mr. Mills preaches a dull sermon, while in the pew sits a great lady, later known as Lady Carlisle, a very fine woman in person.

The volume closes 1667 with church, gossip, and accounts, as Pepys looks back on a year of war, fire, and inquiry. His eye for company never fails, even in a dull sermon. Readers get the diary's year-end mood: tired, watchful, and still curious about everyone in the pew.
5984-the-british-north-america-act-1867:
The British North America Act of 1867 joins Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick into one Dominion under the Crown. Passed on 29 March 1867 as 30 Victoria, chapter 3, it answers the provinces' wish for federal union under a constitution similar in principle to Britain's own.

The Act sets out the legislative authority of the new Dominion and declares the nature of its executive government. It also provides for the later admission of other parts of British North America. This is a founding legal text, plain in form and large in consequence for Canada's government.
al-hariri-the-assemblies-of-al-hariri-vo:
Al-Hariri's Assemblies, in Thomas Chenery's 1867 English version, open with this first volume of rhymed-prose tales. The rogue scholar Abu Zayd charms, begs, and cons his way across the Islamic world. His wit with words wins gold from judges, crowds, and kings.

Each assembly, or maqama, pairs a stray meeting with a feast of eloquence. Plots turn on disguise, quick talk, and sudden unmasking. Arabs of learning once knew these tales nearly by heart. Chenery's version carries their sparkle into English, and the book stands as a summit of Arabic literary art, playful and exact at once.
alaska-purchase-1867:
In 1867 Russia sold Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars, about two cents an acre. Secretary of State William Seward drove the bargain, and critics mocked the deal as Seward's Folly, a frozen wasteland bought for no good reason. Russia, short of money and fearing Britain might seize the colony, was glad to sell.

The treaty text hands over Russia's North American territory and sets the rights of the people living there. Few Americans saw value in the purchase at first. Then gold was found in the Klondike region and, much later, vast oil fields were proved. The sale now looks like one of the greatest land bargains in history.
arxiv-2412-00467:
Del Castillo and Lomelí prove a key assumption in the theory of automorphic forms for a family of groups over function fields. Kim's Assumption A matters for transferring results between groups. The authors settle it for the split classical groups in positive characteristic.

They work in a slightly wider setting, groups of classical kind, which adds quasi-split groups and generalized spinor groups. The proof leans on a local Ramanujan bound. That bound was already known for split classical groups, and the authors prove it for the wider family under a local-global condition. The result firms up a foundation used across the Langlands program.
arxiv-2412-00667:
Lucy Ham and three co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-four on how cells pick their fate, and how math models help us steer that pick. Cells read cues, weigh them, and commit to a type or act. Probes now track this at fine grain. Mixed data types make the picture hard to read as one whole.

The team tours fate systems across the tree of life, from lone cells to complex beasts. Their thread is design principles: rules that recur in how cells decide. Models can tease those rules out of data. The rules can then guide bids to reprogram cells. The piece argues for a sharp, number based view of cell choice.
arxiv-2412-01167:
Pamely Zantou and five co-authors build a privacy-preserving tool to detect birth asphyxia in a 2024 paper. The condition starves a newborn of oxygen during delivery and remains a top cause of infant death. In much of Africa, diagnosis relies on clinician judgment, which can err or come late.

Machine learning can flag cases early, but central training forces hospitals to ship sensitive records away. Their design uses federated learning, where models train locally and share only updates. The software aims to stay friendly and cheap for low-resource settings. Early detection without moving private data could speed care for newborns. The approach suits regions where trust and bandwidth both run thin.
arxiv-2412-01567:
Franz Demmel and Noel Jakse showed that diffusion in liquid metals turns on a contest between two collective moves, in a paper published in 2024. Atom simulations for liquid aluminum and rubidium find a crossover point in diffusion speed at about 1.4 times the melting temperature. Past it, the diffusion law bends away from its standard curve.

Speed echoes tell the tale. Near melting, dense packs cage each atom and slow its diffusion. In the hot fluid, swirl flows lift diffusion and stretch the tail of the echo. The two moves trade the lead as temperature climbs, which bends the diffusion law. The authors frame the crossover as a shift from dense to fluid-like life in the landscape of states.
arxiv-2412-02067:
Lee and co-authors present a 2024 physics paper on focusing hole currents with a magnetic field. Holes are the positive carriers in some thin semiconductor layers, and they feel a strong spin effect. That effect could sort them by spin, making a spin filter. But holes act quite unlike electrons in these focusing tests, which makes results hard to read.

The team models the test in a gallium arsenide layered structure. Their math shows heavy and light hole states mix as the holes move. The split heavy-hole bands turn out not to be spin sorted at all. That casts doubt on spin filtering in this common material setup. The authors then compute transport with spin tracked, giving a fresh way to plan and read such tests.
arxiv-2412-03167:
Aniruddha Mukherjee, Rekha Singhal, and Gautam Shroff present an ensemble system for intraday trading in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Independent data scientists submit models that predict short-term stock moves from five-minute price candles. The system blends their forecasts into one call.

The blend uses a weighted majority rule, and each model's weight updates with its recent performance. Models are scored by accuracy and by a utility measure that stands in for potential profit under a trading strategy. Weights can also serve to reward model owners. On real intraday data, the ensemble beat every single model on both measures, especially when weights were updated over short windows with the utility score.
arxiv-2412-03967:
Victoria Williamson and four colleagues put a new statistic to work on interstellar turbulence, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Gas and dust between the stars churn as magnetohydrodynamic turbulence stirs them. The dense clumps formed there seed new stars.

Tools in wide use, like the two-point correlation function, miss the marks this churn leaves, marks that are not Gaussian in form. The four-point correlation function tracks how sets of four density points relate, through the tetrahedron they form. The team took this measure, for the first time, on a large suite of simulations that mimic interstellar conditions. New functions in the sarabande code made the work doable. To set runs side by side through this rich lens could sharpen ideas of how stars form. The statistic also gives those who watch the sky a fresh probe of real gas out there.
arxiv-2412-05367:
Mario Collura, Jacopo De Nardis, Vincenzo Alba, and Guglielmo Lami measure a quantum trait called nonstabilizerness in a class of fermion states. Their paper from twenty twenty-four calls this trait the magic that sets some states apart for quantum computing. Gaussian fermion states can be strongly entangled, which blocked past measures. The team finds a fast way around that block.

Their method rests on a sampling scheme tied to a point process with a determinant form. It computes stabilizer entropy scores for systems of hundreds of qubits. Random states show a bulk growth like that of fully random states, with a small log-shaped extra term. The team backs this with exact math for linked scores. They also track the trait over time in a random circuit. In a flat fermion model it jumps sharply at phase edges.
arxiv-2412-06667:
Georgios Giannakopoulos and Khushbu Mehboob Shaikh design a compact antenna in 2024 for mobile phone bands. Their dual-band antenna must work on both the GSM and DCS bands while staying small enough for a handset. They built it as a flat patch on a common circuit board material, shaped so it can fold into a box form.

The team first simulated the design in a standard antenna tool, then built it and tested it on lab gear. The measured signal loss matched the simulation well across a wide range of frequencies. They also charted how the antenna radiates in each band. The paper closes with how the feed line match affects performance.
arxiv-2412-06867:
Boyang Zhang and co-authors present a way to shrink deep learning models by factoring their weight tables, without the usual small loss of accuracy, in a 2024 paper. Splitting a weight table into two thinner ones cuts size, but tuning the split alone leaves a gap from the original model's skill. The team traces that gap to the split being tuned apart from the model's own training goal.

Their fix tunes both at once under one joint goal. First they work out how far split errors may stray before model skill moves. They then offer two routines: one that maximizes accuracy while compressing, and one that minimizes size while holding skill steady. Neither needs retraining. In one test, a model shrunk by 70 percent beat the original it came from, across vision and language tasks.
arxiv-2412-07067:
Yinsicheng Jiang and colleagues published a benchmark study in 2024 on mixture-of-experts language models. These models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks. That trick scales models cheaply, but it mixes memory and compute demands. Cost, accuracy, and speed then trade against each other in messy ways.

The authors built a benchmark designed to expose those trade-offs. Their analysis found that current hardware rarely balances all three goals. Systems usually win on two dimensions and sacrifice the third. They call that pattern the MoE-CAP trade-off. A radar diagram visualizes where each system stands. New sparsity-aware metrics measure memory and compute use more fairly. The tools aim to guide real deployment choices.
arxiv-2412-07667:
Lucy Martinez uses symbolic computation to attack the generalized gambler's ruin problem in one and two dimensions. The classic problem asks how a gambler betting repeatedly will fare before ruin or victory. Exact symbolic answers reveal structure that plain numerical simulation hides.

The paper gives efficient algorithms for the generalized problem rather than case-by-case computation. It also introduces a twist: a third kind of step, called the mirror step, added to the usual win and loss moves. For that variant the author derives closed formulas for the probability of ruin and the expected duration of the game. The work doubles as a showcase for symbolic methods in probability.
arxiv-2412-08167:
Zhenpeng Chen, Xinyue Li, and colleagues improve fairness for people who sit at the overlap of several protected groups in a 2024 software fairness study. A hiring model can look fair for each single attribute while failing badly for a specific combination, the intersectional gap. Their ensemble mutates inputs at higher orders, changing several attributes at once to probe those combined subgroups during inference.

Diversity among the mutant ensemble members drives the gains, the authors argue. Checking fairness only one attribute at a time is no longer enough for deployed systems, and inference-time fixes avoid retraining models that owners cannot touch.
arxiv-2412-09867:
Zi Haur Pang and five co-authors present a 2024 paper on an android robot that interviews people like a human researcher. The robot ERICA was fitted with attentive listening, conversational repair skills, and the ability to adapt to a speaker's fluency. It can also analyze and present the results after the interview ends. The system was deployed at a real international dialogue conference, a first for such a setup.

Forty-two participants were interviewed at the event. Sixty-nine percent reported positive experiences. The authors conclude the android conducted interviews comparably to a human in this setting. The study serves as a proof that embodied AI can handle the social give-and-take of interviewing, not just scripted questions. A demonstration video accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2412-10167:
Octavio Roncero and Pablo del Mazo-Sevillano present MADWAVE3, a computer code for quantum chemistry, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The code tracks a wave packet over time for systems of three atoms. It can handle collisions that bounce, react, or break apart under light, even when several electronic states are coupled.

The paper lays out the theory, the modular build of the code, and how to install and run it. Long lists explain each control setting and what it does. A worked case, a hydrogen atom hitting a hydrogen-deuterium molecule, shows the steps and the speedup from parallel runs. Input files and the needed energy surface are shared.
arxiv-2412-11267:
Namdari and co-authors present a 2024 stats method for data that arrive as scattered points in time or space. Such point data show up in medical scans, where a camera counts photons from a tracer in the body. A popular tool called partial least squares mixes model fitting with data squeezing, but it could not take point data as input. The team extends the tool to fill that gap.

Their method, P3LS, works with hidden rate curves behind the point clouds. A new fitting route leans on a known random curve model. Tests on made-up data check how the method behaves. The team then applies it to kidney scans to help spot blocked kidneys. Tools of this kind could also train new radiologists to read such scans.
arxiv-2412-11367:
Wang and five colleagues report a rare case of renewed star birth in a large galaxy in twenty twenty-four. The galaxy, called 3C 59, hosts a bright quasar with strong radio jets. It is an elliptical galaxy, a type that is often quiet and old. Data from many telescopes in space and on the ground trace its past.

The history shows a burst of new stars in the past five hundred million years, after a long quiet phase. Three nearby small galaxies show warped shapes, and two have long tidal tails that point toward 3C 59. The authors argue that small mergers push gas into the big galaxy. That gas fuels new stars and may also feed the quasar. The jets may keep gas hot around the group and curb star birth in the small galaxies.
arxiv-2412-11667:
Di Santo, Tiberti, and Cassioli wrote in twenty twenty-four about a fairer, safer quantum secret sharing protocol. Quantum secret sharing encodes a secret in quantum states split among players. Only authorized subsets should be able to reconstruct it. Past schemes often needed every player and used fixed network layouts. They also lacked player authentication and redundancy. The authors build on a generic distributed quantum network with a threshold rule. A dealer picks the best subset of players using a quantum routing algorithm.

Custom weights guide which players join the reconstruction. Post-quantum cryptography primitives fingerprint and authenticate each player. Identities stay hidden to protect player privacy during the process. Tests against classical and quantum attacks showed strong performance. The protocol improves security measures over the current state of the art. Redundancy means the scheme tolerates missing or faulty players.
arxiv-2412-12067:
Hidetaka Manabe and Yuichi Sano offer a scalable way to load bell-curve probability distributions into quantum computers, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Loading a distribution as a quantum state is a basic step in many quantum algorithms. For a distribution with many variables, the circuit can grow too large and hard to build.

Their method uses tree tensor networks, a way of splitting a large structure into a tree of small parts. They prove that bell curves with chain-like correlation patterns fit this form well. A compiler then searches for the leanest network layout and builds the matching circuit. In tests on random high-dimensional cases, the circuits came out far shallower, with far fewer key gates, than with older methods, while staying faithful to the target.
arxiv-2412-12167:
Evangelia Gkritzali and co-authors present a 2024 paper on Greek2MathTex, a system that turns spoken Greek into typeset mathematics. LaTeX is the standard language for equations, but its code-like syntax shuts out many users, especially people with disabilities and anyone new to it. Speaking a formula is far more natural than typing its code.

The end-to-end system chains speech recognition tuned for Greek with a stage that renders the recognized words as LaTeX commands. It is, to the authors' knowledge, the first such pipeline built for Greek. The work targets classrooms and research alike, opening equation writing to people whom the keyboard has kept out.
arxiv-2412-13667:
ChengAo Shen and co-authors published a 2024 paper on finding cause-and-effect links with help from language models and mixed data. Classic methods for causal discovery rely on numbers alone and miss the meaning inside text and other records. Language models can read those meanings, but tools for causal work with them lag behind, especially when data comes in several forms.

Their system, MATMCD, uses two cooperating AI agents. One agent fetches and prepares extra data from varied sources. The other reasons over the combined material and proposes cause-and-effect constraints. Tools plug into both agents to ground their work. The authors tested the system on seven datasets. Results suggest that adding other data types sharpens causal discovery beyond what numbers alone give. The paper points toward decision tools that use everything a record holds, not just its measurements.
arxiv-2412-14167:
Runtao Liu and six co-authors adapt a preference training method to video generation in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Text-to-video models can now make varied clips, but the clips often miss what users want. Preference training fixed similar gaps in language and image models. The authors bring that approach, called DPO, to video diffusion models. Their pipeline is named VideoDPO.

Earlier image methods judged either looks or text match, not both. The team scores clips on both axes with a combined score they call OmniScore. They gather preference pairs on their own from these scores. Training on the pairs steers the model toward clips people rate higher. The work matters for media tools that must match user taste, not just prompts.
arxiv-2412-14867:
Imed Keraghel and Mohamed Nadif group documents with a graph method that blends named entity links and large language model embeddings. Rich embeddings from models like BERT help text work, but most grouping methods skip entity ties. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The method builds a graph where documents are nodes and edges weigh how alike their named entities are. A graph convolutional network then tunes the grouping. Tests show the approach beats classic co occurrence methods, most of all for documents rich in named entities. The authors argue entity aware graphs give a truer sense of which documents belong together.
arxiv-2412-15067:
Aqeel Ahmed and co-authors work out the fingerprints of hidden sectors in particle physics in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A hidden sector is a set of unknown particles that talk to known matter through a portal interaction. When the hidden part is removed from low-energy theory, it leaves behind specific correction terms.

Working in the standard effective theory framework, the team studies Higgs, neutrino, and hypercharge portals. For each portal, the leading correction terms have fixed forms, no matter how the hidden sector behaves inside. Under conditions tied to causality, even some signs are fixed. The authors fit these terms to precision data, Higgs results, and boson pair production to bound their sizes.
arxiv-2412-16667:
Nicolás Díaz Ferreyra, Sirine Khelifi, Nalin Arachchilage, and Riccardo Scandariato map a research area in this two thousand twenty-four review. Privacy and security are at the core of trusted information systems. Yet developers often lack training, or treat the two as late thoughts. Security engineering has as-code techniques: automatic vulnerability detection and secure code generation. The privacy mates are far less studied: detection of privacy properties in source code, and generation of privacy-friendly code. The team calls this area Privacy as Code.

Their review sets out what is there: methods and tools, and how they are judged. The verdict is that the field is young, most of all for method quality and usability. The team lays out paths for work to come: studies with developers, curated data sets, and the role AI might play. The paper is a map for researchers who enter privacy engineering.
arxiv-2412-17067:
Sheng Jin, Zhe Zhai, Qifu Tyler Sun, and Zongpeng Li study a form of network coding built on circular shifts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. In network coding, nodes blend data as it moves, and shifts keep the math cheap. The plain shift form, though, cannot reach full network speed, so extra symbols must be sent.

Their new form works over a broad field and can reach full speed. Its set of local rules is closed under its own blends, by design. Costs stay much like the old form, and in some cases they drop. The work also yields new array codes, with bounds on their size and fast ways to encode them.
arxiv-2412-18167:
Hariharan and a large team check how model choices affect a giant voltage found in a thundercloud in twenty twenty-four. A telescope in India tracks muons, tiny particles that rain from space. Shifts in their flow showed a cloud voltage of more than a billion volts in twenty fourteen. That claim rests on models of how particles collide and split in the air.

The team reran the work with nine mixes of collision models, high energy and low. Found voltages ranged a bit above and below the first claim. Low energy models caused most of the spread. They checked seven more big storms the same way. The first, lowest value still stands as the safe report.
arxiv-2412-18667:
Jiajie Xu, Xabier Irigoien, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini survey the underwater vehicles and support technologies that could knit the oceans into a smart, sensed network. Their survey appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Oceans cover most of the planet, yet remain sparsely observed. Vehicles that dive, drift, and surface are the network's moving parts.

The authors sort vehicles into tethered, autonomous, hybrid, surface, and animal-like bionic types. Each class is weighed for monitoring, deep exploration, defense, and inspection work. Communication options get the same treatment: sound, light, and mixed links. Support gear includes submerged buoys, docking stations, and wearable localization aids. Stubborn limits include energy, bandwidth, and harsh conditions. Artificial intelligence, they argue, will raise autonomy and efficiency. The classification gives builders a map of the field.
arxiv-2412-18867:
Members of the DarkSide-20k team describe quality checks for light sensors built for a dark matter search, in a 2024 report. The experiment needs a large area of silicon sensors that can catch faint flashes of light deep underground. Each sensor batch must be tested with care, since a weak part could hurt the whole search.

The report covers how the sensors were made, checked, and passed or failed at each stage of production. It explains the tests used to confirm that the parts meet the strict needs of the experiment. For readers, the work shows the scale of effort behind a modern dark matter detector, where careful checking of parts is as vital as the search itself.
arxiv-2412-18967:
Balbeer Singh and Varun Vaidya present a 2024 physics paper on jets of particles flying through dense nuclear matter, as in heavy-ion collisions. The medium watches the jet so often that a new momentum scale emerges, set by the medium itself. Splitting the problem at that scale is needed to separate what can be computed from what cannot.

Working in a new effective theory that treats the jet as an open quantum system, the authors give a precise operator definition for how a gluon's direction spreads in the medium. They show the spread is partly universal: it depends on how the jet is measured and probes the medium at both large and small momentum shares.
arxiv-2412-19567:
Nuraddin Kerimov, Aleksandr Onegin, and Konstantin Yakovlev present a path planner for robot arms in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Planning a safe path in three dimensions is hard for arms with many joints. Moving obstacles make it harder still, because time must enter the plan.

Their planner joins safe-interval search, which tracks time windows when a spot is free, with a fast randomized tree method. A dedicated trick computes the safe intervals quickly. In tests, the planner beat leading rivals on both running time and path cost. The authors have released their code in public for others to use and extend.
arxiv-2412-20067:
Arif Er and Meng-Chwan Tan lift several Floer homology theories one categorical floor higher using physics, in this 2024 paper. Floer theories count solutions of geometric equations on manifolds and organize them into homology groups. Categorification replaces those groups with richer category structures. Working from twisted gauge theories with sixteen supercharges, the authors read them through lower-dimensional Landau-Ginzburg models.

That reading yields new Fueter-type categories that lift three known Floer theories for two-, four-, and five-manifolds. A second reading shows the same objects match Fukaya-Seidel categories. In the eight-dimensional case they climb one rung more, to a three-category for four-manifolds. The paper closes a trilogy and proves several standing math conjectures by physical means.
arxiv-2501-00967:
Leonardo Gonzalez and Victor Zavala detail a smarter optimization setup in a 2025 paper. Bayesian optimization tunes systems that are costly to test, learning a statistical model as it goes. The standard method treats the whole system as a black box and ignores known structure inside it.

Many real systems chain known steps with unknown ones, such as linked plants with sparse connections. Earlier grey-box methods handled that mix with heavy sampling or side problems. The framework detailed here uses adaptive linearization to keep the math tractable. The paper focuses on practical implementation choices that make the method run well. Exploiting structure should cut the number of costly tests a tuning run needs.
arxiv-2501-01467:
Martin Erinin and colleagues built a laboratory cloud chamber in a paper published in 2024. Clouds form when humid air cools and water condenses onto tiny seed particles, but field conditions are hard to control. Their chamber, called REACh, triggers droplet birth with a sudden pressure drop that cools the air, mimicking rising air in the sky.

The mid-sized chamber tightly controls starting humidity, seed type and amount, temperature, pressure, and mixing by turbulent flow. Fast instruments track droplet sizes and counts as the cloud lives and dies. Tests showed the coldest point of each expansion follows dry or moist theory well across humidity levels. Cloud physicists gain a repeatable test bed for nucleation studies.
arxiv-2501-02067:
Many functions in math and optimization are too rough for ordinary calculus, so analysts build second-order tools that act like curvature for jagged cases. Pham Duy Khanh, Boris Mordukhovich, Vo Thanh Phat, and Le Duc Viet study two such tools, proposed very recently by Rockafellar: a generalized form of twice differentiability and objects called quadratic bundles. Unlike older tools, these live in the same space as the problem itself.

The team develops fresh ways to handle these ideas for a broad class of well-behaved rough functions, called prox-regular. They prove new characterizations of the generalized derivative. They also show the quadratic bundles are never empty for these functions, which clears the ground for using them in optimization.
arxiv-2501-04567: Martyn R Dixon, Leonid A. Kurdachenko, and Igor Ya. Subbotin study a class of algebraic objects called left braces. Their 2025 paper gives a detailed account of some nilpotent left braces that are generated by one element. The abstract is brief, and it states the aim and scope of the work rather than listing findings.
arxiv-2501-04867:
Serge Tabachnikov, writing alone in 2025, studies curves traced by bouncing light in odd geometries. The setting is a billiard table whose distance rule is a Finsler metric with straight-line paths. A caustic is the bright curve that reflected rays outline as they bounce. Tabachnikov fixes the number of bounces and asks about the curve's sharp points, its cusps.

He proves that such a caustic always has at least four cusps. The question descends from Jacobi's last geometric statement about shapes on an ellipsoid. Recent work had settled the claim for ordinary Euclidean billiards. This note extends the result to the wider Finsler setting. The proof adds a piece to the long study of how light and geometry meet.
arxiv-2501-05767:
You Li and ten colleagues build the first model that can point to objects across many images from free-form text. Multimodal models read single images well and grasp groups loosely. Precise pointing inside a group, though, has lagged. Chain-of-thought tricks that chain single-image pointing prove shaky.

Their model, Migician, learns the skill end to end. A new data set of over six hundred thousand examples covers many multi-image pointing tasks. It adds fresh free-form instructions generated for this purpose. A dedicated benchmark, MIG-Bench, scores the skill directly. Migician beat the best existing models by a wide margin on it. It even passed models many times its size. Code, model, data, and benchmark are all released openly.
arxiv-2501-05967:
Mihaescu, Isar, and Macovei study a tiny chip trap paired with paired electron dots in this twenty twenty-five paper. The dots act like small gates for charge, and the trap holds a wave field that links to them. The team tunes the pair so the dot beat is twice the trap beat.

Inside, that tuned link gives rise to a rich set of joint acts in the pair. The flow of charge through the dots ties to the wave field in the trap in a bent, non-plain way. Both parts show sharp shifts at key points as the settings change. The light-like flux from the trap can bunch or spread, and at some points the trap acts like a tiny laser at wave-band rates.
arxiv-2501-06367:
Hassan Nassar and four co-authors design a hardware fingerprint that resists both wear and learning attacks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such fingerprints, called PUFs, turn tiny manufacturing quirks of memory chips into unclonable keys for authentication.

Non-volatile memory cells that hold several levels give rich, hard-to-model responses. But frequent writing wears the cells out, shortening the device's life. The team first models how wear degrades response quality. On that model they build a design that spreads writes evenly and eases stress per cell. The result lasts sixty-two times longer than the best prior design. Protection against machine learning attacks stays intact.
arxiv-2501-06567:
Yuru Li, Jiawei Tan, and Qingying Xue prove weighted bounds for commutators of singular integrals in a 2025 paper. These operators sit at the heart of harmonic analysis and partial differential equations. They measure how multiplication and averaging fail to commute, a gap with deep bounds attached.

Working under flexible integral conditions of Young type, the authors first pin the operators down with sparse domination. Dyadic methods then deliver two classic bounds with general weights. A version with numbers sharpens the second bound. Their proof splits a link between the count and a small parameter that earlier work kept fused. The results cover a wide shelf of such tools, from Calderon commutators to Fourier multipliers.
arxiv-2501-06867:
Alice Nardelli and co-authors give a robot arm a personality and test whether people can sense it, in a paper from 2025. Personality shapes how humans read each other, and robot makers use it to smooth teamwork. Past work is scattered and built mostly for human-shaped robots. Factory arms, though, are set to work beside people more and more.

The team loaded a full cognitive model of personality into a Kinova arm. The model rates the arm on traits like care, openness to people, and ease. Those ratings steer how the arm moves, picks acts, and reacts. In a joint game study with many sessions, users played with arms set to unlike traits. Some arms also spoke, while others used only gestures. The study asks whether shape-free robots can still project a clear character.
arxiv-2501-09267:
Abdalwhab Abdalwhab and co-authors ask whether flexible vision-language models are ready to spot pipes, ducts, and wiring parts on real construction sites, in a 2025 paper. Robots with cameras could one day check mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work on their rounds. Open-vocabulary models can look for anything named in words, with no special training, which makes them tempting for messy sites.

The team filmed sites with a ground robot and labeled the parts by hand. They then raced the open models against small detectors fine-tuned on the labeled set. Flexibility did not win: the tuned lightweight models beat the open ones by a wide margin in this special setting. The authors conclude that, for now, site robots still need training on the exact parts they must find.
arxiv-2501-09767:
Tuowei Wang and five co-authors present LeMo, a system for teaching language models to handle longer texts, in a 2025 paper. Longer context windows are in demand, but training for them eats memory, mostly through stored intermediate values. Existing shortcuts cut the cost of weight updates rather than this memory load.

LeMo rests on a pattern the authors call contextual token sparsity: many tokens add little in long texts. The system drops dull tokens layer by layer, predicts the drop pattern cheaply in advance, and uses tuned low-level code to cash the savings. Model quality is preserved while memory use falls. The work opens a path to long-context training on more modest hardware.
arxiv-2501-09867:
G-functions are power series with deep ties to geometry, and Yves André, a solo author, surveys their role in arithmetic geometry, the field where number theory meets shapes. These functions solve the equations that govern how the periods of a family of shapes change as the family bends. Where two such functions meet in an algebraic relation, the meeting point often has extra hidden symmetry.

A principle from Bombieri caps how special such points can be, an idea that fed into a famous conjecture on unlikely meetings in geometry. André closes with the method's recent revival around the Zilber-Pink conjecture, a sweeping claim about when special points can appear. The survey links old results to the newest work.
arxiv-2501-10867:
Gonzalo Herrera shows how dark matter detectors, now fine neutrino catchers too, can probe new physics through neutrinos. The paper from twenty twenty-five offers three ideas. Each turns a low-energy neutrino signal into a test of physics past the Standard Model. The detectors in view were built for dark matter but see solar neutrinos well.

First, solar neutrinos can trigger the Migdal effect through coherent scattering on nuclei, leaving a set mark. Second, a radioactive source near a liquid xenon tank could reveal the neutrino anapole moment by electron scattering. Third, neutrinos tied to a light dark sector may carry boosted electromagnetic traits from loop effects. Herrera weighs how well near-term detectors can test that case. The paper recasts sunk-cost rigs as broad physics probes.
arxiv-2501-11067:
Elad Levi and Ilan Kadar build a testing ground for conversational AI systems. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Chatbots built on large language models must hold multi-turn talks, call the right tools, and obey strict policy rules. Old test methods are fixed sets of cases made by hand. They miss the mess and variety of real use.

Their framework, IntellAgent, is open source and uses several agents working together. It builds varied test cases on its own from policy-driven graphs. It also creates realistic events and runs live talks between a fake user and the system under test. The output gives fine-grained reports on where a system fails. That detail helps builders fix weak spots that coarse scores would hide.
arxiv-2501-12267:
Chaohao Xie, Kai Han, and co-authors fill missing regions in videos with a diffusion model that needs no extra training, in work from twenty twenty-five. Flow guided inpainting copies pixels from other frames, but big holes have no matching pixels at their center. Diffusion models invent rich content, yet naive use breaks time consistency.

Their framework steers the denoising process with valid pixels pulled along optical flow paths. Those pixels constrain the random noise the model starts from. Filled frames then feed further propagation and generation rounds. Different noise seeds give varied but coherent results. Tests beat leading video inpainting methods on both time coherence and fidelity, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-12567:
Cuellar and five co-authors report on gas near distant quasars that also show strong molecular and neutral hydrogen absorption. Their study from two thousand twenty-five uses the X-shooter tool on the Very Large Telescope. They look for absorption from highly ionized nitrogen close to the quasar's own redshift.

Nitrogen lines showed in nine of thirteen quasars, a far higher rate than in systems far from quasars. The ionized gas moved over much wider speed ranges than the neutral gas, so the two seem split in motion. Bluer, outflowing parts showed higher ionization. The team reads these systems as key stages when a quasar still sits in rich gas, before or as outflows start.
arxiv-2501-12667:
Wenbin Zhou, Liyan Xie, Zhigang Peng, and Shixiang Zhu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It spots the moment a data stream's pattern shifts, by way of score matching with noise.

Classic change-point tools lean on set forms for the data before and after the shift. That fails on rich, high-dimensional streams. Here the score of the data law is learned by adding noise, then cleaning it back, a trick called denoising score matching. A CUSUM test runs on those scores, in both offline and online forms. Theory shows the noise scale can be tuned to sharpen the catch. Tests on fake data and on quake precursor hunts back the claim.
arxiv-2501-12967:
Serena Dipierro and co-authors study when a population survives in a hostile region under mixed forms of spread. Their paper appeared in 2025. The model is a logistic diffusion equation, where growth is limited by crowding. Spread is driven by a blend of fractional operators, covering both normal wandering and long jumps. Outside the region, conditions are lethal.

Survival hinges on the spectrum of the region, its size and shape in effect. The authors prove ranges where steady living states exist and where only extinction remains. A striking example shows both normal and jumpy spread alone would kill the species. Yet adding even a tiny amount of a concentration pattern lets it survive. The work clarifies how nonlocal spread changes the fate of populations in poor habitats.
arxiv-2501-13767:
Mingzhao Wang and a team of co-authors solve the traveling salesman problem with a diffusion model that guesses whole tours at once. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Step-by-step solvers are slow; parallel ones are fast but sloppy, and tours suffer.

Their system, DEITSP, denoises many candidate tours simultaneously in a single step, steadied by a self-consistency trick. A dual graph transformer reads both city points and the roads between them, with fewer layers for speed. Iterations alternate adding and removing noise, widening the search beyond earlier diffusion attempts. A noise schedule refines the solution space as it goes. On real and large synthetic instances, the solver matched or beat rival neural methods on quality, speed, and generalization.
arxiv-2501-13867: Antonino Ficarra wrote a 2025 paper in algebra presenting the theory of cotangent functors in the approach of Palamodov. Cotangent functors are tools that measure how algebraic structures deform. Alongside the theory, Ficarra presents a conjecture of Herzog tying the vanishing of certain of these functors to a prized property of rings called being a complete intersection. The abstract is brief, so this account stays at the level of what the work sets out to do.
arxiv-2501-13967:
Haoxuan Che, Yifei Wu, Haibo Jin, Yong Xia, and Hao Chen wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It trains medical image models across hospitals that cannot share their scans, in a way that still works on scans from new places.

In federated learning, each hospital trains locally and only model updates travel. The hard part is handling the style gap between hospitals' images. Older methods remix the traits of known sites, which may never mimic a truly new site. The authors' framework instead invents fresh image styles by pushing generated pictures away from the originals at the feature level, then trains the task model to close that gap. They also note that sites contribute unevenly to the shared model's toughness. The paper builds on that observation to balance the training.
arxiv-2501-14867:
Kaili Cao and Marc Pinsonneault model red giant stars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They focus on two signs of what happens inside such stars. One is the first dredge-up, when surface material mixes with processed matter from inside. The other is a bump in brightness along the red giant path.

They compare survey data on real giants with models built by a standard star code. The models match the broad trends with mass and metal content, but the observed surface change is smaller than predicted. The brightness bump also sits higher in the data than in models. The authors discuss fixes and propose lithium as a sharp test for telling them apart.
arxiv-2501-15767:
Muhammad Maaz and Timothy Chan tackled a new check task for chance based models. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with Markov processes whose rates come from machine learning. A learned rate is not a fixed number, so plain checks fail. For a wide set of models, from linear to neural nets, they cast key checks as a two part math program. Those checks ask if a state can be reached, how long it takes, and what total gain accrues.

Their solve scheme breaks the program and spreads bounds to speed the search. Tests showed solves up to one hundred times faster than top tools. They show use in a real health care case and share a free tool for the work.
arxiv-2501-16067: Joop Niekus traces the path of Brouwer's use of free choice chains in the base of math, up to the year a way to use them well was found. The paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is a work of history and close reading. From the rules of that first good use, Niekus draws a small set of base rules. With just those, he rebuilds Brouwer's work from that year on. The rebuild matches the source with care, and makes clear why the proofs work.
arxiv-2501-16167:
Onur Alican and a team of co-authors built an index to grade how like a true voltage source a power device acts. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with power systems now ruled by electronics. New devices crowd in with wild dynamics. Grid staff need to know how close each acts to the classic source models they trust. Their index is scored per tone band, so gaps show where they live.

Both makers and grid operators can use the score. It flags in which tone ranges a model under study will part from the reference. Readers who plan the new grid get a shared gauge for a mixed fleet. One number per band beats a vague claim of like acts.
arxiv-2501-17467:
Riku Kuze, Shigeo Kimura, and Ke Fang model black hole systems in this 2025 paper. The systems pair a black hole with a normal star that feeds it gas. Some of them shine at extreme gamma-ray energies, and the source of that glow is debated. The team proposes a two-part picture based on how the gas disk behaves.

In their picture, a strongly magnetic disk heats protons and electrons to high speeds. Fast protons then clash with disk gas and light, making very high energy gamma rays and neutrinos. Jets from the black hole add lower energy gamma rays of their own. Added up over many quiet systems, the glow may explain part of the galaxy's diffuse high-energy light.
arxiv-2501-17567:
Emmanuel Irabor, Mariam Musavi, Abhijit Das, and Sergi Abadal wrote a 2025 paper on linking AI chips without wires. AI work keeps demanding more compute, and makers now split jobs across many small chiplets. The links between chips are still stiff and waste power, which caps how far the design can scale.

Wireless links could free chips to talk across a package with less loss. The team weighs what such links can offer multi-chip AI accelerators. Flexible links may let builders mix chip types for each new model family. Their study maps the gains and the hard parts, from signal noise to layout. The work feeds the search for scalable AI hardware.
arxiv-2501-17767:
Ankush Agarwal, Ganesh S, and Chaitanya Devaguptapu answer questions that span tables and prose in a 2025 study. Real questions often need numbers from a table joined with facts buried in text, across several hops. Fine-tuned systems need costly human-made training sets, and language models alone handle single-source text better than mixed sources.

Their hybrid graph approach links table cells and text passages into one structure that a language model can reason over. Building the graph replaces heavy training data with explicit connections. Multi-hop aggregation then follows those links. The design targets accurate answers where evidence is split between structured and unstructured homes.
arxiv-2501-19067:
Hossein Zakerinia, Dorsa Ghobadi, and Christoph H Lampert present a 2025 paper on why deep networks that learn several tasks at once still generalize, despite having far more knobs than data points. One leading account says the real learning happens in a small hidden subspace of the full weight space. The authors test that account in multi-task learning.

They build the network directly inside the small subspace, using random expansion tricks to do so. High-accuracy shared solutions then appear with far fewer free parameters than single-task learning needs. From that low intrinsic size they derive generalization bounds that are not vacuous, meaning the promised error ceiling sits below blind guessing.
arxiv-2502-00267:
Jonathan Owens, Bojun Feng, Jie Liu, and David Moore study how water changes carbon capture in a sponge-like crystal, in a 2025 paper. The crystal is a metal-organic framework fitted with amine arms that grab carbon dioxide in a chain reaction. Its uptake curve has a sharp step, which makes it attractive for capture work.

Using atom-level calculations, the team shows how nearby water molecules twist the chain behavior and the energy of capture. They predict a new arrangement in which water and carbon dioxide braid together down the pore. A simpler grid model, adjusted for water, then reproduces the sharp shift in uptake at low pressure. The braid hints that capture may flip into a phase change, a finding that could guide drier or wetter capture designs.
arxiv-2502-00667:
Maezawa and Saito study an ordering between graphs built from rainbow patterns in colored networks. A rainbow subgraph uses a different color on every edge. One graph sits below another in their order when banning its rainbow form in richly colored complete graphs forces the second form out too.

When one graph contains the other, the order is automatic. Earlier work covered the strange case where a bigger graph still sits below a smaller one. This study turns to pairs where neither graph contains the other. The authors prove many such ordered pairs exist. They also map how those pairs arrange themselves inside the overall order.
arxiv-2502-00867:
Cooper and Okur study how to split a directed network with balanced flow into loops, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such a network is called Eulerian when flow in and out match at each point. They count splits of full tours into a given number of smaller loops. They show a signed sum over all counts cancels to zero.

The only case that escapes the rule is a single directed cycle. Their proof uses heaps of pieces, a picture tool for stacked items. They link heaps to splits and to maps of shared edges. A classic inversion step on the split lattice then gives the result. The proof also ties a key graph polynomial to color counts of shared-edge maps.
arxiv-2502-01567:
Deqian Kong and co-authors proposed a new class of language models built around latent thought vectors in two thousand twenty-five. In these models, hidden thought vectors follow a stated prior model and guide a Transformer decoder as it writes tokens. Thought is thus an explicit part of the model, not just a by-product.

Training uses variational Bayes with two speeds: fast updates for each text's thought vectors, and slow updates for the shared decoder. The models add new scaling knobs, like more thought vectors or more inference steps. With them, the models beat standard autoregressive and diffusion models on perplexity and zero-shot tasks. They also showed early few-shot reasoning that grew with model size.
arxiv-2502-01867:
Anastasiia Soboleva and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on the cold start problem in online advertising. New ads have almost no click history, so click-through forecasts start shaky, and early weak showings can drag an ad down for good. The team builds an upper-confidence-bound algorithm within a multi-armed bandit frame, tuned to position-based auction systems that charge per click.

They derive theory bounds on wasted budget and test the method on synthetic and real platform data. It held up in practice. Alongside long-term gains, they propose a control on how much exploration is allowed, so short-term profit does not bleed while the system learns.
arxiv-2502-02367:
Alexander Kolesov and three co-authors make and move data by use of charge on plates. Their method sets a source spread on one plate of a capacitor. A target spread sits on the other plate, with charge of the flip sign. A neural net learns the field of force between the plates. Points then ride the field lines from one plate to the next.

Points that land, the proof shows, match the target spread. That one trick serves two jobs. It can make new data, and it can move data from one form to next. Toy tasks and image tasks show the method at work. The physics does real work here, not just a nice image. The field's shape moves the points where other plans lean on learned maps or noise steps. Their code is free for all to use.
arxiv-2502-02667:
Amit Kumar and Gojko Vujanovic compute a piece of jet physics in twenty twenty-five. When a fast quark plows through hot QCD matter, it loses energy. Some of that loss comes out as real photons, a process called bremsstrahlung. The authors focus on quarks with very high virtuality and energy.

They work within the higher-twist formalism and build improved emission kernels. Their account includes heavy-quark mass effects and processes that swap fermions and bosons. It also includes coherence effects that older treatments missed. A generalized factorization step, like one used in electron-nucleus scattering, shapes the derivation. Diagrams are sorted by the final particles produced. Readers get sharper kernels for how jets shed energy as light.
arxiv-2502-03567:
Luca Cocconi, Yihong Shi, and Andrej Vilfan study information-optimal mixing at low Reynolds number, in a research paper from 2025. At such scales, flow is smooth and reversible, so mixing is hard to gauge. Mutual information between particle positions before and after mixing gives a universal, assumption-free score of how well mixing erased the starting pattern.

For a planar shear flow with a time-varying rate, the authors derive a compact formula for that information. They solve exactly for the best shearing schedule under limits on total shear or on energy loss. The best schedules are universal and symmetric in time in both cases. A minimum energy cost of erasing information follows for a broad class of systems.
arxiv-2502-03867:
Kay Barshad, Yair Censor, Walaa Moursi, Tyler Weames, and Henry Wolkowicz examine a widely used optimization approach in a 2025 mathematics study. The method starts from an algorithm that seeks a feasible point for convex constraints. Small extra steps then try to lower an objective value without losing feasibility.

The authors ask when those extra steps are guaranteed to end at a better feasible point than the plain algorithm would reach. They give a condition under which steps based on negative gradient descent fail to deliver that improvement. Knowing the failure case matters because any future guarantee must rule it out, and users can avoid the condition in practice.
arxiv-2502-04067:
Matthew Penn and co-authors speed up family tree building for the genome era. Full likelihood and Bayesian tree methods strain under whole-genome data sets. Distance methods are fast but less trusted, since their scores were seen as weaker. The team builds a Bayesian form of distance methods on an entropy-based score for pairs of species.

They show that score ties closely to the classic likelihood of Felsenstein. Tree estimates on three benchmark sets matched past results well. The method then ran on sixty million sites from 363 bird species in a fair time. It exposed deep doubt about bird splits right after the asteroid impact that killed the dinosaurs. Fast Bayesian trees can now serve genome-scale work.
arxiv-2502-04367:
Kiran Sharma, Ziya Uddin, Adarsh Wadal, and Dhruv Gupta build an image classification system for kidney disease in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their hybrid deep learning model sorts kidney CT scans into four categories: normal, stone, cyst, and tumor. The design fuses a pre-trained ResNet101 network with a custom convolutional neural network. Feature fusion is meant to sharpen the accuracy of automated diagnosis.

Trained on a dataset of over twelve thousand CT images, the hybrid model reached very high reported accuracy, including perfect testing accuracy in the authors' experiments. It outperformed a standalone ResNet101 on precision and recall while reducing testing time. The authors present the architecture as a robust, efficient candidate for clinical use in automated kidney disease diagnosis.
arxiv-2502-05067:
Tabares and four co-authors programmed a quantum simulator in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Cold atoms in light grids naturally mimic the Fermi-Hubbard model of interacting electrons. New controls let experimenters steer the grid in time, turning the setup into a programmable device. The team built algorithms to prepare ground states on it.

Their variational circuits are pre-compiled for the native model and beat slow adiabatic recipes. The same style reaches extended models with extra hopping terms tied to superconductivity. A second method mimics imaginary-time cooling to refine energies further. Tests used ladder-shaped grids, but the protocols fit flat two-dimensional setups. The authors aim them at regimes classical computers cannot reach.
arxiv-2502-06667:
Shahar Hod, writing alone, derives the survival chances of a biased random walker who can restart. His 2025 paper studies a Sisyphus-like walk. At each step, the walker has a set chance to step toward an absorbing trap at the origin. With the complementary chance, it jumps back to its start instead. The question is how long the walker survives.

Hod solves the time-dependent survival probability in closed form. He proves it decays in an exponential way at late times. A critical starting distance emerges: beyond it, the restarting walker outlives a standard random walker at late times, despite the trap's pull. Below it, restarting hurts. The result is a neat case where a restart rule flips from harmful to helpful at a sharp threshold.
arxiv-2502-08067:
Han-Jia Bi and Sheng-Wen Li present a 2025 physics paper on using tiny multi-level atoms as refrigerators to quiet microwave resonators. Thermal noise in such resonators limits quantum devices and precision sensors. Their scheme couples the resonator to many three- or four-level systems, then pumps those systems with light.

Pumping herds the systems into their ground states, from which they steadily swallow thermal photons out of the resonator. The authors compute the cooling process precisely and find its limits. For three-level systems, too strong a pump warps the energy levels and breaks the resonance that cooling needs, so the drive must stay in a sweet range. Four-level designs relax the trade-off.
arxiv-2502-08267:
Lars Rohwedder, Arman Rouhani, and Leo Wennmann present a rounding method for allocation problems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Rounding turns a fractional plan into whole assignments while keeping hard limits. Earlier dependent rounding schemes could let the total cost creep up. Their scheme promises the final bill never tops the fractional one.

The method keeps the sharp concentration behavior of random rounding. It applies to a class of assignment problems much like those older schemes handled. As a payoff, the authors pair it with known linear programming tools. Together they build an approximation for a budgeted Santa Claus problem. There, gifts of varied value go to players under a cost cap, while the worst-off player's share is lifted as high as possible.
arxiv-2502-08367:
Peter Hochs and Hemanth Saratchandran wrote a 2025 mathematics paper that generalizes a known trace formula to settings where a group also acts on the space. Guillemin's trace formula gives the trace of an operator that pulls back functions along a flow on a compact manifold. Such traces summarize how the flow carries values around the space.

Their equivariant version holds when the group action is proper and the space remains compact once the action of the group is taken into account. The result is not an end in itself. It lays the foundation for an equivariant form of the Ruelle zeta function, which counts closed paths of a flow, and which the pair construct in a companion paper. To get there, they first had to generalize the trace itself in the same group-aware way. The paper is pure mathematics, aimed at researchers who work on flows and geometry.
arxiv-2502-08867:
Jade Ducharme and Jonathan Pober present a way to locate interference sources in a 2025 arXiv paper. Radio-frequency interference can swamp the faint signals that radio telescopes seek. Knowing where an emitter sits could let astronomers subtract it instead of discarding data.

Their method applies near-field corrections to bring a moving source into focus. In a two-minute observation with an Australian array, an unknown object crossed the view. The focus method put it at about 11.7 kilometers up, moving near 792 kilometers per hour. That profile fit an airplane. Two more observations confirmed the method by again pointing to airplanes.
arxiv-2502-09567:
Negru and co-authors present MorphNLI, a step-by-step method for judging how two sentences relate. The task sorts pairs into entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Their system asks a language model to edit the first sentence, step by step, into the second.

A standard inference model then tracks how the label shifts after each small edit. Those step labels are pooled into the final call. In cross-domain tests, the method always beat strong baselines, with gains up to 12.6 percent. The edit trail also explains the verdict, since each atomic change can be inspected.
arxiv-2502-10267:
Szabolcs Borsányi and co-authors used lattice models in 2025 to fence in one of the most wanted locations in nuclear physics: the key point of quantum chromodynamics. There the shift between normal matter and quark-gluon plasma changes character. They hunted it by following lines of constant entropy density from imaginary chemical potential, where model is safe, toward real values, keeping the matter strangeness-neutral as tests need.

Supporting the search is a new equation of state at zero density. Extrapolated to the continuum from models at four lattice spacings with markedly boosted precision, plus fresh data at imaginary chemical potential. Watching whether the entropy contours converge on a meeting point, the authors find their current precision already excludes. At the two-sigma level, any key point below a baryon chemical potential of about four hundred fifty million electron volts, narrowing the territory where tests should look.
arxiv-2502-11067:
Aronsson, Rahbar, and Chehreghani surveyed in twenty twenty-five ways to buy facts one by one for each case, trading truth against cost. A test or sensor fact can cost time or cash, so blind full reads waste both. They give the first joint frame for the field as a hid-state choice chain.

That frame ties the field to known plan tools for hid-state tasks. Four method kinds are sorted, from cost-wise trees to sim-trained plans. Most past work lacks proof of sound bounds, they note. Ties to step-wise stochastics point to where proofs can come from.
arxiv-2502-11467:
Naoki Takeshita and Masaaki Imaizumi ask how well transformer networks can copy a special kind of formula, in a 2025 theory paper. Transformers are the networks behind most modern language tools. The formulas here take tables of numbers as input and give the same answer when columns are swapped. Such symmetry shows up in many data tasks.

The authors build transformers that copy these formulas and track how network size affects the error. Their proof uses traits of symmetric formulas, a classic topic in algebra. The link they find is explicit, tying size to accuracy in a clear way. Results like this help explain why these networks are so flexible in practice.
arxiv-2502-11667:
Camila Navarrete, Alejandra Recio-Blanco, Patrick de Laverny, and Ana Escorza published this astronomy paper in 2025. It uses data from the Gaia space mission to study red giant stars in pairs. A fresh Gaia release listed about one thousand long-period pairs, the largest sample of its kind with both light and motion records.

The team matched those pairs against the main Gaia catalog and derived sizes, masses, and brightness for 243 of one class and thirty-nine of another. In the main class, the giant often swells nearly to the edge of its allowed space, and orbits grow rounder as the star grows. The unseen partners look like small, dense remnants. At least fourteen pairs match forecasts for the systems that later explode as type Ia supernovae. The two classes seem to differ in age as well.
arxiv-2502-11867:
Yun Li, Neil Yorke-Smith, and Tamas Keviczky present a study from twenty twenty-five on robust plans when the unknown comes in many clumps. In data driven robust design, the set of possible bad cases is key. A union of many subsets gives a tight, flexible set. Two gaps block its use in control: hard math, and plans that play too safe.

They give one mixed integer form for the whole union set. The worst case then falls out of a single solve. A new aim blends robust and distribution robust views to trim the safe bias. A column and constraint method makes the sums run fast. Three case studies back the scheme.
arxiv-2502-12267:
Xi Zheng, Ziyang Li, Ivan Ruchkin, Ruzica Piskac, and Miroslav Pajic set out a frame for trustworthy autonomous systems in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Cyber-physical systems use AI for seeing, planning, and control, but their built-in doubt blocks safety sign-off. The neurosymbolic path swaps some random neural layers for symbolic AI whose steps can be read, bringing back fixed behavior where it counts. Hard spots stay in fusing sensors, adapting, and checking.

NeuroStrata is the team's neurosymbolic frame, built to help design, test, and check self-running systems. The paper lays out its parts, reports results, and sets out plans ahead. The aim is autonomy that can earn sign-off: systems whose choice paths can be inspected and checked, not just sampled. For fields where safety is key, like self-driving cars and medical tools, that is the gap between shippable systems and lab demos.
arxiv-2502-13967:
Roman Bachmann and eight co-authors published this paper in 2025. It introduces FlexTok, a way to compress images into token sequences whose length adapts to the picture. Image generators work on tokens, and fixed-length tokenizers waste effort on simple images while starving complex ones.

FlexTok squeezes an image into anywhere from one to two hundred fifty-six ordered tokens, arranged coarse to fine like a summary that keeps adding detail. A flow-based decoder rebuilds a plausible image from any prefix of the sequence, trained by randomly dropping token tails. In generation tests with a transformer, quality scores stayed strong from eight to one hundred twenty-eight tokens, beating a fixed tokenizer with fewer tokens. Text-conditioned generation worked too. The authors note the tokens behave like a visual vocabulary, describing scenes from gist to detail. Adaptive length, they argue, should be the default for image tokenization.
arxiv-2502-15067:
Cañizares and co-authors track radio waves from a solar burst in a 2025 paper that uses data from five spacecraft. Fast electrons from the Sun make radio waves as they travel outward, but scattering blurs where the waves seem to come from. The team used a burst from December 2021 to trace the true path of the waves through the inner solar system.

Their tracking method placed the sources along a spiral path set by the solar wind, and ground-based images backed up the result. Checks with a probe near Earth also matched. Their measures of scattering fit current models well. The work gives firm proof that scattering explains why electron counts far from the Sun once looked too high.
arxiv-2502-15667:
Diyou Liu and Mohammad Khosravi tackle system identification when sensors mix signals in a paper from 2025. Many systems have linear dynamics but nonlinear, bilinear readouts. The goal is to recover the model parameters from input and output data alone. The authors build two probabilistic frameworks for the task. The first maximizes a likelihood function with a fast first-order optimizer.

The second uses an expectation-maximization approach with a specially shaped cost function. That shape guarantees a single best solution, and the authors derive it in closed form. They also prove the procedure stays feasible step by step. Simulations compare both methods and show accurate parameter recovery. The work targets control problems with bilinear sensing.
arxiv-2502-16867:
Momammad Ali Ranjbar presents a 2025 study on controlling a robot arm so it follows a set path quickly and smoothly. Standard sliding mode control is tough against disturbances but can make the arm chatter, jittering around the path. The proposed method uses a fast terminal form of the control, designed to settle in finite time without the chatter. It was built on the arm's Newton-Euler dynamics and checked with a Lyapunov stability proof.

Simulations on a three-joint arm compared the new controller with two standard rivals. The new method tracked paths more accurately, settled faster, and held steadier. The author presents it as a strong fit for high-precision robot work where both speed and smoothness matter. The study is a single-author simulation paper, so hardware tests remain future work.
arxiv-2502-18667:
Top quarks rarely switch flavor without changing charge, and such flavor-changing interactions would signal new physics if seen. The authors use machine learning to hunt four-fermion interactions in which a top quark decays to an up or charm quark plus an electron pair, giving a three-lepton signal at the LHC. They study top pair and single top production, folding in both reducible and irreducible backgrounds and realistic detector effects.

Machine learning classifiers sharpened event selection and signal sensitivity against the heavy backgrounds from top pairs and boson production. For 3000 inverse femtobarns, the expected 95 percent limits on the interaction scale reach 5.5 TeV and 5.7 TeV in the top pair channel. The single top channel reaches about 2 TeV. The authors also translate the bounds into limits on a heavy neutral Z prime boson in a sample model.
arxiv-2502-19567:
Marcin Spoczynski, Marcela Melara, and Sebastian Szyller present a frame that makes each step of a machine learning pipeline provable, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Open data and models spread fast, and with them the risks of poisoned data and supply chain attack. Rules now press vendors for clear records, yet secrets must stay shut.

Their frame, Atlas, borrows open specs from data and software chain proof. It gathers signed records of where each model piece came from and how it was changed. Trusted hardware and public logs guard the records, while locks keep data private and bar stray hands. A test build weds several open tools, and two case pipelines show the frame can run in real work.
arxiv-2502-19967:
Vimala Soundarapandian and co-authors wrote a 2025 computer science paper on checking copied data types for a strong form of correctness. Copies of data across machines give fault tolerance and fast access. Users gain when each copy's state can be read as some clean order of the updates it has seen.

The authors give a fully automatic way to check that property for mergeable data types. They find new algebra rules for the update and merge steps that are enough to prove the property. Those rules go past the classic trio of rules used in past work. A bottom-up proof method checks the rules on its own. The team proved the method on many complex types, plus a new one for a common data format.
arxiv-2502-20567:
Richard Lebed and Steven Martinez test whether exotic four-quark states are pairs of mesons in disguise. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Tetraquark models often picture two quarks bound against two antiquarks. Meson-meson molecules are the rival picture. The authors join both in one model. A diabatic formalism, generalizing Born-Oppenheimer ideas, does the joining.

Simple molecular potentials are added to an established diquark model. Mixed states emerge, part diquark pair and part molecule. Sweeping the potential's parameters maps the possibilities. Some settings reproduce the masses of two famous candidate states exactly. Other regions yield a pure molecular state. The study shows how both pictures can share one spectrum.
arxiv-2503-01067:
Swamy and four co-authors ask in twenty twenty-five why the best way to tune large chat models is a two-step route. First a score model learns from human picks, then the main model learns by trial with that score. A plain one-step fit on the same picks looks more direct.

They test a few views on why the two-step route wins, with both math and trials. The best-backed view rests on a gap: checks are easy to learn, but good replies are hard to write. The trial step then picks from a small set of replies that pass the easy check. That cuts the data the full task needs.
arxiv-2503-01267:
Engui Fan, Gaozhan Li, and Yiling Yang solve a wave equation exactly using curve-based methods, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The equation is a modified form of a known shallow-water wave model, with an added spread term. Exact solutions are rare for such nonlinear wave models.

Their route builds a Riemann-Hilbert problem tied to the equation. A special function, built from a family of hyperelliptic curves, solves that problem in closed form. A rebuild formula then yields the wave solution in full. The curve family carries a genus set by two size parameters in the setup.
arxiv-2503-02267:
