Sourav Mishra, Shreya Hallikeri, and Suresh Sundaram design a new activation curve for physics-informed networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents REAct. Such networks solve physics problems by learning, but training often stalls. The activation curve inside each unit shapes how well learning travels across problems.

Their curve bends a classic shape with four learnable dials. That lets one curve fit many physical systems. On heat problems, error fell to a thousandth of the classic curve's level. It also held up on finer grids and points beyond the training zone. Inverse tasks with noisy data gave cleaner parameter guesses as well.
arxiv-2503-03367:
Xiaotong Zhang and co-authors present a method to outline liver blood vessels in 3D scans, in this 2025 paper. Surgeons need that map before cutting out part of the liver. Standard methods read scans slice by slice and can lose the vessel tree's overall shape. The team borrows a trick from how CT scans themselves are built.

Their projections keep only the top few brightest points along each view line, mimicking the scan physics. Those projections guide a diffusion model that grows a full 3D vessel tree. On a public liver data set, the method earned the best scores on the three main overlap and detection measures, ahead of prior work. The authors say physics-aware priors help keep vessel structure whole.
arxiv-2503-04467:
Xiang Zhang and two colleagues wrote a 2025 survey on the two-dimensional Burgers' equation. This equation models a flow where the fluid pushes itself along while friction smooths it out. It is a classic test case for the math of fluids.

A model is well-posed if it has exactly one solution and that solution behaves in a stable way. The authors show such results using tools from the study of dynamical systems. Their proof leans on the Galerkin method, which turns the flow problem into a set of simpler equations. Energy estimates and compactness arguments close the case. The survey gathers the key ideas in a short, clear form for new readers.
arxiv-2503-05267:
Amal Alphonse, Ana Djurdjevac, Emil Engstrom, and Eskil Hansen extend a parallel computing method to heat problems on moving domains in a 2025 math study. Parabolic equations on evolving shapes model processes such as molding heated material. Splitting a fixed domain across processors is routine, but a domain that changes shape breaks the usual structure.

Their variational setup carries domain decomposition to the evolving case. Transmission conditions govern how neighboring pieces exchange information across their shared boundaries. The authors prove the structure is sound, opening the way to large simulations on parallel hardware for manufacturing and materials problems with moving fronts.
arxiv-2503-05367:
Jing Zhang and four co-authors tackle dose planning for a cancer treatment in this 2025 paper. The treatment sends radiation straight to tumor cells with targeted drugs. Doctors need a dose estimate tuned to each patient, yet labeled data for training models is scarce.

Their fix learns from many scans that lack dose labels and a few that have them. The method creates likely labels for the unlabeled scans, in a style drawn from a known training scheme. Tests used fake data built with physics simulation. Adding the extra scans improved organ dose estimates over training on labeled scans alone.
arxiv-2503-06067:
Designers often argue their case with example user flows, sequences of app screens that show a task being done, but finding a good example is slow. Daeheon Jeong and Hyehyun Chu tackle that search problem in this 2025 paper, after interviewing practitioners about how they communicate design ideas.

They train a model that links the visual look of screens to written descriptions of flows, using contrastive learning. A survey then confirmed that the system retrieves flows people judge relevant. The authors discuss what their results mean for how software should represent user flows, aiming to make example-based design talk faster and better grounded.
arxiv-2503-06367:
Jiaming Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on an electronic circuit that mimics exotic non-Hermitian systems, where gain and loss are balanced. Two resonators, one amplifying and one damping, are linked by a capacitor. In ideal versions of such systems, two vibration modes merge at a special point and then one grows explosively.

Real inductors always waste some energy as heat, and that small loss changes the story. The team shows, in both bench tests and theory, that the mode merging no longer happens. Instead, the circuit flips from fading to growing oscillations near the expected special points. The work warns that textbook pictures of these systems need the loss term kept in.
arxiv-2503-07067:
Ko and a team of colleagues presented DistiLLM-2 in twenty twenty-five, a method for distilling large language models into smaller ones. Distillation trains a compact student model to mimic a big teacher. Most past work used the same loss rule for teacher-written and student-written training data, ignoring how the two interact.

Their contrastive method raises the chance the student gives teacher-like answers while lowering the chance of its own weaker answers. Extensive tests built strong student models across tasks such as following instructions and writing code. The method also supported preference alignment, tuning toward human choices, and a vision-language extension. The authors argue matching the loss rule to the data type is the key to better distillation.
arxiv-2503-07267: Hervé Henry, writing alone in 2025, simulates how cracks run through uneven materials. Real materials often mix a stiff base with soft inclusions scattered at random. Henry uses a phase field model, which smears the crack over a small zone so a computer can track it in three dimensions. The random mix barely changed the overall stiffness. But it changed the cracking a lot. The less even the spread of soft spots, the more force the material withstood before the crack took off.
arxiv-2503-07867: Roberto Aloisio reviews cosmic ray tests of new physics in twenty twenty-five. The Pierre Auger Observatory is the world's largest cosmic ray detector. Its ultra-high-energy cosmic rays probe two scenarios beyond the standard model. Super heavy dark matter, born in the early universe, could decay into photons and neutrinos that Auger can search for. Lorentz invariance violation, suggested by quantum gravity ideas, would alter particle dispersion and interaction thresholds with background light. Auger data constrain both possibilities.
arxiv-2503-08067:
Ali Veisi, Hamidreza Amirzadeh, and Amir Mansourian improve, in a 2025 preprint, how transformers handle texts longer than any they trained on. Models usually learn position from added bias signals tied to relative distance. Fixed or globally learned biases cannot adapt to what a given passage is about. The authors' method, CABLE, learns a bias per token and per attention head. The bias bends with the input's context. That flexibility targets the sharp failure of models on over-long inputs.

A mid-size GPT-2 fitted with CABLE scored better on long texts than rivals with standard encodings. Tests ran on two large public corpora. A BERT model with CABLE also did better at long-context retrieval. The gains stacked on top of the strongest existing relative encodings. The authors release their code openly. They pitch context-aware biases as a general patch for length limits in deployed models.
arxiv-2503-08767:
Joshuah Heath and six co-authors study a noise source that plagues superconducting qubits. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with two-level systems, tiny flaws inside the Josephson junction at a qubit's heart. These flaws soak up energy and shorten the qubit's useful life, a process called decoherence.

The team treats each flaw as a soft bosonic mode pinned in place, in the oxide skin or in the bulk. They find one flaw can create a local hot spot where the Josephson energy is amplified. That amplification measurably shortens the qubit's energy lifetime, even when the flaw is not on resonance with the qubit. The source of decoherence is specific to the superconducting part itself.
arxiv-2503-11167:
Haonan Wang, Qixiang Zhang, Lehan Wang, Xuanqi Huang, and Xiaomeng Li rebuild videos, in a 2025 preprint, from brain scans of people watching them. Reading moving pictures from fMRI data is hard: the signal is coarse, and motion must stay smooth. Their framework, NEURONS, copies the layered design of the human visual cortex. It splits the job into four linked tasks. These are picking out key objects, naming concepts, describing the scene, and drafting a rough video. Each task feeds the next, much like stages of real vision.

At run time, those outputs become guiding signals for a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model. The model paints the final clip from that guidance. Against leading rivals, NEURONS raised video consistency by about a quarter and scene accuracy by about a fifth. The authors point to brain-computer interfaces and clinics as future users.
arxiv-2503-11467:
Jose-Luis Holgado-Alvarez and co-authors train a legged robot's navigation policy against adversarial moving obstacles, in this 2025 paper. Steady walking is largely solved; dodging surprise obstacles in new places is not. Their setup splits control into a walking layer and a navigation layer. The navigation layer learns while obstacle agents actively try to block it, like opponents in a game.

Unbounded opponents would make training hopeless, so the adversaries follow bounded rationality, modeled with quantal response equilibria. A curriculum raises their cleverness step by step. The method, called Hi-QARL by the authors, is tested in unseen random mazes with several moving obstacles. It holds up well there and transfers to a simulated Unitree GO1 quadruped.
arxiv-2503-12667:
Jacob Chmura, Jonah Dauvet, and Sebastian Sabry test if the stored knowledge of large language models can lift a tool that judges whether an event sounds plausible. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Tools that learn word sense from co-use fail to split events that could happen from those that could not. The team draws out facts held in large models, with light fine-tuning. They train twelve small add-ons, each for a type of fact, such as traits of things or strength of links. They then fuse the add-ons on top of a base model's word codes. The mix is trained across two sets of plausibility tasks. Their code is shared in the open.
arxiv-2503-16167:
Hong Yi Lin and four co-authors present CodeReviewQA, a test set for how well large language models grasp code review notes. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Review notes are often brief, vague, and loose in tone, so a model has to grasp both code and human intent. Past tests score fixes by word match, which hides where a model fails.

The test set breaks a fix into three steps, each posed as a choice task. Steps cover what kind of change is asked, where it goes, and which fix is right. Nine hundred hand-picked cases span nine code tongues. Tests of many new models showed clear weak spots that fix scores alone had masked.
arxiv-2503-17967:
Zeyu Wang computes the murmuration pattern for a family of L-functions tied to imaginary quadratic fields. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Murmurations are ripples in averages of arithmetic data, first spotted with machine learning in modular forms.

Wang finds the density for Hecke L-functions attached to nontrivial characters of these fields. The density shows the same universality seen in the modular form case. Its averages also agree with a famous conjecture about low zeros of L-functions. The fresh feature here is an almost repeating wave in the pattern. That wave lets the murmuration be described without averaging over primes, a shortcut no other family had shown. The result widens a fast-growing topic.
arxiv-2503-18067:
Shahaf Bassan and co-authors build neural networks that explain themselves for business process monitoring in a 2025 paper. Such monitoring predicts what a running case will do next, like its next activity, from logs of past cases. Deep sequence models lead the field but act as black boxes. Explanations bolted on after training can be unfaithful, costly, and brittle on odd cases.

Their approach weaves the explanation into the model itself, so the reasons come out with the prediction, not after it. The design targets the trust problem head-on: a manager who can read why the model expects a delay can act on it. The paper sets out the self-explaining design and tests it on the standard next-activity task. Faithful, cheap explanations are the prize.
arxiv-2503-18267:
Minh-Tuan Tran and four colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on dataset distillation, compressing a large training data set into a small synthetic one that trains models almost as well. Features in data come in two kinds: instance-specific details unique to each example, and class-general patterns shared across a category. Good distillation must keep both.

Earlier approaches tended to favor one kind and lose the other. The authors propose refining the non-critical regions of distilled images, the areas that carry instance detail without disturbing the class pattern. This refinement rebalances the two feature types. Better distilled data sets mean cheaper model training for everyone who reuses them, from research labs to production teams.
arxiv-2503-19567:
Peter Boyvalenkov and Sergii Favorov published this mathematics paper in 2025. It concerns crystalline measures, special patterns of point masses spread through space. Such a measure has a remarkable property: its Fourier transform, which rewrites the pattern in terms of waves, is again made of point masses. The authors ask how fast the total mass of these patterns can grow inside large regions.

They prove two results. First, take the transform's masses, square them, and build a new measure from those squares. That new measure cannot pile up too fast anywhere; it stays translation bounded. Second, if the wave positions inside any fixed-size ball are independent in an integer sense, the transform itself is also translation bounded. These results give concrete conditions a crystalline measure must meet to count as a Fourier quasicrystal. Such patterns matter in the study of ordered materials that are not simple crystals.
arxiv-2503-20267:
Jiabin Wang and co-authors show how a cold atom gas can mimic two universes at once in this 2025 paper. The system is a Bose Einstein condensate with two spin components. Sound waves in each component feel their own curved spacetime metric. That lets one lab system host two expanding or shrinking analogue universes side by side.

By ramping the interaction between the components, one universe expands while the other contracts. The sizes can be read from oscillation frequencies in density patterns. The expansion history shows up in the pattern amplitudes. Both signals are within reach of current cold atom setups. The work opens a lab route to questions about multiple universes that astronomy cannot test directly.
arxiv-2503-21967:
Agustin Munoz Gonzalez, Juan Ignacio Sequeira, and Ariel Dembling wrote this finance paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a hidden cost in crypto markets. People who add coins to automated trading pools can lose value when prices move, a loss known as impermanent loss.

The authors work out the math of that loss for constant-product pools, the kind used by Uniswap and Balancer. They show that a pool's value can be copied exactly with a fixed mix of standard call and put options. Within a set price range, that mix fully covers the loss. A worked example uses real option prices from Deribit, a large crypto options market, to show a strangle strategy in action. The paper gives pool providers a concrete way to hedge a risk many only meet after the fact.
arxiv-2503-22267:
Charalampos Passalidis studies heavy-tailed probability laws that live in more than one dimension, in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. He brings in a new class, the multivariate strong subexponential ones. Such laws fit rare, huge events, like extreme insurance claims. In them, one big jump can swamp the sum of all the rest.

He proves a few basic facts for the new class. One is a form of Kesten's inequality for this case. One says the class stays closed when sums are formed. He then shows the single big jump rule for sums stopped at a random time. The terms he needs are weaker than for the old class of this kind. He also finds sharp bounds for large moves away from the mean. A use in a nonstandard insurance risk model ends the work.
arxiv-2503-22367:
Shakul Awasthi, Hyunggyu Park, and Jae Sung Lee study small random systems whose heat level changes over time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such systems matter for tiny engines, yet the common over-damped shortcut drops the speed of the parts from view. That shortcut then gives wrong values for heat loss and entropy growth.

The authors name these gaps thermodynamic anomalies and derive exact forms for them. One sharp point is that thick fluid and small mass lead to the same motion laws but unlike anomaly laws. Their forms let users judge engine yield without measuring speed. They also give a simple way to gauge the kinetic energy of such a system.
arxiv-2503-22667:
Young discs of gas around newborn stars can grow heavy enough that their gravity stirs them into spirals, moving matter inward and building planets. Starlight heating should calm that unrest, especially in the outer disc. Caitriona Leedham, Richard Booth, and Cathie Clarke ask how much the answer depends on the way heating is put into the model, comparing two recipes in two-dimensional simulations.

When heating was spread by mass, the unrest died out once starlight became the heat source, as expected. When heating was spread evenly by area, the unrest survived under strong starlight and high stability readings, matching theory. Discs could still break into fragments in that regime, though the cooling had to be faster as the heating rose. The team caps the viscosity in that state at roughly 0.03 to 0.09. Their point is practical: the recipe chosen for starlight can flip what a simulation predicts.
arxiv-2504-00267:
Daniel Irving Bernstein and Nathaniel Vaduthala study flag matroids, layered structures built from matroids of rising rank, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their central question is which of these structures can be written with numbers from a given field.

They give a new axiom system that defines flag matroids from scratch. For uniform flag matroids, they pin down exactly when a numeric form exists. For full flag matroids, they list the blocked smaller patterns that rule out a form over the two-element and three-element fields. They also treat the regular case in several matching ways. The results sort out which of these layered structures algebra can actually build.
arxiv-2504-02667:
Thomas Dooms, Ward Gauderis, Geraint Wiggins, and Jose Oramas design neural networks that can explain themselves in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their build, chi-net, fuses the compositional multilinear structure of tensor networks with the expressivity and efficiency of deep neural networks. The compositional structure is the interpretability hook. Tensor networks split computations into pieces whose ways of acting on each other can be looked at, unlike plain weight matrices.

The team also brings in a diagonalization method, ODT, showing linear low-rank structure in a model, shown on a multilayer model for the SVHN digit data set. That shown structure is then used two ways: toward formal, weight-based interpretability, arguing in a strict way about what the network computes. The other way is toward model compression, shrinking the network with its shown low-rank form. The paper sets compositionality as the bridge between performance and interpretability.
arxiv-2504-02867:
Hongliu Cao, Ilias Driouich, Robin Singh, and Eoin Thomas automate the design of language model judges, personalized to each evaluation job. Judging generated text with models is now standard, since overlap and embedding scores miss nuance. Existing judge frameworks, though, adapt poorly to different text and ground-truth styles. Their scores also skew oddly and correlate weakly with human judgment.

The proposed multi-agent system designs a bespoke judge for each application. Agents iteratively refine the evaluation prompts, balancing task fit against alignment with human perception. Experiments show better evaluation accuracy than existing methods. Scores come out better behaved as well as better aimed. The system treats judging as a design problem with a client, not a fixed instrument. Personalized evaluation, the authors argue, is what open-ended generation always needed.
arxiv-2504-03967:
Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, and Ziwen Pan built a translator between quantum software frameworks in a 2025 paper. Simulating quantum circuits on classical machines verifies algorithms before hardware runs them, but mainstream tools run on CPUs and crawl, while graphics processors need code written for entirely different frameworks. Their Q-GEAR system converts circuits written in the popular Qiskit toolkit into kernels for NVIDIA's CUDA-Q platform automatically.

Converted circuits then run far faster: about two orders of magnitude on CPUs and tenfold on GPUs, with little coding effort, per their benchmarks. Linking memory across several GPUs lets oversized circuits fit. Container images tuned for a national supercomputer's scheduler reached near-full GPU use, easing adoption for large simulation campaigns.
arxiv-2504-04067:
Pranab Sen proves new concentration bounds, which are math guarantees that random averages stay close to their expected values, for quantum information tasks. Earlier results for a covering problem in quantum communication gave guarantees only on average, and a classic theorem handled independent samples. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Sen extends the picture in two directions. One result covers several parties at once and gives an exponential strength guarantee. The other covers samples drawn by a random walk on an expander graph, a sparse network that mixes quickly.

The expander result rests on a new proof tool that adapts a classical bounded-difference method to walks, which the author expects to be useful elsewhere. Notably, the bounds avoid any explicit factor for the size of the quantum system. Applications include new one-shot limits for sending private messages over quantum wiretap channels with many separate eavesdroppers.
arxiv-2504-07967:
Md Ferdous Pervej and co-authors built a content-making model in 2025 for wireless channels, the math accounts of how radio signals travel between transmitter and receiver. Builders need true-to-life channel models to design and standardize communication systems. Machine learning makers exist. But most either predict single channel snapshots or cover only signal loss, while a complete account must be double-directional, tracking angles at both ends of the link.

Their maker combines a hybrid Transformer, changed to use a cheaper low-rank focus calculation, with a bidirectional memory network that makes full double-directional channel data. Training is guided by domain knowledge so the generated channels match the figures of real ones. Models showed the generated samples' figures aligned closely with the truth and mostly beat earlier predictive methods.
arxiv-2504-08267:
Borboruah, Malhotra, Patel, Patra, and Sankar build a left-right symmetric neutrino mass model without a scalar bidoublet, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The model mirrors left and right forces with two separate doublets. Charged fermion masses arise through a universal seesaw mechanism. Three singlet neutral fermions carry TeV-scale masses.

Light neutrino masses appear only at one loop, staying naturally small. Careful coupling choices enable resonant leptogenesis at the TeV scale. The lightest right-handed neutrino becomes a warm dark matter candidate. Its mass of a few keV fits that role. Double beta decay signals stay observable in reach.
arxiv-2504-08967:
Rana Elnaggar and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a language-model tool that fuzzes cross-platform compilers to shake out bugs. Compilers that target many chip types have endless code paths, and hand-writing tests for each path eats expert time. Their tool pairs a language model with a retrieval system stocked with compiler knowledge.

Let loose on Intel's SYCL compiler, the tool drafted tests on its own. Within hours it found eighty-seven cases where code gave wrong answers or crashed the compiler across different chips. The testers needed no prior knowledge of the compiler passes involved. The authors say retrieval-guided fuzzing can give small teams the reach of large ones.
arxiv-2504-09467:
Pal, Lahiri, and Saha studied tiny heat engines in twenty twenty-five that run inside flowing fluids. Their engine is a single colloidal bead held in a trap whose stiffness pulses in time, a standard design for a stochastic heat engine. Around it, the fluid shears steadily, and the flow's shape — circular, elliptic, or hyperbolic — can be tuned from outside.

Over long times, the flow's own work swamps the trap's thermodynamic work whenever the flow strays much from circular. Only a perfectly circular flow lets the trap do all the work. A second model tethers a spinning particle near the bead, so its wake stirs the bead's motion. At high spin rates the flow work again dominates, and the engine stops producing useful thermodynamic work.
arxiv-2504-11767:
Qinyan Shen, Karl Gregory, and Xianzheng Huang fix trust checks after model choice in twenty twenty-five. Their case is group test data, where the true scores are seen in part at best. In place of true scores, teams see pooled test scores that can be wrong. The choice of which traits count has to deal with that gap in what is known.

A back and forth max step works out LASSO picked scores with a fine built in. Once choice is done, plain trust bands read too bold, since the same data did double work. The team stretches past choice trust checks, built on the polyhedral lemma, to fit this case. Test runs show their bands hold up more well than plain ones do. The piece gives sound checks for pooled test work, where choice of traits and gauge of traits share one set of data.
arxiv-2504-13967:
Yufei Bai simulates magnetic patterns in thin films in a study from 2025. Films magnetized straight out of their plane form maze-like and bubble-like domain patterns that shift with film thickness and outside field. Bai borrows a model from chemistry, the Lengyel-Epstein model of reaction and diffusion, and applies it to these magnetic patterns.

The simulations reproduce maze, bubble, and in-between states seen in real layered films under a microscope. The shapes and topology of the simulated domains match the observed ones closely. Bai argues that the chemistry analogy is a sound new tool for studying how magnetic domain patterns form and change in thin films.
arxiv-2504-14067:
Justin Ray Angus and Johannes van de Wetering wrote a 2025 physics paper on a computer method for collisions in plasmas. A plasma is a hot gas of charged particles, found in stars and fusion devices. Particles in a plasma constantly deflect each other through electric forces, an effect called Coulomb collisions.

Exact simulation of every encounter is too costly, so codes use statistical collision models. Their method pairs particles at random and applies a screened collision rule, valid when the plasma is weakly or moderately coupled. It matches the standard theory with first-order corrections and reduces to the classic method for small time steps. The code change is about ten lines, so existing simulation programs can adopt it easily.
arxiv-2504-15067:
Péter Gurin and Szabolcs Varga published a 2025 physics paper on sticky particles confined to a narrow channel. Patchy particles carry attractive spots and can bond into chains. Squeezed into a channel barely wider than themselves, their ordering becomes a one-dimensional problem with rotation. The authors extend a theory of association, Wertheim's perturbation theory, to this setting.

With a transfer-matrix method, they prove the theory is exact when the particles' hard cores interact additively, only neighbors touch, and bonding runs along the channel. At constant pressure, every structural and thermodynamic quantity follows from the pressure and the fraction of unbonded sites. Narrow-channel fluids model things, from molecules in pores to colloids in grooves. An exact theory is rare and useful: simulations can be checked against it, and design rules for self-assembling materials can be read off.
arxiv-2504-15267:
Shaorong Zhang and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on translating between two kinds of brain scans with a diffusion bridge model. One scan type maps the brain's wiring in fine detail but takes long to acquire. The other, a standard MRI, is quick and common.

Their model learns to turn the quick scan into the detailed one and back again. That lets clinics enrich their data without long extra scan time. The team judged the outputs by look alike scores, pixel level match, and spread of values. The made up scans kept the brain's structure and the state of its white matter well. A sex sorting test showed the fake data still carried real signal.
arxiv-2504-15367:
Anton Simen and co-authors blend two search styles to solve hard optimization problems in a 2025 paper. Branch-and-bound solves such problems by splitting them into cases and using relaxed versions to bound the best possible score. That trick gets hard when the goal involves higher-order terms, which make the relaxed form non-convex and loose.

Their quantum method uses a counterdiabatic drive, a helper push that keeps a quantum system on track, in digital form. Bias fields stand in for the relaxed solution, and the branch-and-bound loop sharpens results step by step. Tests ran in tensor network simulations with up to one hundred fifty-six qubits. Runs on IBM quantum hardware used up to one hundred qubits. In both, the method beat simulated annealing and a tuned quantum annealing baseline. It found better answers with much less computing effort.
arxiv-2504-15967:
Khalaf, Itani, and Sharafeddine present a study from twenty twenty-five on digital twins for device networks, aided by drones. A digital twin is a live copy of a real system used to test and tune it. Their setup parks several drones at chosen spots to gather data from ground devices. Many devices may watch the same object, so their readings merge into one status. Updates then flow to a base station that holds the twin. They coin a new score for how fresh the twin's status is.

Their goal is to gather the most data while keeping the twin fresh. They state the task as a hard math problem and solve it by stepwise smoothing. Tests show their method beats base approaches. The authors say fresh twins support better data-driven choices.
arxiv-2504-18167:
Fredrik Lohne Aanes, a solo author, speeds up a popular way of explaining model predictions in a 2025 paper. Shapley values split a prediction fairly among input features, but the conditional version is slow when the explainer model is a linear or polynomial regression. Aanes develops three methods, two approximate and one exact, that estimate the needed pieces for all feature subsets at once rather than one by one.

The methods lean on constrained random field theory and fast sparse matrix tools. In case studies they matched the accuracy of the standard sequential software while cutting run times from hours to minutes or seconds. One case handled over two million submodels in minutes. The author recommends the exact method, since it needs no tuning.
arxiv-2504-18567:
Jingxu Wu, Yuwei Yin, and Jianing Shi simulate hot quark matter in a twenty twenty-five paper. They use the two-flavor PNJL model, a model of quantum chromodynamics that tracks both quarks and the phases of the strong force. Heat and baryon density are the two dials they vary.

Two transport traits are their focus: how thick the matter flows, given by viscosity, set against its entropy. They find the shear ratio dips to a minimum, while the bulk ratio peaks, near the line where chiral symmetry is restored. The effect grows at high baryon density. Such marks could point to the QCD critical endpoint in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2504-19067:
Some dark matter models split the dark particle into a ground state and a slightly heavier excited state, with a dark photon carrying force between them. A dark Higgs boson completes the picture: it gives the dark photon its mass and sets the gap between the two dark matter states. Ko and co-authors note that this particle has been little searched for. When it is heavy enough, its decays turn half visible or fully invisible, which defeats the usual searches for light scalars.

The authors study how the Belle II experiment could catch it anyway, through dark Higgs production alongside other particles and through rare decays of B mesons. Two signs look robust: pairs of displaced particle vertices, and missing energy carried off by the dark Higgs decay. They also assess a proposed far detector for Belle II, called GAZELLE, and its reach for this elusive particle.
arxiv-2504-19167:
Tithi Dwary, Khyodeno Mozhui, and Krishna sort which split graphs can also be read as order graphs, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A split graph divides its points into a fully linked clique and an unlinked set. The order side asks whether arrows can point along a ranking without cycles.

A labeling test marks exactly which split graphs qualify. From that test, any such graph needs at most three ranking words to encode it. The bound also re-proves a known cap on the dimension of split orders. Readers in graph theory get a tidy test plus a sharp encoding cap in one pass.
arxiv-2504-19367:
Defant and Lee wrote in twenty twenty-five about a reduced random walk in the hyperbolic plane. The walk comes from Lam's work in hyperbolic triangle groups. Viewed in the upper half-plane model, the walk wanders under group actions. The authors prove it settles almost surely at a point on the extended real line. One special case, the modular group setting, gets detailed treatment. There they give an explicit formula for the limit's distribution.

The formula uses a new function they name the interrobang function. It mirrors many analytic and arithmetic traits of Minkowski's classic question-mark function. Such limit laws connect probability with number theory in striking ways. Random walks on groups often reveal hidden fractal structure. The explicit distribution is the paper's centerpiece result. It opens the special function to further study.
arxiv-2504-19767:
Katherine Lin and five co-authors study how people build a habit of writing in a paper journal over time. Those who keep journals hold strong views on their books, pens, page layouts, and what should go on the page. The team sought to see how those tastes form and settle in.

They went through journal content shared in public on YouTube and Instagram, and they spoke with eleven journalers one on one. Habits, it turns out, are shaped by three forces at once: the stuff used, the person's own life and needs, and the group round them. Those forces also feed how journalers see who they are. The team close with design ideas for tools to come. Good support, they argue, should respect what paper is good at, not press it flat into apps like any other.
arxiv-2504-20267: Aleksander Filip Żarnecki wrote a personal contribution in 2025 to the 2026 update of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. The note concerns the Future Circular Collider, a proposed ring collider put forward as CERN's next flagship project. Żarnecki explains that after joining many discussions and contributing to official documents, he concluded those documents do not give the whole picture. His note sets out his concerns about how the strategy update process is being run. It questions the possible choice of the new collider as the field's leading project.
arxiv-2504-20567:
Chakraborty and five co-authors wrote this study in twenty twenty-five about explaining computer tuning tools to people. Bayesian optimisation is a method that finds good settings for a system when the best settings are unknown. Newer tools add explanations meant to help users trust and use the results. The team asked whether the form of an explanation changes how well people do.

They built a playful task in which people tuned six settings to cook a perfect soft-boiled egg. Over two hundred volunteers got either a bar chart, a list of rules, a written explanation, or no help. Any explanation raised success and cut the number of tries. All three forms worked about equally well. Designers, the authors suggest, can add explanations without fussing over format.
arxiv-2504-21467:
Luc Vedrenne, Sylvain Faisan, and Denis Fortun align many 3D point clouds at once. Their 2025 paper introduces POLAR, a method for multiview registration. Pairwise alignment plus syncing scales poorly as views pile up. Older generative methods falter under big rotations or heavy damage.

POLAR moves the puzzle into the hidden space of a pre-trained autoencoder. A loss built to shrug off damage guides the search there. A multistart strategy keeps the optimizer from getting stuck. On made-up and real data, POLAR beat leading methods by clear margins. It handles many views, wide starting angles, and rough inputs in one frame.
arxiv-2505-00667:
Cian Reeves and co-authors built a practical frame in 2025 for faking lab light tests on a computer. Such tests flash light at matter and read how electrons move in less than a blink, which reveals how a material works. Lab results gain a lot when a matched computer run can check the reading and add insight.

The frame rests on a math form that tracks how many particles act as a team over time. It grows a classic series step by step in real time rather than in fake time steps. The team aimed for a tool that labs can run on real cases, not just toy ones. Good fakes help sort true effects from noise in fast light tests.
arxiv-2505-00767:
Gloria Isbrandt, Frank Pollmann, and Michael Knap explore what happens when spin ice is made anisotropic on a breathing pyrochlore lattice. Spin ice is a magnetic system whose spins obey local constraints, leaving a highly degenerate ground state. The team adds a tunable anisotropic coupling to the standard Ising spin ice Hamiltonian.

The ground state structure changes markedly, visible in the spin structure factor and in reduced residual entropy at low temperature. Depending on parameters, the system either crosses over into a constrained manifold with entropy below the conventional Pauling value, or orders into a symmetry-broken state. Large-N analytical predictions agree well with their simulations.
arxiv-2505-02267:
Mederic Motte gives prospect theory, the classic account of how people judge gambles, a formula that can be computed at once for bell-shaped rewards. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Prospect theory bends values and odds in set ways: losses sting more than gains please. Fitting those bends to data usually means slow numeric work.

Motte crafts bends with three guarantees. They always obey the theory's shape rules. They are rich enough to mimic a wide range of tastes. And for Gaussian gambles they yield a closed-form price. That last trait makes the scheme fast enough for whole populations. Two worked examples show population-level modeling in action. The frame suits risk studies where many agents must be priced quickly. It keeps the theory's spirit while dropping its computational drag.
arxiv-2505-04667:
Olivier Minazzoli writes in twenty twenty-five about the principle of relativity of inertia. He compares how that principle sits in two theories of gravity. One is general relativity, Einstein's well-known theory. The other is entangled relativity, a newer and leaner theory. The newer theory can recover both general relativity and standard quantum field theory in a set limit.

Entangled relativity also rules out spacetime with no matter in it at all. Minazzoli argues this makes the new theory a better fit for Einstein's own vision. He adds that its leaner form is a point in its favor under Occam's razor. Readers get a theory-level argument about what inertia should mean.
arxiv-2505-05467:
Haibo Wang and co-authors present StreamBridge in two thousand twenty-five, a framework that turns offline video language models into live streaming assistants. Models trained on finished videos struggle with two things online: following long multi-turn exchanges and speaking up proactively when something happens.

StreamBridge adds a memory buffer that compresses older context with a decaying scheme, keeping long conversations manageable. A small separate activation model watches the stream and triggers responses, and it plugs into existing models easily. The team also built Stream-IT, a large training set of interleaved video-text sequences for streaming tasks. In tests, upgraded offline models beat even flagship commercial systems on streaming understanding while staying competitive on standard video benchmarks.
arxiv-2505-05967:
Uyoata and co-authors set out to cut the signaling cost of power control in future factory wireless networks. In 6G plans, dense clusters of small subnetworks will serve robots and sensors at short range, and their access points must constantly adjust transmit power to limit interference. Earlier schemes assumed a central controller with perfect, fresh channel knowledge and ignored the chatter needed to gather it.

Their approach lets each access point learn both when to signal and how much power to use, through multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial information. In simulation the learned protocol used eight times less signaling than standard schemes while clearing data buffers nearly as fast as an all-knowing ideal. The authors argue learned protocols suit the messy reality of factory floors.
arxiv-2505-06167:
Chenwei Wang and co-authors propose reading the flight angles of charged particles from the pattern of hits across a satellite's detectors, in a 2025 paper. Their instrument, GECAM, watches the sky for gamma-ray bursts and also catches particle events in low Earth orbit. A particle's pitch angle, its tilt against the magnetic field, is a key clue to its origin. GECAM-style detectors were not built to measure it.

Simulations show the counts across detectors encode the angle well enough to recover it. Applied to a real electron rain event caught by GECAM-C, the method gave an angle near 90 degrees. The authors say the trick opens a new window on space particle events, from electron beams tied to distant storms to those sparked by lightning.
arxiv-2505-07467:
Yui Hayashi, Yuya Tanizaki, and Mithat Ünsal build the semiclassical machinery of confinement on a small twisted box. Yang-Mills theory on a plane times a small torus, with a non-minimal 't Hooft twist, can be treated semiclassically. Their center vortices descend from known monopole solutions through a three-dimensional abelianized picture. The construction assigns each vortex fractional charges.

Its magnetic and topological charges come in N-th parts, fixed by the twist. The action is likewise a fraction of an instanton's. A dilute gas of such vortices then describes the confining vacua. The authors derive how observables depend on the vacuum angle and compute string tensions. They finally test which twist best stabilizes the center at large N, examining a Fibonacci-based proposal from related models. The checks run through both one-form and zero-form center symmetries.
arxiv-2505-08067:
Sorensen and Gibbons wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five tracing a mystery noise in dark matter detectors. The detectors use liquid xenon and watch for faint flashes of light. For nearly a decade, a delayed glow with a slow fading pattern has followed each flash, and in recent years it has swamped searches for light dark matter.

Working with a small xenon cell at a Berkeley lab, the authors ran a broad series of tests. They conclude that the main source is fluorescence from the quartz windows of the light sensors, set off by ultraviolet light. Naming the source gives detector builders a concrete target to fix.
arxiv-2505-10867:
Luca Luceri and five co-authors hunt coordinated fake accounts on TikTok, a video-first platform past methods barely touch. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies coordinated inauthentic behavior around the twenty twenty-four United States presidential election. Text-era detectors lean on signals TikTok lacks. The team adapts network methods to the app's habits instead.

User similarity graphs rest on shared acts: synced posting, near-dup copies of captions, reused clips, and matched hashtag chains. Pruning the graphs exposes dense clusters of likely partners. The data span hundreds of thousands of election videos. Found acts range from synced narrative pushes to semi-automated copying with AI voices and split screens. Some classic signals port well; transcript likeness and Duet links do not. The study lays a first base for TikTok influence research.
arxiv-2505-11067:
Omobayode Fagbohungbe and co-authors present a 2025 paper on training neural networks in analog memory hardware, and how well that training transfers to new tasks. Such hardware promises fast, frugal learning by computing where the data sit. Real devices, though, switch unevenly and vary from unit to unit, which breaks standard training recipes.

The team assessed a newer algorithm built to cope with that mess, one that chops updates to tame the devices' lopsided response. Earlier rival methods demanded unrealistically perfect devices or proved fragile. The study weighs how the analog-trained models perform when moved to fresh tasks, the transfer setting where the hardware's speed could pay off most.
arxiv-2505-11367:
Ji Eun Kim and Libby Hemphill study how moral language shapes online giving in a 2025 paper. Charity appeals often lean on values such as care, fairness, and loyalty. The team measured which values appear in real campaigns and how donations answered.

They analyzed 14,088 campaigns on GoFundMe, sorting appeals by three moral frames. Emergency campaigns reacted most strongly to moral wording. Appeals stressing harm and unfairness drew more donations and comments overall, yet each donor gave a little less on average. Loyalty framing helped everywhere, raising both gift counts and messages of support. The authors suggest platforms could coach fundraisers on framing, while warning that outrage-based appeals have a cost.
arxiv-2505-11967:
Bas Sanders sets out a new way to measure doubt in trade and place-based models, in a paper from 2025. Economists use these models to guess what a policy change would do. Those guesses can steer real choices, so the doubt around them matters. Three snags make the doubt hard to gauge: the data link pairs of places, the count of places is small, and the data feed the model twice over.

The author builds a bootstrap method shaped to fit these snags. The method is simple to run and comes with both short-run and long-run promises of soundness. He then reapplies three well-known past studies with the new method. The reruns show where the method helps in practice. The paper gives trade research a cleaner way to say how firm its forecasts are.
arxiv-2505-13367:
Carsten Henkel solves the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations for waves that bounce in a lumpy condensate. The paper from twenty twenty-five studies the full continuous spectrum near a turning point. A basis swap splits the particle and hole amplitudes, near enough, into two modes. One mode spreads wide and rules phase ripples of the condensate. The other hugs zones where density slopes.

Phase shifts on reflection are worked out by hand math and by numeric runs. Those shifts set the standing wave pattern in the trap. As a use case, Henkel computes mode tones in a gravitational trap with no local density shortcut. A companion paper takes up the warm cloud's density and quantum depletion. The study sharpens the theory of sound-like waves in trapped gases.
arxiv-2505-13467:
Kleischmann and three co-authors report tests on clay in salty water done in space, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The tests ran on the space station, where there is almost no gravity. The team watched how small bits of clay clump into larger lumps over time. They tracked the clumps with photos for ninety-nine days.

They find that tiny shakes on the station sped up the clumping. Clumps grew much faster than they would from random heat drift alone. Computer models back up the same point. Stronger shakes and more solid clay both made growth faster. The result shows a new way that bits in a fluid can join up.
arxiv-2505-13767:
Celso Jorge Villas-Boas and Ciro Micheletti Diniz published a 2025 physics paper arguing that most of the energy in thermal radiation hides where detectors cannot see it. Heat glow, like light from a warm object, is usually treated as a crowd of independent waves. The authors show the crowd organizes into collective modes. Most of those modes are dark: entangled states of light that do not couple to matter.

In a system of many field modes, only one share in M of the energy can interact with matter at all. The rest sits locked in the dark modes. A common way of estimating energy, measuring brightness, can therefore mislead badly. The team tests the idea in a model cavity holding a single lossy atom, where breaking symmetry lets some hidden energy leak into view. The claim reframes what a detector reading means: silence may signal hidden energy, not absence.
arxiv-2505-14667:
Wonje Jeung, Sangyeon Yoon, Minsuk Kahng, and Albert No published a 2025 paper on keeping reasoning models safe without dulling them. Large reasoning models think aloud in long chains, and harmful prompts can hijack that chain toward dangerous outputs. Standard safety training suppresses the harm but often shortens and weakens the reasoning itself. It also cracks under clever jailbreak prompts.

Their method, SAFEPATH, teaches the model a small reflex: when a prompt is harmful, begin the reasoning with a short safety primer, just eight tokens. The rest of the chain is left unsupervised, free to reason at full depth. Across benchmarks, harmful outputs fell while problem-solving performance held. The primer works like a guardrail placed at the entrance, not speed bumps along the whole road. The authors offer it as a lightweight patch for a real tension: models that reason longer need safety that does not reason less.
arxiv-2505-17167: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on a fairer score for AI-written radiology reports. Word-overlap metrics miss clinical truth, while model-based judges wobble, and clinical checklists reward lazy all-normal answers when diseases are rare. Their CRG score grades only the abnormalities the reference report actually names, in binary or structured detail. Penalties are weighted by how common each label is, so rare findings count properly. Any language model can drive the feature extraction.
arxiv-2505-17267:
Odysseas Chlapanis and co-authors introduce GreekBarBench, a test set for language models in Greek law. Their paper appeared in 2025. The questions come from Greek bar exams across five legal areas. Answers must reason in free text and cite the right statutes and case facts. Grading free text is hard, so the team built a scoring system with three dimensions, judged by a language model.

They also built a second benchmark to check the judges against human experts. Simple rubrics tied to text spans made the model judges agree better with experts. They then graded thirteen leading models. The best beat the average expert score but fell short of the top five percent of experts. The work gives Greek legal AI a demanding, well-checked measuring stick.
arxiv-2505-21967:
Juan Ren, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem study attacks on vision-language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. These models take in images as well as text, which opens new attack surfaces. The authors ask why standard adversarial attacks can slip past the safety tools built into such models.

They carry out a systematic analysis of the models' internal representations. They also propose a two-stage scheme for grading attacks, first sorting outcomes into non-compliance, refusal, and true exploitation. The second stage scores how fully the output serves the harmful intent, and sorts refusals by type. A normative schema then sets out ideal model behavior against harmful prompts, as a target for safety work.
arxiv-2505-22367:
Aswathy Menon Kavumpadikkal Radhakrishnan and her four co-authors, publishing in 2025, ask whether the inner structure of oxygen nuclei leaves a fingerprint on particle flow at the Large Hadron Collider. Oxygen nuclei are known to hold clusters of helium nuclei inside them. Colliders have begun smashing oxygen into protons and into itself to study tiny drops of quark-gluon plasma. Flow patterns in the debris reflect the shape of the colliding nuclei.

The team simulates both collision types with a hybrid model that chains several standard codes. They compare clustered nuclei against a smooth standard profile. Clustering barely matters when oxygen hits a proton. In oxygen-oxygen collisions it changes every flow measure they study. The size of the helium clusters also shifts the effect. The work gives experimenters a way to read nuclear structure out of collision data.
arxiv-2505-22767:
Vasilaki asks how chat with a big tongue tool sparks fresh sight in this twenty twenty-five piece. A chat can jolt a mind to see a snag in a whole new way. She frames that spark as fruit of a two-way loop, not tool wit lone.

Inside, each made word turns back as feed for the next word in line. Each reply also loops through the mind, whose fresh read re-shapes the next ask. The tool's part swings tween stock lines and frame breaks that open new paths. A spine of kept past bits could call back the best modes on cue. Past chats, open tools, and brain math make the claims test-ripe.
arxiv-2505-23667:
Lang Cao and co-authors train language models to answer table questions by writing spreadsheet formulas, in a research paper from 2025. Models reason well in words but slip on numbers in complex tables. Formulas offer an exact, checkable path from data to answer.

Their method, called Fortune, rewards the model when its formula runs and lands the right answer. No hand-labeled formulas are needed for training. Across seven table benchmarks, the approach lifted performance sharply, above all on multi-step numeric tasks. The trained model, Formula-R1, shows that executable answers beat mental arithmetic for table work. The framework opens a practical route to reliable data assistants.
arxiv-2505-23767: Mostafa Najafi and Ali Morassaei study functions that stay fully monotone on the plus half-line, in a short math note from twenty twenty-five. A fully monotone function keeps a strict sign pattern through all of its rates of change. The note states key traits of such functions. It then builds fresh classes of them. Worked special functions show the tests in use.
arxiv-2506-00567:
A Aguilera and co-authors study frames built by repeating one operation on a starting set of vectors, in a math paper from 2025. Such frames, called dynamical frames, arise in sampling problems where a signal is probed over time. The head of the paper gives it the title Optimal Dynamical Frames.

The team first settles when an operation can generate a frame of a special balanced kind, called a Parseval frame. Past work gave conditions that were known to be enough; the authors show they are also required. They then define the frame index of an operation: the fewest starting vectors needed to build a frame by repetition. A formula is given for the balanced case. Last, they show that an operation and its adjoint share the same index, by an explicit build.
arxiv-2506-00967:
Zhang, Vorobyov, and three co-authors design a learning system that sets transmit power in cell-free massive antenna networks. Classic optimization methods iterate too slowly for real-time use. Graph neural networks work faster, but earlier versions assumed clean, separate pilot signals for every user.

In real networks, users outnumber the clean pilots, so signals contaminate each other. The proposed graph attention network handles that contamination directly. It also adapts when the number of active users changes, and it trains without costly precomputed answers. Tests show it performs well even against a strong optimization baseline. The authors frame the work as a step toward practical real-time power control.
arxiv-2506-01467:
Dorian Gailhard and co-authors present a stepwise generator for graphs and hypergraphs that keeps node and link features, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Graph generators handle small structures well but stall on large, complex ones. Layered methods scale better, yet often drop the features that real uses need.

Their frame grows a sample scale by scale, through local expansion and polish. A node budget knob controls grain and keeps scales consistent with each other. Tests spanned fake data, three-dimensional meshes, and point clouds. Scores matched or beat the best rivals, while scaling to far larger featured structures.
arxiv-2506-01767:
Sobati-Moghadam proposes in twenty twenty-five a light defence for split-packet attacks in low-power Internet of Things networks. In these networks, packets are routinely cut into fragments to fit tiny radio frames. Receivers store fragments before checking them, so attackers can flood memory with fake early fragments at little cost.

Her system scores each node's behaviour over time, rewarding steady success and punishing suspect patterns fast. A chained hash checks fragment integrity early, catching tampered sequences before they waste memory. Simulations of injection, replay, and flooding attacks kept delivery rates and energy use steady. The author pitches behaviour-based defence over heavy cryptography for tiny devices.
arxiv-2506-02267:
Xue Xia and co-authors present a recommendation model used at Pinterest in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ranking a user's home feed depends on predicting clicks from past actions. Most industry models read only short recent histories, missing long-term taste.

Their model, TransAct V2, reads very long action sequences to improve click prediction. It also adds a next action loss, training the model to forecast the user's coming action within the ranking task. The third advance is serving: the system is built to run these heavy sequence models at scale with low delay. The authors describe the model as a production system, not a lab prototype.
arxiv-2506-03167:
Long Tan Le and co-authors harden meaning based wireless communication against noise and meaning errors with a worst case training method, in work from twenty twenty-five. Semantic systems send task relevant content instead of raw bits, a draw for sixth generation networks. Two failure modes haunt them: garbled features at the source and channel noise in transit.

Their framework trains against a ball of plausible data shifts, using a distance measure borrowed from optimal transport. Theory gives firm bounds on how well the system holds up on fresh data. Image and text transmission tests showed better survival under noise and crafted attacks than prior designs. The authors stress that meaning stayed intact across varied wireless conditions.
arxiv-2506-03967:
Sebastián Daza and João Nuno Mestre study deformation problems with symmetry in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. A deformation problem asks how a structure can be bent or varied while keeping its core rules. The authors work with the algebraic system that controls such problems when a symmetry group acts on them.

Using special operators tied to that algebra, they give a smooth way to list the nearby structures around a given one. Along the way they offer new proofs, both algebraic and fully explicit, of known results on rigidity. Those results say when a structure cannot be deformed at all, and when no obstacles block a deformation.
arxiv-2506-04967:
Claudianor Alves, Rui Ding, and Chao Ji study solitary waves for a generalized wave equation in this 2025 paper. The equation is the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in two dimensions. The waves sought have a fixed total mass, called normalized solutions. An unknown parameter acts as a multiplier to enforce that mass condition.

For a pure power response, the authors prove ground state solutions exist in both the subcritical and supercritical ranges. For a mixed power response, a solution appears as a local minimum of the energy. A second solution with positive energy is also shown for a sequence of small masses. The authors note these are the first such results for this setting.
arxiv-2506-05667:
Yuhan Hao and a large team build DriveAction, a benchmark for human-like driving calls by vision-language-action models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such models steer self-driving cars, but past tests lack scene range, trusty action labels, and scoring tied to human taste.

The set holds over sixteen thousand question pairs drawn from more than two thousand real driving scenes. The scenes were logged by drivers of self-driving cars, and action labels come from what those drivers truly did. A tree-shaped scoring frame links sight, words, and action. Tests show top vision-language models need both sight and words: drop either and accuracy falls, drop both and it falls most.
arxiv-2506-08167:
Sunny Gupta, Nikita Jangid, and Amit Sethi present a federated learning scheme that keeps local training honest when each site's data look different. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains one model across many sites without pooling data. Skewed local data bias each site's classifier and drag the shared model down.

Their method, UniVarFL, fixes the bias at the client, with no help from the global model. One penalty aligns each class's predicted odds with what balanced data would give. Another spreads feature points evenly over their sphere, which aids generalization. Together they mimic training on pooled, balanced data. Tests across several benches beat existing methods in accuracy. The scheme stays light, suiting phones and other weak devices. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2506-08967:
The Step-Audio team at StepFun presents a large audio model that answers spoken questions with speech of its own, in a 2025 paper. Most audio-language models still reply in text, which breaks the natural flow of a voice conversation. Their model, Step-Audio-AQAA, handles the full loop from audio in to audio out. It pairs a two-stream audio tokenizer, capturing both meaning and sound detail, with a 130-billion-parameter language core and a voice synthesizer.

Training after the main build mixed text and audio tokens in one stream so the spoken answers stay coherent. A preference-tuning step, combined with merging model versions, polished quality and expression. The team positions the system for the audio query, audio answer setting, where a user speaks and expects a spoken reply. They frame it as a step toward voice assistants that converse in voice throughout, with feeling intact.
arxiv-2506-09767:
Ali Mohammadian, Milad Poursoltani, and Behruz Tayfeh-Rezaie wrote a 2025 math paper on lean networks that just avoid a given pattern. A saturation number counts the fewest links in a network that lacks a target shape but gains it if any missing link is added. Such minimal-but-ready networks are a classic topic in graph theory.

The team work out how that count grows for two targets: complete multipartite graphs, which split nodes into fully linked groups, and even cycles long enough to behave well. Their results extend a 2010 finding and partly settle a 2013 conjecture by Füredi and Kim. The paper is proof-based, giving growth rates rather than exact counts for every size.
arxiv-2506-09967:
Shangshang Wang and six co-authors show how to move reasoning skill from one language model to another at very low cost. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Their family of small reasoning models is called Resa. The trick is to first train a sparse autoencoder on a strong source model.

The autoencoder learns to spot the inner patterns tied to reasoning. It then guides normal fine-tuning of a target model on checked question-answer pairs. No worked reasoning traces are needed for that step. The tuned models kept nearly all of the skill of far costlier trained peers. Training took minutes and cost about a dollar. Skills lifted from one data set still helped on bigger ones. They could even be bolted onto a third model at test time with no new training.
arxiv-2506-10067:
Andrew A Allocca, Devesh K Verma, Sriram Ganeshan, and Justin H Wilson study, in a 2025 paper, whether the control of quantum chaos follows universal rules. Their test bed is the quantum Arnold cat map, a classic model of chaotic motion. Inspired by classical tricks, their protocol flips at random between the system's own instability and steering steps that push it toward a target.

Exact quantum simulation and a semi-classical shortcut agreed closely on how control takes hold. To explain the pattern, the authors built a simpler stand-in model, an inverted harmonic oscillator, which can be solved on paper. All three lines of work pointed the same way: the shift into control is shaped by the fuzz that quantum uncertainty itself sets, not by interference effects. The authors frame this as a universal feature of such transitions.
arxiv-2506-10467:
Felix Härer reports exploratory research from 2025 on systems where several language-model agents work as a team. Such teams can mix reasoning, code writing, and running software to handle tasks in a single field. Yet teams are often judged piece by piece, and how to specify and grade the whole system is poorly understood.

Härer offers two linked pieces: a schema language for writing down how a multi-agent system is built, and an architecture with a working prototype that runs those specifications and scores the results. Test cases in cybersecurity, covering question answering and server and network defense, were completed correctly by agents using models from two major providers. The work shows the approach is workable.
arxiv-2506-11467:
Carlos Rafael Catalan turns translation evaluation into a game that also recruits its players in a 2025 language technology study. Machine translation for low-resource languages cannot be judged by string matching alone; human judges are essential, yet hard to find for small language communities. A platform that makes evaluation playful can draw in the very speakers whose judgment is scarcest.

Players assess translations as part of the game, and strong players become the recruited evaluator pool. The design treats evaluation and recruitment as one problem. Low-resource communities gain both a scoreboard for their translation systems and a crowd to improve them.
arxiv-2506-11567:
Jens Lucht, Paul Meyer, Leon Merten Lohse, and Tim Salditt present HoToPy, a free Python toolbox for X-ray holo-tomography, in a 2025 paper. The method images tiny objects by reading how X-rays bend and spread through them, then rebuilding the volume slice by slice. Phase retrieval, the hard step, has many competing algorithms. HoToPy gathers them behind one simple interface, for both deep holographic and direct contrast imaging.

The box also handles alignment of the stack, image cleanup, and simulation of experiments. The team shows it on a catalyst nanoparticle imaged at a Hamburg synchrotron beamline. Its modular build suits both quick tests of new algorithms and full reconstruction pipelines at other light sources. The authors offer it as shared infrastructure for the phase imaging community.
arxiv-2506-11867:
Hanchen Wang, William Legrand, Richard Schlitz, and Pietro Gambardella show that an electric current can switch a coupling between magnons on and off. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works with an ultrathin film of bismuth-doped yttrium iron garnet. Two platinum nanostripes bound a region where cavity modes form. Edge traits from the metal contact reshape the magnon spread there.

Cavity modes mix with boundary modes trapped under the capped film, opening a gap where they cross. A spin-wave model with dipole and exchange terms fits the seen modes well. Spin current from a stripe's spin Hall effect breaks the cavity's edge terms. Past a threshold, modes and mixing fade. Microwave power offers a second knob, shifting the gap. The build suits chip-scale magnonic parts that can be set by current.
arxiv-2506-12467:
Fang Qin and Rui Chen set out a frame to steer small states that sit at the corners of a class of materials with special wave traits. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

In these materials, corner states can be trapped at set spots. The team shows that long-range hops of waves let a user tune where the states sit in a round form. Hops in unlike paths shift them in unlike ways. They then test forms with many sides. A corner holds a trapped state when the signs of a mass term on its two edges clash, and holds none when the signs match. The work gives a broad tool to place such states by design.
arxiv-2506-12667:
Alexis Tudor and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how to make AI systems worthy of trust. Large language models can sound sure while making things up, and their choices cannot be audited; pure rule systems can explain themselves but are heavy and complex.

The team proposes a middle path built on s(CASP), a goal-directed reasoner that answers queries with a visible chain of steps. They test it against a well-known list of sixteen traits that trustworthy AI should have, plus two of their own: spotting clashes and weighing other possible worlds. Worked examples include a chatbot and a reasoner inside a virtual body. The authors argue that plain, checkable reasoning can meet the trust list without a giant rule base.
arxiv-2506-13267:
Subbotin and eleven co-authors present a 2025 paper on steering the plasma in a fusion device with a learned controller. A tokamak needs tight control of the plasma's shape and place to run safely. Standard control first rebuilds the plasma state from sensor data, then applies fixed models, which limits speed and flexibility.

The team trained a deep learning agent in a simulator of the DIII-D tokamak. The agent reads raw magnetic signals and sets the coils directly, with no rebuild step. This was the first use of such learning for magnetic control on this mid size device. The authors report stronger and more flexible control across several plasma setups.
arxiv-2506-13767:
Chenpeng Feng presents a 2025 mathematics paper on the surface formed by all planes inside a general cubic fivefold, a five-dimensional shape cut out by a cubic equation. He studies this moduli surface and how it deforms as the fivefold varies. The surface turns out to be smooth and projective, with an ample canonical bundle, placing it among surfaces of general type.

For a particular family of such surfaces, the variation of their degree-one Hodge structures is maximal, meaning the family explores the full possible range. The main tools come from hyper-Kähler geometry and a detailed computation of the surfaces' Hodge numbers. The paper is a specialist contribution to the geometry of cubic hypersurfaces and their moduli.
arxiv-2506-14767:
Li-Wei Chen and four co-authors improve the naturalness of computer generated speech in a 2025 paper. Spoken language models work on discrete speech tokens, but those tokens capture words while dropping tone, rhythm, and other expressive traits, so output sounds flat. Earlier fixes hand added pitch features, which cover only part of what makes speech sound human.

Their method instead learns, end to end, a compact code for the continuous expressive traits and feeds it alongside the word tokens. No manual feature picking is needed. Human raters preferred the speech continuations the system produced over the alternatives tried. The authors release code, samples, and models for others to build on.
arxiv-2506-14867:
Isabel Garcia Garcia, Marius Kongsore, and Ken Van Tilburg build a new kind of instanton, a lump of field with a twist count, out of purely electric-magnetic parts. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Instantons are key events in quantum field theory, but they were thought to need non-Abelian fields. The team shows an Abelian field can carry the twist too.

Each of their setups grows from a closed loop of magnetic charge in four-dimensional space. The field must wind in a nontrivial way along that loop. The result is a dyon loop, part electric and part magnetic, with a nonzero twist count. They place the loops inside a classic unified model to show the setup is complete. There, the whole charge sits in the plain photon sector. Numerically, the loops deform smoothly into the classic small instanton.
arxiv-2506-15967:
Dan-Dan Hu and colleagues work out a rare semileptonic decay of the Ds meson with QCD light-cone sum rules. The decay yields the scalar meson f0(980). That meson is thought to be a mix of two energy states. The states join light-quark and strange-quark parts. To grasp such decays tests both the structure of the meson and the method of work.

The team first works out the f0(980) decay constant with sum rules in background field theory. They then find the first two moments of its leading-twist light-cone distribution amplitude. The mixing-state amplitudes are included. With those inputs they work out the transition form factor for the decay. They extend it across the full region with a series expansion. That gives decay widths and a branching fraction.
arxiv-2506-17267:
Jusheng Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 training method for vision-language models, the systems that link images and words. Such models often lean on surface word-image links and miss the cause behind a scene. They can fail when a small change flips the sense of a picture. The team set out to teach finer and more causal reading.

Their method, CF-VLM, trains models on near-miss fake scenes built to clash with the real one. Three training goals work as a team: keep the base image-word match, hold the true scene steady against fakes, and sharpen care for tiny but key edits. Tests showed steady gains over strong rival methods on reasoning and new-case tests. The models also made fewer made-up claims about images. Stronger causal reading matters for high-stakes uses of such systems.
arxiv-2506-17567: Yoshioka, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, studied whether sheaf stability survives a Fourier-Mukai transform built from the Poincaré line bundle. Sheaves are bookkeeping tools for geometric data on a surface, and stability decides which ones behave well in moduli problems. Working on abelian surfaces, he shows Gieseker stability is preserved under this transform. He also adds remarks on the weak Brill-Noether property, which concerns how many sections certain bundles carry.
arxiv-2506-17967:
Hendriksen and seven co-authors tune sight-tongue tools to grade fake world films in this twenty twenty-five paper. World tools dream films of acts in fake rooms for plan work. No stock grade can tell if a dream film's acts ring true.

Inside, two grade tasks test act reads and face reads in three ask forms. Their tuned judge reads a film's time line, not lone still frames. Drill forms from full to light tune paths met at one judge build. That one judge tied task-tuned kin on each grade task in the runs. Folk grade rounds in seven fake rooms matched the judge with faith.
arxiv-2506-19467:
Ni and eight co-authors test whether reasoning helps language models capture how human annotators disagree, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. When labelers disagree, the split often flags a task that is a matter of taste or a case that is not clear. Keeping that split can matter. Sixty setups span three tasks, model sizes, and ways to steer the models. Reasoning trained with checked rewards is set against plain chain-of-thought prompting.

To the team's surprise, reasoning trained with checked rewards makes the fit to human splits worse. Plain chain-of-thought makes it better for models trained on human feedback. Swapping human labelers for reasoning models risks loss of this useful spread of views. The results warn against the view that reasoning always helps when models judge work. On tasks of taste, the split may need to be kept, not reasoned away.
arxiv-2506-19667:
Ethan Ackelsberg presents a 2025 math paper on patterns inside large sets of fractions. A question from four other scholars asked which shapes must appear in any big chunk of the rational numbers. Ackelsberg proves two such results. In any finite coloring of all fractions, one color holds an endless set whose squares and sums stay in that color. Any set of fractions with positive share holds a shifted copy of the same shape.

Twin claims for whole numbers are both false, so fractions behave in a richer way. The proofs move the puzzle into dynamics, the study of systems over time. New tools there handle averages twisted by polynomial paths. The work gives a clean case where two close number systems split in their pattern rules.
arxiv-2506-20667:
Louis Legrand and colleagues design a safer way to reconstruct how gravity from cosmic structure bends the oldest light in the universe. The bending, called lensing of the cosmic microwave background, is recovered from telescope maps whose noise is uneven because of scanning patterns and atmosphere. If that noise is modeled even slightly wrong, the lensing answer comes out biased. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reshapes the best-fit reconstruction so it only trusts correlations between map splits with independent noise, sidestepping the auto-correlations where modeling errors bite. With many splits, the method stays close to the statistically optimal reconstruction.

Simulations show the recovered lensing measurements stay immune to noise mis-modeling while losing almost no signal. The authors present the estimator as preparation for the next generation of background surveys, where precision goals leave no room for noise-driven bias.
arxiv-2506-20767:
Richard Sarmento and Evan Scannapieco simulate the earliest galaxies in a 2025 paper. They ask how the mass spread of the first stars shapes what a new space telescope can see. Two large simulations are compared, one with detailed light transport and one with a cheaper approximation. Both include a model of turbulent mixing needed to track first-star formation.

Light transport changed little, and both runs matched observations and other simulations fairly. They predict far fewer detectable galaxies at the earlier epoch than the later one. Even with a top-heavy first-star mass spread, those stars contribute almost none of the light of detectable galaxies, because their mass recycles too fast.
