arxiv-2506-21267:
Gracie McGill and nine co-authors read the Andromeda galaxy's accretion history in the horizontal branches of its outer halo star clusters. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents deep Hubble photometry of forty-eight clusters, many tied to tidal streams. New empirical relations, calibrated on Milky Way clusters, yield consistent metallicities and extinctions from the color-magnitude diagrams. One correlation jumps out of the data.

Clusters with very red horizontal branches sit almost always on substructure. Stream-free clusters show extended blue branches instead. The split is the first direct proof that red-branch halo clusters arrive via satellite accretion, an idea fifty years old. A few metal-poor red-branch oddballs suggest recent, young arrivals. Andromeda's merger past looks longer than our own galaxy's.
arxiv-2506-22567:
Shansong Wang and co-authors build a general biomedical vision-language model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models like CLIP link images and text, but biomedicine lacks the huge paired datasets used for natural images. Their model, MMKD-CLIP, learns instead by distilling knowledge from nine expert models.

Training ran in two stages. First came standard pretraining on 2.9 million image-text pairs across 26 imaging types. Then the model matched features from its teachers on over 19 million pairs. The team tested it on 58 biomedical datasets covering millions of images. The aim is one generalist model for many medical image tasks.
arxiv-2506-23267:
Shrikant Utagi and Prateek Chawla test two recent witnesses for non-Markovian behavior in quantum systems, where the environment feeds information back into the system. Both witnesses rest on forms of temporal correlation. Through counterexamples drawn from the literature, the authors show cases where these witnesses flag memory effects that standard distance and entropy measures miss.

The paper then turns one witness into a measure. The pseudo-density matrix behind it links directly to the Choi matrix of the process. That link lets the authors quantify total quantum memory in any process that cannot be split into steps. One witness family, based on temporal steering, may miss a class called eternal non-Markovianity. The pseudo-density approach catches that class faithfully. The authors close by distinguishing weak and strong forms of quantum direct cause in open-system dynamics.
arxiv-2506-23967:
Geerd-Dietger Hoffmann and Verena Majuntke present, in twenty twenty-five, a tool to measure the resource use and carbon cost of software. As computing demand grows, so does interest in software's environmental footprint. Measuring is the first step to cutting it. The Green Metrics Tool runs software in containers, in a controlled and repeatable way. It assesses resource use across key phases of a program's life. The pair argue for fact-based metrics to guide decisions on efficiency.

The tool adds views of the data, cross-run comparison, and rule-based and AI-based tips for savings. Those features can guide developers and researchers to lower-impact software, they say. The talk version came from a workshop on low carbon computing held in Glasgow in late twenty twenty-four.
arxiv-2507-01167:
Atsushi Inoue and two co-authors prove that a classic test for economic models stays valid under wide conditions, in a 2025 econometrics paper. The Anderson-Rubin test checks a subset of model parameters while leaving the rest free. The version here rests on a criterion from a continuously updated estimator. The team treats the data spread in a flexible way, with set rules imposed only under the null claim.

They show the test keeps the right error rate even when parameters are weakly or not at all pinned down. The result covers data with uneven spread, cross-sections, and time series that need not sit still. A fresh proof trick, based on small nudges and smoothing of the estimator's core equations, drives the result. The authors say applied workers can trust the test in more settings than before.
arxiv-2507-02367:
Christian Salomonsen and colleagues teach a network to read a PET scan's input curve so mice need no arterial line. Dynamic PET tracks a tracer through the body, and kinetic models need the tracer's blood concentration over time. Drawing that curve means cannulating an artery, an intricate, terminal procedure in small animals. Longitudinal studies die with the subject.

Their fully convolutional model watches the scan's volumetric frames, extracts spatial features, then reads them over time to predict the arterial input function. It trained and validated on a common glucose tracer's scans with real blood curves. Two further tracers, for dopamine and prostate targets, test its range. Shortened and time-shifted scans probe robustness. The model predicted the input function reliably throughout. Blood-free kinetics could spare animals and unlock repeat imaging.
arxiv-2507-02467:
Vincent Runge, Charles Truong, and Simon Querné speed up the exact hunt for change points in long time series, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Dynamic programming finds every shift in a series' behavior, but slowly. Pruning rules that discard hopeless candidates made it fast, yet each existing rule has a blind spot: one fades when changes are sparse, the other suits only simple models.

Their framework, DUST, judges candidates through a dual function weighed against a threshold. Strong duality holds for the pruning problem under mild assumptions. For single-parameter models it pairs one rival's simplicity with the other's speed, and it shines for non-Gaussian data. A mouse monitoring series shows it recovering the true change structure efficiently.
arxiv-2507-02567:
Maarten van Dijk and colleagues take a census of the particles flowing down a CERN test beamline. The T10 line in the renovated East Area feeds experiments and school competitions alike. Knowing its particle mix at each momentum is basic housekeeping. The team measured it four independent ways.

Pressure scans on a threshold Cherenkov counter vary the gas until species switch on one by one. A lead-glass calorimeter and time-of-flight measurements add cross-checks. A paired-counter method brackets a species' threshold from above and below. The measurement began as a Beamline for Schools proposal, carried out in twenty twenty-three and expanded with more scans into twenty twenty-five. Overlapping data sets are compared into one comprehensive account. The work is metrology in service of everyone downstream of the beam.
arxiv-2507-02967:
Pragya Dhungana and co-authors (2025) test object detection models for inspecting underwater pipelines. The sea floor is a hard place to see: turbidity, bent light, and decayed images defeat ordinary inspection cameras. The team compared two recent YOLO generations, version 8 and version 11, in three sizes each. The task was image segmentation, outlining the pipeline structures in frames shot beneath the seabed. Artificial intelligence enhancement steps supported the detection pipeline.

YOLOv11 beat YOLOv8 overall in their comparisons. The authors report the newer model delineated target structures more accurately under the poor visual conditions. They frame the study as groundwork for autonomous fault diagnosis on subsea lines. Reliable outlining is the first step toward spotting corrosion, cracks, and leaks without divers. The work also gives operators a practical ranking of model variants for this niche, where most published benchmarks use clear land images instead.
arxiv-2507-05167:
Nestor Guillen and Luis Silvestre explain a breakthrough on the Landau equation in an expository note from 2025. The equation describes how particles in a plasma collide and spread. A feared outcome is blow-up, where values grow without bound in finite time. Their recent work rules out blow-up for the case of Coulomb forces, and the note lays out the ideas for a broad math audience.

The key step tracks a quantity called Fisher information along a solution. They show it does not increase over time, which blocks blow-up. A lifted helper equation, built in twice the variables, makes the proof work. For this equation it becomes a family of heat equations on a sphere. Background links round out the note.
arxiv-2507-05267:
Markus Böck reports a full strong solution for the game Connect-Four on its standard board. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The game was solved in the sense that the best move can be found by search. But a full look-up table, giving win, draw, or loss for each state, was thought to be too big to build.

Böck uses a symbolic search based on binary decision diagrams, with a fast code build. On a single core of home-grade hardware, the work took about two days and made a large table. His open tool also adds a search that finds the fastest win or the slowest loss. Game fans and code users can check the result freely.
arxiv-2507-05467:
Gnabasik and seven colleagues measure temperature at the nanoscale with electron patterns in twenty twenty-five. Tiny devices need precise heat maps, but optical and probe methods have limits. Their method reads temperature from electron backscatter diffraction patterns in a microscope. Heat blurs the pattern's bands in a measurable way.

Simulations set sensitivity limits for four semiconductor materials. A Fourier analysis captures the subtle blurring across the whole pattern. On silicon, experiments matched the predicted sensitivity closely. They reached thirteen kelvin uncertainty with a ten second capture. Temperature maps under a heat gradient were also produced. The authors offer the method as a practical tool for device diagnostics.
arxiv-2507-05867:
Nikita Savin, Elena Ambrosovskaya, Dmitry Romaev, and Anton Proskurnikov assess linear control for zero speed fin roll damping in two thousand twenty-five. Ships at rest or slow speed lose the lift that damps roll. A Navis system uses two fins that drag and oscillate to push back. That drag based act works even when the hull stands still.

Their control design stays linear in its core structure. Nonlinear drag forces and actuator limits are still counted in the loop. A high fidelity vessel model built for hardware tests hosts the runs. Simulations show the scheme damps roll well in that setting.
arxiv-2507-06067:
Maximilian Tschuchnig, Lukas Lamminger, Philipp Steininger, and Michael Gadermayr improve synthetic CT images made from cone-beam scans. Cone-beam CT is used a lot in surgery for its speed and low dose. But its images have flaws and look worse than standard CT. To turn cone-beam scans into the CT form is a strong fix.

The team uses learning that joins cone-beam data from surgery with standard CT taken before surgery. The two sets are not lined up by nature. So they add a registration module that can learn, inside the build steps. They test the model on a controlled fake data set and on two real clinic data sets. Adding registration lifted image quality past base methods in most test settings. Gains were largest when cone-beam quality was low.
arxiv-2507-06267:
Fitting a model to data breaks when the outside signal driving it jumps suddenly, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Hyeontae Jo, Krešimir Josić, and Jae Kyoung Kim fixes the jump first. Their method, HADES-NN, alternates two steps: a neural network smooths the jagged signal, then the smooth version feeds standard parameter fitting.

The estimates came out accurate and tight across test cases. Two came from real biology: the body clock driven by light recorded on wearables, and yeast answering a mating signal. The authors say the trick widens the range of real systems that can be fitted at all.
arxiv-2507-07467:
Juyeop Han, Lukas Lao Beyer, Guilherme Cavalheiro, and Sertac Karaman wrote this robotics paper, published in 2025. It plans drone flight paths that actively help the drone know where it is, indoors, where GPS cannot reach.

Map-based localization needs heavy pre-built maps that scale poorly. Instead, a learned estimator predicts 3D scene coordinates for each pixel, giving position directly, and an uncertainty-aware version says how much to trust each patch of view. The planner steers the camera toward trustworthy scenery while a smoother blends the slow visual fixes with fast motion-sensor data. In simulation, position error fell by at least five percent and orientation error by over thirty percent against baselines. Hardware-in-the-loop tests showed the system could run in near-real conditions.
arxiv-2507-07567:
Reza Ghasemi Alavicheh and three co-authors turn amplifier distortion into a shield for wireless links. Their 2025 paper works on physical layer security. Amplifiers bend signals as they near saturation, a flaw engineers usually fight. Bent signals, steered well, could jam eavesdroppers instead.

Their Z3RO precoder flips some antennas so distortion cancels at the true user. Elsewhere, the distortion lands as interference. Eavesdroppers then face a dirtier channel than the intended receiver. Simulations show secrecy rates up to two and a half times the standard method. The gain holds at a ten percent outage level. Dirt in the signal becomes a feature, not a bug.
arxiv-2507-08167:
Md Saif Hassan Onim, Andrew Kiselica, and Himanshu Thapliyal read the feelings of older adults from wrist sensor signals alone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Knowing mood helps care in hospitals and assisted homes, but cameras feel intrusive and miss some states.

Forty older adults wear two wristbands while face-based reads give the truth labels across twelve feeling kinds. Classic learning models then guess feeling strength from body signals alone. The best fits the labels well with tiny error. The path suits people with dementia or trauma stress, and keeps the read private and cheap to run.
arxiv-2507-08567:
Preslav Aleksandrov and nine co-authors present AbbIE, an encoder that loops over its own latent states to model sequences with adjustable effort. Their paper from twenty twenty-five reshapes the encoder-only transformer into a recursive form. Standard scaling buys skill with more weights and tokens. AbbIE adds a third dial: iterations at test time.

The loops run in latent space, with no special data or training scheme needed. Trained with just two loops, it generalizes to any loop count at use. Perplexity beats a standard transformer at matched size. Zero-shot in-context learning gains show up as well. Harder tasks can spend more loops, easy ones fewer. All tests stay at modest model sizes. The authors open a fresh axis for transformer scaling.
arxiv-2507-09067:
Serhan Bahar sets out a coin on screen built to live through quantum screens while it fights the watch risks of coins from chief banks. The ledger named in the title is a token based build. It joins set post quantum locks with hash based proofs that show a fact with no leak of the fact. Its aims are rule by the user, growth, and pried deals.

Parts of the design are short lived proof chains for deals that can not be linked. It has a stake vote that weighs pried use to spread who takes part. A proof way with no leak lets users pick what to show. They can prove facts on a deal with no show of all. Block times of ten to twenty ticks of the clock weigh guard and flow. The design is in thoughts; builds to test it are set as work to come.
arxiv-2507-11967:
Yuchi Ishikawa and five co-authors teach a model to learn from sound, images, and words at once. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Masked autoencoders learn by hiding parts of audio and video and guessing them back. Adding language guidance can sharpen what they learn. The catch is training data: matched sound, image, and text triples are scarce.

The team makes those triples on its own from raw videos. An image captioning model writes frame-level captions first. A filter based on CLAP then keeps only triples where sound and caption align well. No hand labels are needed. Their model, LG-CAV-MAE, adds a pretrained text encoder to the audio-visual setup. It beats prior methods on retrieval and classification tests. The gains show the value of clean auto-made triples.
arxiv-2507-12767:
As populations age, AI agents are being offered as helpers for older adults, from reminders to care coordination. Jiaxin An asks a design question that is easy to miss: how much independence should such an agent take, and how much should it leave with the person? Earlier work mapped the stages of a task and the agent's role in each. An draws on ideas of autonomy from several fields and splits it into four parts for older adults.

The four parts are choosing for oneself, setting one's own goals, staying in control, and carrying social responsibility toward others. An argues the last of these is under studied: an agent used in shared spaces affects family and community, not just its owner. The paper proposes research directions: tackle social responsibility, define agent independence task by task, and build ways to measure autonomy.
arxiv-2507-13267:
Igor Araujo and Zimu Xiang study two properties of oriented graphs in two thousand twenty-five. An oriented graph has edges with a set direction. One property asks if big near tournaments must hold a copy of a given graph. The other asks if they must hold a perfect tiling by that graph.

The pair disprove a guessed full account of the first property. The guess came from a team of six named authors in past work. They also show the two properties can split apart. Some graphs have the first property but not the second. They give a fresh case of a graph with the tiling property as well.
arxiv-2507-14267:
Ziqi Wang and his six co-authors, publishing in 2025, build a team of AI agents that runs materials simulations under strict guardrails. Language model agents can drive long calculations, but their numbers are hard to trust. The team's engine, DREAMS, wraps a standard physics method in a layered safety guard. Every value must trace to a registered source, and checks run both as tools are called and when the final report is written.

The guarded system landed within 1 percent of reference values on a standard lattice benchmark. It also reproduced an expert-level result on a classic surface puzzle. An unguarded twin reached a nearly right answer while a fifth of its essential steps quietly failed. The guard costs about thirteen times more input text. The authors let users switch layers off to trade trust for cost, and frame the design as a path to autonomous labs.
arxiv-2507-14867:
Zhaoqiang Xia, Hexiang Huang, Haoyu Chen, Xiaoyi Feng, and Guoying Zhao wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reads feelings from micro-gestures, the small body moves people make without knowing, using a hypergraph-enhanced transformer.

Micro-gestures are a fresh cue for feeling, but past work on them is thin. The frame has an encoder and a decoder, each built from hypergraph attention blocks that link skeleton joints in groups, plus time-based convolution at many scales. The decoder rebuilds the motion as a self-taught task, which sharpens the subtle moves. A light head then names the feeling. Joint training on both tasks tops past methods on two public data sets.
arxiv-2507-15467:
Daniel Grieser, Álvaro Sánchez-Hernández, and Boris Vertman wrote a 2025 survey paper on a family of curved spaces that pinch into cusps. The catalog title carries a funding note, but the paper itself reviews math for spaces that run off to infinity in a pointed, fibred way. Such spaces appear when smooth spaces break down at a seam, and they pose hard questions about waves and heat on them.

The survey gathers results on spectra, torsion, and index theory for these spaces, in both complete and incomplete forms. It explains the shared tools, which track how heat and waves behave near the cusp in fine detail. It also sketches how the main proofs work and where the forms differ. Surveys like this give newcomers one map of a scattered field.
arxiv-2507-15867:
John Wu, Adam Cross, and Jimeng Sun present a software system in 2025 that hunts for rare diseases in health records. Rare diseases affect one in ten Americans, yet records often miss them. Standard disease codes have no match for over half of the known rare disease codes. Patient notes hold the clues, but they are long, messy, and full of short forms.

Their system gives a language model tools to expand short forms, reason about hidden signs, and match terms to two disease catalogs. It needs no training on labeled examples, which are scarce. A small, cheap model matched or beat larger tuned systems in their tests. Costs fell sharply, and hospitals could run it on site to keep patient data private.
arxiv-2507-16567:
Adith Sai Aramthottil and four co-authors warn that some signs of odd behavior in messy quantum systems can be false alarms. Ordered quantum systems are expected to settle so that local reads match a heat based forecast. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The issue is how reads spread when many messy cases are averaged. A non bell shaped spread can look like a break in the settling rule, the authors argue. Across mess types, the spread of a local spin read mirrors the spread of the mess itself. They trace this to overlap between the read and powers of the system's energy rule, and show how to set the energy window right.
arxiv-2507-17467:
Elena Pitta, Tom Kouwenhoven, and Tessa Verhoef present a study from twenty twenty-five on a test task for models that mix sight and words. The task asks if a claim about a photo is true, false, or unclear. The team used one vision model as their test case. They ask how far scores on this task show real grasp of sight and words.

They tried no-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned runs. Three prompt cases beat none, but more cases added noise. The order of labels in the prompt swayed the calls a lot. With no photo, the model made up content, which hints it leans on word habits. Fine-tuning scored high and gave sound reasons. Yet like scores with weak sight cast doubt on the task.
arxiv-2507-18667:
Police sketches turn witness memories into faces, and drawing them takes scarce expert time. Nicholas Fidalgo and co-authors test whether image-generating AI can help in this 2025 project, comparing three pipelines built on a popular diffusion model.

One plain pipeline was tested against versions that align text and image with a matching model, one of them fine-tuned for the task. Careful tuning of the matching model improved text fit, yet the plain pipeline still scored best on image quality measures and produced the clearest faces by eye. The study suggests simple setups remain hard to beat for sketch generation, at least for now.
arxiv-2507-18767:
Mia Gabriella Escobar, Valentin Garcia, and Anastasiia Minenkova settle an open case about special quantum spin chains in a 2025 mathematics study. Early state exclusion describes chains where a starting state becomes unreachable after the first step. Infinite families of matrices with and without that property were known for even chain lengths, but odd lengths from seven upward stayed open.

For a chain of seven qubits with nearest-neighbor coupling and environmental effects, the authors present infinite families of the relevant matrices in both flavors. Closing the smallest odd case suggests the pattern extends, and gives quantum walks research a complete small example.
arxiv-2507-19867:
Anshul Chavda and five co-authors make made up in car chats full of the stops and self fixes that real drivers make. Sets that live now miss these breaks in speech. Bots trained on them deal poor with real speech. Their frame builds DiscoDrive, with 3,500 chats of more than one turn. The chats span seven car fields, with breaks in speech wove in as they are made.

Models trained on the made up data tied or beat models trained on a stock set took from folk. That held on test sets that fit the task. As a boost with just ten per cent of that stock set, the data gave more gains. Folk who scored the chats judged the made up chats a bit more plain to the ear and more sound as one than the set took from folk.
arxiv-2507-20767:
Alexander Metelkin, Sam Jacob, and Bernhard Vowinckel use learning models to predict forces on round particles in a flow, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fine-grained flow tests are exact but costly, while fast methods need good force rules. Their model reads the space around each particle, not the exact spots of its neighbors.

Local fill fractions on a fine grid serve as the input. Training data came from exact flow runs through random fixed particle arrays. The new model beat models fed with raw particle spots on force and twist accuracy. It also handles mixed particle sizes and shapes more readily.
arxiv-2507-20867:
Džuklevski wrote in twenty twenty-five a short note constructing a set of convex tiles with a rare tiling property. A tile set is called sigma-morphic if it tiles the plane in countably infinitely many truly different ways. Whether a single such tile exists remains an open problem. All known sigma-morphic sets used bumps and nicks on their tiles. Those features force the tiles to be non-convex, with dents in their outlines. Džuklevski instead builds the set entirely from convex tiles.

The construction cleverly splits tiles from a known set into convex pieces. The pieces behave just like the originals when tiling the plane. So the new set inherits the countably many distinct tilings. Convexity makes the result surprising to tiling specialists. It shows dents are not required for this kind of flexibility.
arxiv-2507-21267:
Wilbur Shirley, Carolyn Zhang, Wenjie Ji, and Michael Levin challenge a belief about quantum symmetries in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Folklore said a symmetry that cannot be gauged or made on-site must be anomalous. Anomalous symmetries block simple gapped ground states. The authors build lattice models in two dimensions whose symmetries resist both gauging and on-site form. Yet the models have calm, unique, gapped ground states, the mark of no anomaly.

They sort such symmetries by an index drawn from a cohomology group. The labels come from one-dimensional quantum cellular automata, rules that shuffle quantum data along a line. The counterexamples redraw the map of possible symmetries. Condensed matter theorists who classify quantum phases are the audience.
arxiv-2507-21367:
I-Hsiang Chen, Hua-En Chang, Wei-Ting Chen, Jenq-Neng Hwang, and Sy-Yen Kuo help segmentation models survive new environments in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Domain generalized semantic segmentation must label images from places the model never trained on, where appearance shifts can wreck performance. Recent methods align features back toward the source domain but neglect the latent priors describing how domains vary. Their framework, PDAF, adds probabilistic diffusion modeling to existing segmentation networks.

A latent domain prior captures domain shift and conditions the alignment of source and unseen target features. Three modules cooperate. An extractor predicts the prior by supervising domain shifts on paired real and pseudo-target images. A compensation module adjusts features to cancel shift. A diffusion-based estimator recovers the prior without paired samples. The design iteratively refines features, and extensive experiments across diverse urban scenes validated the gains in generalization.
arxiv-2507-21967:
Adina Feinstein, John Noonan, and Darryl Seligman report early images of 3I/ATLAS, the third known object from outside our solar system, in a 2025 paper. The object was found on July 1, 2025, and telescopes rushed to measure it. The team instead mined older data from TESS, a NASA planet-hunting satellite, which had watched the object's sky area from May 7 to June 2, 2025.

By stacking many faint images, they recovered the object and measured its brightness. Those values match the brightness reported after discovery. Set beside size limits from the Hubble telescope, the brightness hints the object was already active far from the Sun, near six times Earth's distance. The team also built a twenty-day light curve and found no clear sign of a spin period.
arxiv-2507-22267:
Owen Hoffman and four co-authors teach online safety by letting two chatbots act out a scam while learners coach the victim. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Language models make fraudulent chats cheap and convincing, so the public needs practice spotting them.

One model plays the scammer, another the target. Users watch the exchange unfold and feed advice to the target along the way. Learning research says feedback on hypothetical choices sticks better than lectures. Earlier work had shown models can simulate scams realistically enough to train on. The system turns that unsettling skill defensive. The authors presented the design at a conversational AI workshop on ethical agent personalities.
arxiv-2507-22967:
José Lima, Raydonal Ospina, Michelli Barros, and Antônio Macêdo build a diagnostic check for models of extreme wind gusts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Rare, violent gusts cause damage and deaths, and regression models help assess that risk. Yet a single unusual event can bend a model's results, so analysts need ways to spot such events.

The team applies a local influence method to a class of extreme-value regression models. By curving the model's fit surface, they measure how much each data point pulls the parameters. A trial run on simulated data worked as hoped. Applied to real gust records from Itajaí, Brazil, the method flagged one severe storm event, one that caused damage and deaths, as strongly influential. The tool can help scientists judge how much trust a fit deserves.
arxiv-2507-23467:
José Luís da Silva and Mohamed Erraoui wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on a way to split certain random quantities into parts. Some laws of chance have a neat property: a quantity can be written as a product of a shrunken copy of itself and an independent leftover part. The gamma law has this property, and so does the simpler exponential law inside it. That fact has been known since work in 1977.

What was missing was the exact law of the leftover part. The authors find it and write it out using a special function from advanced analysis. For the exponential law, the leftover follows a law known as the M-Wright law. For the wider gamma family, and for the size of a centered bell-curve variable, the leftover follows a related law with different settings. The result completes a picture left open for decades.
arxiv-2508-00967:
Massoud Pourmandi, a solo author, proposes a cooperative perception system for swarms of drones, in two thousand twenty-five. Drone teams that rebuild a scene in three dimensions face tight computing limits and low-bandwidth links. Sending all raw images to one place is too costly, and privacy matters as well.

The proposal has each drone extract scene meaning with a light detection model and update a local neural scene model. A shared diffusion model is trained in a federated way, so drones learn together without pooling raw data. Meaning-aware compression trims what must be sent. The author plans validation in simulation and on real drone testbeds, and frames the system as a step for multi-agent autonomy.
arxiv-2508-01967:
Okan Köksal computes how lowering a crystal's symmetry switches on a Rashba spin effect in a layered oxide sandwich. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Rashba effect splits electron spins by direction when symmetry breaks and spin-orbit coupling is strong. It is a prized knob for spintronic devices.

The stack pairs strontium hafnate with lanthanum aluminate on a buckled honeycomb frame. In the lopsided phase, a clear Rashba splitting appears near two key points, with a helical spin texture. In the symmetric phase, the bands stay spin-degenerate and the effect vanishes. A simplified model built from localized orbitals reproduces the full calculations. Phonon checks confirm the lopsided structure is stable. Measured strengths place the material among solid oxide Rashba candidates.
arxiv-2508-02367:
Federico Viola studies how the symmetry group of a regular tree can act on spaces with a special kind of form in two thousand twenty-five. These actions, called representations, must be continuous and cannot be split into smaller parts. Each one has an index that counts how far it sits from the standard unitary case.

Cases with index zero and index one were already fully known. Viola shows that no such actions exist for any index above one. That result closes the list: the known cases are all there are. Work of this kind maps the full range of ways a large group can act while keeping a fixed form.
arxiv-2508-02567:
Lloyd, Abanin, and Gopalakrishnan show that a recently proposed measure of quantum states also grows under plain classical dynamics. The measure, called Markov length, was meant to flag phase changes in quantum mixed states. The team quenched a low-temperature ordered state into the high-temperature phase.

Ordinary measurements show no growing length scale during that heating. The Markov length, though, grew exponentially with time. That means the heating state drifts ever further from a simple thermal form. The authors built a matrix-product method to compute the measure and tested it on the classical Ising model. Simple information arguments explain the growth in every case they tried.
arxiv-2508-03467:
Mehdi Dabirnia, Hamdi Joudeh, and Albert Guillén i Fàbregas write on source coding in this 2025 theory paper. Source coding squeezes data for sending or storage; here the decoder also holds side information about the source. The authors study how fast error chances fall as codes grow long. They work in the dual domain, where the math runs over a few settings.

They present a trimming method that yields two new error exponents for two styles of random codes. The setup even allows a decoder tuned to the wrong statistics. The better of the two exponents matches a known classic result. Number examples show how the two exponents differ in practice. With no side information, their exponent matches the best possible code's error rate.
arxiv-2508-05367:
Newton Mwai, Emil Carlsson, and Fredrik Johansson present a 2025 paper on bandit learning for personal choices. Bandit methods learn by trying actions and watching rewards. Learning from scratch is too slow when one person faces few choices, as in care or tailored offers. Latent bandit models speed things up if a hidden state model is known. In practice that model is hard to find, and few hidden states may not fit everyone.

People with the same hidden state may rank treatments alike yet rate symptoms on unlike scales. The team relaxes the model to need only the ranking of actions in each state. Rankings survive scale gaps that break raw reward models. Care and product teams get faster personal learning with weaker demands on the model. The paper reframes what a latent model must supply: order, not exact numbers.
arxiv-2508-06867:
Muhammad Awais Khan, Jérôme Droniou, Kim-Ngan Le, and Iuliu Sorin Pop studied solvers in twenty twenty-five for stochastic Stefan problems, which model phase changes like melting under random forcing. Simulating them requires repeatedly solving a nonlinear equation at every time step and for every random scenario, so solver efficiency dominates the cost.

The authors compare a standard Newton method against linearized solvers. The linearized versions reuse one coefficient matrix across all iterations, time steps, and noise realizations, so it can be factored once and for all. Convergence is slower per step, but the total cost can win. Sensitivity analysis with adaptive tolerances, in deterministic and stochastic settings, guides which solver to pick for a given scenario.
arxiv-2508-07067:
Honghao Lin and three co-authors design sampling tools for huge data streams in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A stream passes once, too fast to store, so algorithms must sketch it on the fly. One key task is drawing a random item with chance tied to its frequency raised to a power. The authors give samplers that use nearly the least possible memory. One version updates its sample at every moment of the stream.

They then tackle streams where items can be forgotten, resetting their counts. That twist breaks older estimators with heavy bias. Their near-unbiased estimators cover the full range of powers in this harder model. The results serve the theory of data streams and the systems built on it.
arxiv-2508-07367:
Bilal Ghermoul presents near-complete progress on a number puzzle from 1956 in a paper from 2025. The puzzle asks whether five divided by any whole number can be split into three unit fractions. Unit fractions have one on top, like one half or one third. For most remainder classes modulo five, direct formulas were already known.

The hard class leaves remainder one when divided by five. Ghermoul gives explicit formulas for most of that class, using polynomial expressions. One subcase, tied to multiples of two hundred fifty-two, rests on a stated conjecture. Computer checks confirm the pattern up to about ten billion. The author includes the checking code with the paper.
arxiv-2508-08967:
Kuan-Tang Huang and four co-authors study why speech recognition falters on new recording channels in a 2025 paper. Pre-trained recognizers do well until the microphone or channel changes, when accuracy can drop sharply. Past work blamed mismatch between training and test collections. This study argues the channel itself changes speech traits in ways that fundamentally hurt recognition.

Their fix normalizes the model's internal features toward those of a clean reference channel. That alignment sharply improved performance on unseen channels and even unseen languages. The authors present the method as a general defense against channel variation, a common real-world deployment problem for speech systems.
arxiv-2508-09767:
Shuhei Kato proposed UtterTune in twenty twenty-five, a light method for fixing pronunciation in multilingual text-to-speech systems. Modern speech systems built on language models sound natural, but they often lack an explicit step that maps letters to sounds, so pronunciation control is weak. UtterTune uses low-rank adaptation, a small trainable patch, to steer one language's pronunciation without disturbing the others.

The test case is Japanese, where both segment sounds and pitch accent can be adjusted at the phoneme level. Evaluations, both measured and human-rated, confirm the edits work. Naturalness and speaker similarity hold up in a zero-shot setting, where the voice was never trained on. The method offers precise control for one language at a time inside a shared multilingual system.
arxiv-2508-09967:
Xiang, Li, Zhang, and Li present a study from twenty twenty-five on sorting tissue slides with very few labeled cases. Whole slide images are huge, and expert labels are scarce in clinics. New image-and-text base models can sort slides with no labels, but they trail classic methods. Few-label methods help, yet their fixed sorter designs crack under data scarcity. The team's sorter picks and tunes its own design from a bank of sorter types. A guide part learns how to blend those options.

Their sorter beat prior methods on several few-label test sets. On one lung cancer set, its score rose by a clear margin over the best rival. Gains were largest when just one case per class was given. The authors say the tool suits clinics with very little labeled data.
arxiv-2508-10367:
Pablo Hernandez-Camara and colleagues borrow a classic test of human eyesight science to probe how vision-language models actually see. The contrast sensitivity function charts the faintest contrast a viewer can detect at each spatial scale, from broad stripes to fine ones. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team treats each model as a test subject. It views filtered noise patterns and answers structured prompts, and its yes-no answers are fitted into psychometric curves that yield thresholds, with no peeking inside the model. Several current models were put through the full procedure.

Some models matched the human curve in shape, others in overall scale, but none matched both. Answers also swung with small changes in prompt wording, a fragility the authors flag. The measured curves predicted how models coped with blurred and adversarial images, which the team offers as evidence the test is a useful diagnostic.
arxiv-2508-10667:
Xu and a team including Zhang, Fan, and Zhou teach image models to find a street address from a street photo in this twenty twenty-five paper. Big image-language models can name a town or land, but they often fail at the exact street spot inside a city. Street photos alone give only small local clues.

Inside, the method adds sky-view maps as wide clues and trains the model to match the two views. The team built question-and-answer sets from street photos in Pittsburgh and San Francisco to test it. Their model beat rival models by wide gaps on both sets. The work points to maps as a strong aid for fine place finding.
arxiv-2508-11767:
Kasmanoff and Zalkikar wrote in twenty twenty-five about using imitation learning to spot bad behavior in chat models. Imitation learning copies expert examples when no clear reward exists. Applied to conversation, it yields both a talking policy and a judge. The judge learns to tell expert chats from machine-made ones. The talking policy worked well enough on its task.

The judge's results were the more telling part for the authors. Its scores exposed limits in how dialog models behave. They argue the same trick can audit other data models built for chat tasks. Any flawed pattern the judge catches can guide fixes. The work reframes a training tool as a safety check. It needs no hand-built list of bad behaviors.
arxiv-2508-12467:
Umesh Shankar proves that the rows of a broad family of triangular number arrays always bend the right way. The family is defined by a super-recurrence, a powered version of the rule behind Stirling, Lah, and Eulerian numbers. Many recent generalizations of those classics obey the powered rule. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Shankar gives sufficient conditions for every row to be log-concave, meaning each entry squared dominates the product of its neighbors. The proof reads the array as weighted lattice paths and builds a weight-increasing injection.

The single condition covers the classical examples at once, a unified route to their log-concavity. It also confirms a conjecture about generalized Lah numbers. The paper closes by introducing a two-parameter generalization of the Eulerian numbers, shown palindromic, with remarks on deeper positivity properties.
arxiv-2508-13367:
A bundle of fibers under load fails fiber by fiber, and heat can trigger those failures over time, a slow process called creep failure. The four authors build an equal load sharing fiber bundle model in which transition state theory sets the rate of elementary failures. For uniform fiber thresholds they derive the lifetime distribution, its mean and variance, and their asymptotic limits, all matching simulations closely.

The scaling with fiber number matches earlier analytical results for a Gaussian noise breakdown model at low temperature. For random fiber strengths the lifetime distribution becomes a multi-dimensional integral with no closed form, yet simulations show similar large-bundle scaling. Failures come in avalanches set off by single thermal events, and the avalanche size distribution matches theory for quasistatic loading.
arxiv-2508-14067:
Sonakshi Chauhan and four co-authors present a 2025 study of where language models gather and move information, starting with punctuation. Earlier work flagged punctuation tokens as attention sinks and memory aids. Using interventions that remove or swap parts of the input, the team tested whether punctuation is necessary and sufficient for performance across layers in GPT-2, DeepSeek, and Gemma.

The answer split by model: in GPT-2 punctuation was both necessary and sufficient in many layers, less so in DeepSeek, and not at all in Gemma. The team then asked whether models freeze early summaries of sentence parts or stay sensitive to changes layer by layer. Conditional and universal statements turned out to be processed very differently. The findings warn against generalizing one model's internals to all.
arxiv-2508-14267:
Mihai-Silviu Lazorec and Marius Tărnăuceanu study counts of conjugacy classes of subgroups in two thousand twenty-five. Two ratios gauge how near a finite group sits to a Dedekind group. In Dedekind groups all subgroups are normal, a rare tidy trait. One ratio weighs subgroup classes against the full subgroup lattice.

For nilpotent groups, that ratio fills the whole unit interval densely. A high floor on the second ratio forces a group to be nilpotent. A still higher floor forces an Iwasawa group structure. A final result pins when p groups count as Dedekind. Structure facts ride along with each bound.
arxiv-2508-16067:
Teddy Koker, Mit Kotak, and Tess Smidt train a foundation model for materials science on a shoestring, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Such models predict how atoms arrange and vibrate, but training the leaders costs so much compute that most research groups cannot compete.

Their model, Nequix, is a compact potential that respects three-dimensional rotations and reflections by design. It simplifies a known architecture and adds modern training practices, including a specialized layer normalization and the Muon optimizer. The whole model has seven hundred thousand parameters. Training took one hundred hours on a single class of high-end GPU. On two public benchmarks it ranks third overall, at about a twentieth of the training cost of most rivals. It also runs about a hundred times faster than the top-ranked model. Weights and a reproducible codebase are released openly.
arxiv-2508-17367:
Régis Mélin, Asmaul Smitha Rashid, Romain Danneau, and Morteza Kayyalha revisit the adiabatic limit in large multi-terminal Josephson junctions. Their paper from twenty twenty-five responds to fresh experiments that probe new size and voltage ranges. As bias voltage grows in big devices, the electrochemical potential nears the level spacing of the core. New effects then enter the current.

A counting result anchors the model: correlated pairs from colliding Floquet-Kulik quartet levels form a fixed share set by the channel count. The team then treats the central metal as a continuum under slow-change rules. Andreev modes move through populations tuned by voltage and flux. Set voltage scales emerge for the wobble of critical current. Those scales touch quartet, topology, and Floquet readings alike. Recent Harvard and Penn State tests inspired the frame.
arxiv-2508-17467:
Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata and seven co-authors benchmark mixture-of-experts models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such models reach huge parameter counts while staying efficient, by routing each input to a few expert subnetworks. At inference time, they face load imbalance across experts and extra routing cost.

Their bench study varies batch size, sequence length, and key model settings across several model families. They test optimization tricks on high-end Nvidia GPUs, including pruning, fused operations, speculative decoding, and quantization. Parallel strategies were also compared. Results show how performance shifts across configurations. The authors aim to guide efficient deployment of these models in practice.
arxiv-2508-17967:
Mona Bhukta and co-authors film tiny magnetic whirlpools as they bump into each other in real time, in work from twenty twenty-five. The whirlpools, called skyrmions, sit in a material where spins cancel out. How they scatter shapes plans for fast, small magnetic devices.

The team used X-ray movies to watch a skyrmion grid driven by current pulses. At low drive, free skyrmions hit pinned ones and bounced back over a few billionths of a second. At higher drive, the whole grid moved as one clean sheet. Math fits gave the force range between skyrmions, which matched computer models. The grid ran well at high speed over billions of cycles. Control held even in the messy flow mode.
arxiv-2508-18367:
Minchev and co-authors warn that wandering stars distort galaxy histories in a 2025 paper. Astronomers rebuild a disk galaxy's star formation history from where stars sit today, region by region. That habit assumes stars stayed near their birth radius. In real disks, stars migrate inward and outward over billions of years.

Using zoom-in simulations of galaxy formation, the team measured the bias this creates. In inner disks, early star formation is understated by a quarter to a half, while late formation is overstated. In outer disks, mid-age stars are overstated by up to two or threefold, since many were born inside and drifted out. History peaks flatten and spread, and inside-out growth looks slower than it was. The authors say surveys of nearby galaxies must correct for this drift, using disk mass, bars, and motion as clues.
arxiv-2508-19267:
Sai Teja Reddy Adapala and Yashwanth Reddy Alugubelly present a 2025 paper on a security frame for self running AI agents. As agents act on their own and talk to each other, new risks appear. Old security tools were not built for hijacked control flow or failures that cascade across agents.

Their frame, called Aegis, stacks three parts. The first gives each agent an ID that cannot be faked, based on a web standard. The second guards messages with math that should resist future quantum computers. The third checks that agents follow policy, using proofs that hide private data. The authors test the frame against a standard list of threat types.
arxiv-2508-20367:
Luke Bhan, Miroslav Krstic, and Yuanyuan Shi present a 2025 control study on systems whose actuators respond only after a delay of unknown length. Predictor feedback cancels such delays by forecasting the system's future state, but the forecast has no exact formula for nonlinear systems. The authors replace the forecast with a neural operator, a learned map trained once offline and then run fast online. They build the theory on the delay's description as a transport equation.

A Lyapunov-style proof shows the closed loop settles near the target, with the slack set by the learning error and the delay bounds. Tests on a biological switch system ran about fifteen times faster than standard numerical methods. The work gives learned predictors a firm stability footing for real control tasks.
arxiv-2508-20967:
Ernesto Birgin, Geovani Grapiglia, and Diaulas Marcondes design in 2025 faster ways to minimize bumpy functions whose variables must stay within bounds. Such problems appear across engineering and data work. Their methods combine active-set logic, which fixes variables sitting at their limits, with Newton steps solved cheaply by an iterative solver.

Two escape routes from flat faces are studied: a spectral gradient method and a cube-regularized Newton variant. The authors prove how many function calls each needs to reach a near-stationary point, with the second scaling better in accuracy. Computer tests against existing methods favor their approach, and the cheap solver beat the standard one for Newton directions.
arxiv-2508-21567:
Tan Van Vu, Ryotaro Honma, and Keiji Saito derive, in a 2025 preprint, universal limits on how precise any observable can be in an open quantum system. Such systems leak into their surroundings at any coupling strength. Known uncertainty relations tie precision to thermodynamic cost, but mostly for memoryless, Markovian settings. Memory changes the game, and bounds there were missing. The authors measure each process against its time-reversed twin. The gap between forward and backward paths becomes an asymmetry term in the bound.

For currents that flip sign under time reversal, precision is capped by entropy production plus that asymmetry. For general observables, a floor on relative fluctuation is set by an activity term describing environmental change. The framework covers arbitrary coupling and two-point measurement schemes. The authors present it as the broad map of precision limits that the Markovian results only sketched.
arxiv-2509-00167:
W. F. Lamberti, S. R. Lawrence, D. White, S. Kim, and S. Abdullah run a pilot study in 2025 on generative AI and critical thinking in college classes. Such tools spread fast in education, yet their role in growing critical thought is little studied. Past work casts the tools as tutors or as assignment helpers, not as objects of critique.

Their classes in computational and data science ask students to analyze, critique, and revise AI-generated solutions. The tasks stress that AI output is often flawed in context or plain wrong. Early findings show how well students apply structured critical thinking to those outputs. The pilot lays groundwork for larger studies in future terms on teaching with AI present.
arxiv-2509-00267:
Axel Gross, Samuel Cupp, and Matthew R. Mumpower calculate the particle signals from decaying r-process nuclei in 2025. The r-process, rapid neutron capture, forges heavy elements in extreme cosmic events. Its nuclei decay by beta decay, shedding electrons, gamma rays, neutrinos, and neutrons as they settle.

The team computes emission spectra from first principles, using detailed nuclear structure and decay data for each particle kind. A reaction network simulation then tracks how those spectra evolve over time. The distributions shift strongly with time and are non-thermal, with substantial average energies. Such signals could probe heavy element formation directly, across many messenger types at once.
arxiv-2509-01467:
A tool called NMR reads the states of atomic nuclei. Reading those spins with light could push fine sensing toward single molecules. Evgenij Vasilenko, with eight co-authors, reports optical readout of nuclear spins in a europium-based crystal. Very narrow optical lines let the team prepare and detect the spin states with light.

Radio waves drove two nuclear resonances. Those lines were narrow and clearly linked to the optical line in use. The team ran standard spin tools: Rabi oscillations, spin echo, and decoupling pulses. These steer the spins and shield them from noise. Nuclear coherence lasted up to two milliseconds. The results mark a step toward light-based NMR in precisely built molecular systems for quantum technology.
arxiv-2509-01667:
Adam G Riess leads eleven authors who test whether crowded star fields bias a key cosmic distance measure. Their study uses new James Webb Space Telescope views of Cepheids, which are stars that pulse in brightness on a steady rhythm. The team targets NGC 3447, a supernova host galaxy whose young companion has almost no old stars behind the Cepheids.

Inside, the authors compare telescope data under crowded, clear, and nearly empty background conditions. They find no shift between the parts of the system and much tighter scatter where the background is empty. Combined with other hosts, their value for the Hubble constant stays well above the early universe prediction. The result supports the view that crowding does not explain the gap.
arxiv-2509-02167:
Jing Wang leads four co-authors with AudioRWKV, an efficient bidirectional architecture for audio pattern recognition. Transformer audio models scale poorly with sequence length due to quadratic cost. State space rivals can turn unstable when scaled up. Their design inherits a stable recurrent form from a recent RWKV generation with linear cost.

A two dimensional depthwise convolution replaces the one dimensional token shift to catch local time frequency patterns. The core kernel becomes bidirectional, letting each point see global context while keeping linear complexity. The smallest variant matches a much larger rival model on performance. Long audio over five minutes processes many times faster than the transformer baseline. Throughput stays more stable than competing designs in tests.
arxiv-2509-02867:
Christian A. Schröder, Reinhard Kienberger, and Stephen R. Leone introduced a 2025 physics paper about software for planning a special kind of light source. The source uses high-harmonic generation, where a strong laser pulse makes a gas emit much higher energy light. Such beams support very fast spectroscopy, the study of matter through its light.

Their program is free for anyone to use and change. It models both the tiny single-atom response and the way light builds up across a whole gas target. That breadth lets it fit many setups, from extreme ultraviolet light to soft X-rays. The team checked its output against four common laboratory arrangements. Labs can use it to design and improve these demanding light sources.
arxiv-2509-03067:
Lukas Freter and 5 co-authors developed a 2025 theory of dynamical superradiance in organic materials. Superradiance happens when many excited emitters release energy together into one light mode, faster and brighter than they would alone. In organic matter, electronic states constantly interact with molecular vibrations, which complicates that shared release.

The team studied two models: vibrations as a surrounding bath that scrambles phase, and vibrations built directly into the system. Using symmetry, they solved one model exactly for well over a hundred emitters. That check let them test faster approximations for truly large groups. Vibrational coupling did more than scramble phase; under some tunings it even strengthened the burst. A lopsided rise time across tunings could let experiments spot that help.
arxiv-2509-03167:
Jorge Sanchez Almeida, Angel R. Plastino, and Ignacio Trujillo explored in 2025 how dwarf galaxies can grow broad stellar cores. Many dark matter dominated dwarfs show stars spread in a flat central core rather than a sharp peak. Some dark matter theories say the invisible halo itself slowly softens from a peaked cusp into a core.

As the halo expands, its gravity weakens and the stars it holds drift outward. The authors model stars on purely sideways, purely radial, and mixed orbits under that slow change, using adiabatic invariants, quantities that stay fixed under gentle drift. Cores formed easily in many setups, though their sizes depended on starting conditions. Circular-orbit systems made cores for a stated range of starting slopes. Radial systems made none, which gives observers a useful discriminant.
arxiv-2509-03467:
Soukeina Elhassen and four co-authors wrote a 2025 research paper on recognising continuous Saudi Sign Language from video. Sign language is the main communication route for many deaf people in Saudi Arabia, yet most computer systems focus on other sign languages or on single signs. Their work targets full signed sentences instead.

The team introduces KAU-CSSL, a dataset for continuous Saudi signing built around complete sentences, described as the first of its kind. Their model first extracts picture features with a pretrained ResNet-18 network, then tracks timing with a transformer and a bidirectional memory network. Accuracy reaches high levels when the same signers appear in training, and drops when new signers are tested. The dataset gives later researchers a shared base to improve on.
arxiv-2509-03567:
A 2025 research paper by Alexandre Journeaux and seven co-authors asks how short-range correlations build up in an ultracold Bose gas. Their gas sits near a Fano-Feshbach resonance, a tuning point where atoms interact especially strongly. Watching pair correlations form in real time tests theories of quantum gases.

Using fast optical control, the team jumps the energy of a molecular channel onto resonance in under a microsecond. They then track the two-body contact, a measure of close pair encounters, through losses caused by photodissociation, where light breaks molecules apart. Repeated pulses sharpen sensitivity to early losses from atom pairs. Atom pairs and molecular states stay in long-lived coherence with each other. A two-channel theory with zero-range interactions reproduces the behaviour, explaining how narrow the resonance is and how long the closed channel lives.
arxiv-2509-03667:
A 2025 research paper by Vivek Vasan and four co-authors asks whether entanglement purification still works when classical communication takes real time. Quantum networks distribute entangled particle pairs to distant nodes, but stored pairs lose quality through decoherence, the fading of quantum behaviour. Purification trades several weak pairs for fewer strong ones, yet its coordination messages travel over ordinary networks and impose idle waiting.

Two standard protocols, BBPSSW and DEJMPS, are evaluated under realistic internet protocol delays in city-scale networks. Quantum dynamics are modelled microscopically with a Lindblad treatment, and memory parameters come from current testbeds. Break-even curves map where purification succeeds or fails across network and memory conditions. The authors also count how many pairs a multi-round protocol consumes overall. Resulting memory quality targets, latency budgets, and overhead estimates guide deployment on present and near-future networks.
arxiv-2509-03767:
In a 2025 research paper, part of the ODYSSEUS survey, Caeley V. Pittman and six co-authors examine how young T Tauri stars exchange spin with their surrounding disks. Classical T Tauri stars are young stars fed by gas disks, varying strongly from minutes to decades. Much theory assumes stable spin states, an assumption this work tests directly.

For 47 stars from a space telescope sample, the team measures spin periods and corotation radii. Each corotation radius, where disk material orbits at the star's spin rate, is compared with where the star's magnetic field truncates the disk. Most stars fall in the spin-up regime, hinting at efficient angular momentum loss. Outflows and episodic accretion both appear, consistent with accretion-powered winds. The truncation point varies over days, pushing some stars across stability boundaries. Inclined systems near equal radii show dipper light curves, though dippers occur at all ratios.
arxiv-2509-03967:
A 2025 mathematics paper from Aida Abiad and one co-author examines the Zq-forcing number of graphs. Zero forcing is a colouring game modelling how influence spreads through a network. A player seeds a few blue vertices, and colour spreads by fixed rules until, ideally, the whole graph turns blue. The goal: the smallest seed set that succeeds.

The q-analogue adds an oracle that pushes back, forcing the player toward larger seed sets during play. The structure of several graph families drives the paper's two kinds of results. A SAT-based algorithm computes the exact Zq value and yields optimal strategies for both player and oracle, by encoding the game for a satisfiability solver. For cactus graphs, where cycles share at most one vertex, a polynomial-time algorithm handles the q equals one case. Exact values are proved for further classes, including block graphs, extending earlier tree results.
arxiv-2509-04167:
Peng Zhao and one co-author, Xiaoning Wu, prove that solutions exist for a coupled gravity-and-matter system in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Einstein-Dirac system joins Einstein's gravity equations with Dirac fields, which describe particles with spin, such as electrons. Their setup starts from data given on two crossing sheets of light-like surface, a harder starting style called a characteristic problem. No symmetry is assumed about the solution.

Following a strategy due to Luk, the authors promote certain spinor derivatives to independent variables. That move removes curvature terms from the energy estimates, the bookkeeping that keeps solutions controlled. Smooth solutions then exist across a rectangle-shaped region ahead of the starting sheets. The proof closes at the best possible derivative level.
arxiv-2509-04267:
Masahico Saito and one co-author, Emanuele Zappala, build knot invariants from a cohomology theory for Yang-Baxter operators in a 2025 mathematics paper. Knots and their invariants, numbers that identify knot types, connect deeply with quantum physics through these operators. Cocycles, special bookkeeping functions inside cohomology, earlier produced invariants for a related structure called quandles. The authors reinterpret those building blocks as deformations, gradual bendings, of the operators themselves.

Two construction routes are developed, one through traces and one through pairings between algebraic pieces. The older quandle invariant fits inside the new frame, and the quantum version sometimes separates knots the older one cannot. Even the famous Jones and Alexander polynomials arise as special cases.
arxiv-2509-04567:
Archishman Khasnovis and three co-authors count atomic hydrogen in Green Pea galaxies to explain why some leak ionizing light in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Green Peas are small, furiously star-forming galaxies thought to resemble the universe's early reionizers. The Green Bank Telescope searched thirty of them for the 21-centimeter hydrogen line, finding seven, and literature data widened the sample to sixty. A spectral ratio called O32 flags likely leakers of Lyman continuum light, the radiation that reionized the cosmos.

Galaxies with low O32 were detected in hydrogen over half the time; strong leakers almost never were. High-leaker systems hold less hydrogen, with lower gas fractions and faster depletion times. Their starbursts likely consumed the gas, opening escape routes for ionizing light.
arxiv-2509-04667:
Real-time speech can hide who is speaking without badly garbling what is said. Waris Quamer and one co-author present DarkStream, a streaming speech synthesis model for speaker anonymisation, in a 2025 paper. The system must work under strict latency limits in live communication.

DarkStream encodes content with a causal waveform encoder and transformer layers for context, aided by a short lookahead buffer. It generates waveforms directly with a neural vocoder, skipping slower intermediate steps. A fake speaker embedding, produced by a generative model, replaces the real voice identity. Tests show near-chance speaker verification while keeping words largely intelligible.
arxiv-2509-04967:
Fuzzing a program without its source code often misses bugs hidden in data flow. Kai Feng, lead author with two co-authors, present FuzzRDUCC in a 2025 software security paper. Traditional grey-box fuzzers follow control flow edge coverage, which can overlook how data propagates through a binary.

Their framework uses symbolic execution to reconstruct definition-use chains directly from executables. A heuristic algorithm selects relevant chains without excessive computational cost. Evaluated on a standard utilities benchmark, the fuzzer finds unique crashes that leading fuzzers miss in their tests. The authors present dataflow guidance as a feasible next step for vulnerability discovery.
arxiv-2509-05367:
Safety training that sorts requests into safe or unsafe breaks down on moral dilemmas, Shei Pern Chua and five co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 paper on language model security. Dilemmas force trade-offs, and that reasoning skill itself becomes an attack surface.

Their red-team method, TRIAL, hides harmful requests inside ethical framing over several turns and succeeds against most models tested. In response they propose ERR, a defence that separates answers enabling harm from answers that merely explain an ethical view. It uses a layered, harm-gated tuning design. The defence held up against reasoning-based attacks while keeping the model useful, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-05967:
Teaching a model three-dimensional medical imaging without labels, in a way doctors can follow, is the aim of a 2025 paper by Yiqin Zhang and two co-authors. Self-supervised learning eases the scarcity of labeled medical data, but most designs come from flat image work and hide what the model learns about space. Their method uses tasks a human can observe directly.

Three sub-tasks train the model on spatial relationships inside scans, at several levels of detail, so learning stays stable and interpretable. Results match current methods while making the learning process visible. The authors argue that the extra dimension of medical scans, handled openly, can supply the semantic depth self-supervision usually lacks.
arxiv-2509-06167:
City data fused into one latent picture reveal more than each source alone, test Ximena Pocco and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Urban analytics mixes static data, like land use, with dynamic data, like movement, at street-level detail, and the mix is granular and multimodal. Their visual analytics framework uses autoencoders to fuse the sources and asks whether the fused representation finds deeper patterns.

The analysis says yes, mostly: combined latent representations produce more structured patterns than separate ones, though separate views still win in particular cases. The framework lets analysts explore those latent spaces directly. The authors frame the result as guidance for when fusion is worth its complexity in city-scale data work.
arxiv-2509-06467:
Can a vision model trained only on everyday photos handle medical scans? Che Liu and twenty-three co-authors test that idea in a 2025 benchmark report on DINOv3, a large self-supervised image model. The team asks whether it can serve directly as a shared encoder for medical tasks, with no special medical training.

They run DINOv3 on two- and three-dimensional classification, segmentation, meaning outlining regions in an image, and registration, meaning aligning images, across many scan types. Sizes and resolutions vary to check scaling. The model sets a strong baseline and even beats some medical models on several tasks. Weak spots remain in whole-slide images, electron microscopy, and PET scans, and bigger versions do not always help. Even so, its features look like a solid starting point for medical tools.
arxiv-2509-06567:
When does an energy functional lose its Lavrentiev gap? Michał Borowski answers more broadly in a solo 2025 analysis paper. The gap is a mismatch between the lowest energy found among smooth functions and among rougher ones. Double phase functionals mix two growth rates, weighted by a function that varies across the domain.

Borowski shows that the smoother that weight is, the wider the range of exponents with no gap. When the weight is infinitely smooth, no extra restriction on the exponents is needed at all. For weights with a finite number of smooth derivatives plus a Hölder condition, he establishes the optimal exponent range, extending earlier results that covered only Hölder weights. The pattern is clean: each gain in smoothness buys a matching gain in allowed exponents, closing a question about how regularity controls this gap.
arxiv-2509-07067:
Sara Rastello, Giuliano Iorio, Mark Gieles, and Long Wang model micro-tidal disruption events in young star clusters in a 2025 paper. In a dense young cluster, stars pass close to stellar-mass black holes again and again. A star that strays inside the black hole's tidal radius gets torn apart.

The team ran a suite of direct N-body simulations with a specialised code, adding new recipes for handling the disruptions themselves. Their cluster models were built to look real, with primordial binaries drawn from the Milky Way population as observed. The runs include how stars and binaries change over time, kicks from supernovae, and stellar winds, plus the pull of the Galactic tidal field. They find three routes that make the events: lone star and black hole meetings, contacts helped along by binaries, and messier systems with several stars at once.
arxiv-2509-07767:
Nai-Bo Zhang and 4 co-authors show in 2025 how weighing and sizing one heavy neutron star can limit the dark matter inside it. Some theories let dark matter build up inside neutron stars. That changes their mass-radius relation. Paired mass and radius measurements are stronger than either one alone. The pulsar PSR J0740+6620 gives exactly such a paired measurement, for a massive star.

The dark matter model is fermionic and interacts only through gravity. The nuclear equation of state is well constrained. In that setup, the joint measurement cuts the uncertainty on one quantity by more than half. That quantity is the dark matter central energy density. Other dark matter parameters stay unconstrained. The dark matter fraction is bounded below two percent by maximum mass alone. With the joint measurement, the bound falls below about 0.3 percent. The result supports only a small dark matter admixture in such stars.
arxiv-2509-07967:
Gravity can bend light from a distant galaxy into several images, and the same trick can delay a gravitational wave signal. Sourabh Magare, Anupreeta More, and Shasvath J. Kapadia explore the warning time that creates, in a 2025 research paper. If the first signal from a neutron star merger arrives, lensing may guarantee a repeat performance hours or days later. Telescopes could then watch the merger live.

The team tests whether optical images of the lensed host galaxy can predict that delay. They built mock lenses matching Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based Hyper Suprime-Cam quality. For double images, both telescopes gave similar uncertainty. Four-image systems predicted delays accurately with Hubble, less so from the ground. A real lens case showed day-scale differences between the two. The authors argue high-resolution imaging is essential for this early-warning scheme.
arxiv-2509-08167:
Gene regulatory networks route information most efficiently when their parts decay at matched rates, argue Miguel Ángel García-Ariza and 3 co-authors in a 2025 paper on biological information flow. Cell state changes are driven by networks where deterministic chemistry mixes with molecular noise. To study information transfer, the authors recast a Boolean network model as motion through a space of Gaussian distributions.

That space carries the Fisher information metric, a natural ruler for statistical models. In the new picture, optimal information transfer trajectories become gradient flows of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between distributions. Efficiency demands isotropic decay rates, equal in all directions across nodes. Geometric reframing of this kind can reveal design principles that simulations of single networks would never state plainly.
arxiv-2509-08367:
Jochen Harant and Ingo Schiermeyer bound the independence number of subcubic graphs from below in a 2025 combinatorics paper. An independent set is a group of vertices with no edges among them, and its maximum size is a central graph parameter. Subcubic graphs, where every vertex has at most three neighbours, appear in network design and scheduling.

Their bounds weight vertices by degree: counts of degree-one, degree-two, and degree-three vertices each contribute with their own coefficient, minus a constant. Families of graphs are exhibited showing the bounds are sharp, unimprovable in general. Degree-aware bounds beat one-size formulas because leaves and branching vertices play very different roles in how large an independent set can grow.
arxiv-2509-08567:
Chains of self-driven particles can form a living interface that crawls, bends, and flickers with fluctuations. Arvin Subramaniam, Tirthankar Banerjee, and Rajesh Singh study such an interface in a 2025 research paper. The particles interact through chemistry, and their motion couples spin with drift. The authors map every steady shape the interface can take across its parameter range.

One regime stands out: the interface settles into a curved, C-shaped form and propels itself nonstop. Its height flickers follow a classic scaling family but with wholly new exponents, including super-ballistic growth. Meanwhile, the particles' alignment flickers grow smoother as the system gets bigger, defying intuition. Together, the results point to a new non-equilibrium class. Such classes help physicists predict how whole families of active materials behave from a few shared rules.
arxiv-2509-08667:
Amirali Rayegan and 1 co-author introduce EZR, a framework for explainable optimization in software engineering, in a 2025 paper. Engineers face huge configuration spaces, and labeling examples is costly and error prone. EZR aims to use fewer but better labels.

Active sampling guided by Naive Bayes picks informative examples first. The learned logic is then distilled into short decision trees that explain global and local choices. Across sixty real datasets, EZR reaches over ninety percent of the best known result in most cases. Its explanations beat standard tools on clarity. Code and materials are shared for checking and reuse.
arxiv-2509-08867:
Every large language model answer burns electricity, and developers rarely know how much their choices matter. K. Pronk and Q. Zhao introduce the LLM Efficiency Benchmark in a 2025 research paper. Earlier energy studies often used setups unlike real production serving. Their benchmark runs on vLLM, a widely used, production-ready serving system.

The benchmark varies model size, architecture, and the number of simultaneous requests. It then measures how each factor changes energy efficiency during inference. The point is realism: numbers gathered under production-like conditions can guide real decisions. Developers choosing between models, or tuning request batching, get evidence instead of folklore. The authors hope such benchmarks build climate awareness into everyday AI engineering, where small efficiency choices multiply across millions of daily queries.
arxiv-2509-09067:
Recognizing that someone is using an ATM, not just standing near it, defeats skeleton-only action recognition. Hesham M. Shehata and Mohammad Abdolrahmani add scene awareness in a 2025 research paper. Graph networks reading body poses perform well on general actions. They fail on human-object interactions because the object and its place in the scene are missing from the input.

The authors feed fixed object information from the environment into the model. A multi-task learning setup trains recognition jointly with interaction-area information. They collected real data in public spaces, covering interactions with fixed machines and plain walking or standing. Accuracy rose well above the skeleton-only baseline, reaching near-perfect scores on their dataset. Surveillance, assistive monitoring, and smart buildings all need machines that understand not just how people move, but what they are engaging with.
arxiv-2509-09367:
Li-Jun Zhou and 5 co-authors work toward precise gauge fixing for lattice QCD in a 2025 paper. Lattice QCD solves quantum chromodynamics from first principles on a spacetime grid. Work on off-shell partons has mostly stayed in the Landau gauge, since precise fixing in other gauges is hard.

A universal power law link between parton matrix elements and gauge fixing precision motivates an empirical extrapolation method. Proper definitions of bare coupling and effective gauge parameter support the procedure. The method reproduces gauge dependent renormalization constants for quark operators at a fraction of a percent level. That accuracy holds up to a gauge parameter near one. Wider parton studies may follow.
arxiv-2509-09867:
