The authors use Dyson maps, mathematical transformations named after Freeman Dyson, to restore monotonic entropy growth in such processes. Restoring that steady growth lets researchers apply the standard tools of statistical physics again. The method is general and computationally tractable, meaning it stays practical to run. It applies to a broad class of Markovian systems, those whose future depends only on their present state. The authors present it as a fix for both interpretation problems and inference techniques that detailed balance normally supports.
arxiv-2510-09667:
Huaihai Lyu and six co-authors introduce OmniSAT in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to compress robot actions into short token sequences. Vision-language-action models command robots from images and instructions. Autoregressive versions train efficiently, but action chunks form long, high-dimensional sequences that slow them down, and earlier compression methods either reconstructed actions poorly or barely shortened anything.

The Omni Swift Action Tokenizer first normalises value ranges and time horizons, encoding motion with B-splines, smooth curve pieces. It then applies multi-stage residual quantisation separately to position, rotation, and gripper signals, yielding compact tokens with coarse-to-fine detail. Pretrained on the large Droid robot dataset, the tokenisation shortened training sequences nearly sevenfold and lowered the target entropy. The authors add a cross-embodiment strategy that trains jointly on robot and human demonstrations inside the shared token space, letting skills transfer between different bodies.
arxiv-2510-09767:
Yifan Lu and eight co-authors, among them Imran Razzak, present HeSRN in a 2025 arXiv paper, a network for learning from heterogeneous graphs. Real graphs mix node types, authors and papers, say, with different meanings per type. Graph transformers capture long-range links through self-attention, but they cost quadratically and blur the distinct semantics of each type, limiting scale and wider use.

HeSRN disentangles type semantics with a slot-aware encoder, projecting features into independent slots per type. A retention-based encoder then replaces self-attention, modelling dependencies in linear time. On four real-world mixed-type graph datasets, HeSRN beat leading graph networks and transformer baselines on node labelling each time.
arxiv-2510-09867:
Chen and co-authors tackle few-shot adaptation of vision-language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Models such as CLIP link images and text after training on huge numbers of image-text pairs, and they can classify new tasks with only a few examples. A class is often described by an ensemble, or bundle, of context prompts.

The authors note that the usual approach, averaging the text features of all prompts, often gives weak results. Their cluster-aware method groups prompts first and learns the ensemble with those groups in mind. This keeps distinct prompt styles from blurring into one flat average. The aim is stronger accuracy when only a handful of labeled examples are available for each new task.
arxiv-2510-09967:
Kai E. Yang and a large team present SPIn4D in this 2025 arXiv paper on solar physics. Inferring the 3D structure of the Sun's atmosphere from observations is central to understanding the magnetic fields and currents that drive solar activity. This paper is the second in a series on their deep learning method.

SPIn4D uses physics-informed machine learning to rebuild the 3D solar photosphere, the Sun's visible surface layer, from spectropolarimetric data, measurements of light and its polarization. Physics-informed means the network is guided by the equations the solar gas must obey, not by data alone. The reconstruction aims to recover magnetic structure that telescopes cannot image directly. Better 3D maps would sharpen forecasts of flares and storms.
arxiv-2510-10067:
Liu and co-authors study beamforming in interferometer arrays with cross-couplings in this 2025 arXiv paper in radio astronomy. An interferometer synthesizes a sky image from visibilities, the cross-correlations of voltages received by pairs of antennas. Beamforming steers the array's sensitivity toward a chosen direction.

Cross-couplings, unwanted signal leakage between array elements, corrupt those visibilities. The authors analyze how such coupling distorts beamforming and how to account for it. Precise beams matter for telescopes that map faint cosmic signals, where leakage can masquerade as sky structure. Their treatment gives array designers a clearer model of a real-world imperfection that ideal analyses usually ignore.
arxiv-2510-10167:
Du and Zhaofang Bai characterize preparable entangled states in Gaussian quantum networks in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum information. Large quantum networks overcome the limits of single entangled systems for transmission and storage. Deterministic preparation of entanglement is a key step toward working networks.

No efficient test exists to check whether a given multipartite entangled state can be prepared by a multisource Gaussian network. The authors give features that such preparable states must have, narrowing the question. Gaussian states and operations are the workhorse formalism for light-based quantum systems, so the criteria apply where experiments are most advanced. Their results guide network designers toward states that sources can actually produce.
arxiv-2510-10367:
De Saha introduces a coarse Lusternik-Schnirelmann category for groups in this 2025 arXiv paper in geometric group theory. The classical category counts how many simple pieces are needed to cover a space, a basic complexity measure in topology. A coarse version should measure large-scale complexity, ignoring small detail.

De Saha defines this invariant in the coarse homotopy category for metric spaces and groups. He proves it does not change under coarse homotopy, so it is a genuine large-scale invariant. He also proves a lower bound linking it to an earlier invariant for geometrically finite groups. Such invariants help distinguish groups whose large-scale shapes look alike at first glance.
arxiv-2510-10767:
Jiayuan Sheng and four co-authors study a mismatch in how diffusion models are fine tuned versus used, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Fine tuning with human feedback uses stochastic samplers, which wander randomly and encourage exploration. Deployment usually switches to deterministic samplers for efficiency and stability. This discrepancy creates a reward gap: the model is graded under different sampling than it will face. The team characterizes that gap theoretically.

They prove non-vacuous bounds on the gap for general diffusion models, with sharper convergence rates for two standard Gaussian families. Their method uses a generalized implicit sampling framework that allows any level of stochasticity while preserving the data distribution. In large scale experiments on text to image models, reward gaps consistently narrowed over training. Training with higher stochasticity samplers also improved the quality of deterministic sampling at deployment.
arxiv-2510-10867:
Chris Grossack writes an invitation to one of the deeper corners of modern geometry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Fukaya categories are rich invariants of symplectic manifolds, spaces that underlie classical mechanics. They are notoriously hard to compute explicitly. For surfaces, though, the theory becomes simple and combinatorial, and experts understand it well. Grossack's expository paper aims to bring newcomers into that computable world.

The paper gives an introduction built around many worked examples. Rather than proving new theorems, it assembles the surface case in one place: the objects, the morphisms between them, and the algebraic structures that arise from curves on surfaces. The stated hope is that readers finish equipped to compute Fukaya categories of surfaces independently. Expository work like this matters where knowledge is folklore among experts but scattered across hard sources. It lowers the entry cost for students and newcomers from neighboring fields.
arxiv-2510-10967:
Tanuj Khattar and seven co-authors sharpen a candidate for provable quantum advantage, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Decoded quantum interferometry turns certain optimization problems into decoding tasks. Applied to the optimal polynomial intersection problem, whose dual code is Reed-Solomon, the method needs only near linearly many quantum gates where classical solving takes exponential work. That makes it the first known candidate for verifiable quantum advantage with the best possible speedup. The catch is engineering the reversible Reed-Solomon decoder the method requires.

The team introduces new quantum circuits for the extended Euclidean algorithm, the decoder's bottleneck. A new way of accessing Bézout coefficients implicitly, plus optimized in place layouts, cuts the space to the theoretical minimum while lowering gate counts. Their resource estimates say classically intractable instances, needing over ten to the twenty third classical trials, fall to about 5.72 million Toffoli gates: fewer than breaking RSA-2048 would take.
arxiv-2510-11067:
Backward stochastic differential equations run a random process backward from a known end value, and mean-field versions also depend on the statistical distribution of the solution itself. Weimin Jiang, Juan Li, and Yan Shen study such equations with merely integrable end values in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. They look for L1 solutions that stay integrable, under weak assumptions in one and several dimensions.

In the one-dimensional case, a test function method and a localization procedure give existence when the generator grows slowly enough. Adding monotonicity and continuity conditions yields a comparison theorem, which in turn implies that the solution is unique. For the multi-dimensional case, the authors prove existence and uniqueness under a one-sided Osgood condition with general growth and Lipschitz conditions. They finally treat the general case where the generator depends on the joint distribution of the whole solution.
arxiv-2510-11267:
Many classical symmetry groups of physics, from rotations to symplectic groups, can be built from algebras equipped with an involution, a generalized transpose. Eugen Rogozinnikov extends that construction in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Earlier work used the unit group of the algebra; Rogozinnikov instead builds the symplectic group from any Lie subgroup of the algebra, which widens the construction's reach.

The generalized group recovers several classical Lie groups as special cases and, gives new realizations of spin groups using subgroups of the Clifford algebra, a case the earlier framework missed. He constructs spaces on which the group acts, generalizing the projective line through spaces of isotropic lines. He also introduces invariants for these spaces, including a generalized cross-ratio of positive quadruples of lines. When the subgroup's Lie algebra is Hermitian, he defines the Riemannian symmetric space and gives several models for it.
arxiv-2510-11567:
Training a street-scene segmentation model needs labeled images, and synthetic scenes provide labels for free, except that rendered cities never look real. Denis Zavadski and co-authors close that realism gap without expensive 3D modeling in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Their framework adapts an off-the-shelf diffusion model to a target domain, such as Cityscapes, using imperfect pseudo-labels as supervision.

Once adapted, the model generates high-fidelity, target-aligned images from the semantic maps of any synthetic dataset. The pipeline filters suboptimal generations, repairs misalignments between images and their labels, and standardizes semantics across datasets. It turns weak synthetic data into competitive training sets for real domains. Across five synthetic sources and two real targets, the method gained up to eight percentage points of mean intersection-over-union over state-of-the-art translation methods. Cheap synthetic datasets became as effective as high-effort ones.
arxiv-2510-11767:
Kahori Komaki analyzes a twist on Wythoff's game, a classic two-player pastime played with two piles of stones or, equivalently, a chess queen sliding toward a corner. In the classical game the losing positions for the player to move follow a pattern built from the golden ratio. Komaki's 2025 arXiv paper changes the ending: moving the queen into a small set of six positions near the corner now wins immediately.

For this variant Komaki describes all losing positions exactly. The description involves a correction function built from Hofstadter's G-sequence, a self-referential integer sequence. Two remarkable properties emerge. Far from the corner, beyond coordinate eight, the variant's losing positions under misère play match the classical game's list exactly. At those same positions, the variant's Grundy number, a measure of a position's strength in game theory, equals one exactly on the classical losing positions.
arxiv-2510-11867:
Zelin Gan and eight colleagues sharpen a formula fiber-optic engineers use to predict noise. Intense light in a fiber distorts itself, creating nonlinear interference that limits data rates. The Gaussian noise model estimates that interference, but its standard closed forms struggle in the O-band, the original wavelength window around thirteen hundred nanometers. There, low dispersion changes the physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper supplies a new closed-form model.

The formula adds two ingredients older models miss: the efficiency of four-wave mixing and the coherent build-up of self- and cross-phase modulation across repeated spans. The team checked it against split-step Fourier simulations, the heavy numerical gold standard, and against direct numerical integration. Tests spanned 41 to 161 channels over 80 to 800 kilometers. The model's error in predicted signal-to-noise ratio averaged below a fifth of a decibel.
arxiv-2510-12167:
Minghan Wang, Thuy-Trang Vu, Ehsan Shareghi, and Gholamreza Haffari test whether thinking in continuous vectors can borrow text reasoning's favorite trick. Inference-time scaling, sampling many solutions and re-ranking them with reward models, reliably boosts language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper transplants the recipe to COCONUT, a model that reasons in continuous thought space rather than words.

Feasibility checks pass: dropout-based sampling generates diverse reasoning paths, and pass-at-N analysis shows headroom akin to the discrete case. The gains refuse to materialize. Discrete-space recipes for training process and outcome reward models unlock only marginal improvements in continuous space. Probing geometry and trajectory dynamics reveals why: continuous thought representations lack the inductive biases a reward model needs to discriminate correct from incorrect reasoning. The authors argue continuous-reasoning training must build in such biases explicitly, optimizing not only for accuracy but for thoughts that can be judged.
arxiv-2510-12367:
Li and colleagues simulate a world where language models both write papers and review them, and find systematic unfairness, in a 2025 arXiv paper. They built a simulation with a research agent that writes and revises papers and a review agent that scores them.

Human annotators compared the model reviews with human judgments, and two misalignments stood out. Model reviewers inflated scores for model authored papers, rating them markedly higher than human authored ones. They also kept underrating human papers with critical statements about topics like risk and fairness, even after several revisions. They trace these effects to a bias toward model generated writing styles and an aversion to critical statements. On the positive side, revisions guided by model reviews improved paper quality under both model and human evaluation, with clear value for early stage researchers if the biases are managed.
arxiv-2510-13067:
Yang and co-authors improve infrared and visible image fusion with a new training loss in this 2025 arXiv paper. Fusion merges a thermal infrared image with an ordinary visible image into one useful picture, serving night surveillance, detection, and scene enhancement. Most learning methods train with structural similarity, intensity, and gradient-magnitude losses, but collapsing gradients to magnitude alone throws away direction.

Their direction-aware, multi-scale gradient loss supervises horizontal and vertical gradient components separately and preserves their sign at every scale. That gives models clear directional guidance at both fine and coarse resolutions, promoting sharper, better aligned edges and richer texture. The loss drops into existing pipelines without changing architectures or training protocols. Experiments on an open-source model and several public benchmarks showed the approach works for edge fidelity.
arxiv-2510-13167:
Li, Lu, and Wu study quantum resources near a higher-dimensional black hole in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their gravity model is Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, an extension of general relativity motivated by string theory, with a spherically symmetric black hole. They examine two three-party entangled states of a fermionic field, the GHZ and W states, under Hawking radiation, the quantum emission that slowly evaporates black holes.

Two cases are compared: quantum memories sit near the horizon while the measured particle stays far away, and the reverse. Above five dimensions, measurement uncertainty falls steadily as the horizon grows while coherence rises; in exactly five dimensions both move unevenly, a sign of unusual thermodynamics. The W state preserved coherence better, while the GHZ state resisted uncertainty growth better. Coherence was always lower when the memories sat near the horizon, helping guide state choices for information processing in curved spacetime.
arxiv-2510-13267:
Artioli, Tashtarian, and Timmerer model video streaming engagement with digital twins in this 2025 arXiv paper, from a multimedia systems conference. Streaming providers care intensely about engagement, the share of a video a user watches before quitting. It drives loyalty, personalization, advertising relevance, and testing. Standard adaptive bitrate algorithms assume all users react alike to quality changes and network problems.

Their system, DIGITWISE, builds a digital twin of each user from past viewing sessions. Streaming events feed the twin, and gradient-boosted machine learning models predict it for new sessions, with a unified model combining the twins. Modeling personal sensitivities cut prediction error noticeably compared with user-blind models. It can also identify which features maximize engagement, guiding content and delivery decisions. The authors report average gains from that optimization.
arxiv-2510-13367:
Kachaev and co-authors ask whether transformers can serve as strong models for online reinforcement learning. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies continuous control, where an agent learns by acting in its environment. Transformers excel in offline settings, yet their use online has stayed limited. Small design choices make them sensitive to training setups, the authors note. Earlier success came mostly from fixed datasets collected in advance.

The team tests how inputs should be conditioned for the policy and value networks. They also test whether those networks should share parts, and how sequences should be sliced for training. Their experiments find stable designs that perform well across many tasks. The results hold for fully and partly observable tasks, and for both vector and image inputs. The authors offer these findings as practical guidance for online use. This makes transformers credible baselines for online model-free learning.
arxiv-2510-13467:
Li, Du, and Huang build NetMCP, a platform that makes language model tool routing aware of network conditions. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends the Model Context Protocol, a standard way to connect models with outside tools. Current routing matches requests to tool descriptions by meaning alone. That makes deployments fragile when latency spikes or servers fail.

NetMCP provides a testbed with five representative network states for controlled experiments. It also supplies a benchmark of latency sequences and server datasets. On this platform the team proposes SONAR, a routing algorithm that weighs meaning and network quality together. SONAR consistently raised task success rates over semantic-only and model-based baselines. It also cut completion times and reduced the number of failures. The code for the platform is publicly available, the authors note.
arxiv-2510-13967:
Julian Demeio, Sam Streeter, and Rosa Winter prove results about rational points, solutions whose coordinates are fractions, on a class of geometric surfaces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The surfaces are del Pezzo surfaces of degree one, from algebraic geometry. The property at stake is the Hilbert property. It says rational points cannot be trapped inside thin exceptional sets.

Working over fields built finitely from the rational numbers, the authors establish the Hilbert property for degree-one del Pezzo surfaces. These have Picard rank one, a measure of how few curve families the surface carries. They generalize work by Demeio on elliptic surfaces and borrow constructions that Desjardins and Winter used to prove density of rational points. The results are the first for minimal degree-one del Pezzo surfaces lacking a conic fibration, a structural shortcut whose absence had blocked previous approaches.
arxiv-2510-14667:
Zubovas and Tartėnas ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, why winds blown out by active galactic nuclei speed up once they leave the center of their galaxy. Recent observations of ten galaxies show a shared pattern. The outflow moves at a roughly steady speed inside the central bulge, then accelerates rapidly beyond one to three kiloparsecs. The authors test whether this is simply what happens when a wind clears the bulge's gas and breaks into emptier space.

They ran a one-dimensional semi-analytical model, Magnofit, for each galaxy, holding the central engine's brightness constant and treating the bulge's gas fraction and mass as free parameters. The simplest model fit six of the ten velocity profiles essentially perfectly. A bulge with a shallower gas density profile fixed a seventh, and it improved the central fits of the remaining three, though those still accelerate faster than the models predict.
arxiv-2510-14867:
Iorsh and Titov propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new explanation for a magnetic resistance effect usually credited to bulk spin currents. In metal-ferromagnet bilayers, such as platinum on yttrium iron garnet, resistance depends on the magnetization direction, an anisotropy blamed on the spin Hall effect. They show the interface alone can do it, with disorder's help.

In their model, charge transfer at a clean interface creates a spin filter. One spin direction passes with little backscattering. The other is strongly scattered, when interfacial exchange and Rashba spin-orbit coupling act together. The predicted anisotropy peaks at a few nanometers of metal thickness. It reproduces the size and angular patterns usually assigned to spin Hall magnetoresistance. Unlike that mechanism, the maximum effect scales with whichever coupling is weaker. The model predicts strong sensitivity to charge transfer and disorder, giving experimentalists a way to tell the two stories apart.
arxiv-2510-15067:
Munizzi and Schnitzer build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a topological construction kit for quantum states beyond the easy class. Stabilizer states are easy to simulate and geometrically well understood; non-stabilizer states, the resource behind quantum advantage, are not. The authors work in SU(2) level-one Chern-Simons theory, a topological field theory, and use its Kac-Moody algebra.

They build Pauli and Clifford operators from path integrals over manifolds with Wilson loop insertions, lines that record the passage of particles. This yields topological realizations of W and Dicke states, two families of entangled states of this kind, together with their entanglement entropies. They show that Clifford group action corresponds to modular transformations generated by Dehn twists on surfaces, tying the mapping class group of a surface to quantum operations. The work extends constructions from the stabilizer class to these families, sharpening the geometry of entanglement as a quantum resource.
arxiv-2510-15167:
Nina Cao and nine colleagues argue that machine learning for x-ray absorption spectroscopy needs shared infrastructure, not just clever models. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes a technique that reads the local chemistry around atoms from how a material absorbs x-rays. Machine learning already speeds that analysis and cuts human bias, but models trained on simulated spectra often stumble on real experimental data.

The first case study shows why: a model trained only on simulations predicted the wrong trend in titanium oxidation states across a zinc titanate film. After the team mapped the real spectra into a simulation-like form, a step they call spectral domain mapping, the same model recovered the correct trend. A second study explores universal models trained across the whole periodic table, letting them borrow patterns shared between elements. The authors sketch a full pipeline of benchmarks, databases, and workflows aimed at real-time analysis.
arxiv-2510-15467:
Lingfeng Xuan and five colleagues rebuild driving scenes in 3D from the camera rings that modern cars carry. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents MRASfM, a structure-from-motion system tailored to multi-camera driving data. Structure-from-motion estimates camera poses and a point cloud of the surroundings, feeding tasks like high-definition mapping. On driving footage it often stumbles, with shaky poses and stray points littering the road surface.

MRASfM exploits the fixed geometry of the camera rig during registration, which steadies pose estimates. A plane model deletes road points that cannot lie on the surface. Treating the camera set as one unit in the final optimization cuts variables and speeds the work. Scene association modules then stitch separate drives into larger maps, coarse to fine. On the public nuScenes dataset it reached a low pose error, and real-vehicle tests covered difficult conditions.
arxiv-2510-15567:
Eduard Andrei Cristea, Petter Molnes, and Jingyue Li use language models to detect malware and name the weaknesses it exploits. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that commercial detection tools are costly, and almost no tool links a malicious program to the specific catalogued vulnerabilities, known as CVEs, that it abuses. That link helps defenders understand old attacks and prevent new ones.

Their proof-of-concept, MalCVE, works on Java archive files. It decompiles and deobfuscates the code, summarizes it with a language model, and searches for similar known code. A second model then classifies which CVEs the malware likely exploits, guided by retrieval-augmented generation. On a benchmark of about thirty-eight hundred Java executables, mean detection accuracy reached ninety-seven percent at a fraction of commercial costs. Its vulnerability matching, the first of its kind for binary malware, scored a recall at ten of sixty-five percent.
arxiv-2510-16167:
Archie Chaudhury, writing alone, asks where inside a language model its good behavior lives. Models learn manners through training with human feedback, a method called RLHF, but no one knew which parts store the change. He probes the small Llama-3.2-1B model by swapping inner activity between the raw model and its tuned twin.

The swap tests show the change sits in a tight spot, not spread through the whole model. Middle layers hold a small set of signals that drive reward-pleasing replies, while early and late layers barely change. A second test with sparse math finds only a few layers carry the effect at all. If this holds for bigger models, fixing bad behavior may one day mean patching a few layers, not retraining the whole system.
arxiv-2510-17067:
Ioannis Anagnostides and five co-authors study a classic learning rule for games in this 2025 paper. The rule, regret matching, shifts play toward moves that would have done better. It drove big wins in poker, yet its math beyond two-player duels stayed unclear. A plus form of the rule also shines on hard limit tasks.

The authors prove the plus form reaches a near-best point under limits quite fast. Bounded regret can make that speed even better. By contrast, the plain rule can take vastly longer in some shared-payoff games. That gap is the first of its kind shown for these rules. The work gives the plus form a firm base as a solver.
arxiv-2510-17167:
Telling whether one factor truly causes another is hard when some hidden factor shapes both. Yong Wu, together with four co-authors, builds a test for that problem using a stand in variable called a negative control outcome. Earlier control based methods were limited to categories only, or they leaned on strong assumptions to reach an answer.

Wu and his co-authors set out a general approach that handles both category and measured data with only one control variable. A new equation links the outcome and the control, and modest conditions make the causal claim identifiable. Their kernel based test is more efficient than older ones, and adding a second control restores answers in cases where the first control alone fails.
arxiv-2510-17367:
Contact binary stars are pairs so close that they share an outer layer, and Atila Poro with eight co-authors studies five such systems of the W Ursae Majoris type. The team gathered light curves in several colour bands using telescopes in both the northern and southern hemispheres. Those curves record how the combined light rises and falls as the stars circle and eclipse each other.

Poro and his co-authors find that two systems show slowly shrinking orbital periods, while one light curve needed a cool starspot to fit well. A tight link between orbital period and the spacing of the pair gave the most reliable route to masses and sizes. The team also classifies the systems by subtype and traces their likely past evolution.
arxiv-2510-17567:
Statisticians build new families of probability distributions to fit data whose shapes older curves cannot match, such as data with two humps or a heavy bathtub shaped risk curve. Alexsandro A Ferreira and Gauss M Cordeiro develop one such family, the modified odd Burr XII-G family, which grows out of an earlier exponentiated class of distributions. The construction is meant to bend a wide range of baseline distributions into more flexible shapes.

Ferreira and Cordeiro derive the mathematical properties of the new family and build a regression model inside it, so that outcomes can be tied to explanatory variables. They estimate the parameters by maximum likelihood and run simulations to check that the estimates settle near the true values as samples grow. Three real data sets show the practical value of the proposals.
arxiv-2510-17667:
Graciana Puentes evaluates machine learning methods for fluidic lenses in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fluidic lenses are optical lenses whose shape can change, and their flaws are described by Zernike variables. These variables form a standard basis for optical aberrations, meaning distortions in an image. Her data was coarse experimental data, so careful statistics were needed.

Three supervised tools sorted out which variables matter most. Principal component analysis found two components explaining about 95 percent of the total variance. Factor analysis showed a small tolerance still kept the essential information. Hierarchical clustering grouped similar variables, with a fit value close to one. By cross checking methods against each other, the study lays groundwork for stronger future analyses of such lenses.
arxiv-2510-17867:
Jian-wei Liu, with two co-authors, surveys two close families of neural networks: recursive and recurrent designs. The review sorts them by network shape, by the goal used in training, and by how the learning method runs. It then walks through many named variants in a set order.

The first group covers basic, memory-based, and folded forms, plus highway and multi-way designs. A second group covers forms built for grids, graphs, time, and layered data. For students entering the field, the survey maps a crowded area and shows how each variant grows out of the basic loop idea.
arxiv-2510-17967:
Soumen Roy and four co-authors build a waveform model for black hole pairs that sit inside clouds of light scalar particles. Such particles appear in many extensions of known physics and could serve as dark matter. Near black holes they can grow dense, and if the cloud lasts through the final spiral, the gravity waves change shape.

The model is checked against full numerical simulations, then used on the public LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA catalog. Most pairs give firm upper limits on nearby scalar density. Two events stood out, with plain vacuum sitting outside the likely range under the stated assumptions.
arxiv-2510-18167:
Robert Griffiths, writing alone, builds Gaussian fields on the corners of a high-dimensional cube from long-range random walks. The field's covariance comes from the Green function of walks that wander the cube and die at a set rate. A coupling then lines the fields up across dimensions so they form a Markov chain in the dimension itself.

When the walk steps are exchangeable, the field links to spin glass models. A natural step choice from a de Finetti sequence extends the walk to the infinite cube. The paper characterizes the Green function and a strong form of the field through a point process.
arxiv-2510-18367:
Naoki Otani and Takeru Matsuda study statistics for data that live on a circle, such as angles or directions, where the end of the scale wraps back to its start. They examine estimators built by projecting the observed data distribution onto a model, using the Wasserstein distance as the measure of closeness. A formula for that distance on circles makes the projection practical to compute.

Numerical tests covered three circular distributions: the von Mises, the wrapped Cauchy, and a skewed version of the von Mises. On clean data, the projection estimators matched the accuracy of maximum likelihood, the usual benchmark method. When noise was mixed into the samples, the projection estimators held up better, showing a robustness that matters for messy real measurements.
arxiv-2510-18467:
Yili Wang and her four co-authors propose a simpler network for learning from graphs that change over time and mix several types of nodes and links. Such graphs appear in areas from finance to social platforms. Existing attention-based models usually learn time patterns and link patterns in separate stages, which weakens how the two interact and makes the models heavy.

Their design, SE-HTGNN, folds time modeling into the spatial learning step through a dynamic attention method that carries attention information from past snapshots forward to guide later rounds. Large language models also supply prior knowledge about node types, helping the network grasp hidden traits of each kind. In experiments, the model ran up to ten times faster than leading rivals while keeping the best forecasting accuracy, a rare gain on both fronts.
arxiv-2510-18567:
Yiding Feng works with Mengfan Ma, Bo Peng, and Zongqi Wan. They study a repeated deal between a principal and agents. Each round, the principal offers contracts. The offers rest on context and past feedback. The principal does not know the agents' true costs or rewards. The setup extends classic contextual pricing. There, the only real choice is a price. Here, agents can take much richer actions.

The results are sobering. One regret bound grows almost exponentially with context size. A second, classic regret bound is also proved. Even three actions and two context traits make the problem vastly harder. Contextual pricing, by contrast, admits near-optimal learning. The authors blame a structural trap. They call it contextual action degeneracy. Crafted contexts can make some actions strictly worse. The principal then cannot lure agents to try them. Exploration gets blocked at the root.
arxiv-2510-18867:
Anarya Ray and Vicky Kalogera reexamine a claimed gap in black hole masses. Theory says pair instability in massive stars should block a high-mass range. Black holes should not form there. The fourth gravitational-wave catalog now probes that idea directly. It covers the population of merging binary black holes.

The authors use flexible models that avoid rigid assumptions. They find no evidence now for a sharp drop-off in the expected gap region. They also trace how mass ratios and spins change across the population. The heavy, broadly spinning subgroup often has fairly equal masses. That sits awkwardly with a story of systems built from earlier merger generations. Star cluster simulations do not rescue that story. A gap may still appear as samples grow, the authors caution.
arxiv-2510-18967:
Ritam Basu and three co-authors measure the stabilizer complexity of Hawking radiation from an evaporating black hole. In quantum computing terms, they ask how much magic, tracked by Wigner negativity, the radiation carries, since that sets how hard it is to simulate with classical methods.

In a toy gravity model they compute the negativity directly and find it stays small before the Page transition, then grows hugely after it. They also derive a general formula that links the two regimes. A second toy model supports the same picture of radiation becoming far harder to fake classically late in evaporation.
arxiv-2510-19367:
Yasser Hamidullah, Josef van Genabith, and Cristina España-Bonet present a sign language translation method that replaces gloss annotations with sentence embeddings as the training signal. Gloss labels, the written notes for signs, are rarely available at scale and differ between datasets. This has long limited systems that learn through them.

Embeddings of the target sentences, learned from raw text alone, play the gloss role without any manual annotation. The approach also supports several languages naturally. The authors test it on German and American sign language datasets with both single-language and multilingual embeddings, checking where embedding supervision helps most.
arxiv-2510-19567:
Takahiro Suzuki and Keisuke Okumura study pathfinding for swarms of identical agents that must stay connected at all times. This connected, unlabeled variant of multi-agent pathfinding fits swarm robotics jobs like self-reconfiguration and marching, where ordinary planners give no connectivity guarantee. The problem is simple to state but has lacked practical algorithms.

The authors first build an integer linear programming solution that is optimal in makespan but scales poorly. They then propose PULL, a lightweight rule-based algorithm that picks each next configuration while preserving connectivity and moving toward the target. PULL runs fast per step, is complete, and quickly solved random instances with hundreds of agents that the exact method could not handle.
arxiv-2510-19667:
Yuxing Fei and four co-authors present Dara, a system that automates the interpretation of powder X-ray diffraction patterns for materials with several crystal phases at once. Reading such patterns is still largely manual and expert-driven, and because diffraction gives only structural information, several phase combinations can fit one pattern, inviting mistakes. Dara searches exhaustively over plausible phase combinations within a chemical space.

Each candidate is checked with a robust Rietveld refinement routine, with database filtering and clustering of structurally similar phases keeping the search manageable. When the evidence stays ambiguous, Dara reports multiple hypotheses for experts or other instruments to decide between. The goal is reliable phase identification that scales to realistic, complex patterns and self-driving laboratories.
arxiv-2510-20267:
Saraf Anzum Shreya, MD. Abu Ismail Siddique, and Sharaf Tasnim build a real-time phone system that identifies currency and speaks the result aloud for visually impaired users. Handling money without help is a daily difficulty, and a camera phone with machine learning offers a practical aid. Their detector is trained on thirty classes of notes and coins covering United States dollars, euros, and Bangladeshi taka.

The system uses a YOLOv8 nano model with a custom detection head that adds deep convolutional layers and squeeze-and-excitation blocks to sharpen feature extraction. Reported results include accuracy near ninety-eight percent with strong recall and precision scores on their dataset. Voice feedback after each detection lets the user confirm the denomination independently.
arxiv-2510-20767:
Tomás Cabrera, Antonella Palmese, and Maya Fishbach study black hole mergers in active galaxy disks. Active galactic nuclei, called AGN, are bright centers of galaxies. Their disks are rings of gas around a central black hole. Detectors have found over three hundred pairs of merging black holes. No matching flash of light has been confirmed yet.

Some past searches found AGN flares near merger events in time. Theory says a flare could come from the merged black hole. It would interact with gas in the disk around it. The authors test how likely such matches are by chance. They find less than three percent of mergers produce visible flares. Up to about forty percent could still start in AGN disks. For each pair, background flares explain the match better. Better tests are needed to tell real matches from chance ones.
arxiv-2510-20967:
Sraavya Sambara leads seven co-authors on 3DReasonKnee, the first data set for grounded reasoning over three dimensional medical images, built from knee MRI scans. Clinicians reason step by step about named anatomy, yet vision language models struggle to locate regions in volumes and explain findings in that workflow.

Nearly half a million high quality quintuples are derived from almost eight thousand knee volumes, each linking the scan, a question, region grounding, reasoning steps, and an answer. Training on such data aims at outputs that match diagnostic practice and can be checked by clinicians. Trustworthy collaboration between doctors and AI is the stated goal.
arxiv-2510-21067:
Raul Cavalcante Dinardi leads three co-authors on a simple heuristic for parallel test time reasoning, pick the shortest solution among several sampled attempts. Reasoning models gain from sampling many solutions, but scoring them usually adds cost and complexity.

Shortest selection proves highly effective in their tests, a counterintuitive result explained by two operating regimes in model behavior, where correct solutions tend to be direct and wrong ones ramble through overthinking. Brevity thus acts as a cheap quality signal. The trick could cut the cost of test time scaling for mathematics and coding assistants substantially.
arxiv-2510-21167:
Dogyun Park leads three co-authors on Blockwise Flow Matching, which splits the generative trajectory of flow matching models into time segments, each handled by a smaller specialized network. A single large network must capture every stage of the path from noise to data and is costly to evaluate repeatedly.

Distinct signal character across timesteps strains the one network design, and full model calls at every step inflate inference cost. Segment specialists can be lighter and better tuned to their slice of the trajectory. The framework aims at high quality image generation with materially lower compute per sample.
arxiv-2510-21567:
Youngmin Park and Thomas G. Fai model how molecular motors haul cargo vesicles into dendritic spines, the tiny bulbous compartments where neurons receive signals. Whether a vesicle makes it through the spine's narrow neck shapes the connection's strength, and disorders linked to excess long, thin spines make the geometry question clinically relevant.

Starting from a detailed agent-based model of myosin motors, they prove that second-order fluctuations in motor attachment times can be safely ignored, leaving a far simpler description governed by mean attachment times. Simulations confirm the trimmed model keeps the original's key behavior while making delivery times and success chances computable directly. Sweeping motor parameters shows thin spine shapes sharply cut delivery odds, and tuning the motors can compensate only up to a point.
arxiv-2510-21667:
Qihui Yang, Randal Leistikow, and Yongyi Zang generate virtual instruments that keep one consistent voice across every pitch and playing strength. Sampled and modeled instruments live or die by that consistency. Note-by-note generators tend to let the tone wander as notes change. That betrays the illusion of a single instrument.

Their FlowSynth reworks flow matching so the model's velocity field is itself a distribution. The model can admit uncertainty instead of committing to one average path. That honesty pays off at generation time. The system samples several trajectories and weighs them by the model's own confidence. It keeps the output that best preserves timbre across notes. Against the leading TokenSynth baseline, FlowSynth wins on single-note quality. It also wins on cross-note consistency, edging toward instruments fit for live performance.
arxiv-2510-22067:
Zheng Qi, Chao Shang, Evangelia Spiliopoulou, and Nikolaos Pappas try to stop vision-language models from hallucinating content that neither the picture nor the question supports. Earlier fixes boosted attention to image regions, but attention itself often pools on irrelevant areas, and boosting sight alone can leave the model misreading what the user actually asked.

Their method, GIFT, watches where the model's visual attention moves in a helpful direction while it absorbs the question. Builds a saliency map from those gaze shifts before answering begins. That map then guides a balanced fusion of image and query, strengthening the right regions instead of amplifying whatever already glows. The authors present the approach as a simple correction to a specific failure: models answering from language habits rather than from what they were shown.
arxiv-2510-22267:
Weijian Li and Andreas A. Malikopoulos add a conscience about risk to the workhorse of control theory. The linear quadratic regulator balances state error against effort with elegant mathematics. It says nothing about how wildly the state may swing, and in safety-critical systems the swings are the danger.

Their risk-constrained version appends a statistical limit on state variability to the classical problem over an infinite horizon. Reformulated as a max-min game, the problem yields an actor-critic learning scheme that needs no model of the system and learns online. The critic prices actions by temporal-difference learning, the actor improves the policy by gradient steps, and a dual variable climbs to enforce the risk cap. The three updates run on separate time scales, the standard recipe for keeping such a trio stable while it learns.
arxiv-2510-22367:
Haowen Zhou, with nine co-authors, reports a limit on using high lying electronic states to laser cool large molecules. Earlier theory, using simple approximations, pointed to a third excited state as the best cooling route for alkaline earth phenoxides. The team measured that state in two such molecules in detail for the first time.

Spectroscopy showed that coupling among the first three excited states mixes them and opens extra decay paths. The coupling is small, yet many vibrational states in a large molecule make the mixing matter. The finding suggests that only lower states may be safe targets for cooling complex molecules.
arxiv-2510-22467:
Jing Yang and four co-authors introduce GradLite, an optimizer meant to cut the memory cost of training large language models. Full fine tuning stores activations and optimizer state, which eats memory fast. Past fixes change the network or trade memory for extra computation, leaving the optimizer itself untouched, and GradLite targets exactly that gap.

GradLite works with rough gradients instead of exact ones when activations are dropped or approximated. A low rank shortcut shrinks error signals, while an error feedback step saves and repays past mistakes. Theory keeps the estimates unbiased, and tests cut memory use by up to half with equal or better results.
arxiv-2510-22767:
Not all layers in a large model help on every task. Omar Naim, Krish Sharma, Niyar R Barman, and Nicholas Asher use that fact in 2025. Their method is called TALE. It removes task harmful layers at inference time. No retraining is needed.

TALE stands for Task-Aware Layer Elimination. Across nine tasks, it matched or beat baselines. It was tested on five model families. Both zero shot and few shot settings were used. It also cut compute costs at the same time. Fine tuning plus TALE gave further gains. Setup for a new task needs only modest resources.
arxiv-2510-23167:
Zhao Yang and five co-authors guide skill discovery in reinforcement learning with foundation models. Learning varied skills without hand-made rewards could speed later tasks, but pure diversity seeking can produce useless or dangerous behavior. A cheetah robot, for instance, may learn to roll in every direction instead of running safely.

Their FoG method uses a foundation model to steer discovery toward skills humans would prefer. The robot still explores broadly, yet avoids flipping or entering hazardous areas. Guided discovery promises reusable skill sets that are both diverse and aligned with what people actually want.
arxiv-2510-23267:
Klaus Mattis and Timo Weiss prove an equivalence between two ways of forming the derived category of Frobenius modules over a scheme in characteristic p. Frobenius modules generalize the pushforward action that defines much of positive-characteristic geometry. Their result covers quasi-compact Fp-schemes with affine diagonal, including all separated quasi-compact schemes.

The equivalence is t-exact and generalizes their earlier theorem for regular Noetherian schemes. As a byproduct they settle the needed derived category properties in this generality. Algebraic geometers working with Frobenius actions gain a cleaner foundation for derived methods. The authors present their evidence and methods in full for readers to judge.
arxiv-2510-23367:
Aaron C Trigg leads a team of nineteen researchers searching archival Fermi data for overlooked giant flares from magnetars in other galaxies. Magnetar giant flares are rare, extremely bright gamma-ray bursts from highly magnetized neutron stars. At extragalactic distances they mimic other bursts, so only a handful are confidently known.

The study expands the candidate sample with improved identification methods applied to Gamma-ray Burst Monitor archives. A larger population would clarify how often such flares occur and how much energy they release. Better samples also sharpen the line between true giant flares and ordinary short bursts.
arxiv-2510-23467:
Shreya Khisa, Ali Amhaz, Mohamed Elhattab, Chadi Assi, and Sanaa Sharafeddine study joint uplink and downlink resource allocation for pinching antenna systems. Their setup uses two waveguides, one for transmission and one for reception, each holding several pinching antennas at preset positions, all tied to one base station.

The station serves uplink and downlink users at the same time on the same spectrum. The authors formulate a sum-rate optimization that jointly chooses resources and which antennas to activate. Smart activation could raise total throughput while cutting energy in future flexible-antenna networks.
arxiv-2510-23667:
Amin Heyrani Nobari and four co-authors introduce Optimize Any Topology, a foundation model that designs load-bearing structures without the usual grid restrictions. Topology optimization decides where material should go inside a part. Classic solvers are slow, and learning-based ones accept only fixed square grids and a few hand-coded supports. That rigidity has kept such models out of real design work.

Their system pairs an autoencoder that ignores shape and resolution with a decoder based on implicit neural fields, driven by a conditional latent-diffusion model. Training used OpenTO, a new corpus of 2.2 million optimized structures spanning two million support and load setups. On public benchmarks and two unseen hard tests, the model cut mean compliance by up to ninety percent versus the best prior models. It answers in under a second on one GPU, at sizes from small grids to wide ten-to-one shapes.
arxiv-2510-23767:
Timothy De Deyn and a co-author reframe how ideals are sorted in noncommutative tensor-triangular geometry. In this field, algebraic objects are studied through a geometric spectrum, much as rings are studied through their prime ideals. Balmer's spectrum sorts the radical thick tensor-ideals in the well-behaved setting, but the genuinely noncommutative case stayed open.

Given the Balmer spectrum of any small category of the right kind, the authors sort its semiprime thick tensor-ideals by a dual built from that spectrum. The proof passes through support data for lattices and frames, where Stone duality turns algebra into topology. They also pin down when the spectrum acts like a classic spectral space, and show that rigid, centrally generated categories pass that test. The work answers a question from Negron and Pevtsova about one-sided ideals and cohomological support.
arxiv-2510-23967:
Mu-Lin Li and two co-authors prove that a positivity property of certain line bundles cannot appear or vanish as a smooth family of algebraic varieties deforms — with careful conditions. The bundles in question are adjoint bundles, built from the canonical bundle twisted by a relatively semiample partner. The first result says: if the adjoint bundle is nef on one fiber of a family over a disk, it stays nef on every fiber.

The authors extend the same stability to semiampleness. From there they prove deformation invariance of plurigenera, assuming just one fiber has a semiample canonical bundle, and sharpen earlier rigidity results. One striking case: a family over a projective line or elliptic curve with one big, nef fiber has all fibers isomorphic. A companion result for threefolds runs the other way — if one fiber's canonical bundle is not nef, its deformations cannot have one either.
arxiv-2510-24367:
Junda He and seven co-authors review the use of large language models as judges for software engineering outputs. Models now generate huge volumes of code and other artifacts, creating a bottleneck: human review is slow and costly, while simple metrics like BLEU miss nuanced quality. Using a model to judge outputs promises human like nuance at automated scale.

The review maps the young field, covering how judge models are prompted, where they succeed, and where they fail against human standards. As a forward looking paper, it lays out a vision and a road ahead, including reliability checks and better alignment with expert judgment. The authors aim to guide trustworthy automated evaluation for software work.
arxiv-2510-24467:
Stanisław Halkiewicz writes alone on a trader who knows all future prices. The trader is lazy and trades rarely, due to costs or slow tools. Knowledge is perfect, yet each trade has a real price in time or fees. Halkiewicz asks how often such a trader should act for best profit. He links that choice to how rough the price path is.

He derives a closed-form profit rule from a geometric setup. He proves one best trading pace exists and is unique. The best pace can be read from the path's fractal dimension. Fractal dimension measures roughness at finer and finer scales. A random-path version uses fractional Brownian motion and its Hurst exponent. Tests on real share data match the predicted scaling well.
arxiv-2510-24567:
Pablo Bilbao, Thales Silva, and Luis Silva, three authors, study plasma accelerators. Wakefield accelerators surf particles on waves in a plasma. New driver beams carry huge charge in ultra-short bursts. In dense plasma, the beam sheds betatron radiation as it wiggles. Betatron motion is the sideways bounce of a beam in a channel.

The team show this radiation cools the beam in a shaping way. Cooling here means energy loss that sorts particles by amplitude. The sorted beam forms bunched rings in its phase space. Phase space pairs each particle's place with its momentum. Outer rings gain population, an inversion of the usual order. Analytic timescales match particle-in-cell simulations of the beam. Such self-structured beams could emit coherent betatron light.
arxiv-2510-24767:
Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Zhe Huang, Jing Lin, Xuefei Zhe, Jian Li, and Haoqian Wang aim to make video captions name fine moves of the human body well. Past caption tools often give vague lines or lines that clash with the clip. Their model adds body mesh based move traits right into the word choice step.

Those move traits stress how the body shifts, which cuts fake claims and lines up words with the clip. To train and test such work, they built a set of more than one hundred thousand clip and line pairs on human moves. A bench set goes with it. Their model beat past tools on hard move clips.
arxiv-2510-25167:
Hayk Stepanyan leads a team with seven co-authors who built a repeat pipe to grow culture rich data for AI models, in many tongues. Such models act less well in far culture zones and tongues than in the core ones. Plain data top ups boost mean scores but do not aim at those gaps.

Their pipe runs on more than one prong, to find, check, and add data that is rich in local culture sense. Such data can gauge how far a model truly works round the world. Gaps found that way can then be aimed at and closed on a next pass. The pipe is built to scale and to be run again.
arxiv-2510-25367:
Muhittin Mungan, Eric Clement, Damien Vandembroucq, and Srikanth Sastry review self-organization. Their 2025 review covers driven disordered systems. Such systems live under a fluctuating environment drive. They can organize into history-dependent response patterns. The system retains a memory of past driving. Sheared amorphous solids provide a clear example.

In those solids, mechanical instabilities emerge persistently. Driving can trigger the same instabilities repeatedly. That leads to highly reversible mechanical states. System response becomes correlated with environment dynamics. That correlation can act like a sensing mechanism. Similar phenomena appear across soft matter systems. The authors suggest they are generic in nature. Little may depend on specific underlying details. They discuss lessons for living matter too. Simple organisms may sense and adapt similarly. Their review links materials physics with biological adaptation.
arxiv-2510-25667:
Tribikram Choudhury, Yacine Haddad, and Michael Doser review infrared quantum dots. Their 2025 paper focuses on narrow band emitting dots. Infrared quantum dots operate across several wavelength regions. Near-infrared through long-wavelength infrared ranges are covered. They show promise in optoelectronics and nanotechnology. Military surveillance is another likely use area.

Bandgap energy and output wavelength are precisely tunable. Particle size, composition, and surface chemistry control tuning. Wide tunability attracts basic research interest. Health and space technology uses also motivate work. The paper focuses on polymer-based infrared quantum dots. Possible uses span high-energy physics tests. Medicine could use infrared dots for imaging. Astrophysics and space uses are also explored. Narrow band output suits sensing and finding needs. The review maps materials progress to use prospects.
arxiv-2510-25767:
B J Ramshaw and Steven A Kivelson argue that old BCS theory fits overdoped cuprates well. Their 2025 view piece deals with cuprates, the best known odd superconductors. Cuprates work at heat levels far past what sound-based pairing would give. Most experts took BCS theory as a wrong start.

The pair argue for a shift as doping grows. Lightly doped cuprates do need a fresh frame, they grant. Past a shift point, the overdoped side may fit BCS-like views. That holds at low power scales, near the gap and below. The catch is that mess and flaws in the stuff must be counted in. Traits that clash with their view can stem from those flaws, they argue. They close with sharp, testable calls for a flaw-free overdoped cuprate.
arxiv-2510-26267:
Amartya Sengupta, Dejan Stojkovic, and L. C. R. Wijewardhana explore what the universe would look like if the strong force symmetry broke in the late cosmos. Only two gauge symmetries remain unbroken today: the color symmetry of the strong force and electromagnetism. The authors ask why they must stay unbroken forever, and build a model with a new colored scalar whose potential allows a first order phase transition through bubble nucleation.

Expanding bubbles of the broken phase would produce particles in several ways, from direct nonthermal production at the wall to frictional heating in a shocked layer. Their benchmark transition temperature lies below the relevant particle masses, so a hot broken phase bath would restore the symmetry instead. They formulate a freeze out estimate below that temperature for the surviving broken phase particles.
arxiv-2510-26967:
Riley Grossman, Michael Smith, Cristian Borcea, and Yi Chen measure sneaky design in cookie consent banners. Aesthetic manipulation means styling that draws the eye to the button that allows data sharing. The team visited thousands of websites, sorted their banner types, and used a vision model that predicts where people look to score how strongly each element stands out.

About forty-five percent of relevant sites have fully compliant banners, yet thirty-eight percent of those still use aesthetic manipulation, more than earlier studies found. The method also reveals new tricks such as button placement. European sites use manipulation more than non-European ones, and some sites change design when the visitor appears to be in the United States.
arxiv-2510-27067:
Marouane Benbetka, Merwan Bekkar, Riyadh Baghdadi, and Martin Kong improve how quantum programs are fitted onto real quantum hardware. Qubits on current processors can only interact with near neighbors, so compilers insert SWAP gates to move quantum states closer together. Each added gate lengthens the program and raises error, making swap placement a critical cost.

The new mapper exploits dependence information, meaning which operations must wait for which others, through affine abstractions that make those links computable. Circuits are split by dependence distance and each layer gets its own weight. Tested on IBM and Rigetti processors against four baseline tools, it improves circuit depth and swap count while scaling competitively on large benchmark suites.
arxiv-2510-27167:
SeongHee Jeong, Seulip Lee, and Sijing Liu design a monotone finite element method for optimal control under strong convection. The state follows a convection-diffusion-reaction equation in a regime where flow dominates, a setting prone to nonphysical oscillations in naive numerics. Their method builds on the edge-averaged finite element scheme, which preserves a discrete maximum principle for such problems.

The discretization inherits monotonicity from the continuous problem, so the computed optimal state respects desired bounds and stays free of spurious wiggles. Analysis combines a consistency result with a discrete inf-sup condition to prove well-posedness and optimal convergence order. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and show robustness across convection-dominated cases. The scheme suits control problems where overshoot would break physical or safety limits.
arxiv-2510-27567:
Einan Gardi and Zehao Zhu tackle a key piece of particle physics in 2025: how soft radiation shapes the chance of a collision outcome. They work out a full three-loop term, called the soft anomalous dimension, for cases with one heavy colored particle and any count of light ones. QCD, the theory of the strong force, sets the rules for the work.

Their method expands line-based tools along a light path and splits the work by region. The final form uses broad log-like functions in three variables. It matches known limits when mass fades and when particles move in line. Precise terms like this sharpen forecasts for collider tests.
arxiv-2511-00067:
Zhixing Li, Arsham Gholamzadeh Khoee, and Yinan Yu tackle domain generalization for vision-language models without domain labels. Models must stay robust when deployment domains shift, yet labels for domains are often unavailable or ambiguous. Their idea represents an unseen target domain as a combination of latent domains discovered automatically from training data.

Latent domain prompt learning then lets the model transfer knowledge across those discovered domains adaptively. Computer vision readers get a label-free route to robustness. Prompt learning is the adaptation mechanism, so the base model stays frozen while domain mixtures are expressed through learned prompts.
arxiv-2511-00567:
Marcello Di Costanzo reports, in conference proceedings for the ALICE Collaboration, how charm quarks flow inside the fireball made by lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Elliptic flow measures how the almond shape of the collision zone imprints itself on particle motion. Charm hadrons are ideal probes: prompt ones come straight from charm quarks, while non-prompt ones arrive later, through beauty hadron decays.

Using fresh Run 3 data at midrapidity, the analysis measures flow for several charm mesons and, for the first time, a charm baryon, with record precision and reach to low momentum. A splitting between baryon and meson flow appears in the charm sector for the first time. Non-prompt particles flow less, as expected from the heavier beauty quark, sharpening the picture of the fireball.
arxiv-2511-00867:
Yassin Tesfaw Abebe and co-authors model conflict deaths in Ethiopia across nearly three decades, from 1997 to 2024, using event level records from the ACLED project. They treat deaths as two linked outcomes: whether an event kills anyone at all, and how many die when it does.

Their Bayesian model mixes measured factors, such as event type, season, and distance to cities and borders, with a latent spatial and time process that captures clustering. Airstrikes, shelling, and attacks carry the highest risk and counts, and communal and rebel actors account for the most deaths. Fatal events are more likely in summer, border proximity raises intensity, and distance from cities lowers it. The results aim to guide protection planning and resource allocation.
arxiv-2511-01167:
Sara Morrissey and colleagues report seven cold, distant brown dwarfs found with the James Webb Space Telescope. Brown dwarfs are objects too small to fuse hydrogen like stars, and cold distant ones are hard to spot. The seven turned up in spectra from the RUBIES survey, taken with the telescope's near infrared spectrograph.

Comparing the spectra with standards gives types from L1 to T8, among the coolest classes, and distances from about eight hundred to three thousand parsecs. Fits to three model grids mostly agree with those classifications, though the L dwarf fits suggest the models miss some ingredient. Three of the dwarfs sit far above the galactic plane and likely belong to the thick disk, and two look metal poor, possibly thick disk or halo members.
arxiv-2511-01467:
Naqueeb Ahmad Warsi, Ayanava Dasgupta, and Masahito Hayashi study privacy for quantum data. Quantum differential privacy limits how much a mechanism's output can reveal about its input states; the authors approach it by defining when one pair of quantum states is more informative than another.

Their key result: if the hypothesis-testing divergence of one state pair dominates another's, the dominance holds for every f-divergence at once. That ordering completely characterizes private quantum mechanisms by identifying their most informative allowed state pairs. From it they derive precise limits for privatized hypothesis testing and for quantum parameter estimation. The limits include tight upper bounds on quantum Fisher information under privacy. They also get near-optimal contraction bounds for private quantum channels.
arxiv-2511-01667:
Qian-Nan Huang, Zhiping Xue, and Tao Yu report an unexpected resonance while driving a high-quality ferromagnet hard with microwaves. Scanning the transmission, they found a Fano resonance, a distinctive asymmetric peak, when the magnetization swings widely and the drive frequency sits close to, but not at, the ferromagnetic resonance.

Scattering theory explains the shape. The driven Kittel magnon, the uniform precession mode, interacts through a three-magnon process. Its partners are pairs of magnons with opposite wave vectors, at half the drive frequency. The measured signal probes fluctuations of the pair modes around the driven state. Those fluctuations damp far more slowly than the Kittel mode's. So the resonance betrays pairs with a record long lifetime. Such durable modes are prized for magnonic quantum information devices.
arxiv-2511-01867:
Zhengdong Hu, Chong Han, Wolfgang Gerstacker, and Robert Schober estimate wireless channels in the hardest setting going: millimeter-wave and terahertz systems with ultra-massive antenna arrays. These bands promise the bandwidth next-generation networks need. But severe path loss forces huge arrays with hybrid beamforming. The channel must be inferred from few radio-frequency chains. Near-field and far-field patterns mix as well.

Classical compressive sensing relies on fixed sparsifying dictionaries that cannot capture that hybrid structure. DiffPace instead learns the channel distribution with a diffusion model. The model is built on a hybrid spherical- and planar-wave channel model. DiffPace then uses it as a plug-and-play prior inside the estimation procedure. The learned prior replaces hand-made sparsity assumptions, improving channel estimation accuracy for the ultra-massive systems these future bands require.
arxiv-2511-01967:
Andrea Cozzumbo and four colleagues play detective on a cosmic embarrassment. Combined microwave background and baryon acoustic oscillation data lately prefer a total neutrino mass. The value sits below the minimum that oscillation experiments allow. It is even negative. Something in the analysis chain must be off, and the authors suspect gravitational lensing.

They introduce an effective neutrino mass parameter, allowed to go negative. They study its link with two extra parameters. These describe lensing's imprint on the microwave background. One covers the smoothing of the spectrum's peaks. The other rescales the lensing potential's amplitude. With lensing data from Planck and ACT and distance data from DESI, the inferred effective mass comes out consistent with the oscillation minimum. The apparent negative-mass preference, they conclude, is a short blanket. Late-time probes see more lensing than the Planck spectra imply. It is the known CMB lensing anomaly in disguise.
arxiv-2511-02067:
Ben Cassese, David Kipping, and six colleagues report what the James Webb Space Telescope saw during a rare event: the Jupiter-like planet Kepler-167e crossing its star. The planet's orbit takes over a thousand days, and the October 2024 transit was watched for nearly sixty hours. One goal was to measure the planet's oblateness, its flattening from spin, and to look for large moons.

Spherical and flattened planet models fit the data equally well, and slow drifts during the long exposure weakened the measurement. Using their most cautious analysis, the team bounds the flattening below about 0.097 with high confidence, which would mean a rotation period of at least about 7.11 hours if the spin axis lies in the sky plane. Other analysis choices gave tighter bounds.
arxiv-2511-02267:
Stoimen Stoimenov and Malte Henkel, theoretical physicists, derive the expected shapes of correlation functions for systems that are still ordering themselves after a quench. Phase-ordering kinetics describes domains growing as a disordered system settles, and its fingerprints are correlation functions measured at one time and at two times. The work concerns the case where the dynamical exponent takes the value two, the classic diffusive setting.

The authors obtain the generic forms of these correlators from the covariance of four-point response functions. Behind the calculation sits a new non-equilibrium representation of the Schrödinger algebra, a symmetry algebra of non-relativistic physics, and the scaling forms of the correlators follow from imposing that symmetry. The short paper, based on an earlier longer work by the same authors, presents the symmetry route as the organising principle for these ageing systems.
arxiv-2511-02367:
Shuning Zhang and ten co-authors measure a privacy risk hiding in ordinary home videos: what a vision-language model can infer about a person, beyond what is plainly shown. Inferential privacy is the danger that sensitive attributes get deduced from behaviour over time. To study it, the team crowdsourced 508 everyday personal videos from 58 individuals and benchmarked model inferences against human evaluators.

The models proved superhuman at this inference, beating the human judges by leveraging behavioural patterns across the temporal stream rather than merely recognising objects. The risk grew or shrank with video characteristics and with how the model was prompted. Worryingly, the models' own explanations for their inferences were unreliable: the objects they cited as evidence often were not what actually drove the conclusion, making everyday items misleading confounders in their accounts.
arxiv-2511-02467:
The NEXT Collaboration reports a calibration milestone for its newest detector in the search for a hypothetical nuclear decay that would rewrite neutrino physics. NEXT-100 is a high-pressure xenon gas chamber, holding about seventy kilograms of xenon, built to spot neutrinoless double-beta decay, an event so rare it has never been observed. Finding it demands superb energy resolution, and xenon gas technology is designed to deliver under one percent.

Using a thorium-228 calibration source, the team demonstrated a linear energy response and measured a resolution of 0.90 percent at the thallium-208 photopeak, full width at half maximum. Extrapolated to the decay's endpoint energy, the resolution is 0.93 percent, confirming the detector can measure energies precisely enough for the search. The result validates the design of the largest NEXT detector built so far.
arxiv-2511-02667:
Giacomo Camposampiero and four colleagues study compositional generalization, the skill of handling new mixes of known ideas. A model might know red and squares yet fail on a red square it never saw paired. Their 2025 paper notes that tests for this skill lack shared standards, and that big vision models lack the built-in biases the skill seems to need.

They offer a stricter test protocol that cuts the computing cost from combinatorial to constant. They also trained more than five thousand models to take stock of current vision backbones. Their Attribute Invariant Networks set a new balance point, lifting accuracy by over 23 percent over baselines while adding only 16 percent more parameters, far less than fully split designs.
arxiv-2511-02767:
Tyler Zhu and four colleagues run the first broad study of how video and text representations line up. Alignment between image and text encoders has revealed much about those models, but video adds time, which earlier work mostly skipped. Their 2025 study probes modern video and language encoders side by side.

Alignment strength depended heavily on how rich the test inputs were, both in frames and in captions. The team fit parametric test-time scaling laws that predicted the observed behavior well. Strong alignment with text also tracked with better scores on semantic and some non-semantic tasks, hinting at general-purpose video understanding. Temporal reasoning tests built on alignment gave the models a hard challenge. Video-text alignment, they conclude, is a cheap zero-shot probe of encoder power.
arxiv-2511-02967:
Edouard Sonin revisits the theory of ballistic SNS junctions, sandwiches where a normal metal sits between two superconductors. A recent theory said that, when the layers share the same Fermi speed and mass, phase gradients inside the superconducting leads cannot be ignored. His 2025 paper works out what that change does to the current-phase relation, the junction's basic fingerprint.

At zero temperature, the relation flips from forward-skewed to backward-skewed for short junctions. At moderate temperatures, the current stays flat with temperature and falls as the fourth power of the length, not exponentially as the old theory claimed. With mismatched Fermi speeds, the junction reverts to a standard Josephson weak link. Sonin also suggests the new picture explains backward-skewed curves seen in indium arsenide nanowire junctions.
arxiv-2511-03267:
Bingyang Guo and colleagues release IEC3D-AD, a new data set for spotting defects in factory parts with three-dimensional scans. Bearings, rings, and bolts from real production lines were scanned at fine detail, and flaws were marked with care. Older data sets, the authors say, miss the subtle faults and messy conditions found on actual shop floors.

Because the scans come straight from working lines, models trained or tested on them face problems closer to real use. Finer point clouds and sharper flaw labels make small defects harder to hide. The set targets methods that learn only from good parts and must flag odd ones without examples. Such a resource can help lift the safety and trust of automated checks on core equipment.
arxiv-2511-03467:
Lapo Santi and Nial Friel merge a classic ranking model with a clustering model so tied groups get ranked together. The Bradley-Terry model ranks items from pairwise wins and losses, while a stochastic block model clusters items into groups. Their combined model ranks the clusters, with items inside one cluster sharing a tied rank.

A Bayesian setup learns cluster count, cluster strengths, and assignments all at once. A fast Gibbs sampler, built through a Thurstonian augmentation trick, keeps the learning efficient and its summaries readable. The motivating case ranks men's tennis players from two decades of tour results. Top players fall into broad tiers, a picture fans and analysts can grasp faster than a strict list.
arxiv-2511-03667:
Luigi D'Amico and colleagues tame prior dependence in hierarchical Bayesian fits for pulsar timing arrays. Those arrays hunt gravitational waves by watching clock-like stars, yet their models tangle astrophysics, pulsar noise, and nuisance terms in a high-dimensional web. Results can hinge too much on prior choices where parameters lean on each other.

A reparameterization using normalizing flows untangles the hierarchy, separating prior-governing terms from the astrophysics of interest.
