Meng Hua and co-authors blend in-context learning with deep joint coding for image sends. Joint source-channel coding sends images over noisy links in one learned step. Over MIMO links, with many antennas, the task gets harder. Channel states shift fast.

Large models can learn from a few examples in context. The team uses that skill to adapt the coder on the fly. Few-shot adaptation avoids retraining for each new channel. Adaptive coding could keep image quality high on mobile links where conditions change by the second. Context examples ride in the signal itself, so the receiver needs no side channel to learn the sender's code for each new image.
arxiv-2512-01667:
Qingyang Liu and co-authors detect model flaws in Bayesian inverse problems. Bayesian inference is optimal when the model fits. When it does not, results can fail badly. Many post-Bayesian fixes have been offered for that risk.

Their method uses variational gradient descent to spot misspecification. Predictively oriented views lift the model itself during checks. A clear flaw alarm lets users fix the model before trusting its answers. That guard matters in imaging and geophysics, where inverse answers guide costly acts. The check runs after fitting, so it guards real workflows where a flawed model has already shaped the data analysis once.
arxiv-2512-01767:
Tsvetana Stoyanova proves non-integrability of the Sasano system of a stated affine type. The system is a four-dimensional nonlinear set of differential equations. It has affine Weyl group symmetries. It is also a time-dependent Hamiltonian system, seen as coupled Painleve III systems.

Non-integrability means no full set of conserved quantities exists. Proving it rules out exact solution by classic means. The result guides scholars to numeric or asymptotic tools for this system. Coupled Painleve systems arise in random matrices and statistical physics. Hamiltonian form sharpens the proof's bite, since integrable Hamiltonian systems are common enough that a ruled-out case saves much wasted search.
arxiv-2512-02067:
Dark energy drives the cosmos to expand faster and faster. How strong it is hangs on how the growth of structure is counted. Mauro Carfora and Francesca Familiari give in 2025 a shape-based route to that link. They compare lightcones, the full records of all light that can reach one watcher.

Their route skips step-by-step approximations. It lets a standard watcher gauge a distance that shifts with scale and ties to the dark energy share. Such work counts, since the standard model's tale of late-time structure still grates against its dark energy claims. A cleaner gauge could help settle how much of the cosmos is dark energy at all.
arxiv-2512-02267:
Partitions split a whole number into parts. Some chance rules on them tie into growth and random matrix work. Jimmy He and Michael Wheeler study two such rules in 2025. Both have a free edge: the q-Whittaker process and the Hall-Littlewood process.

They prove a neat fact about one gauge of the q-Whittaker rule. After a random shift, that gauge gains a symmetry in two dials at once. The proof broadens past work by Imamura, Mucciconi, and Sasamoto, and a later growth of it by He. Such symmetries are the hinges of this field. They turn one solved case into a spring of exact formulas.
arxiv-2512-02667:
Haozhuo Zheng, Cheng Wang, and Yang Liu generate new molecules with a two stage transformer system. Designing molecules with wanted traits is slow when each candidate must be built and tested. Diffusion models generate well but cost heavy compute, while step by step models can drift into errors.

Their Graph VQ-Transformer first compresses molecules into high fidelity discrete codes. A transformer then writes new codes, which decode into full molecular graphs. The design aims for diffusion level accuracy at lower cost, helping chemists search larger chemical spaces for drugs and materials. Codes that keep the shape of the whole graph keep the traits that make a drug work or fail.
arxiv-2512-03067:
Difu Feng and five co-authors measure how easily a user could escape a recommendation filter bubble. Recommender systems shape what users see by modeling their preferences closely. That strategy reinforces existing tastes, trapping users in filter bubbles linked to group polarization.

Reasonable measures of bubbles are needed before platforms can fix them. Their behavior aware measure uses contrastive simulation to score escape potential. A number for escapability lets platforms compare designs and prove that a change truly widens what users can discover. A score for how stuck a user is turns a vague gripe about feeds into a mark. Shops can be held to that mark when they tune what folks see each day.
arxiv-2512-03167:
When two theories meet at a surface, energy can cross or bounce. Avik Banerjee and Giuseppe Policastro study that meeting point in this 2025 work. They look at conformal field theories changed by a known deformation, joined by an interface.

Such interfaces show a broad pattern in how much energy passes and how much reflects. The authors examine those shares for the deformed case. Their results add to the theory of defects in quantum systems. That theory helps model wires, junctions, and other sharp joins in physics. Reflection shares guide how energy moves in devices built from joined quantum materials.
arxiv-2512-03367:
A neat correspondence links operators to pairs of simpler objects. Weixi Chen, Mee Seong Im, Mikhail Khovanov, Catherine Lillja, and Nicolas Rugo extend that link in this 2025 work. Tom Leinster gave a bijection between operators on a vector space and certain pairs.

Each pair holds a nilpotent operator and a vector. The authors study pairs of eventually constant maps and nilpotent pairs. Over a finite field, such counts give exact probabilities, like the chance an operator is nilpotent. The work blends algebra and combinatorics in a clean way. Counting over finite fields turns an abstract bijection into exact, testable numbers.
arxiv-2512-03467:
Chronic diseases progress in a few typical patterns, not random ones. Hongtao Hao and Joseph Austerweil present a Bayesian event-based model in this 2025 work. They build on work with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

Their model infers disease subtypes and stages from mostly cross-sectional data. It estimates how many subtypes exist, the order of progression for each, and each patient's subtype. Knowing a patient's pattern can guide prognosis and trial design. The method aims to capture structured differences among patients. Subtype labels could refine prognosis, since two patients at one stage may face different futures depending on their progression pattern.
arxiv-2512-03967:
Dataset distillation squeezes a huge training set into a small synthetic one that teaches models almost as well. Keith Ando Ogawa and colleagues survey how that idea has been adapted from images to text in a 2025 technical report. Vision research built a large literature first, while text lagged behind, partly because words are discrete and resist the smooth tricks used on pixels.

The report traces milestones: transformer-based methods, techniques generating genuinely discrete synthetic text, and scaling to decoder-only models over a billion parameters. It then catalogues the open problems honestly. Benchmarks are not yet standardised, complex tasks remain hard, and clear real-world applications are still scarce. The authors present the area as maturing rather than finished. Their review maps the main distillation strategies and the key contributions behind each, giving newcomers a structured entry point.
arxiv-2512-04367:
Yun Piao and seven co-authors introduce AgentBay, a sandbox service that lets people step into an AI agent's work at any moment. Agents built on large language models can run multi-step tasks on their own. Yet they still stumble on odd real-world cases, so human backup stays vital for high-stakes work. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the handoff into the system from the ground up.

AgentBay gives each task a safe, sealed workspace across Windows, Linux, Android, web browsers, and code tools. An agent drives the space through standard program interfaces. A human operator can seize full manual control at any time, then hand the task back. A custom streaming protocol, built for this swap, keeps the view smooth where older remote tools lag. The design aims at smooth joint work between people and agents.
arxiv-2512-04567:
Sotiris Kotitsas, Marco Romito, and Zhilin Yang revisit how random ripples in a moving fluid settle into a simple Gaussian pattern at large scales. Their equation, the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz Navier-Stokes system, adds thermal noise to fluid flow. Earlier work by another team derived the large-scale limit at and above the critical dimension. Their 2025 arXiv paper redoes the analysis and corrects part of it.

With standard diffusive scaling in three or more dimensions, and a weaker coupling scaling in two, the ripples converge to a stochastic heat equation. Its key coefficient comes out nontrivially renormalized by the noise. The team also expands that coefficient in higher dimensions and shows a published conjecture for it was wrong. Their proof tracks how the flow's vector twists under the Leray projection case by case. Clean limits like these anchor theories of fluctuating fluids.
arxiv-2512-04667:
Fedor Gnetov and Valentin Konakov prove limit theorems for a random walk that moves through rank-one symmetric spaces, curved worlds that generalize hyperbolic space. This family includes quaternionic and complex hyperbolic spaces, plus the Cayley plane. On such ground, plain addition fails, so even defining a walk takes care. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the walk from a non-Euclidean summation that extends Möbius addition beyond constant curvature.

With that walk defined, three classic results follow. A law of large numbers fixes the walk's drift. A central limit theorem and a local limit theorem describe its spread. Properly rescaled, the walk converges to the heat kernel of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, which plays the role of the normal law here. The proofs lean on harmonic analysis with spherical functions. These are the first such results in this setting, and they anchor probability on curved spaces.
arxiv-2512-04967:
Jasmaine Khale and Ravi Prakash Srivastava present a few-shot learning framework that diagnoses retinal diseases from fundus photos when labeled examples are few and lopsided. Eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy and macular degeneration are rising worldwide. Standard deep learning needs large, balanced, hand-labeled sets that clinics rarely have. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on the Retinal Fundus Multi-Disease Image Dataset, focusing on its ten most common classes.

Even those ten classes are badly imbalanced, with common diseases dwarfing rare ones. The framework answers with balanced episodic training: each practice episode draws classes evenly, so rare diseases get fair rehearsal. Sampling and training choices reinforce the balance. The goal is a model that spots the rare case, not just the frequent one. Fairer few-shot tools could carry specialist-level screening to clinics with small archives.
arxiv-2512-05167:
Fang Li describes a two-part course design for teaching artificial intelligence that deliberately bridges old and new. Students first learn traditional machine learning — the established techniques behind classification, regression, and clustering — and then move on to contemporary large language models and their applications. The sequence is meant to show how the field evolved while building working skill with both the classic toolkit and the newest one.

Li details the course architecture, the strategies used to run it, how students were assessed, and what they learned, drawing on a summer delivery spread over two seven-week terms. The integrated approach, she reports, deepened students' grasp of the wider artificial intelligence landscape and left them better prepared for industry needs. The design offers a template for programmes struggling to honour the fundamentals without short-changing the technology employers now expect graduates to know.
arxiv-2512-05267:
Osvaldo Simeone and Yaniv Romano review how AI should handle not knowing — the uncertainty that comes from having too little training data. In fields like robotics, telecommunications, and healthcare, data scarcity is the norm, and the uncertainty that results, the kind more data would cure, caps performance. The review organizes the field's answers along two lines: measuring that uncertainty honestly, and fighting the scarcity itself with made-up data.

The tour covers generalized Bayesian learning, which softens the classical posterior to cope with flawed models, and post-Bayes frameworks beyond it. Bounds from information theory then tie the amount of training data to predictive uncertainty, grounding the Bayesian story. The review continues with methods carrying finite-sample guarantees, including conformal prediction and conformal risk control, and ends with recipes that stretch limited labelled data using abundant model predictions. Throughout, information measures supply the common currency.
arxiv-2512-05967:
Francesco Granata, Francesco Poggi, and Misael Mongiovì add a factual compass to retrieval augmented tutoring in Italian. Retrieval systems fetch passages by semantic similarity, which can misfire in specialized fields where terms are ambiguous. ELERAG links entities in a question to Wikidata, and uses that signal to re-rank what was fetched. Reciprocal re-ranking rewards passages both signals agree on.

The testbeds are a custom academic dataset and the Italian version of a standard question answering benchmark. In the specialized, educational setting, ELERAG beat both plain retrieval baselines and strong cross-encoder configurations. On the general domain set, the cross-encoders won instead. The authors read that split as the domain mismatch effect in action: no single ranking strategy rules everywhere. The upshot is a tutoring assistant whose answers lean on identified facts.
arxiv-2512-06167:
Nima Ghafari Cherati, Arsalan Hashemi, and Ádám Gali catalog the ways extra carbon atoms can hide inside diamond. These defects shape diamond's electronic behavior. With density functional theory and potential models, the team studies clusters of one to six interstitials.

Clusters grow more stable as they compact; a four interstitial platelet is especially stable. Bonding in the cores turns more polar. Clusters of one, two, five, and six add gap states; three and four stay silent. Core vibrations are fingerprints in infrared spectra. The 3H center is identified as a neutral di-interstitial. Experimentalists get a naming guide.
arxiv-2512-06267:
Seomgeun Shim studies a two player game played on points inside a shape system, where each move must dodge a trap. Players take turns picking points, one by one. The loser is the first player whose pick makes the closure of all picked points swallow a fixed target set. Such dodge games sound simple, yet who wins can hinge on fine details of the shape system in play.

Shim rebuilds the theory of these games from the ground up. He works out their nim numbers, a classic score that tells which player holds the edge and how plays combine. The results cover point systems drawn from trees, both from their corners and from their edges, plus cases where the target set is made of the extreme points of the system. The work ties a playful game to deep tools from the math of shapes and games.
arxiv-2512-06367:
Yidong Zhou, Mingxian Zhong, and Shenwei Huang settle a case of a classic puzzle about coloring networks. The puzzle asks whether the points of a network can be painted with three colors so that no linked pair shares a color. Some networks ban a path of a set length as a clean sub pattern. Others are forced to have all their odd cycles, loops with an odd count of points, at exactly one set length.

The authors focus on networks that ban the ten point path and whose odd cycles all have seven points. They give an algorithm that answers the three coloring question for any such network in a reasonable run time. Coloring questions like this one are usually hard in general, so carving out families where a fast answer exists is a steady theme in graph theory. Their result adds one more settled family to that map.
arxiv-2512-06467:
Florian Kammuller builds a machine checked proof of privacy for learning systems spread across a swarm of satellites. In federated learning, small devices train a shared model and send only updates to a server, which suits tiny hardware in orbit. That setup invites a newer attack that leaks training data from the shared updates themselves. Defenses exist, but few rest on rigorous proof, and that gap is what this study attacks.

Working inside the Isabelle proof assistant, with a framework for insiders and infrastructure, Kammuller extends a formal account of differential privacy for such dynamic systems. He ties that account to the notion of attacker advantage, a measure of how much an attack really gains. The satellite swarm serves both as the driving example and as the test case where the theory is applied. It gives a verified base for judging privacy claims in such systems.
arxiv-2512-06667:
Yu-Hao Wang and three co authors map a family of wave packets that hold their shape in a three part medium. The packets are vector solitons: linked waves with one dark dip and two bright humps, in a Manakov model where the parts repel each other. Nondegenerate forms, where the bright parts carry differing counts, turn out to come in far more variety than expected.

For fixed particle counts and speed, the team finds four distinct branches, differing in their density shapes and phase patterns. Two branches carry positive mass and two negative. Their energy speed curves pair up into two closed loops, independent of each other, and all branches share one top speed set by the larger bright count. Small disturbances leave every branch stable. In wider systems with more components, the branch count doubles with each added part, in a clean pattern the authors work out.
arxiv-2512-06867:
John Licato, Stephen Steinle, and Brayden Hollis test whether giving a language model a persona changes how well it plays a strategy game,. Their arena is PERIL, an open-source board game of world conquest released with the study. Some personas, especially ones linked to strategic thought, are turned into game heuristics, the rough rules a player uses to judge moves.

Raw personas alone did not help. Gains appeared only when a mediator step translated the persona into numeric heuristics in a structured way. That translation borrows from factor analysis, a classic tool for turning questionnaire answers into trait scores. Heuristics built this way proved more reliable and more sensible than ones the model guessed directly. The authors argue the mediator idea gives researchers a cleaner way to study persona effects on machine decisions, with lessons for any setting where models must act, not just chat.
arxiv-2512-07267:
Samuel Rey and Gonzalo Mateos learn the wiring diagram of cause and effect inside data that unfolds over time. Several series are assumed to drive each other through a linear model with both instant links and delayed ones. The instant links must form a directed acyclic graph, a web with no loops, to read as causal structure. Recent learning methods enforce loop-freedom with smooth but non-convex conditions, leaving solvers stuck at possibly second-rate answers.

The key assumption here is friendlier: all instant links carry non-negative weight. Under that sign rule, loop-freedom can be imposed with a convex constraint instead, turning the whole recovery problem convex. A method-of-multipliers solver then finds the answer with a guarantee no non-convex rival can offer: the solution is globally optimal. On synthetic time series with known ground truth, the method beat existing alternatives.
arxiv-2512-07467:
Ben Moews wrote this 2025 criminology paper on how crime risk shifts across a city over time. Police prevention work depends on reading patterns in space and time. Hot spots, where incidents cluster, are the usual focus of that effort.

Moews studies Chicago crime reports covering more than two decades. His cluster analysis allows hot spots of different densities rather than one fixed size. He then tracks how the mix of crime types inside each cluster changes. Some risks look permanent, while others flare up and fade away. The COVID-19 pandemic left a clear mark on the crime mix. Its effects also depended on what each city area is mainly used for. Some crime types prove harder to shift than others. Spatial checks show clusters differ in how evenly incidents spread around them. Moews closes by weighing data bias, a risk he says criminology too often neglects.
arxiv-2512-07667:
Gracjan Góral, Marysia Winkels, and Steven Basart wrote this 2025 paper on honest language models. A model can know the right answer inside yet state a falsehood aloud. That is a failure of honesty, not of knowledge, and it corrodes trust.

Steering offers a fix that needs no retraining at all. A nudge to the model's inner activations can draw out truthful reporting. Earlier work applied that nudge at a single layer, which proved brittle. The authors spread the nudge across the network's depth instead. A Gaussian schedule weights the middle depths most heavily. They test seven models from three well-known families on the MASK benchmark. That benchmark is built to separate honesty from raw knowledge. The Gaussian schedule improves honesty in nearly every model tested. Careful ablations show the depth pattern matters beyond total strength. Random, uniform, and flat allocations all lose to the bell-shaped one.
arxiv-2512-09067:
Luis Rangel DaCosta and Mary Scott study how well neural networks for electron microscopy generalize. Networks are effective for hard scientific tasks, but they often degrade outside the training distribution. Ground truth is hard in real experiments, so simulated data offer control.

The team trains and tests thousands of segmentation networks on synthetic high resolution transmission electron microscopy data. Structures are sampled randomly and images are simulated with a standard multislice method. Using the contrast transfer function of the microscope, they build a framework to compare information content across data sets and to quantify domain shift. Segmentation stays fairly stable, yet it worsens smoothly and predictably as imaging conditions move away from training. The authors also discuss limits of their approach for other shifts, such as atomic structure changes.
arxiv-2512-09167:
Pekka Koskela, Tapio Rajala, and Yi Ru-Ya Zhang work in geometric analysis. Their question is when functions defined inside a flat region can be extended to the whole plane without losing control of their derivatives. Regions with that property are called extension domains. The authors settle the borderline case for a Sobolev space where only first derivatives are measured in the weakest useful way.

They prove a bounded, simply connected planar region is such an extension domain in exactly one case. Any two outside points must be joinable by an outside curve satisfying a stated integral bound. As consequences, a Jordan domain has this extension property exactly when it has the bounded-variation extension property, and exactly when its complementary region is an extension domain for bounded derivatives. The equivalence ties together three notions that had been studied separately.
arxiv-2512-09467:
Yezi Liu and colleagues propose a new fairness regularizer for machine learning, a penalty term added during training. It keeps predictions from depending on sensitive attributes such as race or sex. Existing ones are built from mismatched distance measures and design choices, making them hard to predict and their results uneven across tasks. The authors start by asking what traits a good one should have.

They sort in-process methods into three families: matching prediction statistics across groups, aligning internal states, and directly cutting the link between predictions and sensitive traits. From that survey they identify desirable traits for the underlying distance metric, including tight generalization bounds and scale robustness. Their Cauchy-Schwarz regularizer penalizes a divergence between group prediction distributions, with theory showing tighter bounds than several divergences. On four tabular benchmarks and one image dataset it improved fairness while keeping accuracy competitive and stable.
arxiv-2512-09567:
Chung-Lin Shan reports, in a conference paper, a 3D picture of how dark matter particles would scatter inside a detector. The particles in question are WIMPs, weakly interacting massive particles, a leading dark matter candidate. Theory usually gives the velocity spread of all dark matter particles in the galaxy, but a detector only ever sees the ones that happen to scatter off its target nuclei.

Shan's effective velocity distribution describes that scattering subset. It comes from a double Monte Carlo run that follows 3D elastic collisions between WIMPs and nuclei, event by event. The results display an asymmetric forward-backward pattern in the effective spread, a feature the raw galactic spread does not show in the same way. The paper is based on earlier published work and was prepared for the TAUP 2025 conference on astroparticle and underground physics, aimed at researchers designing and interpreting direct detection experiments.
arxiv-2512-09967:
Maryam Babaei, Peter Rucz, Manfred Kaltenbacher, and Stefan Schoder combine two methods to sharpen solutions of partial differential equations. The finite element method gives solution values at mesh nodes, but little between them. Their hybrid adds least squares support vector regression with Legendre polynomial kernels. The regression produces a closed form formula inside each element, consistent with the finite element values on its boundary. The effect is element wise super resolution: a cheap low order computation gains high order detail, without rewriting the original solver.

The authors report accuracy far above the base finite element solution. Their hybrid matches a standalone finite element run using the same higher order basis. Convergence studies on four elliptic boundary value problems support the method's reliability. The algorithm works as a plug in for low order solvers, and even for expensive or under resolved experimental data.
arxiv-2512-10067:
Jiahao Liu and Senhao Cao propose Independent Density Estimation, a method for teaching vision language models to compose ideas. Big models caption images and generate images from text impressively, yet they generalize poorly to new combinations of familiar elements, unlike people. The authors' idea is to learn the link between each individual word and the matching image features separately. Composition then happens at inference, by combining the per word predictions with an entropy based rule. Two models embody the philosophy, one using fully disentangled visual features, the other learning partially disentangled features with a variational autoencoder.

Across several datasets, their models generalized to unseen compositions better than current alternatives. The gain supports the core bet: compositionality improves when a model is forced to ground words independently before combining them. End to end training lets a model memorize whole captions and their images, which fails exactly when a new pairing appears.
arxiv-2512-10167:
Anwesh Majumder leads a team using the XRISM satellite's Resolve instrument to measure gas motions in the core of Cygnus A, a famous radio galaxy inside a galaxy cluster. Their long exposure resolves X-ray emission lines sharply enough to read velocities. The intracluster gas comes in two temperatures. The hotter phase moves with a broad velocity spread and a modest bulk drift relative to the central galaxy. The cooler phase, nearer the center, is broader still, and the two phases can differ in line of sight velocity by several hundred kilometers per second.

The team reads the large spreads as turbulence plus bulk motion driven by the cocoon shock from the galaxy's radio jets. The kinetic energy in the motions matches the energy of the central radio source. Energy injection exceeds radiative cooling, so the jets are winning.
arxiv-2512-10767:
Andrea Conti and Ricardo Stuardo build holographic models of defects inside maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. A defect is a lower-dimensional slice of the theory with its own physics, and here the defects, of codimension two, twist the theory's R-symmetry as one circles them, a monodromy. Through holography, each such gauge theory setup corresponds to a solution of type II supergravity, and the authors construct three of them.

The solutions come from branes wrapped on spindle geometries, with parameters tuned and boundary conditions imposed to land on a genuine defect. The authors give a prescription for the entanglement entropy of the effective theory living on the defect. And find it proportional to the free energy of the surrounding theory. A parallel attempt with a wrapped D5-brane refuses to cooperate: adjusting its domain yields a circle compactification instead of a defect, a useful negative result.
arxiv-2512-10967:
Subham Kumar and colleagues audit speech recognition tools used to record clinical visits in India. Reliability in multilingual, diverse health settings is still largely unknown, so the team tested leading systems on real clinical interviews. The speech covers Kannada, Hindi, and Indian English, including mixed and everyday spoken forms.

Some systems handled Indian English fairly well but failed on code-mixed or local speech. Errors also varied with who was speaking, with gaps linked to patient versus clinician roles and to gender. The authors provide a broad multilingual benchmark and fairness analysis. Their message is that clinical speech tools for India must be built and tested with local languages and diverse speakers in mind.
arxiv-2512-11067:
Guorui Xiao and colleagues propose KathDB, a database system that answers questions over mixed data such as tables, text, images, and video. Traditional database systems run precise SQL queries but only over structured tables, and writing complex SQL is hard. Newer multimodal systems either expose low level controls or hand everything to a black box language model, losing clarity.

KathDB keeps relational meaning and strong query guarantees while using foundation models to reason over the unstructured parts. People stay in the loop at three stages: while the query is parsed, while it runs, and while results are explained. Users can steer the system step by step and still receive explainable answers. The design aims to combine database reliability with modern AI flexibility.
arxiv-2512-11167:
Anatole Jacquin de Margerie, Alexis Roger, and Irina Rish reproduce and probe a vision language model that reads high resolution images by cutting them into tiles. Reproducibility is a stated foundation of science, yet complex multimodal models often lack clear implementation details or usable training code. The original Monkey model used tiling to recover fine detail while keeping computation manageable.

Working from open checkpoints, the team rebuilt the training pipeline and repeated the experiments. They confirmed the central claim that tiling does recover local details. They then varied the design by adding a view of the whole image alongside the tiles, studying how global context changes results. Effects differed from the original report in size, depending strongly on the task and on how fine the tiles were cut, a caution for future high resolution modelling.
arxiv-2512-11367:
John Tanner and colleagues test quantum machine learning on the practical problem of spotting illegal fishing from radar satellite images. Unreported fishing costs the world economy tens of billions of dollars yearly and undermines ocean governance. Synthetic aperture radar sees through weather and darkness, but classifying small objects in its grainy images is hard.

The study applies quantum kernel methods, which map data into quantum states to measure similarity, to real radar image chips from the SARFish dataset. Two tasks were tackled: telling vessels from non vessels, and fishing vessels from other vessels. Against classical kernels in a kernel only comparison, quantum kernels on real valued chips matched or beat the best classical results in the best case. A quantum encoding of the full complex radar data, however, overfitted and performed poorly. As the first such application to maritime radar, the work maps both promise and present limits.
arxiv-2512-11867:
Daniil Zverev, A Sophia Koepke, and Joao F Henriques warn against training models on their own output over and over. Synthetic data can top up training sets, but repeated cycles risk drift and quiet collapse. The team studies the danger through continual learning, where models learn task after task.

The closest cousin is Generative Experience Replay, where a model rehearses its own fakes to avoid forgetting. Stats analysis shows synthetic data adds bias and variance that weaken standard training logic. Experiments show popular generators collapse under repeated self training. Top replay methods also fail to keep their inner maps aligned. The findings urge care wherever fake data feeds future models.
arxiv-2512-11967:
Kaito Kobayashi, Benjamin Sappler, and Frank Pollmann propose holographic tensor networks that can hold far more entanglement than standard ones. Matrix product states and their kin excel when entanglement obeys an area law. Highly entangled, volume law states force them into exponential cost.

The new states add one extra dimension of tensors, mimicking a holographic bulk, while keeping each tensor isometric so calculations stay cheap. Random cases already show volume law entanglement at fixed bond size. Built and tuned cases cover fermionic Gaussian states, Clifford states, rainbow states, and briefly evolved states. A time evolution algorithm runs on the new states, though errors build over sweeps. The ansatz widens what tensor methods can touch.
arxiv-2512-12067:
Martine S Lenders and co-authors show that a binary web format, CBOR, could slim the modern web. Speed work has focused on transport and static files. Dynamic content, served as JSON or DNS over HTTPS, keeps growing and adds delay, worst for users on weak links.

Swapping JSON for CBOR cut data by up to 80 percent and load times by up to 13.8 percent for large objects, even on local tests. For DNS, name only compression with plain CBOR saved 52.2 percent, while packed CBOR reached 95.5 percent. Their tiny name decoder fits in 314 bytes of code. Parts of the work already shaped IETF standards, a sign the idea has legs beyond the lab.
arxiv-2512-12167:
Yoav Gelberg, Koshi Eguchi, Takuya Akiba, and Edoardo Cetin offer a simple fix for a language model limit in a 2025 paper. Models read only as much text as they saw in training, unless users pay for costly extra training on longer text. Their method, DroPE, drops position codes after training ends.

Position codes help models learn fast, the authors argue, but they also block use on longer text. After a short recalibration, models without the codes handled longer text with no long text training at all. Results held across models and data sizes. DroPE beat both special designs and common scaling tricks for rotary position codes.
arxiv-2512-12467:
Bichan Wu and Jonathan Pillow offer a tutorial on reduced rank regression for neural communication in a 2025 paper. The method finds a low dimensional linear map between high dimensional inputs and outputs. Neuroscientists use it to find communication subspaces, the small sets of patterns through which one brain region talks to another.

The tutorial covers the math from the ground up and compares the method with singular value decomposition, principal components analysis, and canonical correlation analysis. It derives extensions with ridge regularization and non-spherical noise. New metrics measure communication strength and how well communication axes align with main activity modes. Practical guidance runs throughout for applying it to neural data.
arxiv-2512-12967:
Weizhou Shen and co-authors introduce QwenLong-L1.5, a language model trained to reason over very long texts. Many tasks need a model to link facts spread across a huge document. Simply stretching the context window does not solve tasks that run past millions of tokens.

Three ideas drive the work. A pipeline builds hard multi-hop training tasks from split-up documents. A steadier form of reinforcement learning suits long texts. A memory system handles inputs past four million tokens. Built on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking, the model gained 9.90 points on average over its base. Its memory agent added 9.48 points on ultra-long tasks.
arxiv-2512-13067:
Michael Choi, Ryan Lim, and Youjia Wang study Markov chains that are averaged over a group action, a symmetry of the state space. Adding symmetry based moves can help a sampling algorithm mix faster. They compare three ways to build such moves, based on Gibbs, Metropolis-Hastings, and Barker rules.

They also study sandwiches and mixtures that combine the base chain with these orbit moves. Every sandwich has a spectral gap at least as large as the original reversible chain, a sign of faster mixing. For one key case they bound the variance and identify the chain as an information projection. A Curie-Weiss example shows polynomial mixing where standard dynamics is exponentially slow.
arxiv-2512-13167:
Kathrin Bringmann, Jay Jorgenson, and Lejla Smajlovic study a generating function built from Niebur-Poincare series, special functions tied to a Fuchsian group with a cusp. A generating function packs a whole sequence of such series into one object that can be studied at a special point.

At that point, they link the generating function to the resolvent kernel of the hyperbolic Laplacian and to a non-holomorphic Eisenstein series. For whole-number values of the parameter, the function equals series built from polylogarithms. A second generating function, built from derivatives, is expressed using the Rogers dilogarithm and the Kronecker limit function.
arxiv-2512-13467:
Maike de Jongh, Cristian Spitoni, and Emilio Cirillo search for optimal strategies to grow a lattice structure from two starting seeds. Similar growth problems appear in crystallization and in biofilm formation on patterned surfaces. Their model is a two-dimensional, zero-temperature system of short-range spin interactions.

Starting from two positive clusters, the goal is to steer the whole lattice to the uniformly positive state as efficiently as possible using external tweaks. They cast the task as a Markov decision process and compare growth geometries. Optimal strategies are identified across three representative regimes, showing how the best steering depends on the starting shape and interaction setting.
arxiv-2512-13667:
Cristina Aggazzotti and Elizabeth Allyn Smith ask whether speech transcripts alone can reveal who spoke. Forensic work often needs to name an unknown speaker from ransom calls, covert recordings, or anonymous messages. Voice traits fail when a speaker disguises their voice or uses text-to-speech tools.

Their method, StyloSpeaker, uses character, word, token, sentence, and style traits drawn from authorship studies. It judges whether two transcripts came from the same speaker. Normalized transcripts, stripped of capitals and punctuation, gave higher scores in most tests. The strongest topic control gave the best results overall. They also compare their explainable model with black-box neural methods and rank which style traits split speakers best.
arxiv-2512-13967:
Emma Dinowitz and co-authors study potentially positive elements in free groups, a topic in group theory. A word in a free group is potentially positive if some automorphism turns it into a word written with only positive exponents. Sorting such words, and counting them, is hard.

The authors develop automata to analyze traits of potentially positive words. With those tools, they give new bounds on the long-run growth of such elements in free groups with 2 to 7 generators. For the two-generator case, the bounds are tight, fixing the growth function up to a constant factor. They also show that certain restricted automata cannot recognize the set of potentially positive elements, a limit on machine-based approaches.
arxiv-2512-14067:
Yonggan Fu and co-authors present Efficient-DLM, a family of diffusion language models made from autoregressive ones. Diffusion models generate in parallel and can be fast, but training them from scratch learns more slowly than autoregressive training. Converting a pretrained autoregressive model is their route to speed without losing accuracy.

They compare attention patterns and find keeping pretrained weight patterns is key for conversion. Their block-wise attention stays causal across blocks while allowing bidirectional modeling inside each block, which also enables KV caching. A position-dependent masking strategy closes the gap between training and test mask patterns. Efficient-DLM 8B beat Dream 7B by 5.4 points of accuracy at 4.5 times the throughput, and Qwen3 4B by 2.7 points at 2.7 times the throughput.
arxiv-2512-14167:
Jakub Kusnir and four coauthors build a detailed simulation of transient grating spectroscopy in a 2025 paper. The method uses a brief laser pulse to create thermal and acoustic patterns on a material surface, and reading those patterns reveals elastic and thermal traits from one test.

Their finite element model fully couples heat and motion fields and also models the optical detection step. Custom two dimensional elements make it suited to anisotropic solids, whose traits differ by direction and lack simple formulas. The model captures very early acoustic features that carry extra data on elastic traits. It also lets researchers test changes to the experiment in software first.
arxiv-2512-14467:
Neelakantan Padmanabhan speeds up a shortcut for thermal engineering. The LPLSP method builds a small, fast model of how a device heats and cools, replacing heavy fluid simulations. Earlier versions needed many separate simulation runs, one to excite each heat source. His version extracts every model coefficient from a single run where all sources vary at once.

Two extra tricks, rank reduction and a two-stage split of the estimation, keep the cost down for larger systems. The small models matched full simulations within about five percent on average temperature. Building one takes seconds, so fresh digital twins can be generated automatically.
arxiv-2512-14867:
F. Mireles and E. Ortiz study a jittery quirk of electrons in crystals called Zitterbewegung, a rapid trembling motion predicted by quantum theory. In systems with several energy bands, this trembling was already known to link with charge flow, Berry curvature, and the Chern number. The authors ask what it says about spin based effects.

They show that optical spin conductivity and the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity are also tied to the size of the trembling. For multiband models of Dirac type, spin textures, the patterns of spin direction across states, connect directly to the trembling as well. That link lets researchers tell whether the oscillations are present just by reading spin textures. Worked examples show cases where certain trembling modes are suppressed.
arxiv-2512-14967:
Felipe J. P. Antunes and two coauthors build a deep learning method for a hard class of equations in finance and economics. McKean-Vlasov forward backward equations describe systems where each agent reacts to the average of all agents, like banks lending to each other. Common noise, shocks that hit everyone at once, makes them far harder to solve.

Their method mixes Picard iterations with a trick from forecast scoring called elicitability. That trick yields a path wise loss, so neural networks can learn the backward process and the needed averages without nested Monte Carlo runs. A recurrent network handles the mean field term, and a hybrid network handles the backward part. On an interbank lending model with a known answer, the method recovers the true solution well. It also handles quantile based interactions and a complex growth model with no closed form answer.
arxiv-2512-15067:
Zijiang Yan and four coauthors forecast radio wave exposure levels with a diffusion model that knows its own uncertainty. Wireless growth has raised the need to predict electromagnetic field levels for safety compliance and network planning. Most earlier work forecast one wideband total, missing how levels vary by operator and by frequency band.

Their system, EMFusion, forecasts many narrow band series at once. A residual U-Net with cross attention folds in context like time of day, season, and holidays. An imputation based sampler treats forecasting as filling a gap, which keeps the output coherent when measurements are irregular. Instead of one number, it gives probability intervals drawn from the learned distribution. On test data it beat the best baseline by 23.85 percent in CRPS and 13.93 percent in normalized error.
arxiv-2512-15367:
Benoit Cadorel, Ya Deng, and Katsutoshi Yamanoi study hyperbolicity of complex quasi projective varieties in a 2025 math paper, the second part of a three part series. Hyperbolicity concerns which varieties admit no nonconstant holomorphic maps from the complex plane. The team works with varieties that carry a big and reductive representation of their fundamental group.

For every Galois conjugate variety, they prove the generalized Green Griffiths Lang conjecture. When the representation is also large, the special sets marking the non hyperbolic locus agree across conjugates. Under a semisimplicity condition, a proper closed subset traps all entire curves. The results extend earlier theorems from projective to quasi projective varieties.
arxiv-2512-15467:
Vladimir Muller and Yuri Tomilov prove time dependent versions of classic operator results in a 2025 paper. The classic results concern compressions of bounded operators, which restrict an operator to a smaller space, and diagonals, the entries along the main diagonal. Here operators are replaced by continuous functions whose values are operators.

The authors also treat the setting of smooth operator valued functions. Their results have no analogues in the earlier literature and rely on a new technique. The findings are especially transparent for selfadjoint operators, whose matrix form equals its own conjugate transpose. The paper is set to appear in the Journal of the London Mathematical Society.
arxiv-2512-15767:
M. Gorpinich and co authors present a graph neural network based hybrid twin framework in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Physics simulations, such as finite element models, miss real effects through simplifications, leaving an ignorance gap. Pure data driven models could fill it, but they demand dense data that real settings rarely provide.

The hybrid twin models only the ignorance part, which is simpler than the full response. A graph neural network learns its spatial pattern from sparse measurement points and varied geometries. Tests on nonlinear heat transfer across meshes, shapes, and load positions show the network generalizes corrections well. Simulation accuracy and interpretability improve while data needs stay low.
arxiv-2512-15867:
Tony Menzo and co authors present HEPTAPOD, a framework that lets language models orchestrate high energy physics workflows, in a 2025 paper. Modern language models can run multi step tasks through tools and structured context, and physics workflows in theory, simulation, and data analysis stand to gain. Trust and oversight, though, must survive the automation.

HEPTAPOD gives models an auditable layer between researchers and computing infrastructure, with transparency and reproducibility built in. A case study validates a beyond Standard Model Monte Carlo signal, spanning model generation, event simulation, and analysis in one reproducible pipeline. The goal is human in the loop, agent assisted work across high energy physics.
arxiv-2512-16667:
Viacheslav A. Emelyanov compares two ways to describe quantum particles near a black hole, within quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Lab tests of free fall and gravity-driven interference fit plain quantum mechanics well, but the field theory view is the deeper one.

Emelyanov computes how a Hawking particle moves far from the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole. The propagator he finds differs from the one given by the path-integral method, the very method that matches the lab tests. That clash matters because it shows the two standard routes part ways even in a mild gravity zone, a point tests of gravity and quantum theory must face.
arxiv-2512-16867:
Bineet Dash and coauthors measure electric fields inside a continuous radio-frequency plasma without touching it, using Rydberg atoms seeded in rubidium vapor. Rydberg atoms, with electrons far from the nucleus, shift their spectral lines sharply in electric fields.

Narrow lasers read those shifts through electromagnetically induced transparency, a trick that makes vapor clear at set tones. With no plasma, the spectra show sidebands from the drive coil. With plasma on, the sidebands vanish as the plasma screens the drive field. Line shapes then reveal the plasma microfield spread, letting the team read density and broadening across pressures and drive powers, a path to field maps in process plasmas.
arxiv-2512-17167:
Zack Boone studies removable sets inside Carnot groups, which are spaces with a stretched sense of distance used in geometry and physics. A set is removable for a class of functions if deleting it does not change what those functions can do. Boone tests four classes, from rough integrable functions to smooth Lipschitz ones.

For three of the classes, he pins down exactly which sets are removable using a size tool called capacity, tied to a broad family of operators. For Lipschitz functions, the test uses one special operator, the sub-Laplacian. The results give a clean rule for when a hole in the domain can safely be ignored.
arxiv-2512-17267:
Michael J Ryan and five co-authors present AutoMetrics, a way to grade open-ended AI output when human grades are scarce. Judging a travel plan or a chat reply takes real user feedback, which early projects rarely have and cannot wait for. Their framework builds a stand-in metric from fewer than 100 human data points.

AutoMetrics pulls ready-made measures from MetricBank, a curated set of 48 metrics, and adds judge criteria written by a language model. A regression step blends them to track human scores as closely as possible. Across five tasks, the blend matched human ratings up to 33.4 percent better than a lone model judge. The team releases the full toolkit for others to use.
arxiv-2512-17467:
Shoumik Debnath and four co-authors design a lead-free light-emitting diode on the computer before anyone builds it. The glowing layer is a perovskite mixing tin and germanium, safer than lead versions and tunable across the near-infrared. Its weak point is light trapped inside the device, and basic optical data for each mix were missing.

The team first computes those constants from quantum theory for five blends. Bandgap widens from 1.331 to 1.927 electron volts as germanium takes over. Then light-flow simulations add gold-and-glass nanorods that boost emission, reaching a 12.1-fold Purcell boost for one blend. The half-and-half blend struck the best balance, extracting 25 percent of its light. The guidelines target wearable, flexible light sources.
arxiv-2512-17767:
Piotr Michał Bies studies how heat and elastic motion interact inside a solid body, a field called thermoelasticity. His paper treats the nonlinear model on bounded, convex domains in two and three dimensions. He proposes unusual new boundary conditions for the displacement, paired with a Neumann condition for the temperature.

Bies proves that, for small starting data, the model has one global solution that stays regular over time, and that the temperature stays positive. He then traces the long run behavior. The twisting part of the displacement keeps oscillating, while the other part is strongly tied to heat flow and fades away. The temperature settles toward a constant value.
arxiv-2512-18167:
Alexei V. Tkachenko and coauthors at Brookhaven model what happens inside concentrated zinc chloride solutions as water is removed. Such solutions matter for zinc batteries, and drying them pushes dissolved ions to clump together and finally to gel.

Their minimal model, guided by molecular dynamics simulations run with a machine learned potential, tracks the loss of solvent sites, the correlated binding of chloride ions, and loops inside zinc chloride clusters. Losing water drives two sharp changes, both set by the zinc coordination number Z. Near Z equal to 2, lone ions give way to chloride bridged clusters, and near Z equal to 3 the clusters link into a gel. The model matches the simulations closely, and its cluster size exponent matches percolation theory.
arxiv-2512-18267:
Eduard Feireisl and Maria Lukacova-Medvidova tackle the wild math of gas flow. The Euler equations for a gas can have many rough, spread out solutions for the same start, so theory needs a fair rule to pick one. Their rule works in two steps: first favor the solution that makes disorder fastest, then the one with the largest energy defect.

If a plain rough solution exists, the first step finds it at once. Otherwise the pick is a true spread valued flow, which they name a turbulent solution, and its energy defect fades away over time. The picks shift with the starting state in a tame, measurable way, a step toward a well posed theory of rough gas flow.
arxiv-2512-18467:
Supratim Das and three co-authors test whether skill, not luck, decides who wins at fantasy cricket. The question matters in India, where the games are hugely popular and regulators must judge whether they count as games of skill. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, studies a new contest format where players pick from four expert-designed teams and share prizes by total score.

Mixing simulations with real data from the 2024 Indian Premier League, the authors find that informed team selection beats random choice again and again. They quantify how team makeup, overlap between teams, and player behavior shift the odds, and they identify setups where skill clearly dominates. The findings give players strategy pointers and help platforms design contests that stay fair and within the rules.
arxiv-2512-18667:
Avner Bensoussan and five coauthors argue that quantum software tools need live fingerprints of hardware noise, in this 2025 vision paper. Today's quantum computers are noisy, and each platform's noise model differs in hidden ways, which breaks compilation, debugging, and porting of programs. Full reconstruction of the noise scales exponentially and goes stale fast. Their pipeline, SimShadow, borrows classical shadow tomography to build deviation fingerprints from direct observations instead.

A prototype tested with Qiskit and Cirq under IBM Boston and Quantinuum H2 profiles shows fingerprints with clear channel-specific structure and readable heatmaps. Matched settings still gave large cross-platform gaps, measured by Frobenius distance at a fraction of tomography cost. Across 69 MQTBench programs, bigger fingerprint gaps tracked bigger output differences.
arxiv-2512-19367:
Christian Hägg, Kathlén Kohn, Giovanni Luca Marchetti, and Boris Shapiro build neural networks from a 1965 constructive proof. Sprecher's form of the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem writes any multivariate function from shifted one-variable functions. Each block of their Sprecher Network uses just two shared learnable splines plus a shift and a mixing vector.

Stacking blocks gives deep, compositional models, with an extra output block for vector answers. An optional lateral mixing step links output channels at slight cost. Because weights are vectors, not matrices, parameter counts grow linearly with width, not quadratically as in dense networks or spline-edge rivals. Wide, shallow designs are the natural target.
arxiv-2512-19467:
Simon Geyer and four co-authors switch the driving mechanism of a hole-spin qubit in place. Hole spins in silicon quantum dots can be flipped purely electrically, thanks to strong spin-orbit coupling. Two microscopic routes can do the flipping: shifting the g-factor, or displacing the wavefunction. Which route dominates has usually been fixed by the device.

By sending microwave drive to two different gate electrodes, the team rotates the local electric field inside a silicon fin transistor. Measurements of the g-factor, its tunability, and the Rabi rate, read through a g-matrix analysis, track each route's share. One electrode choice gives g-factor control; the other adds strong displacement drive.
arxiv-2512-19767:
Bibek Poudel and Weizi Li teach a reinforcement-learning system to draw bus networks from scratch. Transit route design is NP-hard with an enormous search space, and cities have traditionally relied on manual planning. Their framework builds networks sequentially, guided by a graph attention network that reads the road graph as routes accumulate.

Credit assignment over such long horizons is handled with two-level rewards: incremental topological feedback during construction plus simulation-based scores at completion. Training and testing use a new Bloomington, Indiana dataset with accurate road networks, census-derived demand, and the real existing routes. Learned policies beat both the real network and standard heuristics, posting higher service rates, shorter waits, and better bus utilization across initialization and adoption scenarios.
arxiv-2512-19967:
Thorsen Rivera-Thorsen and thirteen colleagues report starlight escaping from an unlikely birthplace: a bridge of gas stretched between two merging galaxies at redshift three. Their target system, LACES104037, shows a companion offset by only about 450 kilometers per second, with tidal features confirming an early-stage interaction. The ionizing-radiation cluster of interest sits inside the tidal bridge, roughly 2.7 kiloparsecs from the main galaxy's core.

The cluster is faint in ordinary starlight yet glows weakly in hydrogen and oxygen emission, suggesting feedback has dispersed much of the surrounding gas in the bridge's shallow gravity. Comparing direct Lyman continuum escape with local hydrogen emission gives an escape fraction near fifty-seven percent. The cluster's youth, under about six and a half million years, means it formed in place after the closest encounter.
arxiv-2512-20167:
Florian De Leger studies algebraic structures called operads, which encode rules for combining operations with several inputs. His paper takes up Kontsevich's Swiss cheese conjecture, a long-standing question linking the Swiss cheese operad to Hochschild constructions. Starting from a coloured operad and an algebra over it, he builds a new operad and a Hochschild object on which it acts.

De Leger proves that when the starting operad is the little n-disks operad, his construction matches the Swiss cheese operad. That yields a weaker form of the conjecture, without its universal property. He then applies the result to show an extra level of algebraic action on a Hochschild-Pirashvili cochain complex. The work gives researchers a concrete combinatorial route into a conjecture usually handled with heavier tools.
arxiv-2512-20467:
Guillermo Ballesteros, Jesús Gambín Egea, and Flavio Riccardi streamline a painful calculation in early-universe physics. In the in-in method, loop effects describe how quantum ripples during inflation act on each other. Pulling out the short-distance parts of these integrals, for graphs with any number of legs and vertices, was slow and messy.

Their method uses dimensional regularization, a standard device that shifts the dimension count slightly, to sort the work. Along the way they flag a likely snag: cancelling the infinities with Hamiltonian counter-terms looks hard in this method. They also stress that the finite parts of loop effects can be told apart from their counter-terms, so they carry real information. As a test, they compute the one-loop three-point signal in the effective theory of inflation and pick out a part that stands apart from its tree-level twin.
arxiv-2512-20567:
Emily Micklethwaite and Adam Lowe merge two machine learning traditions: radial basis function networks and quantum kernels. Quantum kernels have mostly served support vector machines. Moving them into an RBF network creates a hybrid quantum-classic method with a different balance of strengths.

Synthetic examples demonstrate the idea on interpolation and classification tasks, serving as proof of concept. The practical selling point is classification shape. A standard support vector machine handles multi-class problems only through workarounds that bolt several binary classifiers together. An RBF network classifies into many classes natively, in its basic architecture. Pairing that convenience with quantum kernel functions may suit problems where quantum feature maps help but classes come in more than two flavours.
arxiv-2512-20667:
Juan J Font and Sergio Macario approximate functions whose values are fuzzy numbers. A fuzzy-number-valued continuous function assigns each input an entire fuzzy quantity rather than a point, modelling uncertainty directly in the output. Best approximation asks for the closest member of a chosen family to a given such function.

The authors first introduce a way to measure distance between a fuzzy-valued function and an ordinary real-valued one, bridging two different worlds. With that metric in hand, they prove a best approximation always exists within the space of real-valued continuous functions. The proof leans on the Michael selection theorem, a deep tool from topology. Existence results of this kind license numerical schemes to search for approximants without fearing the target set is empty.
arxiv-2512-20767:
Waltraud Lederle works in group theory, the branch of mathematics that studies symmetry and algebraic structure. Her subject is the free group acting on its Cayley tree, a graph that pictures the group. She studies special subgroups called boomerang subgroups and a growth measure known as the critical exponent.

Lederle constructs boomerang subgroups whose critical exponent comes as close as desired to that of any given finitely generated subgroup. The abstract states this single construction result, so the paper's weight rests on how the subgroups are built. For specialists, the result clarifies how flexible these exponents can be inside the free group.
arxiv-2512-21367:
Satellites used to worry mostly about collisions; now the attack surface runs through radio links, supply chains, and software updates. Mark Ballard, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu compare cyber threats across low, medium, and geostationary orbits. Their evidence base is sixty publicly documented security incidents, cross-read against command-link anomalies, encryption weaknesses, and environmental stress.

Altitude shapes the threat. Geostationary systems are hit mainly through high-frequency uplink exposure, while low-orbit constellations suffer from tight power budgets, constrained hardware, and radiation faults. Across every orbit, weak encryption and irregular command paths best predict attacker success. The authors also tie security to sustainability: compromised satellites retire early and feed the debris problem.
arxiv-2512-21767:
Priyanka Priyanka, Cristiano Nisoli, and Yair Shokef ask whether disordered magnetic materials can remember how they were driven. Artificial spin ices are arrays of tiny magnets arranged to frustrate each other, creating rich states. Memory usually means holding an ordered pattern, but constrained disorder might remember a sequence of manipulations instead.

The authors compare two contrasting systems, in theory and in simulation. Square spin ice settles into an ordered state and shows no sequence dependence. Shakti spin ice, whose disorder is topologically constrained, responds in a sequence-dependent way: the same set of drives in a different order leads elsewhere. Even its smallest repeating unit shows deterministic and stochastic forms of sequence memory, depending on interaction strength. Retracing the same drive path strengthens retention.
arxiv-2512-21867:
Divyansh Srivastava, Fan Du, and their co-authors make autoregressive image generation cheaper by letting the model choose how finely to tokenize each region. Standard image generators use a fixed token grid, so token counts grow with the square of the resolution. Flat and detailed regions pay the same price.

Their model, DPAR, merges tokens into larger patches where the information content is low. The merging signal is the prediction entropy of a small autoregressive model: where the next token is predictable, tokens can be grouped. Training with dynamically sized patches makes the representations robust to patch boundaries, so larger patches can be used at generation time. On ImageNet generation, DPAR cut token counts roughly in half. It reduced training compute by up to forty percent, converged faster, and improved image quality scores by up to about twenty-seven percent.
arxiv-2512-22367:
Ángel Aso-Mollar, Diego Aineto, Enrico Scala, and Eva Onaindia help automated planners cope with actions whose numeric dials can be set to anything. Numeric planning with control parameters lets action parameters be free variables, creating infinitely many applicable actions per state, which breaks standard goal-distance heuristics. The authors isolate a tractable family, controllable simple numeric problems, and compile them optimistically into usual simple numeric tasks.

The compilation abstracts control-dependent expressions into bounded constant effects and relaxed preconditions. That makes subgoaling relaxation heuristics usable again for estimating distance to the goal. Tests show the approach is effective and computationally feasible, extending traditional numeric heuristics to a setting with infinitely many actions that earlier sat beyond the state of the art.
arxiv-2512-22767:
Daniel Cole, Vikas Buchemmavari, and Mark Saffman redesign a classic Rydberg atom gate so it works well outside the strong blockade regime. Rydberg gates use highly excited atoms to entangle qubits, and the original pi-2pi-pi pulse sequence needed a strong interaction between atoms to reach high fidelity. The new design keeps that pulse structure but adds a detuning to the middle pulse on the target qubit.

With that change, the gate comes close to the best fidelity allowed by the finite lifetime of Rydberg states, for both equal and unequal driving strengths on the two qubits. The authors extend the scheme to arbitrary controlled phases and shape the target pulse for a range of interaction strengths. They also show the simple constant-phase version is fastest at fixed laser power, and add control tricks that keep the gate steady when experimental settings drift.
arxiv-2512-22967:
Andrei Mironov, Hisham Sati, Vivek Kumar Singh, and Alexander Stoimenov study a famous knot invariant, the HOMFLY-PT polynomial, for a special family: reverses and parallels of torus knots and links. Using a decomposition of the fundamental representation of a quantum group, with the Rosso-Jones formula, they show these polynomials take a curious shape. The authors call it a panhandle shape, and the polynomials themselves earn the nickname panhandle polynomials.

That rigid shape has geometric payoffs. Combined with an invariant denoted l, it extends a result of Etnyre and Honda about arc index and the maximal Thurston-Bennequin invariant from torus knots to torus links. Consequences follow for braid index, for Bennequin surfaces of banded and Whitehead doubled links, for the Bennequin sharpness problem, and for when quasipositivity and strong quasipositivity coincide. The authors close by discussing how the l-invariant might be defined for general links.
arxiv-2512-23167:
Yifan Zhang and co-authors built SPIRAL, a planning framework that wraps three specialized language model agents inside a Monte Carlo tree search. Language models plan poorly over long horizons because their linear reasoning cannot backtrack from early mistakes, while plain tree search flounders when rewards are sparse and cannot use the model's semantic sense. SPIRAL's agents divide the cognitive labor: a Planner proposes creative next steps, a Simulator predicts realistic outcomes to ground the search, and a Critic scores positions through reflection.

That division turns brute-force search into a guided, self-correcting process with dense feedback. On the DailyLifeAPIs and HuggingFace datasets, SPIRAL beat chain-of-thought planning and other leading agent frameworks. Its accuracy on DailyLifeAPIs reached the mid-eighties percent, more than sixteen points above the next-best search framework, using tokens more efficiently. Code, appendices, and experimental data are released for reproducibility.
arxiv-2512-23367:
Yilun Luo and co-authors shrink Huawei's openPangu language models so they run efficiently on Ascend Atlas A2 hardware. The embedded one-billion and seven-billion parameter variants support chain-of-thought reasoning, but long reasoning traces inflate memory use and latency on the chips. Their remedy is post-training quantization, converting sixteen-bit floats into cheaper integer operations.

A low-bit inference framework supports both eight-bit weights and activations and a tighter four-bit weight scheme, tuned for the openPangu models on the Atlas A2. On the HumanEval and MBPP code benchmarks, eight-bit quantization kept more than ninety percent of the full-precision accuracy while speeding up the prefill stage by about one and a half times. The four-bit scheme cut memory consumption at a moderate accuracy cost. The authors conclude that low-bit quantization makes chain-of-thought deployment practical on Ascend hardware.
arxiv-2512-23767:
Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta bring equation discovery to small edge devices. Self-driving systems in the field must understand and predict physical dynamics in real time, under tight limits on latency, computing power, and energy. Model recovery, identifying a system's governing equations from sensor data, gives safe, explainable monitoring, but leading methods lean on neural ordinary differential equations whose iterative solvers resist hardware acceleration.

Their framework, MERINDA, reformulates the problem for an FPGA chip: recurrent GRU-based dynamics replace the neural ODE, joined by dense inverse-ODE layers, sparsity-driven dropout, and lightweight solvers, all arranged for streaming parallelism. Across four benchmark nonlinear systems, MERINDA matched state-of-the-art recovery accuracy while using over a hundred times less energy than GPU versions, a far smaller memory footprint, and faster training. The work appeared at the Asilomar Conference.
arxiv-2512-24067:
Dan Zhou and co-authors introduce the Antarctic TianMu project. The plan watches the sky for changing objects. A fleet of small telescopes will work on the Antarctic plateau. Months of unbroken polar night make the site ideal. But the cold is hard on instruments. So are scarce power and thin network links. No crew stays on site to help.

The paper describes the prototype built for those conditions. It has an eighteen-centimeter aperture. Its camera uses drift-scan technology. The telescope reached Zhongshan Station in October 2022. It came with China's thirty-ninth Antarctic expedition. Since then it has run steadily for over two years. The authors present its design choices and early results. They treat the prototype as proof the approach works. A full array would follow.
arxiv-2512-24367:
David Alonso-Gutiérrez, Javier Martín Goñi, and Joscha Prochno study distances between random points in high-dimensional balls. The balls use the l-p norm, for any p from one to infinity. Two points are drawn uniformly, inside the ball or on its boundary. Their Euclidean distance is the random quantity.

As dimension grows, that distance obeys a central limit theorem. It concentrates like a Gaussian around its mean. The authors also give a compact new proof for the sphere case. Hammersley had proved that case earlier. Large deviation principles complete the picture for p at least two. Those principles price unusually large or small distances. The work belongs to asymptotic geometric analysis. Random points in convex bodies reveal clean laws once dimension is high enough to wash out detail.
arxiv-2512-24467:
Ulle Endriss asks what it would mean to call a proposal divisive. Citizens on digital democracy platforms rank public policy proposals. Some proposals plainly split opinion more than others. A platform might want to surface the most divisive ones. That service could track how deliberation progresses. It could steer debate toward issues still needing discussion.

Endriss explores definitions for selecting the most divisive set. The tool is the axiomatic method of social choice theory. Seemingly mild fairness demands are stated as axioms. The analysis then shows they clash in fundamental ways. No selection rule satisfies all of them at once. The difficulties are structural, not a matter of clever design. Anyone building deliberation platforms faces the same wall. Measuring divisiveness under ranked preferences is harder than it looks.
arxiv-2512-24967:
Juan Esteban Rodriguez Camargo proves a Cartier duality for gerbes of vector bundles, in both algebraic and analytic settings. The duality is an anti-equivalence of Hopf algebras in a category of kernels of analytic stacks. Gerbes generalize bundles by one categorical level, and duality exchanges such objects with dual data. The result is then applied to rigid analytic geometry in mixed characteristic.

As a consequence, solid quasi-coherent sheaves on the Hodge-Tate stack of a smooth rigid variety correspond to weight-one sheaves on the Bhatt-Zhang Simpson gerbe. Algebraic geometry readers get a duality that organizes categories on stacks central to recent p-adic geometry.
arxiv-2601-00167:
Junkai Luo and coauthor Yinglun Zhu retrain Decision Transformers with pure reinforcement learning signals. Decision Transformers treat offline learning as sequence modeling. They work well before deployment, but online tuning is less explored. Most online versions still lean on supervised goals. The authors find a clash in one standard step.

Hindsight return relabeling helps supervised learning a lot. Yet it clashes with importance sampling methods like GRPO. That clash makes RL based tuning unstable. Their fix adapts GRPO to the transformer setting. Sub trajectory training sharpens credit assignment. Sequence level goals add stability and speed. Active sampling pushes search into unsure regions. Wide tests beat earlier online baselines. The results set new best scores on several benchmarks. Pure RL tuning, done right, can lift a sequence model further.
arxiv-2601-00767:
Diego Garza and nine co-authors ask, in 2026, whether dark energy changes over time, and how we could tell. Dark energy drives the late growth spurt of the cosmos, yet its nature is unknown. Fresh data from a big survey hint that its push may not be constant. The team test that hint in a new place: the forest of absorption lines from hydrogen gas between galaxies.

They ran cosmos simulations with dark energy that shifts over time, within the survey's bounds. In those runs, the forest's power pattern tilts in a way that grows with scale and age. The gas between galaxies also runs hotter, and blocks less light, than in the standard model. That split gives a fresh check on the hint, from data the survey did not use. If real skies show the tilt, the case for shifting dark energy gains weight.
arxiv-2601-00967:
Pierre Bourhis, Cristian Riveros, and Amaranta Salas formalize how event-stream systems summarize data as they recognize patterns. Complex event recognition scans streams from markets or sensor networks for meaningful pattern combinations, and aggregation, turning many values into a maximum, sum, or average, is a core operation. Yet query languages for this task usually allow aggregation only in restricted forms, with undefined semantics.

The authors extend Complex Event Logic, a formal query language for the domain, with proper aggregation operations. That requires rebuilding its semantics around bags of tuples rather than sets of positions. They pair the language with an automata model for evaluating queries. The work is a first step toward event languages whose aggregations mean exactly what they say.
arxiv-2601-01567:
Sainik Karak studies a smoothness property of Banach spaces tied to a classic extension theorem. The Hahn-Banach result lets a linear rule defined on part of a space be stretched to the whole space without growing. Smoothness asks when that stretching can be done in only one way, a question with strong geometric meaning.

Karak focuses on spaces whose dual is an L1 space, and on spaces of affine functions on convex sets. He fully sorts which such spaces hold the property, and shows a related class always allows a second dual description lacking a weaker form. Results on extreme points guide which subspaces keep unique extension.
arxiv-2601-01767:
Fen Long, Songbai Chen, and Jiliang Jing compute the shadow of a rotating black hole that arises in Horndeski gravity, a generalized scalar-tensor theory beyond Einstein's general relativity. Their solution, a circular disformal Kerr black hole, carries a deformation parameter set by the scalar field.

For a non-rotating hole the shadow stays a perfect circle whose size ignores the deformation. Once the hole spins, shrinking the deformation parameter shrinks the shadow and flattens its shape. Observers away from the equatorial plane see the shadow's center shift, north or south depending on the sign of the deformation and on their hemisphere. Such fingerprints could one day let telescope images of black hole shadows test this wider theory of gravity.
arxiv-2601-02067:
Indium antimonide is a semiconductor. Its electrons behave as if extremely light. Shine far-infrared light through it in a magnetic field and cyclotron resonance appears. The electrons circle between Landau levels. M. Bal and three co-authors built a new setup. It records magneto-transmission spectra and the light-induced voltage at the same time. The work runs at liquid helium temperature. Fields reach up to twenty-five tesla.

The conductivity followed the classical Drude response. The induced voltage mixed thermoelectric and resistive parts. Both parts were marked by cyclotron features. They match theory for spin-up electrons moving between the first two Landau levels. The extracted effective mass was about one point four percent of the free electron mass, as expected, and the thermoelectric signal even hinted at a light-driven metal-insulator transition.
arxiv-2601-02167:
