One spread model, fed coarse photoelectron guesses, mimics lifelike wave traces from photoelectron runs. A second model, trained on those fakes, rebuilds the runs from real wave traces. The two refine each other, honing the marks of overlapping signals. Tests show sharpness close to a set ideal for small photoelectron counts. The frame is fully data driven and needs only raw wave traces plus coarse guesses. It targets particle and nuclear physics tests that rely on these sensors.
arxiv-2602-05867:
Cites that cannot be traced to any real paper have begun showing in published science. Amanda Bienz, Carl Pearson, and Simon Garcia de Gonzalo built a self-running pipe to measure the problem. They checked four major high performance computing meetings, weighing cite truth between the 2021 and 2025 editions.

No 2021 paper held a mystery cite. Every 2025 set did, touching a small but real share of published papers. Errors in paper titles and author names climbed steeply in the same period. All four meetings required authors to disclose AI-made citations, yet none in the data did. The authors conclude that current rules are too weak and call for stronger cite checks. The short paper is a warning to editors and reviewers: cite lists can no longer be taken on trust.
arxiv-2602-06167:
Chemists often work with reduced density matrices, compact summaries of a many-electron state that keep only a few particles' worth of information. Ofelia B Oña and 7 co-authors address a basic question: could a given matrix actually come from a real ensemble of electrons? That test is called ensemble N-representability.

Their framework embeds the mixed ensemble into a pure state on a larger space, a trick called purification. A variational quantum algorithm then nudges that state until its reduced matrix matches the target closely. The match distance itself measures representability. Tests on two, three, and four electron systems, including warm molecules, worked robustly. The method can also repair faulty matrices.
arxiv-2602-06267:
Finding the exact point where a data stream changes character, and saying how sure you are, is the changepoint problem. Rohan Hore and Aaditya Ramdas study it with almost no assumptions: data before and after one change are drawn from unknown distributions, with only exchangeability assumed. The goal is a confidence set for the change index with a finite-sample guarantee.

Their method, CONCH, builds such sets from conformal inference arguments. A new lemma in the Neyman-Pearson style yields score functions that keep the sets small, and the sets shrink toward the true point under weak conditions. They also prove any assumption-free method must be a version of CONCH. Tests included image and text data.
arxiv-2602-06367:
Speculative bubbles end in busts because each trader, guessing what others will pay, races to sell. Kieran Hymas and 7 co-authors built a prototype quantum stock market to see whether entanglement between traders can calm that dynamic. Reinforcement learning agents trade a single commodity in their market.

When the agents' valuations were quantum-correlated through entangled qubits, prices stabilized and the traders' net worth rose. In the classical version, the same agents slid into mass selling that collapsed the asset's value. The team explains the effect through a quantized guessing game: entanglement removes the single bad equilibrium that drives classical collapse, while mixed strategies stay healthy. Quantum links act as a built-in stabilizer.
arxiv-2602-06467:
Adding numbers sounds trivial until the inputs are not numbers but ranges, as happens when analog measurements land between digital values. Johannes Bund and 2 co-authors study codes that keep such uncertainty from growing during addition. Metastable bits, caught between zero and one, are a real source of this trouble in circuits.

Binary encoding amplifies the imprecision, so they seek recoverable codes that preserve the combined uncertainty of the inputs. Unary encoding works but wastes space. The authors prove a rate ceiling for any preserving, recoverable code at a given uncertainty budget. They then design a code that meets that bound asymptotically, and discuss how to build adders for it.
arxiv-2602-06567:
Most reward learning chases the best average reward, but some problems ask for a whole spread of outcomes instead. Nicole Bäuerle and Athanasios Vasileiadis study distributional Markov decision processes, where the goal is to steer the law of total reward toward a chosen target pattern. The setting covers cases where matching a shape matters more than raising a mean.

Their solution is a policy-gradient method over random rules, defined on a larger state space and scored by a loss estimated from samples. Under mild smoothness and growth conditions, they prove settling to steady points using random methods. Tests matched complex target patterns, recovered standard best rules where they exist, and exposed many-answers effects intrinsic to distributional control.
arxiv-2602-06867:
Peter Johnson and Shayne Nochumson count the distinct shapes of spanning trees in a complete bipartite graph. Such a tree links every vertex with as few edges as can be, and two trees count as one shape when a relabeling turns one into the other. Degree lists and overall shape interact in rich ways, so the count is far from plain.

For parts of sizes a and b, the pair gives lower bounds in terms of partition counts: ways to split a+b-1 into a parts, and into b parts. They also give an upper bound that uses only a and b. Together the bounds fence in how much shape variety these trees can show, without listing every tree.
arxiv-2602-06967:
Siqi Song and five co-authors coordinate teams of unlike robots with language models that bargain like human teams. Long multi-robot jobs under space limits and uncertainty are hard to plan from the top down, and the promise of language models for coordinated control has been little tested. Their system, CLiMRS, gives each robot its own language model agent and forms subgroups on the fly through a general proposal planner.

Inside each subgroup a manager leads perception-driven talks among the agents to yield action commands, and feedback from robot moves and world changes closes the loop. To test the idea the team built CLiMBench, a benchmark of hard mixed-robot assembly jobs. CLiMRS beat the best rival by over 40 percent in efficiency on complex jobs without losing success on simple ones.
arxiv-2602-07067:
Angélique Campaniello and three co-authors test a striking prediction about waves in disordered matter. Disorder usually scatters waves hard. Yet theory says a special kind of correlated disorder, stealthy hyperuniformity, can mute scattering at long wavelengths. A material could then stay structurally disordered and far from simple homogenization, yet act transparent. Direct evidence inside a medium had been scarce.

The team uses water waves as a test bed. They image both amplitude and phase as the wavefield moves through a two-dimensional disordered structure. From those images they pull extinction lengths and statistical fluctuations. They also map energy-flow patterns, and they pin down the edge of the transparency regime in direct form. The results give quantitative backing to the predicted transport regimes, and they show correlated disorder as a practical route to steer waves across optics, acoustics, mechanics, and condensed matter.
arxiv-2602-07167:
A random drift-diffusion process and a geometric Brownian motion on matrix groups turn out to be linked. That link carries a striking feature: intermittency, where rare bursts dominate the average.  Sefika Kuzgun and two co-authors quantify that intermittency for geometric Brownian motion on SL(n) in dimensions above two.

They do it two ways: by finding the exponential growth rate of higher moments and its unusual dependence on the moment order. By showing a precise form of non-tightness in the normalized squared size.  The note is brief and technical, but it pins down how bursty this process is, with consequences for the drift-diffusion process it mirrors.
arxiv-2602-07267:
Benchmark scores are hard to translate into human terms: what does a model score mean in hours a person would need?  Fengyuan Liu and five co-authors build BRIDGE, a psychometric method that learns a latent difficulty scale from model responses and anchors it to human task completion time.

A two-setting item response model jointly figures task difficulty and model capability, and difficulty turns out to vary linearly with the logarithm of human completion time.  That lets the method predict human time for new benchmarks from model results alone and forecast frontier capabilities in human terms.  Evaluators get a bridge, as the name promises, between leaderboard numbers and real effort.
arxiv-2602-07467:
Which 3-by-3 matrices commute with each other over a finite prime field? Ivan-Vanja Boroja and two co-authors fully describe the unital compressed commuting graph of that matrix ring, combining linear algebra, field theory, projective geometry, and combinatorics.

Vertices are sorted by Jordan form with neighborhoods described, and the core subgraph for non-scalar derogatory ones is pinned down through a bijection with point-line pairs in the plane. The rest are attached afterward, and an algorithm builds the whole graph. As a consequence, the usual commuting graph, open for years, is described too. Algebraists get a finished classification for a long-standing case.
arxiv-2602-07567: Jae-Myoung Kim studies when weak solutions of incompressible non-Newtonian fluids in three dimensions stay smooth.  The paper offers a regularity test based on the weighted gradient of the velocity field, drawing on the Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg inequality.  Short and technical, it gives analysts a weighted-gradient criterion for regularity of suitable weak solutions.  The criterion is aimed at analysts working with weak solutions whose smoothness cannot be taken for granted.
arxiv-2602-07667:
AI agents now populate social platforms, but can they sustain extended back-and-forth coordination?  Aysajan Eziz studies Moltbook, an AI-agent social network, through a first-week snapshot, introducing reply half-life: how fast a comment's chance of a direct reply fades with age.

Across tens of thousands of commented threads, discussions are dominated by first-layer reactions rather than chains: most comments never receive a direct reply, reciprocal exchanges are rare. Replies that do arrive come within seconds, implying persistence of minutes rather than hours.  Aggregate tests also find no reliable four-hour heartbeat rhythm.  Social AI teams get a sobering measurement of agent conversation: fast reactions, little sustained dialogue.
arxiv-2602-07767:
Personalized health apps must choose interventions for each user, learning from complex, nonlinear behavior patterns. Ruizhe Deng and three co-authors combine Thompson sampling, a classic exploration strategy, with Bayesian additive regression trees, a flexible probabilistic model built from sums of trees.

Their method, BFTS, is the first to put this tree model directly inside the bandit exploration loop. Theory gives a Bayesian regret bound growing like the square root of the horizon, and a variant achieves frequentist minimax optimality. For mobile health and other contextual bandit problems, the paper offers a principled alternative to brittle neural models and biased linear ones.
arxiv-2602-07967:
Diffusion models can generate human motion, but aligning them with downstream goals through differentiable rewards is inefficient and memory-hungry. Xiaofeng Tan and three co-authors trace the problem to recursive dependence between denoising steps and propose EasyTune, which fine-tunes each step separately instead of optimizing the whole trajectory at once.

Decoupling the steps enables dense, fine-grained, memory-efficient optimization. To handle the scarcity of preference data for motion, they add self-refinement preference learning, which dynamically identifies preference pairs and builds a reward model from them. Motion-making teams gain a usable alignment method that spends compute where it matters, step by step rather than all at once.
arxiv-2602-08167:
Vision-language-action models reason in chains of thought, but rigid templates for thought primitives can force models to process irrelevant details. Milan Ganai and four co-authors offer R&B-EnCoRe, which bootstraps embodied thought from internet-scale knowledge through self-supervised refinement.

Treating thought as a latent variable in importance-weighted variational inference, the model generates and distills a dataset of embodiment-specific thought strategies without external rewards, verifiers, or human labels. Validation spans simulated and hardware manipulation and legged navigation. Robotics teams gain a route past the chicken-and-egg problem of thought quality: better thought no longer waits for successful policies to verify it, nor vice versa.
arxiv-2602-08267:
Data are often warped by unknown changes, and undoing them means sampling from an after-odds over the change group. Jinwoo Kim and four co-authors model that after-odds as a Boltzmann spread over a general Lie group. They offer Transformation-Inverting Energy Diffusion (TIED), a spread process that stays on the group surface using only Lie-algebra math.

A new simple target-score rule makes score-based sampling of the change after-odds lean. As a key use, test-time balance uses the method to improve ready networks' toughness to input changes. Machine-learning teams working with rotated, shifted, or otherwise transformed data gain a sound inversion tool that respects the geometry of the change itself.
arxiv-2602-08367:
Planning a real trip means juggling choices where one booking can break every later step, yet most agent benchmarks use loosely linked tasks. Zexuan Wang and twenty co-authors introduce WorldTravel, a benchmark of 150 real trips across five cities, each carrying fifteen or more interlocked time and logic constraints. Their arXiv paper pairs it with a web environment of over two thousand rendered pages.

Agents read constraint details straight from page layouts, not from tidy text. Ten leading models were tested, and even the best managed only about a third of trips in text form, dropping to under a fifth with visuals. Failures cluster past roughly ten constraints, exposing separate perception and planning bottlenecks. Readers get a hard, realistic gauge for travel agents.
arxiv-2602-08467:
Spotting faults in complex systems means finding both when something goes wrong and which variable is to blame. Charalampos Shimillas and three co-authors study how Transformers learn multi-variable time series, linking their attention to classical statistical methods. Their arXiv paper builds on those links to propose a low-rank attention model and a localization method.

The model, ALoRa-T, keeps self-attention patterns simple and low-rank, and its companion score captures the temporal shape of anomalies. ALoRa-Loc then attributes anomalies to specific variables by measuring links among series. Tests on simulated and real data show clear gains over leading methods on both detection and localization. Readers get theory-backed diagnostics for safety-critical monitoring.
arxiv-2602-08567:
Value alignment is usually tested on single models, but deployed systems increasingly chain agents that react to each other's outputs. Jinnuo Liu and two co-authors ask how a perturbed value in one agent spreads through such a system. Their arXiv paper introduces ValueFlow, a framework built on a 56-value dataset drawn from the Schwartz survey.

Drift is split into agent-level response and system-level structure, tracked by two measures: eta-susceptibility for single agents and system susceptibility for final outputs. Tests across values, backbones, personas, and topologies show susceptibility varies sharply and is shaped by interaction structure. Readers learn that alignment in multi-agent systems is a property of the whole network, not just its parts.
arxiv-2602-08667:
Recommenders usually compress recent behavior into one vector aimed at one next item, ignoring how a user's motives shift over time. Yicheng Di and three co-authors propose SRSUPM, a frame that models motive shift explicitly. Their arXiv paper targets sequential recommendation where evolving motives drive choices.

A shift-assessment module measures motive change, a construction module builds multi-level shift states, and a decomposition module regularizes representations across shift levels. A matching module then strengthens collaborative patterns tied to shift. Tests on three public benchmarks show consistent wins over representative baselines across sequential tasks. Readers get a motive-aware upgrade for sequential recommenders.
arxiv-2602-08767:
Steadying a vehicle with spread-out tire dynamics is harder than steadying a lumped model, because tire forces evolve along the contact patch. Luigi Romano and four co-authors present a backstep design that exploits passivity for semi-linear single-track models coupling ODEs and PDEs. Their arXiv paper uses the passive trait of the tire part to steady the link-up in a rapid way.

A Lyapunov score mixing lumped and spread states yields enough rules for local well-posedness and fast settling. Controls built for both state feedback and output feedback are given, the latter with a chained watcher. Sim tests with shocks, unknowns, and non-ideal cases confirm robust steadying of twitchy cars at high speed. Readers get a safety-relevant control grounded in passivity theory.
arxiv-2602-09067:
DNA base models often trail niche tools at flu forecasting, for reasons that were unclear. Yue Pei and two co-authors present AntigenLM, a generative DNA language model trained on flu genomes with functional units kept intact and aligned. That structure-aware training lets the model absorb evolutionary constraints and transfer across tasks.

Fine-tuned on time-ordered hemagglutinin and neuraminidase sequences, the model predicts coming antigenic variants across areas and subtypes, including unseen ones, beating phylogenetic and evolution-based rivals. It also nears perfect subtype classification. Ablations show that fragmenting or shuffling the genome wrecks performance, proving unit integrity matters.
arxiv-2602-09167:
Bounded results between zero and one, like rates and shares, often show heavy tails that standard beta fitting handles poorly. Arno Otto and three co-authors propose beta scale mixes: each family member times the given beta scale by a mixing random variable, whose single-setting spread governs tail behavior. The build widens the reachable range of skew and kurtosis.

Tests on fake and real data show the mix model beating old beta fitting and rival methods for bounded replies. For analysts shaping shares with rare extreme values, the family offers greater bend without dropping the known beta setup.
arxiv-2602-09267:
Arctic shipping is expanding as sea ice retreats, raising the question of how far away vessels disturb narwhals. Fanny Dupont and four co-authors introduce a lasso-penalized threshold hidden Markov model that estimates the disturbance distance while testing whether the threshold reflects a real behavioral shift rather than noise. Simulations show the penalty correctly shrinks spurious threshold effects toward zero.

Applied to narwhal telemetry, the analysis suggests animals react to vessels up to 3.4 kilometers away, moving less persistently and spending more time in deeper water, with average maximum depth near 356 meters. The framework generalizes to other species and disturbances, giving regulators a principled basis for slow-down zones and avoidance areas.
arxiv-2602-09467:
Links between contributions and source code help developers trace design reasons, limits, and security worries behind a change. Past work mapped accepted contributions, but declined ones were ignored, even though their debates record why features were refused and developers often revive them later. Sota Nakashima and six co-authors make the first attempt to link declined contributions to code, using proposals from the official Go repository.

Their language-model pipeline picks the right level of detail for each declined proposal most of the time, and roughly two-thirds of the links it draws at that level prove correct. A failure analysis shows where linking breaks down: debates that repeat themselves without concrete detail about how a feature should be built. The study thus maps both a working method and the discussion habits that defeat it.
arxiv-2602-09867:
Adrian Aguirre-Tamaral and two co-authors argue in their 2026 review that morphogenesis turns on a dialog between the local and the global. Tiny contacts between pairs of cells, they propose, steer the shape and substance of whole tissues. That link between local adhesion and global topology, not either side alone, sits at the core of how embryos take form.

During development, cells must coordinate to build tissues and organs with the right shape, structure, and spatial pattern. Fine-tuned shifts in adhesion rank among the most active forces along that path. Those shifts allow the precise physical deformations that produce organs with complex geometries. Although adhesion is defined only where two cells touch, its changes reshape embryonic tissue topology. They also set the geometry and makeup of early tissues. Local pair-wise contacts thus guide tissue-level form, closing the loop the review describes.
arxiv-2602-10067:
Language models learn internal features for abstract ideas such as factuality, usually used only to monitor or steer outputs. A 2026 paper led by Aaditya Vikram Prasad, with six co-authors, turns those features into rewards instead. Its RLFR pipeline targets hallucination reduction, an open-ended goal, by teaching a model to intervene and correct completions when unsure of their factuality.

A probing framework first identifies candidate hallucinated claims, and the same reward features later guide test-time compute. Applied to a Gemma model, the policy hallucinated fifty-eight percent less often alongside the probing harness, while standard benchmark performance held. Interpretability, the authors argue, can supply scalable supervision for open-ended tasks.
arxiv-2602-10167:
Good brain segmentation masks are scarce, and hand-labeling non-contrast CT scans is costly and inconsistent. A 2026 paper led by Lucia Borrego, with five co-authors, proposes an anatomy-preserving generative framework for synthesizing multi-class brain masks, including ischemic infarcts. A variational autoencoder trained only on masks learns an anatomical latent space, and a diffusion model in that space generates new samples from pure noise.

At inference, denoised latents decode through the frozen decoder, with optional rough control over lesion presence through a binary prompt. Generated masks preserve global anatomy, discrete tissue meanings, and realistic variability, avoiding artifacts common in pixel-space models. The framework offers a simple, scalable route to anatomy-aware masks for data-scarce imaging.
arxiv-2602-10467:
Jihwan Oh and four co-authors study how to make language models bargain better in a 2026 paper. Bargaining rewards plan and adaptation to human factors, yet current models handle it poorly and benchmarks rarely expose the weakness. The paper answers with a feedback-centered system built on utility theory.

Its benchmark, AgoraBench, spans nine demanding settings including deception and monopoly, with metrics grounded in agent utility, negotiation power, and acquisition ratio. A human-preference dataset and learning pipeline then strengthen models through prompting and fine-tuning. The authors report improved bargaining that tracks human preference more closely, offering a path from fluent talkers to negotiators that serve their principals.
arxiv-2602-10567:
Xingzhi Huang and Ji Wang design fast stabilization for a fluttering elastic plate in a 2026 paper. The motivation is active wing flutter suppression at high Mach numbers, where aeroelastic instability threatens the structure. The plate is modeled as coupled flat wave rules with internal anti-damping terms.

Using Fourier expansion, the authors decompose the problem into a large straight-line system and design full-state edge feedback through a backstepping transformation. The decay rate can be assigned arbitrarily by the user, a strong promise for a control design. A state observer extends the method to output feedback, estimating distributed states from edge readings alone. Lyapunov analysis confirms the closed-loop steadiness.
arxiv-2602-10767:
Athanasios T. Papadopoulos and six co-authors improve symbol finding under non-Gaussian interference in a 2026 paper. Single-carrier systems facing added interference with Nakagami numbers break the Gaussian beliefs behind usual sensors. Random interference size and non-uniform phase reshape best choice regions, making straight-line distance sensors weak.

The authors develop the maximum-chance Gaussian-phase rough sensor, a low-hardness rule that closely nears true maximum-chance finding while staying useful. The sensor plainly folds the interference numbers into its choices. The work gives signal builders a sensor matched to real interference rather than to a handy Gaussian fiction, lifting symbol-level results where interference rules.
arxiv-2602-10867:
Hugo Tabanelli and three co-authors explain why depth helps learning in a 2026 paper. Learning theory still has no settled answer on whether deep networks truly beat shallow ones at computation. The team studies compositional target functions in a controlled large Gaussian setting with a stated three-layer fitting model.

Though the target is a high-degree formula overall, its nested parts let a learner tackle it piece by piece. An intermediate model reveals structure invisible at the input level, reducing learning to simpler spectral estimation problems. Any shallow estimator must resolve all parts at once. Under Gaussian universality, the analysis yields sharp sample-hardness separations between two- and three-layer learning, quantifying depth's edge.
arxiv-2602-11167:
Fake citations can coax models into confident falsehoods. Nathan Mao and five co-authors offer FalseCite, a data set built to capture hallucinations triggered by misleading or fabricated citations. They run three models through it and find deceptive citations raise hallucination activity, most sharply in one leading small model.

From those replies they also study internal states, visualizing and grouping hidden vectors. Hallucinating and non-hallucinating states alike trace a distinct horn-like shape. The authors offer FalseCite as a base for future work on measuring and curbing citation-driven hallucinations, a risk that grows as models lean on cited-looking evidence.
arxiv-2602-11467:
Anatomical shapes change with growth, and doubt varies across space. Yining Jiao and ten co-authors offer PRISM, a frame joining implicit neural forms with doubt-aware numerical shape analysis. It models the conditional spread of shapes given covariates, giving continuous values of mean shape and covariate-dependent doubt anywhere.

A closed-form Fisher information metric enables fast local time doubt quantification by automatic differentiation, a key theory part. Tests on three built data sets and one clinical data set show strong results on shape evolution, personalized forecast, and anomaly finding in one unified frame. Doubt values remain interpretable and clinically meaningful throughout.
arxiv-2602-11967:
A truthful single-item auction gives the seller revenue and the buyers surplus, and mechanisms trace a frontier of tradeoffs between the two sides. Moshe Babaioff and three co-authors characterize that Pareto frontier completely under natural distributional assumptions. When values are drawn independently from a distribution that is both regular and anti-monotone-hazard-rate, every Pareto-optimal mechanism is a second-price auction with a reserve no larger than the monopoly reserve.

Viewing mechanism choice as two-sided bargaining, the authors analyze the Kalai-Smorodinsky and Nash solutions from cooperative bargaining theory. In large markets under the same assumptions, both yield near-optimal welfare. Under worst-case monotone-hazard-rate distributions, however, they diverge sharply: Kalai-Smorodinsky guarantees half of optimal welfare, while Nash may achieve only an arbitrarily small fraction. Fairness, the paper shows, is only as robust as the distributional assumptions behind it.
arxiv-2602-12367:
Hubble's WFC3 infrared channel slowly loses sensitivity, and photometry must be corrected for that drift or fluxes will skew. Annalisa Calamida led this work with four co-authors, presenting new time-dependent inverse sensitivities for WFC3/IR. They combine sensitivity-change slopes from earlier work with photometry of five CALSPEC standards, four white dwarfs and one G-type star, collected from 2009 to 2023.

The new values account for losses of 1 to 2 percent over 15 years, varying with wavelength, and give internal photometric precision better than 0.5 percent for wide, medium, and narrow filters. An updated calwf3 version 3.7.2, with a new time-dependent photometry table, will update header keywords after MAST reprocessing. Users can also compute values for a specific date with stsynphot.
arxiv-2602-12667:
Geometric congruence asks whether two point sets are identical up to shift and turn, while congruence hashing seeks compact codes supporting fast congruence queries. Yen-Cheng Chang led this work with three co-authors, studying these problems in the streaming model under finite-precision rational inputs. Each coordinate is p over q with absolute values of p and q at most U.

Two randomised small-space methods are given for two-dimensional congruence identification, which also requires outputting a valid transform when congruent. With chance at least 1 minus delta, a 3-pass product-anchor method uses space polylogarithmic in n, U, and 1 over delta. A 1-pass method with slightly larger space is also given. Readers get the first streaming methods for 2D congruence with near-optimal space and high success chance.
arxiv-2602-12767:
Quantum backflow is a strange effect in which probability flows backwards even though the momentum is almost all forward. Yuchong Chen and Yijun Tang propose a way to prepare such states in a non-interacting Bose-Einstein condensate, using large-momentum-transfer atom interferometry. Their scheme extends an earlier single-pulse idea: one arm of the interferometer takes a tunable series of momentum kicks before rejoining the freely moving arm.

For realistic strontium-88 settings, the protocol yields states with tunable flow and almost no negative-momentum contamination. The authors check both the probability current and a critical-density test, and find regimes where the backflow signal beats the single-pulse version. The result offers cold-atom labs a flexible route to making and studying backflow states in practice.
arxiv-2602-12967:
Cryptographic protocols are often written as Alice-and-Bob scripts, but each role is described separately, losing the whole-protocol view. Sebastian Mödersheim and four co-authors present CryptoChoreo, a dance-script language that covers rule sets as a whole. It extends Alice-and-Bob shorthand with choices left open, branching on rules, and memory that persists and changes.

Meaning comes from mapping to a process math, which fixes how agents read and verify inputs and build outputs, even under any algebra theories and choices by other parties. That meaning raises no-answer algebra problems, but the authors build a typical theory and connect the mapping to ProVerif. Case studies show the approach is doable in practice, giving rule-set builders a high-level yet strict spec tool.
arxiv-2602-13367:
Small models are often treated as narrow specialists, but Nanbeige4.1-3B aims to be a generalist at just 3 billion parameters, covering agentic behavior, code generation, and general reasoning in one model. Training blends point-wise and pair-wise reward modeling for aligned responses. Complexity-aware rewards push code that is both correct and efficient, and turn-level supervision supports deep search with long tool-use chains.

The model reliably executed up to 600 tool-call turns on complex problems. Tests show it beating prior models of similar size, including its predecessor and Qwen3-4B, and even topping the much larger Qwen3-30B-A3B on some measures. The authors present it as the first open-source small model with this breadth. Chen Yang leads the work with fourteen co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13567:
Teacher-student training shrinks large language models by training a student on a teacher's outputs, but the teacher's middle thought process usually stays a black box. Feature-based methods try to open it, yet standard losses ignore the uncertainty profiles that shape final outputs. DistillLens aligns student and teacher thought processes evenly, projecting middle hidden states into vocabulary space through the Logit Lens and enforcing a structural match with a symmetric gap objective.

That constraint penalizes both excess and weak confidence from either side, keeping high-entropy information channels needed for final deduction. Tests on GPT-2 and Llama models show DistillLens beating standard teacher-student training and feature-transfer baselines on instruction benchmarks. Manish Dhakal leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13767:
Impostor feelings affect a large share of the software engineering workforce, yet they are usually viewed through an internal, solo lens. This position paper reframes their spread as Human Debt, akin to technical debt, which arises when short-term goals are put over long-term structural soundness. Human Debt instead grows through gaps in mental safety and inclusive support within socio-technical systems. It weighs heavier on underrepresented engineers and researchers facing layered challenges in ranked structures and academic settings.

The paper proposes cultural rework, openness, and active upkeep through allyship, arguing that leaders and institutions must address the environmental factors worsening these feelings to keep an ecosystem for all professionals. Framing impostor feelings as debt makes a personal struggle into a shared structural responsibility. Paloma Guenes leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14467:
Kexin Quan and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv choice-help helper for info search under doubt. Real choices need sampling proof and picking when to stop, yet doubt about how telling proof is spread can lead to weak choices. AI help often targets outcomes, with less care for scaffolding search with no added mind load.

SERA, a language-model helper, gives either gist or word-for-word feedback during search. Two tests with 54 people each weighed SERA-Gist, SERA-Verbatim, and a no-feedback base across three settings varied in doubt. Settings differed in info-gain patterns: fading gains for low doubt, a local dip for mid doubt, and no pattern for high doubt. The study maps which feedback style helps in each setting.
arxiv-2602-14667:
Flows of charged fluids need a scheme that stays calm when friction runs low. Alessandro De Rosis offers a new lattice scheme for such flows, with no squeeze and with a magnetic field. One part tracks the field with a plain scheme, while the fluid part gains a fix.

The fix rebuilds the off-balance part from sound Hermite terms, with no need for speed slopes. A fourth-order spread on a nine-point grid keeps high-order balance and screens fake modes. The scheme keeps the right fluid-magnet limit and cuts grid flaws. It gives a firm base for like schemes in mixed physics.
arxiv-2602-14867:
Artem Chuprov and others give a quick, true quasi-atom plan for solids run at two scales at once. Tight spots like touch zones, cracks, and rims get full atom detail, while the rest of the solid runs as a bulk of quasi-atoms of mixed size.

Link strengths midst quasi-atoms are tuned to match the bulk's spring traits to the atom stuff's, by a trick much like live machine learning, so the plan stays fast. Plain atom codes plus a learning tuner can run it with ease. Solids thus gain a twin-scale run that spends atoms just where they count.
arxiv-2602-15067:
Pate and colleagues build an attention-gated recurrent residual U-Net model for brain tumor segmentation and survival prognosis. Gliomas rank among the most common primary brain tumors and vary widely in aggression, outlook, and histology, complicating treatment and surgery. Their 2.5D model joins residual, recurrent, and three-plane designs to sharpen feature representation and segmentation quality while staying fast.

On the BraTS2021 validation set, whole tumor outlining reaches a Dice score of nine tenths, comparable to leading models. The network also extracts 64 features per plane model for outlook calls, cut to 28 with an artificial neural network. That outlook model reaches about 46 percent accuracy, a mean squared error near 108 thousand, and a Spearman rank correlation near one third on the test set.
arxiv-2602-15267:
Polasek and Rela prove sets exist of zero Fourier size on the real line. The Fourier transform can be limited to them on a non-trivial range. That builds on Mockenhaupt's Limit Theorem, which could only be applied to sets of positive Fourier size. The team shows that a measure with polylogarithmic Fourier decay joined with full Hausdorff size 1 on the real line is enough to ensure limits.

To do this, they join two tools. One is a tweak of a build from a recent work of Li and Liu producing a set with given Hausdorff and Fourier sizes. The other is a wider version of the Stein-Tomas-Mockenhaupt Limit Theorem.
arxiv-2602-15467:
Pavone and colleagues report super-extensive charging power in an extended cluster-Ising model across a broad span of system sizes. It sits in the group, hitting up to 1,000 spins in proper parameter regimes. Quantum cells, tiny gadgets able to hold and free energy on need, are hopeful both because their inner energy and time sizes can mirror those of other quantum tools.

They also raise the intriguing chance of super-extensive charging power. That stronger scaling already turns up in several other settings, yet most researchers had judged it barred from Jordan-Wigner integrable spin chains driven by quantum-quench protocols. The authors trace that striking anomalous scaling to a matching super-extensive build-up of stored energy. That effect stays confined to large yet finite systems and does not survive into the thermodynamic limit. It also stands up to finite-temperature effects.
arxiv-2602-15567:
Long and colleagues give robot motion models a way to obey rules after training. Robot paths are often multi-modal, and streaming flow policies capture that spread well by integrating learned velocity fields straight in action space for smooth, reactive control. But those policies have no built-in way to adapt once trained, so safety limits and task constraints cannot be imposed at run time. The team answers with Constraint-Aware Streaming Flow, or CASF.

Each constraint, in workspace or configuration space, becomes a differentiable distance function turned into a local metric and pulled back into control space. Far from barred regions the metric is just the identity, while near a boundary it gently slows or steers motion away. Tests in simulation and on real robots show smooth, feasible, constraint-respecting paths that keep the multi-modal, reactive character of the base policy and beat post-hoc projection baselines.
arxiv-2602-15667:
Lüders works alone to introduce relative volutive categories, with lax volutive categories as a special case. The drive comes from a neat contrast: every rigid symmetric monoidal category carries a volutive structure, while every closed one carries a lax one. The paper builds basic theory for the relative notion and gives several equivalent formulations of the lax case.

Examples give the theory weight, including complete bornological vector spaces and modules over star-rings. Unbounded operators between Hilbert spaces and Morita 2-categories get their own discussion, the latter inside fully closed symmetric monoidal 2-categories. Category theorists gain a new frame that sorts these objects by how much rigidity or closedness each one actually enjoys, with the lax case covering the closed but not rigid side.
arxiv-2602-15767:
Kashyap and colleagues explore robot-assisted dining out in the wild, beyond lab and home tests. Robot-assisted feeding already lets people with disabilities eat independently and with dignity, but social dining in restaurants remains largely unexplored, with dynamic, unsupervised settings a robot must handle and respond to. Through speculative participatory design with people with disabilities, plus semi-structured interviews and a custom AI-based visual storyboarding tool, the team uncovers ideal scenarios for social dining out.

Their key insight frames the robot as a white glove service. Such a robot supports multimodal inputs and unobtrusive outputs, shows contextually sensitive social behaviour that prioritises the user, takes on expanded roles beyond feeding, and adapts to other relationships at the table. The work carries implications for group contexts of robot-assisted feeding in public life.
arxiv-2602-16167:
Binghang Lu leads a team of three authors improving tuning for scientific machine learning. Physics-informed neural networks and neural operators often suffer severe tuning trouble. The Muon optimizer helps by orthogonalizing updates in the singular-vector basis of the slope. Yet its unit-singular-value steps can prove overly aggressive and lack explicit stability pledges for physics-informed learning.

Their optimizer, SpecMuon, merges Muon geometry with a mode-wise relaxed scalar auxiliary variable design. Matrix slopes are split into modes, with auxiliary updates applied along dominant spectral directions. That lets SpecMuon regulate step sizes by global loss energy while keeping Muon scale-balancing traits. Theory establishes a modified energy dissipation law, positivity and boundedness of auxiliary values, and global convergence at a linear rate under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz rule. Experiments show faster convergence and better stability than Adam, AdamW, and first Muon.
arxiv-2602-16367:
Zahid Ali leads four coauthors on a multihop rendezvous protocol for cognitive radio networks in emergency response. Existing channel-hopping algorithms were designed for single-hop use, and in multi-node topologies they bring increased delay and coordination problems. The proposed Multihop Dual Modular Clock Algorithm extends modular clock-based meeting to wider settings while keeping channel coordination efficient.

The scheme picks two channels per timeslot and adds a lightweight three-way handshake to improve links among intermediate nodes. Simulations under worst-case conditions, including high primary user activity, asymmetric channel availability, and dense network settings, show the scheme significantly cuts meeting time against older approaches, by up to twenty-four percent. The results support its use for timely node discovery in dynamic emergency response work.
arxiv-2602-16567:
Romain Canu-Blot and co-authors model how solar wind ions scatter off and sputter atoms from the lunar surface. The result is emission of negative ions. Airless bodies take the full solar wind. The model is constrained by data from the NILS instrument aboard the Chang'e-6 lander. Prior knowledge is updated by Bayesian inference. A new physics-based account of scattering sits at its core.

The model matches the NILS data well. A precipitating solar wind proton has roughly a one-in-five chance of scattering in any charge state. Its chance of sputtering a surface hydrogen atom is smaller. A departing hydrogen atom has a high chance of leaving negatively charged. Surface roughness controls emission angles near grazing incidence. Energy losses point to longer paths through regolith than assumed.
arxiv-2602-16767:
Leopoldo Pando Zayas and Jingchao Zhang prove a universality theorem for the quantum thermodynamics of near-extremal black holes. The one-loop contribution from tensor modes to thermodynamic entropy is shown to be universal. The proof spans asymptotically flat, Anti-de Sitter, and de Sitter black holes, with spherical, axial, and planar symmetries.

Black hole setups with and without matter sectors are covered, including Abelian gauge fields and neutral scalar fields with arbitrary potential. Under stated conditions, the tensor-mode contribution takes a simple form tied to Hawking temperature over a quantum temperature scale. The proof also shows how Schwarzian modes arise universally in near-extremal geometries in four, five, and six dimensions, with Kerr-de Sitter black holes as an explicit example.
arxiv-2602-16967:
Yongzhong Xu studies early-warning signals of grokking via loss-landscape geometry. Grokking, the abrupt shift from memorization to general skill after prolonged training, has been linked to confinement on low-dimensional execution manifolds in modular arithmetic. Whether that mechanism extends beyond arithmetic remains open. The paper studies two sequence-learning benchmarks: SCAN compositional generalization and Dyck-1 depth prediction.

Across both tasks and a wide range of learning rates, the commutator defect rises well before generalization. That defect is a curvature measure from non-commuting gradient updates. Its lead times follow a superlinear power law, consistent with prior results on modular sums. Causal interventions show a mechanistic role: amplifying non-commutativity accelerates grokking markedly on both tasks, while suppressing orthogonal gradient flow delays or prevents it. Three task families form a spectrum of causal sensitivity, yet suppression delays or prevents grokking in all cases, establishing necessity.
arxiv-2602-17367:
James Bryson led a seven-author team tracing a trigger for widespread planetesimal formation. Planetesimals were integral to the cascade that built the terrestrial planets. The team develops a refined thermal model, including chemical reactions and phase changes during heating plus natural variation in constituent phase shares, to date meteorite parent bodies.

Parent bodies of non-carbonaceous and carbonaceous iron meteorites began forming at very similar times, just under a million years after calcium-aluminium-rich inclusion formation. Their windows overlapped, while chondrite parent bodies formed later in separate periods. Combining ages with isotopic mixing shares yields motion records for the protoplanetary disk. Those records argue both material types crossed the disk barrier after that early time, with motion onset matching planetesimal formation. That suggests one phenomenon drove motion, triggered formation, and served as the semi-permeable barrier. Its identity stays uncertain, but its effects now constrain disk models.
arxiv-2602-17467:
Greta Damo led a four-author team presenting PEACE 2.0, a tool for grounded explanations and counter-speech against hate expressions. Hate speech volume on online platforms keeps rising, posing significant societal challenges. While language processing methods now detect hate speech effectively, responses to it, called counter-speech, remain an open challenge. PEACE 2.0 not only analyzes and explains why a message counts as hateful or not, but also generates a response to it.

The tool adds three new functions, all built on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline: grounding hate speech explanations in evidence and facts, automatically generating evidence-grounded counter-speech, and exploring the characteristics of counter-speech replies. By combining these capabilities, PEACE 2.0 supports in-depth analysis and response generation for both explicit and implicit hateful messages, giving moderators and researchers a fuller picture of each message and a drafted reply grounded in evidence.
arxiv-2602-17667:
Cheng Cheng and team present WeWrite, a system for personalized demand-aware query rewriting in video search. User history gives rich clues to search intent, yet standard methods that use implicit history features suffer signal dilution and delayed feedback. WeWrite tackles when to rewrite, how to rewrite, and how to deploy at speed.

A posterior-based mining strategy pulls high-quality samples from user logs, marking cases where personalization is strictly needed. A hybrid training mix pairs supervised fine-tuning with group relative policy optimization to align output style with retrieval. A parallel Fake Recall design keeps latency low. Live A/B tests on a large video platform show click-through video volume up by about one percent and query reformulation down by about three percent.
arxiv-2602-17867:
João Cardoso and team introduce ADAPT, a hybrid prompt tuning method for language model feature viewing. Grasping what features are stored by learned paths in activation space requires inputs that fire them hard. Feature viewing tunes inputs to maximally fire a target path, offering an alternative to costly dataset search, but it remains underexplored for language models given the discrete nature of text.

Existing prompt tuning tricks suit this domain poorly, which is highly prone to local minima. ADAPT combines beam search start with tuning gradient-guided mutation, designed around those failure modes. Tests on sparse autoencoder latents from Gemma 2 2B use metrics grounded in dataset firing stats for strict comparison, showing ADAPT always beating prior methods across layers and latent types. Results show that feature viewing for language models is doable, but requires design guesses tailored to the domain.
arxiv-2602-17967:
Hanxiao Chen and Debarghya Mukherjee study multi-source transfer learning under conditional drift. Transfer learning improves target inference by borrowing from related sources, yet success hinges on cross-domain mix modeling and control. When covariate links vary across domains, blind pooling can cause negative transfer, hurting performance versus target-only.

The team proposes a semiparametric domain-varying coefficient model, where domain ties are encoded through a seen tag. That frame extends varying-factor models and bridges invariant and mixed regimes. Building on that model, they develop a tuned estimator borrowing from useful sources while guarding against negative transfer. Their estimator is efficient and easy to implement, minimax rate-optimal, with a derived long-run distribution enabling valid uncertainty scoring and claim testing despite tuned pooling. Results characterize the play among domain mix, smoothness of the mean function, and source count, backed by number tests and two real uses.
arxiv-2602-18567:
Gabriel J. Gregory and six co-authors control qudits with multi-photon transitions. Their 2026 paper notes quantum computers use arrays of two-level systems, but array size is limited by laser power, cooling, and control lines. Using more energy levels per carrier raises processing power, yet common control techniques offer limited connectivity between additional states.

The team experimentally demonstrates transitions between electronic angular momentum states differing by three, four, and five in magnetic quantum number. They use resonant stimulated Raman transitions with four and six photons in a single trapped atom. Rabi frequencies follow the standard two-photon treatment with adiabatic elimination of intermediate states, verified experimentally. The authors discuss pathways to raise multi-photon transition fidelities above ninety-nine point nine nine percent, providing efficient, high-fidelity qudit control and single-atom logical qubits.
arxiv-2602-18667:
How do operators hold a tokamak plasma in the right shape while also keeping it upright? J. T. Wai, with seven co-authors, offers a 2026 tutorial on inversion-based shape control. IBSC, a widely used way to steer magnetic fields in fusion devices, with a worked design for the NSTX-U machine.

The guide explains the core trick first: turn a plasma balance into a sensitivity map, then invert that map to find the coil currents or voltages that give the wanted shape. It also covers less familiar variants, such as dynamic voltage maps and control limits set by quadratic programming. It shows how untangling shape control from vertical control removed a wobble on NSTX-U and strengthened its vertical control.
arxiv-2602-18767:
Proving theorems in Lean 4 means searching through expressions and tactics, a space so large that existing agents struggle. Leni Aniva, with three co-authors, introduces Nazrin in 2026, a graph neural network prover built on a small, finite set of atomic tactics claimed to suffice for any provable statement.

A transposing atomization algorithm rewrites arbitrary proof expressions as sequences of those atomic tactics, and a compact ExprGraph structure represents Lean expressions for the network. Because Nazrin dispatches only atomic tactics, it sidesteps many obstacles faced by other agents and runs for training and evaluation on consumer hardware. Demonstrations on Lean's standard library and on Mathlib show the approach has real potential.
arxiv-2602-19167:
Finding subgraphs similar to a query is fundamental across domains. Qi Wen, with four co-authors, defines a new similarity semantics in 2026 called generalised neighbor difference. It weighs both keyword-set relations between vertices and edge-weight differences. Prior metrics miss that combination.

A learning-based approach tackles search under the new semantics. A keyword hypergraph is built from the data graph. A hypergraph neural network learns high-quality keyword embeddings. Pruning strategies rule out false alarms at keyword, vertex, and graph levels. A tree index speeds query answering. The query algorithm traverses the index, prunes candidates, and returns exact answers. Tests on real and synthetic graphs confirm effectiveness and efficiency. Protein discovery, social analysis, and recommendation all stand to benefit.
arxiv-2602-19267:
Protons have internal structure described by gravitational form factors, curves that encode how mass and spin are spread inside the particle. Measuring those curves is hard because data are sparse and noisy. Herzallah Alharazin and one colleague rebuild them with a generative machine-learning method based on denoising diffusion, a technique that learns to turn noise into realistic curves.

The generative prior comes from a large set of synthetic curves drawn from ten distinct families rooted in different theories of hadron structure. Applied to the proton's three main form factors, the reconstructions match lattice quantum chromodynamics results across the full range studied. They stay steady even when only one or two data points are kept as guides, which matters for real experiments where good data are scarce.
arxiv-2602-19367:
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis claims that models trained on different modalities converge on a shared latent structure of the world. Pratham Yashwante and Rose Yu test whether time series join that convergence, a case little examined beside vision and language. Independently pretrained encoders for time series, vision, and language turn out nearly orthogonal in geometry without explicit coupling. No shared structure appears on its own.

Post-hoc alignment with contrastive projection heads over frozen encoders improves with model size, but asymmetrically. Time series line up more closely with visual representations than with text. Images can serve as intermediaries between time series and language. Richer textual descriptions help only up to a threshold, with denser captions adding nothing further. The findings guide multimodal systems involving time series.
arxiv-2602-19567:
Low-width layouts like Dragonfly and Slim Fly see growing use in fast number-crunching and server-farm nets. Tommaso Bonato and five co-authors note that current load sharing either leans on closed in-net gears or fails to use full path range. Their framework, Spritz, moves smart layout-aware routing to the edge boxes, using only standard Ethernet traits.

Two methods are proposed: Spritz-Scout and Spritz-Spray, which scout and smartly cache fast paths using plain jam alerts, packet trimming, and timeout feedback. Test runs on Dragonfly and Slim Fly layouts with more than 1000 edge boxes show Spritz beating ECMP, UGAL-L, and earlier sender-based methods by up to 1.8 times in flow finish time, with up to 25.4 times gain under link failures.
arxiv-2602-19667:
Load flow math underpins modern power grids, yet classic Newton-Raphson solvers are precise but slow, limiting big scenario studies. Timon Conrad and four co-authors test how much training data ML load-flow stand-ins need, a question still thinly studied for fixed-topology grids. They compare one Multilayer Perceptron against two Graph Neural Network variants on a modified IEEE 5-bus system.

For this grid size, Graph Neural Networks post the lowest losses. Still, having large training sets matters more for performance than picking an architecture. Readers get a clear sample-efficiency read: data volume beats model choice when grids stay fixed.
arxiv-2602-20067:
Most turbulence breaks large flows into smaller eddies. Some flows instead organize themselves into large structures. A 2026 arXiv paper by Anna Frishman and two co-authors reviews a perturbative theory of such organized turbulence. The theory rests on two quantities that never change sign and stay conserved.

Two-dimensional turbulence is the example. Large mean flows called condensates emerge there. The review compares two-dimensional Navier-Stokes flow against the large-scale quasi-geostrophic equation. Both sit at opposite limits of that shallow water equation. The first shows long-range interactions between fluid elements, the second local ones. In rotating 3D turbulence, jet-type condensates yield a flow profile and a symmetry breaking. In the shallow water quasi-geostrophic equation, varying the Rossby deformation radius yields condensates in every regime tested. Above the forcing scale they follow two-dimensional Navier-Stokes behaviour; below it, the large-scale quasi-geostrophic equation.
arxiv-2602-20167:
Assembly programming is a core undergraduate topic, yet its abstract, low-level ideas trip up many students. Simulators and visual tools show machine states but keep students as watchers, with little hands-on work. A 2026 arXiv paper by Elliott Wen and seven co-authors offers Playsemble, a game-based system that turns machine-code instructions into playable tasks.

Students steer Pac-Man to grab items, dodge ghosts, and reach goals, writing assembly as they play. One browser-based space holds an editor, a CPU emulator, and visual debug tools. Nothing needs installing or configuring, and students can work offline. Feedback arrives at once, shaped by large language models into learning guidance. The team deployed Playsemble in a college computer architecture course with one hundred and seven students.
arxiv-2602-20267:
Arjun Bagchi and three co-authors reframe the region just outside a black hole in geometric terms. Their 2026 study treats the near horizon of a generic non-extremal black hole as a Carrollian geometry with two null directions, called a String-Carroll geometry. Here the base is a sphere, or a plane for a black brane, and the fibre is two-dimensional Rindler spacetime.

The first part builds particle paths and scalar fields in that geometry. The second part tests the picture on Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes, the BTZ black hole, black branes, and Lifshitz black holes. For each case, they map the example onto the new geometry and check it against the near-horizon limit in the original setting. The cases support String-Carroll geometry as the near-horizon shape of non-extremal black objects. They open the way to studying its quantum side.
arxiv-2602-20567:
Learning over directed nets lets nodes share information even with one-way links, but its stability and generalization are less clear than its convergence. Yifei Liang and three co-authors build a unified uniform-stability account for Stochastic Gradient Push that captures directed nets. A key tool is an imbalance-aware bound for Push-Sum, which controls consensus drift through two quantities: the stationary distribution imbalance and the spectral gap governing mixing speed.

That split separates statistical effects from net-driven bias. The paper proves finite-iteration stability and optimization bounds for convex goals and for non-convex goals meeting the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. For convex problems, it gives an excess error bound and pins down the best stopping time. For Polyak-Lojasiewicz goals, it gives convex-like rates where problem conditioning and directed nets couple multiplicatively. The analysis clarifies when Push-Sum correction is needed over plain SGD.
arxiv-2602-20867:
Language-model agents increasingly rely on reusable procedural modules called skills, which package know-how with rules for when and how to run. Yanna Jiang and six co-authors map that skill layer across its full life cycle in this 2026 survey of the field. They cover discovery, practice, distillation, storage, composition, evaluation, and update.

Two taxonomies organize the survey: seven design patterns for packaging and running skills, and a representation-by-scope grid spanning language, code, policy, and hybrid forms across web, operating-system, software, and robotics settings. Security gets close attention, including a case study in which nearly twelve hundred malicious skills infiltrated a major marketplace. The paper closes with open challenges for robust, verifiable skills.
arxiv-2602-21367:
Ruben Lier and one co-author study a two-dimensional gas of hard disks that collide in a chiral way, keeping energy and momentum intact. Their simple chiral collision rule is meant to mimic collisions of spinning, non-round particles without tracking spin or orientation as separate variables.

Even though the rule breaks time-reversal symmetry at the microscopic level, the H-theorem still holds, so the gas relaxes toward equilibrium when no outside forces act. A Chapman-Enskog expansion then gives analytic formulas for shear viscosity, odd viscosity, and thermal conductivity. Nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations back up those predictions, giving a compact kinetic picture of chiral disk gases.
arxiv-2602-21467:
William Youngwoo Chung and five co-authors build a generalizable world model grounded in Vector Symbolic Architecture as a geometric prior. Most world models represent transition dynamics with unstructured neural networks. That limits clarity, sample efficiency, and handling of unseen states or action combinations.

Their approach maps states and actions into a high-dimensional complex vector space. It uses learnable Fourier Holographic Reduced Representation encoders with learned group structure. Transitions become element-wise complex multiplication. Training codes to be nearly unchanged under group actions enables strong multi-step chaining directly in latent space. On a discrete grid world, the model hits about 88 percent zero-shot accuracy on unseen state-action pairs. It gains about 54 percent accuracy on 20-step rollouts. It shows four times the noise robustness of a multilayer perceptron baseline.
arxiv-2602-22367:
Fast heart simulations use the lead-field method to turn torso geometry into ECG signals, but clinical scans usually focus on the heart and skip the full torso. Arsenii Dokuchaev and four co-authors note that no current method combines anatomical fidelity, low data needs, and computational speed. Their answer is a shape-informed surrogate model that drops into forward ECG simulations in place of the full model.

The framework's first component encodes geometry, mapping anatomical shapes into a form the surrogate can use, letting simulations keep full geometric fidelity without full torso imaging. The design aims to sidestep the lead-field method's linear cost scaling with electrode count, opening high-density recording settings to fast simulation.
arxiv-2602-22567:
Jianmin Wang and two co-authors quiet a quantum amplifier with its own feedback. Amplifiers normally add noise through coupling to inner parts, but quantum correlations can suppress that extra noise. Here the team feeds part of the Stokes light back into a Raman amplifier, exploiting an established link between the Stokes field and atomic spin waves.

The payoff is a noise cut that does not depend on feedback loss at high gain, reaching 6 decibels at best. The single-path design reacts to feedback phase, a sensitivity that suits precision measurement uses. The authors note the same idea should carry over to integrated optics and fiber systems, where low-noise amplification matters for sensing and communication.
arxiv-2602-22767:
Marc Magaña and two co-authors prove that vortex-patch boundaries stay smooth under the quasi-geostrophic shallow-water equations. Those equations extend the Euler equations with an extra parameter, the Rossby radius, which reshapes the link between streamfunction and potential vorticity. Smoothness of the patch edge persists in time.

The team also proves that shallow-water solutions converge locally in time to the matching Euler solutions as the Rossby parameter tends to zero, measured in little Hölder spaces. For fluid mathematicians, the paper secures both the regularity of moving vortex edges and the shallow-water-to-Euler limit in one stroke.
arxiv-2602-23067:
Samuel Lemes-Perera and three co-authors build a GPU-sped-up AES-GCM setup for sky-survey archive access. Large surveys produce image archives needing fast, secure access before release, when secrecy and soundness matter. Usual restricted-phase security lacks fine detail or brings speed penalties.

A bendable policy engine joins GPU AES-GCM proof-of-origin encryption. The key novelty is a side-by-side tree-reduction strategy beating the speed choke point in proof-of-origin encryption: the by-nature stepwise Galois Counter Mode hash, GHASH. Tuned GPU AES kernels from recent code-based speedup work join here first. The high-speed, FITS-aware setup for sky-survey data combines proof-of-origin, two-key access control, and standard Python fit. The setup turns stepwise GHASH computation into a highly side-by-side log-time process, reaching proof-of-origin encryption speed for analysis.
arxiv-2602-23267:
Maik Gröger and one co-author give a full account of tameness and nullness for minimal machine-made systems built from basic constant-length swaps. In the study of shapes in motion, tame and null systems capture low-complexity motion that never repeats. But concrete, easily usable tests for their presence in a standard class of systems have been hard to come by.

The authors pin down both traits through amorphic complexity, a number-based score newly coined for zero-entropy systems. They derive a usable closed formula for this score in the swap setting. The payoff is sharp: for endless machine-made systems, both traits match the score taking the value one, turning an abstract motion trait into a single checkable number.
arxiv-2602-23467:
Rohan Thomas and one co-author test whether machine learning can recover interpretable math structure from raw numbers, using real-root patterns of polynomials up to degree five as a benchmark. They trial decision trees, logistic regression, support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting, XGBoost, symbolic regression, and neural networks.

Neural networks reach 84.3 percent balanced accuracy on quintic classification from raw coefficients alone, far ahead of decision trees at 59.9 percent. But given one explicit feature tracking sign changes at critical points, decision trees match neural performance at 84.2 percent and yield explicit rules. Distillation shows that single invariant explains 97.5 percent of the extracted structure. The networks, the authors argue, learn geometric approximations rather than scale-invariant symbolic rules.
arxiv-2602-23767:
Anilkumar Mailvaganam and six co-authors build an empirical model that predicts how much dust dims light in each small patch of a star-forming galaxy. The 2026 paper uses spectra from the MaNGA survey, covering thousands of galaxies and nearly two million star-forming patches.

The model leans mainly on local star formation density, and it predicts dust dimming within about a third on scales of a thousand light-years. It also works in reverse: starting from uncorrected star formation, repeated use of the relation recovers the dust-corrected values with little bias. Maps match observed ones across varied shapes and tilts, including edge-on galaxies, and radial trends track galaxy mass and star formation strength. The tool helps read galaxy structure where dust would otherwise hide it.
arxiv-2602-23867:
Karolina Drabik and five co-authors study merge-width, a recently introduced graph parameter that unifies several classic width measures. The 2026 paper proves that several alternative definitions of merge-width coincide, showing the notion is robust rather than an artifact of one definition.

A characterization through definable merge-width, using vertex orderings drawn from sparsity theory, yields the first nontrivial approximation algorithm for the parameter. The authors also give a new ordering-based characterization of bounded clique-width. Graphs of bounded merge-width admit sparse quotients with bounded coloring numbers. They sit close to graphs of bounded expansion. They admit neighborhood covers with constant overlap. Further variants and links to adjacency labeling schemes round out the study.
arxiv-2602-23967:
Hongpei Li and four co-authors present PDHCG-II, an enhanced first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming. The 2026 paper builds on the recent PDHCG framework, which matters because quadratic programs underpin decision-making and machine learning, yet large instances remain hard to solve efficiently.

The method exploits the quadratic structure of the objective and adds several innovations. One innovation is Halpern-type acceleration. A second is a PID-controlled adaptive update of the primal-dual weight. A third is a refined termination rule for inner subproblems that avoids over-solving. A fourth is an infeasibility detector for ill-posed cases. Tests on standard benchmarks show consistent speedups over PDHCG, by several times. A CUDA-C implementation is released as open source, supporting reproducibility and adoption for large-scale optimization in practice.
arxiv-2602-24067:
Thom Vaughan and Pedro Ortiz Suarez audit color contrast compliance on the web at large scale, using Common Crawl's archive rather than live crawling. The 2026 paper examines the most frequently crawled registered domains, analyzing homepages with static CSS analysis to keep results reproducible and avoid loading target servers.

Across hundreds of homepages the team found thousands of unique foreground-background color pairings. About two in five failed the standard contrast threshold for normal text. The median site passed about three in five pairings, while only about one site in five achieved full compliance across all detected pairings. Contrast thus remains, on the most prominent websites, a widespread accessibility barrier, with marked variation across domain categories, suggesting that prominent sites still routinely exclude readers with low vision.
arxiv-2602-24267:
K. Andrzejewski studies a spinning particle and its dynamics in pp-wave spacetimes, especially plane gravitational waves and shockwaves. The 2026 solo paper presents a step-by-step procedure, in direct analogy with geodesic motion. It takes the original problem down to transverse-coordinate dynamics.

That reduction uses a spin supplementary condition, which fixes the particle's center-of-mass worldline among the choices that spinning allows. Constants of motion from conformal Killing fields, and Hamiltonian formulations, complete the picture. By isolating the transverse dynamics, the procedure makes spinning particle motion in wave spacetimes tractable. It offers a route to trajectories for spinning test bodies in wave backgrounds.
arxiv-2603-00267: Gong and colleagues propose WKGFC, a multi-agent system for fact-checking that draws evidence from several sources instead of text similarity alone. Earlier methods lean on patterns learned from training data and miss subtle links between evidence and claims, especially across multi-hop relations. Their system uses an authorised open knowledge graph as its core evidence source, topped up with web content. A reasoning language-model agent picks actions step by step under a Markov decision process, tuned by prompt optimisation for fact-checking.
arxiv-2603-00367: Garbagnati studies K3 surfaces carrying a symplectic involution, where dividing by the symmetry and smoothing the result yields a K3 surface, often with a changed Néron-Severi group. When the involution comes from a two torsion shift on an elliptic fibration and the Picard number is minimal, the two Néron-Severi groups match. She finds endless two codimension families outside that type whose typical members still match. She maps the cohomological action and isolates a five dimensional family where the two surfaces coincide and carry complex multiplication.
arxiv-2603-00567: Telikani and Gandomi attack neural contextual bandits with AdvBandit, a black box adaptive method that poisons contexts without seeing victim parameters, rewards, or gradients. The attacker builds a surrogate from observed context action pairs via maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning, then optimises perturbations with projected gradient descent. A Gaussian process guided by upper confidence bounds steers arm choice, and a budget control limits detection risk. Theory gives sublinear attacker regret and victim regret linear in attack count, and experiments beat state of the art baselines on Yelp, MovieLens, and Disin.
arxiv-2603-01067: Chen and nine colleagues probe the strength of proactive watermark defenses for machine-made images, which aim to stop misuse. Their Hide&Seek suite offers versatile, low-cost attacks that reliably strip embedded watermarks while keeping images looking clean. The work exposes how fragile current protections can be, inviting stronger defenses for generated media.
arxiv-2603-01367: Turok, De Sa, and Kuleshov offer DUEL, a plan joining masked diffusion samplers that use fixed spot selection. They prove DUEL samplers admit exact odds math under the test-time spread, giving masked diffusion models proper odds and proper surprise for the first time. That proper surprise matches auto surprise as a natural twin, letting the team revisit masked diffusion questions. Masked diffusion models turn out much better: the surprise gap to auto models shrinks by up to 32 percent on in-domain data and 82 percent on zero-shot benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-01767:
Bosen Lin, Feng Gao, Yanwei Yu, and Junyu Dong enhance underwater photos for machine vision, not just for human eyes. Their 2026 work notes that murk and color shifts blur targets for segmentation and detection tools. Most past enhancers please human viewers yet drop the fine detail that recognition needs.

Their framework, DTI-UIE, uses a model of human perception to guide enhancement toward task gains. A two-branch network with task-aware attention mixes features built for recognition from the start. Training runs in stages with a perceptual loss tied to downstream task success. The team also auto-builds a task-inspired data set with help from task-specific networks. Test results show clear gains in downstream task performance, which reframes enhancement as a servant of recognition, not of looks alone.
arxiv-2603-01967:
Qiming Hu, Baogang Xu, and Miaoxia Zhuang study graphs that just fail a splitting property called perfect divisibility. Their 2026 work defines a perfectly divisible graph through every induced subgraph splitting into two parts. One part must induce a perfect graph, while the other must lower the largest clique size.

A weighted version swaps clique size for maximum clique weight under any positive integer weights. The team investigates how plain and weighted divisibility relate to each other in general. For graphs free of two small patterns, or free of claws, minimal counterexamples have no clique cutset. A clique cutset is a full-connection set whose removal disconnects the graph. That absence conditionally answers a question posed by Hoang, narrowing where minimal non-divisible graphs can hide.
arxiv-2603-02167:
Laura Gómez Paz, Justin Schirmann, Adam Yanis Chaou, and colleagues study a new kind of disordered matter in this 2026 paper. Gyromorphs lack regular spacing, yet their parts share a loose turning order on average. Such systems might block waves evenly in all directions. The catch is that their turning order is only average, not exact.

Standard tests for protected edge states assume exact symmetry, so they can fail here. The team shows gyromorphs can still host higher-order protected states. Those states rest on the average turning order alone. Three tools are compared: a marker based on an effective model, a local probe, and a scattering test. All three draw the same phase map, which supports the claim.
arxiv-2603-02267:
Yunlong Gao, Xinyue Liu, Yingbo Wang, and colleagues help text classifiers learn from few examples in this 2026 paper. Few-shot sorting must label new classes from a handful of labeled texts. Training tricks abound, but test examples are picked at random and may mislead. A badly placed example can drag a new text toward the wrong class.

Their fix uses label words as guides in both training and testing. A training loss pulls each text's code toward its label's code. At test time, a scaler shifts codes using label meaning as well. Shifted examples land closer to their true class centers. Paired with two standard learners, the method beat prior best models by clear margins across many tests.
arxiv-2603-02367:
Yaxi Chen, Simin Ni, Jingjing Zhang, and colleagues personalize knee MRI analysis in this 2026 paper. Radiomic features turn scan patterns into numbers that simple classifiers can use. Such pipelines are transparent, but fixed feature sets chosen for whole populations often underperform. Adaptive methods rank single features, which can admit duplicates and miss paired value.

Their framework picks one compact feature set per patient instead. Random diverse candidate sets are sampled first, then scored by a learned function. The best set feeds a downstream classifier for the final diagnosis. The search closely matches an exhaustive check, with tiny error at the high end. Tasks include ligament tear detection and arthritis grading, where tailored sets should aid clear, patient-level calls.
arxiv-2603-02467:
Ravi Goyal, Victor De Gruttola, Natasha Martin, and colleagues release a network generation package in this 2026 paper. Researchers simulate networks to test methods and reflect real-world uncertainty. Classic models fix network traits or let the model dictate their spread.
