arxiv-2604-08267: Ye factors the Ghilardi-Zawadowski sheaf view of finitely generated free Heyting systems into profinite limits. He then places their dual category inside a sheaf topos as a full subcategory of that topos. That dual category is infinitary, broad, and regular, with completion exactly that sheaf topos, the K-topos. Uniform interpolation traits extend to all such algebras, from the K-topos's internal logic.
arxiv-2604-08467: Patti and seven colleagues speed up tensor network simulations of noisy quantum systems by fixing three bottlenecks in batched trajectory sampling. Unified path variation, non degenerate sampling, and a flexible contraction setup lift data collection to over 100 million times the rate of standard trajectory methods. The same tools also give more than a thousandfold speedup for broader quantum simulations, with special strength for non proportional sampling.
arxiv-2604-08567: Yang and seven colleagues study language model agents that must serve several users at once, not one main user. They formalize multi user interaction as a multi principal decision problem and build a unified protocol with three stress tests for instruction following, privacy, and coordination. Frontier models often fail to hold stable priorities under conflicting goals, leak more privacy over long chats, and stall when coordination needs repeated information gathering.
arxiv-2604-08667: Balkin and six colleagues build a unified two to three setup for production of single particle states in forward proton motion for the future Electron-Ion Collider. It covers spin zero and vector mesons, axion like particles, and dark photon carriers. Its model based rates fit photo and production data and admit steady polish. Benchmarks against matching photon estimate accounts agree closely at near real photon energy, while finite energy links matter for fine grained measures.
arxiv-2604-08767: Dmitrii Stoliarov and seventeen colleagues show a high power O-band soliton microcomb for short reach data center links. It combines an 834 gigahertz self locked silicon nitride microcomb spanning 1050 to 1650 nanometres with a bismuth doped fiber amp. The system gives over 0 dBm per carrier for 21 O-band lines over 100 nanometres with low noise. A 25 km coherent test reaches 7.23 terabits per second total throughput, a usable route to multi terabit links.
arxiv-2604-08867: Kang, Fang, and Li build AudioGuard, a unified guardrail for audio safety across diverse threat models. Audio risks go beyond unsafe text spoken aloud, spanning harmful sound events, speaker traits like child voices, impersonation and voice cloning, and risky voice content combinations. Large scale red teaming uncovers system vulnerabilities and yields a policy grounded risk taxonomy plus AudioSafetyBench, the first benchmark for audio safety built on policy. AudioGuard pairs SoundGuard for waveform level detection with ContentGuard for semantic protection, beating strong audio language model baselines at lower latency.
arxiv-2604-09467: Greenstreet and six colleagues refine multi-stage trials that test several treatments at once and drop the weakest at each interim check. Their design also halts the whole trial early when one treatment proves clearly superior, cutting both the expected number of participants and the maximum enrollment funding must cover. An atrial fibrillation example shows it beating standard drop-the-loser designs on expected size.
arxiv-2604-09867: Taylor constructs a stepwise coherator, a model for endless groupoids with a base round set, using sharing series of monads. The setup supports a stepwise strategy for the broad Homotopy claim, moving model structure from n-groupoids to (n+1)-groupoids. Taylor gives a needed and enough condition for the transfer to succeed, and shows that if transfers complete in turn, the broad Homotopy claim holds.
arxiv-2604-10467: Adak caps how many edges a crown free linear hypergraph can hold. A linear hypergraph lets each vertex pair share at most one edge. His k-crown joins one base edge to k separate edges, each meeting the base once. The new cap beats a recent Zhang, Broersma, and Wang bound for all ranks from four up. Small cases match short linear paths and get their own direct treatment.
arxiv-2604-10867: Barkan, Heuts, and Shi compare routes into homotopy theory at chromatic height n: T(n)-homology versus v_n-periodic groups. Building on Bousfield's observation that the two differ greatly, their tool is parametric T(n)-equivalence, a map inducing an equivalence on local systems valued in T(n)-local spectra. Results are sharpest for infinite loop spaces, including a T(n)-local Kuhn result on Morava K-theory of the Whitehead tower. They give the L_n^f-localization of Omega-infinity E with vanishing L_{n-1}^f.
arxiv-2604-11167: Inoue and three colleagues test whether a torsion-bar detector can sense Yukawa-style departures from Newtonian gravity. Two rotating mass systems cancel the leading Newtonian torque, leaving a residual that maps to a strain signal below one hertz. Sensitivity peaks near eight meters, reaching a coupling strength of 0.000024 at that range, limited by imperfect cancellation and source-mass geometry rather than statistical noise.
arxiv-2604-11367: Santos and eight colleagues calculate how strain-induced curvature reshapes monolayer graphene. Curvature under a set strain constraint stabilizes the sheet. As curvature grows, Van Hove peaks in the electron density of states approach the Fermi energy, with flat and linear bands coexisting near that level, a promising mix for heat-to-power uses. The sheet stays dynamically stable across the studied strains. The flexural acoustic mode shifts from quadratic to linear form, boosting phonon scattering and lowering lattice heat flow, which strain can thus tune.
arxiv-2604-11467: Labarta and four colleagues make explanations actionable with activation steering. Their web tool combines sparse-autoencoder scores with steering for instance-level concept analysis in vision models. In expert interviews with eight experts doing debugging tasks on CLIP, steering shifted work from inspection to testing ideas by intervening for all eight. Most trusted observed responses over explanation appeal. The tool lets users test ideas by intervening, not just by looking. Users favored suppression and flagged ripple effects and limited generalization of instance fixes.
arxiv-2604-11867: Sadasivan reports a three-arc negative result on teaching small language models dispositions like self-verification and uncertainty acknowledgment. An internal draft claimed large gains, but a second check falsified them: the HumanEval gain was a truncation artifact flipping to minus 8.0 points at longer outputs, and the other gain vanished under fair scoring. Across model families, attention-head tempering, and a frozen-base sidecar, no method shifted judge-measured disposition without harming content or collapsing into mimicry. One Gemma model, too, asserts at 91 percent whether it is right or not.
arxiv-2604-12467: P. Lassègues and 31 colleagues report the first measurements of high excited states in francium atoms. They measure absolute energies and radiative lifetimes of the 9p and 10p levels. The work uses collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy on a beam of francium-221 atoms. No experimental data had existed for francium p-states above level eight. Results test relativistic coupled-cluster theory for the heaviest alkali metal. Lifetimes and relative energies agree well, despite a global offset in absolute energies.
arxiv-2604-12967: Sohyun An and four colleagues train search agents without gold answers. Gold supervision scales poorly, yet most methods depend on it. Cycle Consistent Search treats a good trajectory as a lossless encoding of question intent. High-quality trajectories preserve enough information to rebuild the original question. Naive cycle goals leak through lexical cues, so bottlenecks block that shortcut. Excluding the final response and masking named entities force reliance on retrieved observations. Tests match supervised baselines and beat prior gold free methods.
arxiv-2604-13267: Saha and ten colleagues report the first direct detection of ionizing photons from faint early galaxies, using deep ultraviolet imaging from AstroSat and Hubble. The photons emerge from stacked Lyman-alpha emitters at redshift 5.9 to 6.0 in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, implying greater transparency of interstellar and intergalactic media than models predict. The stacked spectrum shows a hard slope and an escape fraction near 0.8. Very blue continua, young ages, and low metallicities point to hot massive stars powering reionization, plus evidence that helium reionization had begun.
arxiv-2604-13467: Raphael Grondin proves that a classic entropy-rate theorem survives a flexible way of cutting data into blocks. As long as the block count grows more slowly than the data itself, the average surprise per block still settles on the entropy rate. The result also withstands small changes to the blocks, and Grondin shows the slow-growth condition cannot be loosened, by building a counterexample.
arxiv-2604-13967: Yan and Li study a power function with a Niho exponent, a family prized in sequence design, coding theory, and cryptography. By analyzing certain polynomials over a finite field, they determine the function's differential spectrum. The result shows the function is locally differentially 4-uniform, filling a gap in the known spectra for Niho-exponent power functions.
arxiv-2604-14267: Wang and six colleagues improve search agents with Contribution-Weighted GRPO, which folds process supervision into group relative policy optimization. Rather than optimizing process rewards outright, an LLM judge scores retrieval utility and reasoning correctness each round, and those per-round scores rescale outcome-based advantages along the trajectory. The approach gives fine-grained credit without sacrificing optimization stability, beating standard GRPO by about 5 percent on Qwen3-8B and about 6 percent on Qwen3-1.7B. Winning trajectories show contributions bunched in specific rounds, a clue for future search agent design.
arxiv-2604-14367: Coskun and Chitra develop a route to the many-body density of states for isolated, interacting quantum systems from generalized coherent states and Simon-Lieb bounds on the partition function. The framework bounds ground-state energy in each sector and supports microcanonical observables across the spectrum. Tests on the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model recover quantum phase transitions and excited-state transitions across spin sectors. On a ferromagnetic Ising chain under a transverse field with power-law interactions, the top spin sector's density of states matches the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick pattern.
arxiv-2604-14767: Kadosawa, Nakamura, Ohta, and Nishimoto map ground-state magnetism in an easy-axis spin-1/2 XXZ antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice. They track sublattice moments as anisotropy grows. At the isotropic point the positive moment is 0.217. In the easy-axis regime the moments stay near a Y-like two-m, minus-m, minus-m pattern, reaching 0.419 positive and 0.209 negative at huge anisotropy. The Y state beats the up-down-down state at zero field, so fluctuations preserve nontrivial order rather than saturated Ising order.
arxiv-2604-14967: Wang and seven others propose UniDoc-RL, a unified reinforcement learning framework for visual retrieval-augmented generation. Existing visual RAG systems use generic retrieval signals that miss fine visual semantics needed for complex reasoning. Their agent jointly performs retrieval, reranking, active perception, and reasoning, refining evidence from coarse search to fine selection and region cropping. A dense multi-reward scheme guides each action, and group relative policy optimization aligns behavior without a value network. Tests on three benchmarks show gains over baselines, up to 17.7 percent over prior RL-based methods.
arxiv-2604-15467: Gatza and Huang build a part-based reduced-order modeling scheme for large rocket engines, where full high-fidelity runs stay out of reach. Each part, injectors, combustor, and nozzle, gets its own reduced model trained on small-domain runs with enforced system-level responses, then the parts couple into full-system runs. On a seven-injector combustor with self-excited dynamics, predictions track spectra and field features well.
arxiv-2604-15667: Yu, writing for the sPHENIX Collaboration, reports open-charm baryon-to-meson ratios in proton-proton collisions at RHIC. The fully commissioned sPHENIX detector recorded 100 billion unbiased proton-proton collisions in 2024, with more high-statistics data in 2025. The sample enables the first Lambda-c over D-zero baseline at RHIC energies, opening questions on baryon hadronization and strange-to-light flavor ratios.
arxiv-2604-15967: Zhang and nine colleagues expose a flaw in text-to-image models called multi-concept compositional unsafety. Individually safe concepts, combined in one request, can yield harmful or sensitive images, without adversarial prompts, model access, or banned content. They build TwoHamsters to measure the threat: 20k prompts, 51 concept pairs, and six risk categories, tested on 13 models. Prompt-faithful models fail most: FLUX.1 shows a 99.35 percent unsafe alignment rate with a defense rate under 2 percent. Three defenses, filtering, detector tuning, and concept erasure, all fail against unseen combinations.
arxiv-2604-16067: Guransh Singh presents AEGIS, a buffer-free orthogonal gradient projection framework for vision-language fine-tuning. Fine-tuning creates a stability-plasticity dilemma: flow-matching experts send regression gradients into cross-entropy backbones, harming vision. AEGIS measures activation stats from pre-training data as an anchor, then a Wasserstein-2 transport penalty creates an anchor-repair gradient. A backward pass projects updates aside during conflicts. The method sheds only 0.62 percent of energy, halting drift. On LIBERO, it preserves visual question answering and holdout loss while matching action convergence, without buffers.
arxiv-2604-16167: Puglisi, Anand, and Migliaccio train a Cycle-GAN to simulate carbon monoxide emission in the Milky Way, learning from Planck dust maps and HI survey data. They target two CO lines measured by Planck, keeping only sky regions with strong signals, and judge the output by its angular patterns and statistics. The goal is better CO models at high galactic latitudes, where recent surveys have barely looked.
arxiv-2604-16267: Yadav, Woodward, and Forsman improve desalination by grafting polymers onto electrodes. CDI promises efficient water treatment, but suffers weak ion uptake and poor charge use. Their grafted block copolymers boost performance strongly, without changing pore structure. Computer models based on density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations support the gain. Even simple neutral polymers help, while a designed block architecture helps more.
arxiv-2604-16567: Dufresne and colleagues survey the graph reconstruction conjecture in an overview article. The conjecture claims each graph with three or more vertices is fixed by its deck of vertex-deleted subgraphs. Their invariant approach asks whether polynomials telling apart decks also tell apart original graphs. That move turns a graph problem into an algebraic one. The article surveys the conjecture and its algebraic approach for a broad readership.
arxiv-2604-16867: Chitrao and Ghate compute the reductions modulo a prime p of certain semi-stable representations. Their results cover weights from p plus 5 to 2p and from 2p plus 6 to 3p plus 1, for primes p at least 5. This extends earlier methods beyond the weight range where they previously worked, and sharpens a bound on the valuation of the parameter given by Bergdall, Levin, and Liu.
arxiv-2604-17167: Aronoff and four colleagues assess risks as GENIUS stablecoins scale into mainstream payments and settlement. Redemption at par may hinge not only on backing quality, but on Treasury and repo markets, dealer balance sheets, and blockchain rails. Even soundly backed stablecoins face stress from redemption surges, market bottlenecks, or tech failures. Lasting stability likely needs joined-up market infrastructure, prudential regulation, and software governance.
arxiv-2604-17367: Ye and Zhu prove a Petersen-Wei type volume comparison theorem for weighted Riemannian manifolds, spaces with a notion of curvature twisted by a potential function. The result holds under bounds on the Bakry-Emery Ricci curvature and on the gradient of the potential. As an application, they give a modified proof of a volume comparison and monotonicity result for Kähler-Ricci flow, with an improved error estimate. The work extends comparison geometry to a weighted setting where curvature is controlled only in an averaged sense.
arxiv-2604-17467: Cheng, Peng, Zhang, Zhou, and Pan compare seven dissipation channels in warm Higgs inflation, built from low-temperature, high-temperature, and threshold channels. One unified treatment of background evolution, complexity penalties, and boundary checks maps best-fit points, rankings, and warmness indicators. Except for the pure high-temperature channel, the other six cluster together. The pure low-temperature channel stays top-ranked under a broad scan and a 1,200-point rescoring. Warmness diagnostics place the leader in the strong warm regime.
arxiv-2604-17567: Yang and three colleagues offer tool-free calibration for multi-camera rigs in stick-based sports like golf, baseball, and hockey. Calibrating camera positions is normally costly, yet multi-camera setups are standard for capturing athletes and gear in 3D. Their method jointly uses body keypoints of unknown scale from synced videos and a stick of known length. A three-stage optimization refines camera positions, rebuilds human and stick paths, and fixes scale from the stick length. The paper also releases the first dataset for this task, covering four sports.
arxiv-2604-17667: Ghorbanpour and six colleagues present Peerispect, a hands-on system for claim-level checking in research peer reviews. Reviewers often include claims that are opinion-based, showy, or off-target for the sent-in work, and manual grounding checks cannot scale to modern meetings and journals. Peerispect extracts check-worthy claims from reviews, pulls proof from the paper, and checks claims through natural language logic. Results appear in a visual display flagging proof in the paper, built as a modular search setup for reviewers, authors, and program panels.
arxiv-2604-17767: Yoon shows single-particle interference is set by the phase shared by ready state and detector-defined basis, a value usual interferometers cannot access. With biphoton sources seeded in step, scanning pump, seed, or signal phase gives same sine fringes with contrast near 0.99, a three-scan match absent in two-mode devices. Fringe contrast is tuned through idler overlap, showing quantum which-path info without idler sensing. The bright-dark structure unifies population trapping, EM-induced transparency, discrete photonic patterns, and single-slit diffraction, varying only in dark size.
arxiv-2604-17967: Baaj and Prade establish a precise link between binarized neural networks and Sugeno integrals, which represent input importance and interactions through if-then rules. For a hidden neuron at inference time, they show a hidden neuron's activation threshold test equals a Sugeno integral over binary inputs. That yields an explicit set-function form for each neuron decision and a rule-based representation. They also express the last-layer score as a Sugeno integral, and discuss richer interactions and extensions beyond the binary case.
arxiv-2604-18067: Millar and three colleagues introduce PhysioLite, a lightweight model for ECG and EMG analysis on microcontroller-scale neural processing units. Recent Transformer models perform well but are too large and power-hungry for such hardware, and their dynamic attention clashes with micro-NPU constraints. PhysioLite uses learnable wavelet filters, hardware-aware layer design, and CPU-offloaded positional encoding. It matches Transformer models on ECG and EMG benchmarks at under 10 percent of their size, about 370 kilobytes with 8-bit quantization. Tests on two micro-NPUs confirm viability for wearables.
arxiv-2604-18167: Sambandham and Schön introduce Embedding Arithmetic, a tuning-free way to reduce social bias in text-to-image models at run time. The method adjusts embeddings directly, leaving model weights, prompts, and data sets untouched. A control knob sets the strength of the correction while keeping backgrounds, layouts, and styles intact. Tests on FLUX and Stable Diffusion models show it beats existing baselines on diversity while preserving meaning, judged by a new Concept Coherence Score.
arxiv-2604-18667: Rata presents linear-space data structures for frequency questions on tree paths, including the most common element, the least frequent element, and minority queries. The new structures answer path mode and least-frequent queries faster than the previous best bound, and a randomized method cuts the minority query time further. A general framework for maximum-value color queries on paths covers both the mode and least-frequent cases.
arxiv-2604-19267: Dezons and colleagues propose ViLiNT, a navigation policy for ground robots that blends camera images, 3D laser scans, a goal embedding, and a description of the robot's own body shape. A transformer merges those cues and conditions a diffusion model that draws candidate routes. A clearance head then scores and ranks those routes against the robot's dimensions. The design aims to keep collision avoidance working when environment, robot, or sensors change, and it improves success rates across three simulated settings.
arxiv-2604-19767: Qin, Wan, Mudunuri, and Manoharan benchmark EAGLE3 speculative decoding for PayPal's Commerce Agent, which runs on a fine-tuned llama3.1-nemotron-nano-8B-v1 model. Tests run through vLLM against NVIDIA NIM on identical 2xH100 hardware across 40 configurations. The gamma-3 setting lifts throughput by 22 to 49 percent and cuts latency by 18 to 33 percent at no added hardware cost. Acceptance rates hold steady near 35.5 percent for gamma-3 across all conditions, while gamma-5 gives diminishing returns.
arxiv-2604-19967: Burlak and seven colleagues report a curved microjet and four Herbig-Haro objects near the young star FN Tau, tracing a bipolar outflow dubbed HH 1267. The jet bends rather than running straight, likely because the inner protoplanetary disk precesses, tilting the jet axis under 20 degrees from the line of sight. About 60 years ago the star flared by roughly two magnitudes for several months. The authors link those outbursts to the onset of the microjet.
arxiv-2604-20367: Ji and Luo prove improved lower bounds of Brezin-Li-Yau type for mean sums of Dirichlet eigenvalues for the Laplacian and poly-Laplacian on bounded Euclidean domains. The key step is expanding two binary polynomials that may interest readers on their own. Their bounds improve several existing bounds of this kind in the literature. They are optimal in the sense that the expansions capture all positive terms, whereas earlier work captured only a subset of the positive terms in these two polynomials.
arxiv-2604-20467: Tempest and two colleagues present an open-source tool bringing mechanistic interpretability to AI weather models. These models now rival traditional weather prediction, yet how they reach forecasts is poorly understood. The tool gathers latent representations from the model processor and supports early checks, including cosine similarity and PCA, so users can spot latent directions tied to weather features. Applying it to the graph neural network GraphCast, they show case studies for mid-latitude large-scale waves and specific humidity, finding latent channel mixes matching features a human can read.
arxiv-2604-20567: Savaré studies the rest shape of a thin, elastic, inextensible ribbon, which cuts its bending energy to a minimum. As ribbon width tends to zero, that bending energy tends to the Sadowsky functional. He looks at bent anisotropic ribbons with a possibly curved reference shape. He proves Gamma-convergence still holds under set affine edge rules, including those met by a Möbius strip.
arxiv-2604-20767: Sen, Gangopadhyay, and Vedral study gravity-mediated entanglement of phonons in condensates. They use two slow condensates in traps with same rates, set apart under a gravity model with gravitons as go-between. For low gaps, the entanglement is much higher than that for the mass-entanglement scheme, although its fall is faster than the pair case. When the number of atoms in the cloud is grown, the entanglement for a smaller separation distance becomes higher. That allows for a more robust plan using this phonon protocol.
arxiv-2604-21067: Thomas Schincariol turns conflict deaths into three-dimensional shapes spread over place and time, then matches new outbreaks against past patterns to forecast fatalities. His adapted ShapeFinder method, paired with a distance measure between shapes, beats the established Views ensemble benchmark. The approach gives early-warning work a pattern-matching tool for reading how violence spreads and where it may strike next.
arxiv-2604-21167: Mikhailo Dokuchaev, Emmanuel Jerez, and José Vilca-Rodríguez extend partial group actions to algebras where the grouping of products matters. They solve the problem of building a global version of each partial action inside a chosen variety. Their Lambda-construction gives the needed trait and also covers covariant representations in usual and Lie settings, linking the two sides by an adjoint pair. They further show the construction plays well with semidirect products of Lie algebras.
arxiv-2604-21267: Sodbaatar Adiya and four colleagues find exact invariant solutions for a class of linear time-fractional diffusion-wave equations with variable coefficients, using Lie symmetry analysis. They first pin down the tiny symmetries tied to those coefficients, one by one. Those symmetries then yield solutions in terms of Mittag-Leffler functions, generalized Wright functions, and Fox H-functions. The equations model odd transport and wave motion in many real physical systems, giving the symmetry route a direct payoff in physics.
arxiv-2604-21567: Nusrat Nadia and five others propose an AI system coupling demand forecasting with supply chain optimization for textiles and protective equipment. A Long Short-Term Memory forecasts demand, tracking time patterns, while mixed integer programming sets refills and allocation. It cuts forecasting error and cost. Textile and supply datasets, it beats statistical and deep baselines. Mean absolute error falls from about 15 to about 13 and percentage error from about 10 percent to about 8 percent. Stock cost falls about 5 percent, stockouts 28 percent, and service rises from about 96 percent to about 98 percent.
arxiv-2604-21667: Olufunke Sarumi and colleagues model why annotators disagree, treating each annotator's written reason as a fine-grained signal of that person's view. Their system predicts labels and reasons jointly, using who each annotator is and their profile facts through a User Passport that shapes inner vectors. It offers two explainer designs, one prompt-based and one that links label-model vectors into a text maker. Adding reason modeling beats a simple annotator-aware model on guesses, with the bridge design giving steadier label match.
arxiv-2604-21767: Matos and four colleagues move video misinformation detection from whole-video verdicts to pinpointing the offending span. They transcribe video audio to text and annotate the segments carrying fact-checked false claims, building two datasets with more than 500 videos and over 2,400 annotated segments. Classifiers built on state-of-the-art language models then locate misinformation spans with an F1 score of 0.68 overall. Datasets, transcripts, audio, and videos are released publicly.
arxiv-2604-21967: Romancino studies random entanglement percolation in varied quantum networks, where edge singlet-conversion chances are drawn from a spread rather than fixed. After noting random classical and random quantum entanglement percolation, the paper focuses on polarisation loss as a physical source of random edge entanglement in light networks. In this setting, polarisation imbalance gives a simple map from this loss size to edge singlet-conversion chance. The map is shown for typical loss models, and effects for entanglement percolation are noted.
arxiv-2604-22167: Angell and six colleagues propose a sample-efficient way to estimate harmful-output probabilities for any query. They build unsafe model versions, making harmful outputs more probable through importance sampling. On misuse and misalignment benchmarks, their estimates match Monte Carlo estimates using 10 to 20 times fewer samples. A probability of 10^-4 can be estimated with just 500 samples. Harm scores also reveal input response and predict deployment risks, showing rare-event estimation is critical and feasible for safety evaluations.
arxiv-2604-22267: Bhat and Kumar derive new identities in number theory from summation formulas of Ramanujan and Bailey. They first obtain a few theta function identities at level ten. From those identities they derive a new modular equation of degree five. They then establish Eisenstein series identities, also at level ten. Theta functions and Eisenstein series are both families of functions with rich symmetry properties in number theory.
arxiv-2604-22567: Muirhead and Wigman present strong sign-balance for Laplace eigenfunctions, spurred by small-scale sign patterns. Random eigenfunctions are sign-balanced above one fixed scale, almost always. That scale is best up to a log power of energy. Results cover spherical harmonics and band-limited random waves on Riemannian manifolds. For any level, they fix the best scale above which random eigenfunctions are volume-balanced for non-zero levels. The results also model a guess on the best scale at which deterministic Laplace eigenfunctions are sign-balanced.
arxiv-2604-22867: O'Connor outlines the kinematics of a three-body decay under leading-order changes from a Lorentz-violating quantum field theory. A Dalitz plot, the tool named in the title, maps a three-particle decay onto a plane. It uses pairs of invariant masses, so where events fall inside the allowed region reflects the underlying dynamics. Here the kinematics show how small Lorentz-violating effects reshape the allowed decay region. The paper sets up that analysis for such decays.
arxiv-2604-23067: Padmakumar and three colleagues train a general-purpose red teaming model that extends to arbitrary adversarial goals, including ones it was never directly trained on. Most current automated red teaming targets safety and content moderation, using safety models as evaluators and optimizing to circumvent them. Their pipeline needs no ready-made judge at training time. Fine-tuning small models with it greatly improves attack generation for both in-domain and out-of-domain goals.
arxiv-2604-23267: Ghosh and seven colleagues compare fine-tuning and in-context learning in large language models through formal language tasks with controlled sampling. A discriminative test counts an LLM as proficient when it assigns higher probability to in-language strings than to out-of-language ones. Fine-tuning beats in-context learning on in-distribution generalisation, while both match on out-of-distribution generalisation. Inductive biases look similar at partial learning but diverge at higher proficiency, while in-context learning varies more across models and reacts to token vocabulary.
arxiv-2604-23467: Yadav and Zhao speed up language-model inference by splitting the work between two execution styles: fixed parts replay through CUDA graphs while changing parts run through just-in-time compiled kernels. The hybrid keeps runtime flexibility during token-by-token generation, cutting the wait for the first token by up to about two-thirds against a strong baseline. Tests on a 7-billion-parameter model cover short prompts, where launch overhead matters most.
arxiv-2604-23567: Rahaman, Granot, and Beniamini build a unified analytic framework for synchrotron emission from late-time blast waves once shocks slow into the deep Newtonian regime. There, only a fraction of electrons reach relativistic energies. The transition yields a shallower flux decay for gamma-ray burst afterglows. For kilonova remnants, radio fluxes run several times higher than estimates that ignore the regime. Even non-detections then constrain ambient density and outflow energy.
arxiv-2604-24267: Wang and colleagues describe the GRM pipeline for SVOM's Gamma-Ray Monitor, which detects bursts from 15 keV to 5 MeV. The GRM Instrument Center processes data in real time through X-band, enabling rapid response to high-energy events. An event-driven design handles massive data efficiently with real-time monitoring. Through data production, the system generates L1B and C level products via a task scheduling system, with modular design and automated workflows converting detection data precisely.
arxiv-2604-24467: Zeybek, Mukherjee, and Schmelcher present a gradient-free matrix product state sampling heuristic for discrete quantum optimal control. The matrix product state defines a score function over control parameters, giving a sampling distribution over candidate sequences. The distribution refines step by step by picking better sequences and tuning local tensors to favor the best. Tests on single-qubit state transfer, Bell-pair preparation, qutrit gate implementation, and open-system population transfer show stable convergence. Performance is competitive against established gradient-free baselines.
arxiv-2604-24567: Li, Hong, Tang and Zhong develop a correction adaptive two-grid finite element method for elliptic problems that are nonselfadjoint or indefinite. An earlier adaptive two-grid method required symmetric positive-definite problems. An extra step solves a small residual problem on the coarse mesh at tiny cost, lifting the corrected solution's accuracy. The authors prove convergence through a contraction property and confirm the gains numerically. The method thus widens the reach of two-grid methods to a broader class of problems.
arxiv-2604-25167: Shi and nine colleagues propose Interpretability-Guided Data Selection, a framework that turns interpretability insights into training actions for large language models. It first finds causal task features through frequency recall and interventional filtering. It then selects feature-resonant data that maximally activates those features for fine-tuning. On math, summarization and translation tasks in Gemma-2, LLaMA-3.1 and Qwen3 models, the method beat full-dataset fine-tuning on math by 17.4 percent on Gemma-2-2B while using only half the data. Analysis links stronger feature amplification to better task performance.
arxiv-2604-25467: Zhu and three colleagues propose SSF, a subspace method for federated learning. It does heterogeneity-corrected work in a low-dimensional subspace using only projected quantities, with backfill updates that keep full control information. Federated learning runs large models where links, memory, and compute are scarce. Non-IID client data induce drift that hurts local training. Old fixes such as SCAFFOLD correct heterogeneity, but add link and memory costs. Under assumptions, SSF attains a rate of order 1 over T plus 1 over square root of NKT. Tests show good trade-offs.
arxiv-2604-25667: Träff presents two message-passing exclusive scan algorithms for prefix sums over vectors held by ranked units. In message-passing systems with bounded one-ported links, such scans have been far less addressed than inclusive scans. From natural rules, he gives two methods efficient in both round count and operator uses. The first joins inclusive and exclusive phases, trading rounds against uses. The second adapts a round-optimal all-reduce algorithm, with extra work set by the popcount of the rank count minus one.
arxiv-2604-25867: Brown gives new tools for central limit theorems for Lipschitz functions in Markov chain Monte Carlo, by extending weak convergence bounds. His main step turns weak bounds for transition kernels into variance bounds for the kernel acting on Lipschitz functions. When the chain is reversible and the starting density is Lipschitz, weak rates yield chi-squared divergence bounds. The paper applies the machinery to high-dimensional Metropolis-Hastings stability, stochastic gradient descent, and stochastic delay equations.
arxiv-2604-25967: Himanshu Tiwari, Kar, and Priyanshu Tiwari propose digital-twin-assisted belief-state reinforcement learning for latency-robust integrated sensing and communication in 6G. Centralized radio control loops suffer telemetry latency, giving stale observations and unstable control. A digital twin rebuilds a synchronized belief state from delayed telemetry with an Extended Kalman Filter. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent jointly handles beamforming and power allocation. At 50 milliseconds latency, throughput rises 12 percent and sensing error falls 7 percent versus a twin-only controller. At 100 milliseconds it keeps about 88 percent of zero-latency throughput.
arxiv-2604-26067: Nasser and five colleagues present RADIO-ViPE, a system that maps moving scenes from ordinary single-camera video. It links spoken queries to three-dimensional regions and objects in those scenes. Unlike methods needing calibrated depth cameras and known starting poses, it works straight from raw video. It fuses vision and language embeddings with geometric scene information throughout initialization and optimization. Robust kernels handle moving objects and rearranged furniture. Tests on a dynamic benchmark beat prior methods while staying competitive with offline approaches using calibrated data.
arxiv-2604-26167: Saglam and Kalogerias steer aligned language models toward safer outputs at test time by tuning input word embeddings. Earlier work showed this only for cutting profanity in short text completions. Aligned models pose a harder control problem because their outputs split between refusal and compliance, not smooth variation. Their method estimates gradients of a black-box moderation score for the embeddings with no inside access. Gradient descent on those embeddings then reduces the harmfulness of generated text. In their experiments the method neutralizes every safety-flagged response on benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-26267: Pachon asked which kinematical groups let local algebras of canonical quantum fields commute at unequal times. Under Galilean symmetry, a commutation rule at unequal times would also hold at matching positions, clashing with the canonical rules at short separations. With positive energy and Bargmann covariance, sharp-time algebras commute only for separations in a closed null set, bounded below by two quantum speed-limit times. Algebras over open regions with time-smeared fields never commute.
arxiv-2604-26667: De Rosa and Liguori ask whether post-release faults in Python systems can be predicted from software metrics. Using a balanced set of more than 4,000 labeled faults with 83 metrics spanning product, process, statistical, and Python-specific traits, plus normalized code representations, they run cross-project experiments. Large language models and unsupervised models fail to separate residual faults from others, while supervised metric-based models reach recall between 85 and 90 percent and cut missed faults roughly tenfold. Process metrics - age, churn, and developer activity - plus class and file size prove most predictive.
arxiv-2604-26967: Bond and six colleagues propose literate execution, inverting the literate programming idea where code sits inside a static narrative. Here docs and other explanatory bits become first-class artefacts, computed alongside a running program and woven into a view of its execution. They explore the idea through Fluid, a language whose provenance runtime records fine-grained links between inputs and outputs. Those links surface as interactions letting readers trace how middle values shape a result. Merging pictures, provenance, and exposition aims to make programs more explorable and clear.
arxiv-2604-27067: Kerr and eight colleagues trace the origins of 16 low-mass associations using Gaia data and traceback. Three groups of separate populations share birth sites, forming the Leo, CaNMoS, and AquENS associations. Twelve link likely to complexes, six forming while moving outward. Feedback from relatives explains the shapes of the Local and Orion-Eridanus Bubbles, plus Sco-Cen and Orion OB1. Most show triggered star formation, and Leo's vertical speeds and slowdown suggest it formed from a slow cloud hitting Orion gas.
arxiv-2604-27167: Lekeas and Stamatopoulos open up large instruction-tuned language models playing the Prisoner's Dilemma to find why they cooperate instead of playing the Nash equilibrium. Three larger models lock onto full cooperation, while a smaller 8-billion-parameter model stays near Nash play. A logit-lens readout shows early layers leaning toward Nash before a late cooperative surge wins. In the small model one controllable direction in the residual stream can dial the choice monotonically.
arxiv-2604-27467: Zheng and ten others present ScaleBox, a high-quality, scalable system for checking code made by large language models, for both RL training and tests. It makes and manages special judges, runs test cases at once across nodes, and offers a test suite. Tests show it lifts checking accuracy and speed, and RL trials show gains on LiveCodeBench and stable training, ahead of simple-matching rivals. By supplying a high-throughput setup, it supports better large code training research.
arxiv-2604-27567: He and six colleagues detect entanglement in multi-mode Gaussian states from intensity correlation moments up to sixth order, without a local oscillator. Quantum invariants of a state's covariance matrix, drawn from such moments, reveal it through the Peres-Horodecki criterion. Their states come from spontaneous and cascaded parametric down-conversion driven by a pulsed laser, read by a detector built from 32 superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. The method works for two-mode and three-mode states and extends to states with more modes.
arxiv-2604-27667: Ou and Dümbgen offer TFM-S3, a tabular local-global hybrid for robot policy learning on a tight rollout budget. They interleave frequent local updates with rounds of global search, building a low-dimensional policy subspace by SVD for surrogate-guided refinement. A pretrained tabular foundation model scores candidates from a small context set, opening large-scale screening on a tight rollout budget. Tests on continuous control benchmarks show faster early convergence and better final performance than TD3 and population baselines under the same budget.
arxiv-2604-27967: Lerner and colleagues build models that forecast patchy hospital time series while showing the links between variables. Their StructGP method learns a short, ordered list of influences, and an extension adds shared hidden pathways to track how patients change over time. On septic shock records it beat separate-task baselines at short horizons and improved long-horizon creatinine forecasts, with strong calibration throughout.
arxiv-2604-28067: Imamura studies the limits of AI systems that may abstain instead of answering, in yes-or-no formal domains where forced answers cannot avoid hallucination. Abstaining always would dodge error trivially, so the real question is how large a domain of guaranteed correct answers can survive. Using separation in the arithmetical hierarchy, he derives a computability trade-off: dodging hallucination through abstention shrinks guaranteed coverage, and vice versa.
arxiv-2604-28167: Bai and Le map the Vicsek phase diagram for collective motion, such as bird flocks, as noise, density and particle speed vary. A neural classifier trained on polar-order labels picks new simulations near uncertain crossovers. The map resolves a disordered gas at high noise, a polar ordered regime at low noise, and a middle coexistence candidate. That middle window widens with density. Independent diagnostics show the middle regime holds dense ordered bands within a dilute weakly ordered background.
arxiv-2605-00067:
Bruno Buonomo, Eleonora Messina, Claudia Panico, Mario Pezzella, and Gaetano Zanghirati present EPITIME, a software framework for integral epidemic models. Such models describe an outbreak through its history. The system covers two classes: an age-of-infection model and an information-dependent behavioural model, in which people change their conduct as news of the disease spreads.

Its schemes are non-standard finite difference methods. They are built to preserve the continuous models' key traits: positivity, boundedness, invariant regions, and correct long-term behaviour. This holds whatever the time step, with first-order convergence. Versions in MATLAB and Python add parameter handling, input checks, speed tests, and a graphical interface. Experiments cover long-run behaviour, rebuilding an infectivity kernel from COVID-19 case data, and conduct dynamics under different memory kernels.
arxiv-2605-00267:
Daniel Zhu and 3 co-authors test whether jailbreaking a guarded language model weakens the model itself. Earlier work had found a jailbreak tax: the tricks used to slip past safeguards also degrade task performance. The authors ask whether that tax shrinks as models grow more capable, and they run twenty-eight jailbreaks across five benchmarks.

Weaker models paid heavily, losing about a third of their benchmark performance on average when jailbroken. The strongest model tested lost only a small fraction, even though reasoning-heavy tasks degraded more than recall tasks across the board. One leading jailbreak method slipped past classifiers almost perfectly with near-zero loss. The authors recommend that safety cases for frontier models never count on jailbreaks dulling a model's abilities.
arxiv-2605-00767:
Zhenghua Huang reviews what is known about magnetic loops in the Sun's transition region, the thin layer between the visible surface and the million-degree corona. These arcade-like loops, at temperatures from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand degrees, are a basic building block of the layer, born of the coupling between magnetic field and plasma. Their dynamics govern how energy and mass move through the region.

Drawing on observations since the IRIS spectrograph launched, the review covers the loops' morphology, dynamics, plasma parameters, ties to emerging flux, and heating. These loops prove distinct from their better-studied coronal cousins, hosting small-scale phenomena that betray the physics of energy transfer. The author closes with the critical open questions, arguing that sharper instruments and more realistic simulations are needed.
arxiv-2605-00967:
Hollis Williams shows that gravity-induced entanglement tests need not rely on free-fall setups. Such tests could probe the quantum nature of gravity, but free-fall interferometry with massive superpositions imposes severe experimental constraints. Williams argues that systems with effectively inertial motion over short times accumulate the same gravitational phase that generates entanglement.

Deviations from the free-fall phase enter only at a small second-order scale set by the ratio of interaction time to the period of constrained motion. A representative design using carbon nanotube pendula keeps the correction small in relevant regimes, with negligible change to the interference visibility used to certify entanglement. Constrained systems thus broaden options for the Bose-Marletto-Vedral type of experiment.
arxiv-2605-01067:
James Butterworth and two co-authors introduce a variational Bayesian extension of deep symbolic regression, a method that searches for explicit interpretable equations without assuming a functional form in advance. A Bayesian approach adds a probability spread over candidate formulas, quantifying uncertainty with noisy, limited data. The standard method finds a single best expression rather than a posterior over models.

Their DVISR replaces the original reward with the integrand of the evidence lower bound and extends the network to output a spread over constants inside formulas. Posterior inference then covers both formula trees and their constants. Tests show recovery of the true one in simple settings, with and without constant tokens, and examine performance as the search space grows.
arxiv-2605-01167:
Tam Nguyen and three co-authors tackle a side effect of activation steering, a method for guiding a large language model's behavior by pushing its internal activations toward a target feature direction. The standard approach, adding a fixed vector, also shifts activations along many other directions. The authors call this collateral damage: the model changes in ways nobody asked for, which can hurt tasks unrelated to the target.

The damage happens because standard methods treat all non-target directions as if they cost the same. The authors define the damage precisely and recast steering as a constrained optimization problem. Their method picks a new activation that keeps the expected squared collateral change as small as possible, weighted by how activations actually vary in practice. That weighting charges more for shifts in costly directions. The result is finer control over the target behavior with less harm to performance on unrelated tasks.
arxiv-2605-01667:
Lucas O Lyra, Antonio E Fabris, and Joao B Florindo add a classic pattern summary to modern hybrid image networks for medical classification, where labeled scans are often scarce. Fisher vectors, an orderless encoding that pools local features against a fitted mixture model, have long helped plain convolutional networks punch above their data weight.

The team wire Fisher encoding into hybrids that pair convolution with vision transformers, aiming at one model that serves small and large data sets alike. The bottleneck is cost: fitting the mixture grows with the data, so they add a method that caps that growth as sets scale. Tests span a wide range, the MedMNIST suite, a chest CT collection, and a skin lesion set. Scores beat the published benchmarks across the MedMNIST sets and stay competitive with the literature on the two larger clinical collections.
arxiv-2605-01867:
Dipendra Gupta and Gregory Bewley present lab measurements of shear turbulence at high Reynolds numbers, reaching values near 1400 on the Taylor scale. They used a very small hot-wire probe and very long records to measure gaps between speeds at two points. Their aim was to see how the scaling of those gaps changes for higher-order measures.

For lower orders the scaling follows past work, but for order twelve and above the exponents level off near a value of about 2.2. The tails of the speed-gap data line up in the same way, which supports the levelling. The authors link the result to thin, intense vortex filaments that dominate the flow at those scales.
arxiv-2605-01967:
Yavuz Yarici and Ghassan AlRegib study multimodal models that must work in new places where recording conditions differ from training. Most systems train separate encoders for each input type and a fusion step together, end to end. The authors argue that joint training lets encoders lean on links between modalities that only hold in the source setting, a failure they call fusion overfitting.

Their fix, MER-DG, adds a loss term that raises the entropy of each encoder's features, keeping them diverse. It fits into existing frameworks without changing their shape. On EPIC-Kitchens and HAC tests, the method improved average scores by about five percent over standard fusion training.
arxiv-2605-02067:
Vedat Levi Alev, Daniel Frishberg, Michail Sarantis, and Prasad Tetali bound how fast random flips mix among triangulations of a convex polygon. The flip chain moves between ways to cut a polygon into triangles. Past work gave a mixing time near the cube of the size, while the best lower bound sits near size to the power three halves.

The authors prove a relaxation and log-Sobolev time near size squared, up to log factors, which gives the same order for mixing. That moves toward Aldous's conjectured order. Their advance develops transport flow methods further, using combinatorial decompositions to get functional inequalities for Markov chains more efficiently. They suggest the ideas may serve other chains.
arxiv-2605-02267:
Yang Huang and Jingrun Chen predict the traits of materials from their chemical makeup, using formulas a reader can inspect. Their method learns both a formula form and a weight for each element in that formula. No fixed descriptors are needed first. Max and min steps inside the formula enforce natural limits, such as a band gap that cannot go below zero.

Search joins tree search with genetic programming, plus gradient steps and parallel work. On MatBench tasks, scores stay close to top black-box models, while the output stays a clear formula. On semiconductor alloys, trends vary smoothly with makeup. Learned element weights also show a sensible periodic pattern across the table.
arxiv-2605-02567:
Thanasis Pantsios and five co-authors tackle a moving target: detectors that flag AI-generated images lose accuracy as new generators appear. Their answer is data-centered. Detectors, they show, need both images gathered from the open web and images made by current generators to adapt well, and either source alone falls short.

An automated pipeline builds web datasets from fact-check articles, with weak supervision rather than hand labeling. Even a small share of generator-made images in training helps a detector handle a new model, and mixing both sources in a continual learning setup limits forgetting of older generators. Tests on two leading detectors gave clear gains in average accuracy. The work frames detection as ongoing data work, not a one-time training job.
arxiv-2605-02767:
Vajrala and seven colleagues slim down diffusion models for image super-resolution. Diffusion models restore images well, but their size and step-by-step sampling make them expensive to run. Their framework, TOC-SR, first finds a compact diffusion backbone, then distills it into a single-step generator that sharpens a low-resolution image in one pass. Surrogate blocks built by feature-wise generative distillation replace heavier parts of a sixteen-channel latent model, and constrained Bayesian optimization trims complexity while guarding fidelity.

The compact backbone cuts parameters about sixfold and compute about threefold against the expanded model. Adapted for super-resolution, it keeps strong reconstruction quality in experiments, showing that careful architecture search plus distillation can deliver practical one-step enhancement. For phones and other constrained devices, the approach promises sharper images without the wait or the power bill of full diffusion sampling.
arxiv-2605-02867:
Lingxiao Kong and three co-authors use an explanation method to find which reinforcement learning choices drive generalization in robotics. Learning agents are sensitive to algorithm and tuning choices, and the gap between training and new settings blocks real deployment. Prior work studied generalization, but not how much each specific choice adds to the gap, nor how to use that split when choosing a setup.

Their framework scores agent performance across robot settings, then applies Shapley-based explanations to assign impact to each configuration choice. A theoretical link ties those values to generalizability. Patterns proved consistent across tasks and settings, so a guided selection rule could pick better-generalizing setups. Practitioners get concrete guidance on which knobs matter, instead of folklore.
arxiv-2605-03067:
Dimitris Avramidis, Alexandra Lassota, Ulrike Schmidt-Kraepelin, and Adrian Vetta settle the cost of computing Thiele voting rules when preferences have interval structure. These approval rules give fair committee outcomes, but finding the outcome is hard in general.

On the candidate interval domain a linear program works, yet the voter interval case stayed open for years. The team proves the standard program still has an integer optimum there and gives a fast method to find it. The result extends to broader domains, clarifies how two of them relate, and shows a tree-based version turns hard again.
arxiv-2605-03167:
Alexander Dorsey and Ankit Goel design a guidance law that guarantees interception for a pursuer chasing an evader with nonlinear motion. Their base method uses feedback linearization to steady the line-of-sight rates, but steady sight rates alone can still miss, since internal range dynamics stay unconstrained.

They add a zero-dynamics correction that forces the range to close, so sight alignment truly means a closing path. The law stays simple enough for real-time use. Wide Monte Carlo tests over starting geometries show better reliability, smaller miss distance, and steady convergence versus the base method and classic proportional navigation.
arxiv-2605-03267:
Mingzhe Yang, Shuo Wang, and Jiang Zhang propose Partial Effective Information Decomposition, a framework for synergistic causation among many variables. Complex systems often act through joint effects no single source explains, and intervention-based tools for splitting those effects have been missing.

Their method decomposes the influence of several sources on a target under maximum-entropy interventions into unique and synergistic parts. In the three-variable case it fits the main axioms of partial information decomposition, and the setup supports causal graphs with hyperedges and downward causation. A test on air quality forecasting pulled readable station-level causal structure from a learned model.
arxiv-2605-03467:
Camille de Valk, Milou van Nederveen, Koen Reerink, and Werner van Westering estimate the quantum resources needed to reconfigure distribution grids for lower power losses. Finding the best grid topology is NP-hard, and classical solvers strain on real networks, so quantum feasibility needs honest costing.

They frame the problem as a higher-order binary optimization with no auxiliary variables, saving qubits, and apply it to a real Dutch medium-voltage network. For each connected component they count logical qubits and gates, then map to physical resources and runtimes. Needs depend on structure like connectivity and cycles, not size alone.
arxiv-2605-03567:
Antonio Bernini, Stefano Bilotta, and Elisa Pergola study Dyck paths, lattice walks that rise and fall but never drop below their start, under two extra restrictions. The paths may reach height at most h, and they cannot have a certain run of consecutive valleys just below that ceiling. Dyck paths are counted by the famous Catalan numbers.

The authors give a combinatorial description of this restricted class and derive counting formulas with classical lattice-path techniques. As a byproduct, the analysis produces an identity involving Catalan numbers that, to their knowledge, does not appear in the existing literature. The identity grows naturally out of how the restricted path families relate to each other.
arxiv-2605-03767:
Julian Jacobs and Jordan Canedy ask whether United States worker retraining under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act cut workers' exposure to automation. They use over twenty-three million program records from 2017 to 2023. Their Retrainability Index measures outcomes through post-program wage recovery and shifts in how routine the tasks are, a proxy for automation risk.

They find retraining rarely moved workers into less automation-exposed work; many of them simply returned to their prior field. Apparent successes were driven mostly by wage gains, possibly simple catch-up, rather than a change of occupation. Prior skills and local economies moderated outcomes, and employer-led programs such as apprenticeships showed the highest success rates, suggesting current programs support wage recovery better than large cross-industry transitions.
arxiv-2605-03867:
Samuel A. Ballas, Ferhat Karabatman, and Tom Needham prove a dual concentration result in frame theory, the study of redundant coordinate systems used in signal processing. It is known that a random frame whose vectors are drawn uniformly from the sphere is nearly Parseval with high probability. The authors prove the complementary statement about randomly chosen Parseval frames.

Random Parseval frames, sampled with respect to Haar measure, turn out to be nearly equal-norm with high probability. Their proofs are geometric, relying on general measure concentration principles on Riemannian manifolds rather than direct computation. Using the same techniques, they also give a novel probabilistic upper bound for the Paulsen problem. That problem asks how closely a frame can be adjusted to be both Parseval and equal-norm.
arxiv-2605-04067:
Kavinda Athapaththu and five co-authors present SemiConLens, a visual analytics system that pairs human experts with machine learning to discover new two-dimensional semiconductors. Such materials promise relief from the performance decline of thinning silicon. But discovery methods based on density functional theory or machine learning face small datasets and trust problems. Sparse, patchy data is the core obstacle.

The team first develops a correlation-aware multivariate imputation method. It uses models such as autoencoders that learn from little data while revealing uncertainty. That improves semiconductivity prediction. On top of that sits a display module with three linked views. They let users filter, discover, and compare materials, supported by a novel circular glyph design and a cluster-aware layout.
arxiv-2605-04167:
Ravi Sankrit and thirty-six co-authors present the new Hubble Spectroscopic Legacy Archive. The resource coadds spectra of single targets observed over the lifetimes of two Hubble instruments. They are the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph. The archive draws on data in the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes. It produces new coadds on its own whenever fresh data become public.

Targets are defined by coordinates with proper motions accounted for, and target classes are gathered from SIMBAD, NED, and the original observing proposals. Coadded spectra are produced per observing mode. Far-ultraviolet spectra are kept separate by instrument lifetime position. A full-range spectrum is built by abutting selected modes. Each target also gets a readable metadata file, and the coadding code is publicly released for reuse.
arxiv-2605-04267:
Burnat studies how to split a budget between testing solutions and asking the decision maker what they want. Interactive multi-objective optimization trades off competing goals, but each objective evaluation can be expensive, and preference questions also cost time. Cheap pairwise statements are noisy, while indifference adjustments are richer but costlier. QUIVER, a surrogate-assisted evolutionary optimizer, chooses at each step between evaluating objectives and asking either kind of question, picking whichever promises the most decision-quality gain per unit cost.

Across standard DTLZ and WFG benchmarks under simulated decision makers, QUIVER reached the lowest final utility regret on hard WFG problems, beating baselines by about twenty-five percent. The mix adapts to difficulty: on easy problems it asked pairwise questions eighty percent of the time, but on hard problems it shifted to thirty-five percent indifference adjustments. Cost-aware querying, the results suggest, beats any single question type.
arxiv-2605-04767:
Gongyu Ni and Lester Ho study how a quantum network should schedule many simultaneous requests for entanglement, the shared quantum resource behind future quantum communication. At metropolitan scale, requests compete for limited quantum memories, channels, and paths, and links differ widely in quality.

They build a test framework spanning the physical and network layers. It has request queuing, retries, and concurrent distribution. They then propose a central scheduler that runs the memories, channels, and routes. Three strategy families are compared: heuristics, an exact integer optimisation, and a reinforcement learning method. The heuristics expose a core trade-off. The variants are delay-cutting, success-boosting, and balanced. They behave distinctly.
arxiv-2605-04867:
Ali Mohammadi asks a small question with surprising reach: does knowing who serves first change how many games a tennis match is expected to last? He assumes each player's chance of winning a point on serve stays fixed through the match. That simple setup lets the first-server effect be isolated and measured exactly.

Mohammadi maps the regions where the effect matters and shows it is never large, at most well under half a game. Still, it can shift the chance of a long match by several percent when the players serve unequally well. Data from professional matches support the fixed-probability assumption for modelling total games.
arxiv-2605-04967:
Lovro Dulibić, Blaženka Melić, and Ivan Nišandžić update predictions for how long doubly heavy baryons and one related meson live before decaying. These particles contain two heavy quarks, and their lifetimes test heavy-quark theory in detail. The authors include higher-order corrections to several contributions, including the chromomagnetic term and spectator effects where the light quark takes part.

They compare results across three mass schemes used in particle theory and give lifetime orderings for each baryon family. For one family they present predictions under both possible spin assignments of the heavy pair. A revisited lifetime for the Bc meson and the effect of a newly included Darwin term are also discussed.
arxiv-2605-05067:
Francesco Campanella and Fabio Riccioni extract the gravitational multipole structure of rotating objects from scattering amplitudes, in four and in higher dimensions. Multipoles describe how a body's mass and motion shape its gravitational field beyond the simplest point-mass picture. In four dimensions only mass and current moments are independent, and the authors show how the Kerr black hole's structure arises from minimally coupled spinning fields.

Extending to non-minimal couplings gives the most general rotating solution with spin-induced moments up to octupole order. In five dimensions a new infinite family of stress moments appears, and different matter fields produce qualitatively different quadrupoles, a contrast the authors trace through the stress-energy tensor.
arxiv-2605-05267:
Kaifeng He and nine co-authors systematically review quality problems in code written by large language models and trace them back to training data. Language models frequently emit defective code, from logic bugs to security holes, and data quality is one contributor among several. Earlier literature had not connected specific data issues to specific code outcomes in one synthesis.

Reviewing more than one hundred papers, the authors build taxonomies of generated-code quality dimensions and training-data issue groups. They synthesise a dozen recurring relationship families linking the two, each traced to its supporting evidence and limits. Detection and mitigation methods across the data, model, and generation stages are also gathered, with provenance flagged as an open need.
arxiv-2605-05467:
Serving many users from one set of graphics cards means juggling urgent chats against relaxed background jobs. Vikranth Srivatsa and four co-authors present Nitsum, a serving system for large language models. It treats tensor parallelism, the splitting of a model across cards, as a dial it can turn while running.

Nitsum adjusts that split, divides cards between reading and writing stages, and schedules requests together. Weight reuse and fast memory migration make the changes cheap enough to use often. On real workload traces it improved the share of requests meeting their speed targets by up to about five times.
arxiv-2605-05567:
A classifier moved to a new domain may meet classes it never saw in training. Chuan-Xian Ren, Cheng-Jun Guo, and Hong Yan tackle those private classes under extreme label shift. Older methods assume private classes look like obvious outliers, but a shared class can vary internally more than a private class differs from it.

Their score, built on local transport mass from optimal transport theory, separates shared from private samples. A full method, ReOT, then learns while keeping the two groups apart, avoiding bad matches. They prove a target-risk bound and validate the approach on benchmark experiments.
arxiv-2605-05867:
AI code generators pass functional tests while quietly shipping security holes. Ali Soltanian Fard Jahromi, Amjed Tahir, Peng Liang, and Foutse Khomh systematically investigate how to harden generated code after the fact. Their study spans fine-tuning and prompting strategies, measured against a list of common weakness types.

Earlier mitigations, from static-analysis-guided generation to prompt engineering, varied wildly in effectiveness across models and settings. The authors assess how far each strategy actually improves security, and where the improvements stop. The result is a map of which repairs are worth their cost for which models.
arxiv-2605-05967:
Davide Maran and Csaba Szepesvári sharpen error guarantees for kernelized bandit optimization when the model is misspecified. In such problems a learner picks actions and is scored against a reward function that may sit slightly outside its kernel model. Past bounds charge for that mismatch at a rate tied to kernel complexity, which can be steep.

The authors show the penalty can grow only logarithmically for a large class of kernels. Offline, a spectral constant governs the extra error, while online, a domain splitting algorithm keeps local errors from swelling globally. Their online regret bound drops an extra factor that earlier results carried. The shared idea is localization, in spectrum for one setting and in space for the other.
arxiv-2605-06067:
Maxim Fishman and four co-authors show that a normalized language model architecture is naturally suited to 4-bit training. Low precision training is critical for efficiency, but standard models need extra tricks to keep quality at such widths. The nGPT design constrains weights and hidden states to a unit sphere, which changes how signal and noise behave.

In this design, quantization noise stays uncorrelated while weak positive signal correlations build up across the hidden dimension. That yields a higher signal to noise ratio and a flatter loss landscape, with the benefit growing at larger sizes. The team validate stable end to end 4-bit training on a dense model and on hybrid mixture of experts models. No random transforms or per tensor scaling were needed.
arxiv-2605-06367:
Flavio Nicoletti and four co-authors examine how data structure and class imbalance shape the learning dynamics of diffusion models. Real datasets mix classes with different spreads and frequencies. Models usually move from generalizing to memorizing, but older theory assumes uniform data, leaving open how uneven classes change that order.

Using a random-features model trained on Gaussian mixtures, the authors derive which classes generalize or memorize first. Class variance matters most, centroid geometry second, and sampling imbalance can reverse the order or delay minority classes. Tests with U-Net models on Fashion MNIST support the predictions, warning that some classes may memorize while others stay underlearned.
arxiv-2605-06467:
Johannes S. Schmidt and five co-authors examine how topological deep learning models should be evaluated. These models work on higher-order data such as manifold triangulations, which allow operations that graphs do not. Evaluation practice has lagged, and earlier benchmark claims suggested a clear advantage for higher-order methods.

The team extends the MANTRA benchmark to more manifold types and finds both graph networks and higher-order methods can saturate it, given the right representation and features. Under a stricter protocol using varied representations and refinements, no model shows generalization beyond the data's combinatorial structure. Their protocol gives future work a firmer test for true topological understanding.
arxiv-2605-07167:
Simon Pfreundschuh and three co-authors present GPROF-IR, a neural method for estimating rainfall from a single infrared satellite channel. Merged global precipitation products blend microwave and infrared sensors, but infrared estimates are weaker and can leave artifacts. Geostationary infrared views, though, are available almost continuously across much of the globe.

A convolutional network reads sequences of half-hourly infrared images to exploit motion over time. Checked against ground and ship measurements, the method beat the infrared retrieval in the current product version and rival methods. In some regions it even beat microwave estimates, supporting its use in the next product version and in long historical records.
arxiv-2605-07267:
Elahe Khatibi and six co-authors learn personal causal graphs for healthcare that change over time. Cohort models give stable but generic cause-and-effect maps, while single-patient discovery is unreliable because individual records are short and noisy. PerCaM-Health starts from a knowledge-guided population graph, then cautiously adapts it with each patient's own temporal evidence.

Rolling updates produce an auditable sequence of graphs, and linked equations support what-if questions about short-term outcomes under behavior changes. On a semi-synthetic health benchmark, the framework beat cohort-level and per-patient baselines at recovering graphs, tracking changing edges, and judging intervention direction. Personal and time-varying structure, jointly modeled, proved more reliable.
arxiv-2605-07567:
David González-Andrade and twelve co-authors report a new way to couple light and sound inside silicon chips. The effect they use, stimulated Brillouin scattering, links optical signals with gigahertz vibrations and serves microwave photonics. Earlier silicon devices were dominated by bulk effects, because designs that touch the device boundaries paid for it in optical loss or awkward frequencies.

Their devices use transverse-magnetic light modes and vertical breathing vibrations in suspended silicon membranes with patterned claddings, so the moving-boundary effect dominates. They measured forward Brillouin interaction at a record 12 gigahertz, with very high gain and millimeter-scale amplification using under 15 milliwatts of pump power. The result points to a scalable platform for high-frequency on-chip signal processing.
arxiv-2605-07667:
Ushangi Goginava and Farrukh Mukhamedov study maximal operators built from dyadic martingale transforms of Walsh-Fourier partial sums, a corner of harmonic analysis. The weights involved are required to satisfy a uniform dyadic variation condition and a bound at the top scale. The question is when these weighted Walsh-Carleson operators obey weak-type estimates and when the series they govern diverge.

Along subsequences, they prove weak type estimates for the maximal operators, and they give divergence criteria tied to the weights' behavior near the top dyadic scale. Applications follow for matrix transforms of Walsh-Fourier sums, including several classical averaging methods. Among the consequences are a Walsh-Paley analogue of the Leindler-Tandori theorem and everywhere-divergence results for multiple summability methods.
arxiv-2605-07767:
Xuanshuo Fu and two co-authors enhance badly lit images by mining the information already inside them, instead of building ever larger models. Their network, SIMI, splits a low-light image into bit-plane components and works with those pieces in an unsupervised framework, so no external paired training data is required.

Working from the image's own intrinsic information speeds convergence and lowers computational overhead compared with data-hungry approaches. The unsupervised design also makes the method easier to apply in real settings, where matched bright reference photos rarely exist. On standard low-light enhancement benchmarks, SIMI reached state-of-the-art performance according to the authors' experiments.
arxiv-2605-08067:
Dipranjan Chatterjee and a large team probe a puzzling magnetic state in Y-kapellasite, a spin one-half kagome antiferromagnet. Frustrated magnets can lock their magnetization at fractions of full saturation, and theory predicts a plateau at one ninth. That feature is rarely seen in experiments, and its origin is unclear.

Using pulsed-field magnetization on single crystals and high-field chlorine NMR, the team found plateaus at one third and one ninth, plus a weaker low-field feature. Across the one-ninth plateau the spins settle into an ordered pattern and low-energy fluctuations are strongly suppressed. The behavior fits a gapped fractional state rather than a gapless one.
arxiv-2605-08167:
Fatma Betul Buyuk, Gozde Karatas Baydogmus, Ali Buldu, Ayaulym Tulendiyeva, and coauthors detect forged digital images with transfer learning. Cheap, powerful editors have made manipulated pictures common, and forensic tools must catch edits that leave only faint traces.

Their framework pairs pretrained convolutional networks with a hybrid input: the plain RGB image plus compression-difference features that expose subtle artifacts left by editing. A per-model threshold, tuned with the Youden index, balances true and false positives for each network. Tests on the CASIA v2.0 dataset with several pretrained architectures show how the added compression channel and tuned thresholds improve classification reliability.
arxiv-2605-08367:
Miroslav Maksimović and Velichka Milousheva simplify the description of marginally trapped surfaces in Minkowski space. Such a surface is spacelike. Yet its mean curvature vector is lightlike at every point. That borderline case has physical interest. In general, such a surface is pinned down by seven functions. Those functions obey a system of differential equations.

The authors introduce special canonical principal parameters. Every surface of general type admits them, at least locally. In these coordinates, a fundamental theorem holds. The surface is determined, up to a rigid motion, by three smooth functions. Those functions satisfy a partial differential system. Fewer free functions make the class far easier to work with.
arxiv-2605-08567:
Xue and six colleagues build a benchmark for world models that predict video from actions. Current benchmarks mostly cover first person navigation or narrow robot sets, leaving rich physics play untried. Their benchmark, ACWM-Phys, tests action conditioned prediction under varied physics in a clean, controllable simulator.

It spans particle motion, kinematics, rigid body dynamics, and deformable object interactions, with tests shifting interaction patterns or scene layouts.
