The authors compare trends by age, race, and social and income status. Poor mental health at the low end of a health scale stands in for despair. The work cannot prove that these problems caused the deaths in the deaths of despair story. It can still guide health plans by showing which groups lost ground in health and hope across the two survey waves.
pmc-10736067:
Rose Lin, Jingjing Su, and Kathi Heffner pool trials of mindfulness training for adults with mild memory loss. Mild cognitive impairment marks an early stage before dementia for many people. Past trials of mindfulness for thinking skills gave mixed results. The team searched six data bases for randomized trials on the topic.

Twelve trials with 530 people met the bar for pooling. Mindfulness gave a small to mid gain in overall thinking scores. Gains also showed for space skills and long-term memory. Short-term memory, planning, and focus showed no clear gain. Study quality and program traits did not shift the effect in checks. The authors call for larger trials to firm up the claim.
pmc-10737367:
Fred Kobylarz and five co-authors study how often doctors billed Medicare for advance care planning talks. Their 2023 paper looks at people who died in 2019. Such talks let patients state what care they want if they can no longer decide for themselves, and new billing codes from 2016 let doctors charge for them.

The team linked claims and other files for more than two million people who died. About one in six had a billed planning talk in the last two years. Talks were a bit more common under fee-for-service care than under Medicare Advantage plans. Most talks were short, and most took place in hospitals. The paper also tracks how use varied by race, place, and type of care.
pmc-10737867:
Mei-Ching Chang, Yu-Tai Lo, Wei Lee, and Sheng-Yu Fan find a simple cut-off that flags frailty and disability risk in older clinic patients, in a 2023 study. A World Health Organization scale grades six inner capacities: thinking, moving, nutrition, hearing, vision, and mood. The team tested 397 outpatients aged 65 and over at a medical center. They compared the scale against standard frailty and daily-living measures.

Three or more failing capacities marked the danger line for both frailty and disability. Thinking, mobility, and nutrition problems drove frailty risk. Hearing joined that trio for disability. The scale discriminated well in both cases. The authors urge clinic staff to watch elders with failing capacities closely, since those failures arrive before the frailty they predict.
pmc-10738167:
Hyunjin Noh, Haelim Jeong, Denise Kan, and Lewis Lee ask rural older adults in Alabama how they view trimming pain drugs and trying drug-free care, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Phone talks reached elders with lasting pain and several health issues. Views on cutting back meds were mixed and wary.

Many feared losing drug gains while also fearing side effects. Doubt about drug-free options ran high, and cost plus travel blocked access. Plain lack of word about what exists was also common. The authors urge teaching and advocacy to build know-how and trust. Readers get the elder view that any pain plan must answer first.
pmc-10738967:
Dokyung Yoon, Eileen Crimmins, and Jennifer Ailshire studied neighborhood ties and well-being in older adults with dementia, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. They used a national survey of adults aged sixty-five and older in the United States. The question was whether a strong sense of trust and closeness nearby softens the harm dementia does to well-being.

People with likely dementia reported lower well-being than others. People in close-knit areas reported higher well-being. The gain from close local ties was larger for those with dementia than for those without it. The authors say building trust among neighbors may help protect people living with dementia.
pmc-10740867:
Iris Heinsoo and co-authors review chest infection treatment in dogs in this 2023 paper. The condition, pyothorax, is pus in the chest cavity. Common bacteria include mixed anaerobes and several named species. Guidelines suggest certain first choice antibiotics while culture results are pending. The team checked whether those choices match real culture data.

Records covered 53 dogs treated at two referral centers between 2014 and 2020. Just over half had a positive fluid culture. Pasteurella species were the most common isolate, followed by Escherichia coli. Sensitivity of each isolate to tested drugs was tallied. The results were compared with a national poster guide and other published guides. Mismatches point to where first choice advice may need updating.
pmc-10741967:
Mierzwa and co-authors report a 4-year-old boy found by chance to carry two rare gene changes. One change sits in the RET gene and causes MEN2B, a syndrome with early thyroid cancer. The other sits in the RyR1 gene, linked to muscle disease and a risk with anesthesia.

Testing began because of short stature and slow motor growth, and the mixed signs slowed diagnosis. Scans of his thyroid looked normal, but a blood marker was high at 34, far above the normal limit. Surgeons removed the thyroid, and lab checks confirmed medullary thyroid cancer.
pmc-10743567:
Barbara Carrese and co-authors test tiny drug-carrying particles against breast cancer grown as three-dimensional balls of cells, in a 2023 paper. The particles are built from a blood protein and loaded with doxorubicin, a standard cancer drug. Such balls of cells mimic real tumors better than flat cell layers, so the team used them to judge how well the particles enter, kill, and show up on imaging.

The particles entered cancer balls more deeply than healthy breast cell balls. The drug spread through the cells over a day, and the balls died mainly at the highest dose. Adding laser light, which heats the particles, killed cells at lower doses and shorter times. The particles also gave off a sound-based imaging signal that grew with dose. The authors argue the mix of drug, heat, and imaging could cut the drug dose patients need.
pmc-10743967:
Jacob Schoffl and colleagues report the first test of heart rate variability biofeedback in adults with spinal cord injury. The therapy trains self-control of cardiac autonomic activity and has helped other clinical groups, but spinal cord injury disrupts the autonomic pathways it acts through. The article sets out a lab framework and a case series of two adults with chronic injuries at different levels and degrees.

The program ran ten weeks, mixing face-to-face and telehealth sessions with daily home practice. Body measures included heart rate and blood pressure variability and baroreflex sensitivity. Both people showed some improvement in the body measures. They also reported gains in mood, fatigue, pain, and quality of life. With two participants nothing is proven; what it gives is feasibility and a measuring framework ready for a powered trial.
pmc-10745067:
Jungim Lee and colleagues published a 2023 survey of worm infections in northwestern Tanzania. Two parasite groups burden the region. One spreads through contaminated water contact. The other spreads through soil. The team tested schoolchildren and adults across many villages.

Urine and stool samples were examined with standard methods. Thousands of children took part in the survey. Questionnaires explored exposure risks at home and school. Infection in adults ran near one in twelve for one parasite. Results guide where mass treatment should focus. Knowing risk factors helps target water and sanitation efforts.
pmc-10746967:
Silvia Gabrielli and a team of co-authors describe building a virtual reality game with, not just for, teenagers with autism. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The game, called Zentastic, aims to train social skills through shared adventure play.

Small groups of teenagers play together online while therapists guide the sessions. Teenagers and therapists joined the design work from the start. They reacted to an early version in an acceptability study, then tested the finished game over several sessions. The players took to the game well. Their social skills also rose from the start of training to the end. The authors offer early proof that such games can help, while noting the study was small and exploratory.
pmc-10749967:
Liu and seven co-authors improve a deep learning network for coconut scan segmentation, in work from twenty twenty-three. Coconut breeding relies on manual experience because the fruit inner structure is hard to observe. Seeing internal traits accurately and in time would speed breeding decisions.

Computed tomography scans give cross sections of the whole coconut. Their model, based on the DeepLab network, replaces one pooling module with a denser version and adds an attention module. Image segmentation then labels tissue regions automatically. Better segmentation turns slow expert reading into repeatable measurement for breeding trials.
pmc-10771967:
Nikhila Chelikam and co-authors reviewed the rise of point-of-care ultrasound, the practice of scanning patients at the bedside during examination and treatment. The method is fast, radiation-free, and repeatable, and it began as a way to find internal bleeding in trauma patients. It has since spread through emergency rooms, intensive care units, and operating theatres as a life-saving diagnostic habit.

The review traces that history and surveys where the scans help most today. It also names barriers inside general internal medicine, including training gaps, while noting that new pocket-sized probes put the tool within easy reach. The authors recommend a focused, binary decision style of scanning and proper training in medical curricula to spread its benefits.
pmc-10894067:
Giesbrecht and co-authors test whether ground penetrating radar can find drowning victims trapped under ice. Each year people fall through ice on lakes and rivers and drown. Bodies may float up under the ice sheet, where divers face risk and poor odds of success. A contact-free search tool would keep rescue teams off thin ice. The team placed three euthanized pigs under ice as stand-ins for human victims.

Radar units at 500 MHz and 1 GHz were dragged across ice from 5 to 26 cm thick. Both units picked out the rough shape of the targets through ice up to 42 cm. A signal matching method helped flag the buried shapes. The results support radar as a safer first search step.
pmc-10905567:
Ryszard Zamorski and co-authors present a 2023 study of why some rice varieties store a wall sugar called glucomannan in their grains while others store none. Cell walls shape plant growth and the quality of food and materials made from plants. How wall makeup varies within one species was poorly understood.

Under the microscope, grain walls from many varieties fell cleanly into two groups: with the sugar or without it. The sugar made up a tenth or more of the starchy walls where present and sat close to cellulose fibres. Gene comparisons pointed to one gene whose form differed sharply between the two groups. Finding the exact gene could guide breeding for grain quality.
pmc-10984667:
Ajay Kumar Jain leads a large clinical research network team asking whether what children with fatty liver disease actually eat tracks with how severe the disease is. Pediatric fatty liver is spreading, and lifestyle change is the main treatment, yet rigorous diet measurement has been missing. One hundred nineteen children from ten tertiary centers had their diets scored with the Healthy Eating Index.

Children averaged about thirteen years old, and most were boys and Hispanic. Those in the healthiest diet tier weighed less and had better blood lipids: triglycerides fell steadily from the lowest to the highest diet-quality group, while protective cholesterol rose. The pattern supports diet quality as a measurable lever in pediatric liver disease care.
pmc-11019967:
Collins, Moons, Dhiman, and co-authors publish TRIPOD+AI, updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models. Such models estimate a patient's risk or likely outcome, and they may use plain statistics or machine learning. A first TRIPOD statement in 2015 set minimum reporting rules for these studies.

The update extends those rules for an era when learning algorithms are common in medicine. Authors are told what to report so readers can judge if a model was built and tested fairly. Clear reporting helps hospitals avoid weak models and helps good models earn trust faster.
pmc-11090167:
Yu-Jie Guo and eight co-authors develop a scale in 2024 to measure how ready cancer patients feel to return to work. Research on this topic in China is still new, and no tool existed for this specific skill. The team built draft items from theory and prior studies, then refined them through expert rounds and a pilot survey.

A large survey of three hundred seventy six patients was used to test the scale. The final version has twenty four items in three groups: focusing on recovery, rebuilding confidence, and adjusting plans. Scores were highly consistent and held up over a two week retest. The authors say the scale can guide support for patients who plan to work again.
pmc-11225467:
Rita Nassanga and eight co-authors describe chest scan findings in Ugandan patients thought to have COVID-19 lung infection, at a time when lab test kits ran short. Fine chest scans were used to guide care in place of the gene test. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

The team reviewed scans of hundreds of patients and the gene test results where they existed. Cloudy patches in both lungs were the most common find. Only a part of patients had the gene test, and few of those tested positive, yet most who tested negative still had scans classed at the highest COVID like level. Scan exactness beat the gene test, the authors conclude.
pmc-11532267:
Duoping Zhu and six colleagues published a 2024 study predicting where an endangered plant, Pyrethrum tatsienense, can grow in China as the climate changes. The plant is critically endangered, and protecting it requires knowing which habitats suit it now and in the future.

The team used a computer model called Maxent, tuned for accuracy, with records of 127 places where the plant occurs. They fed in climate data for the distant past, the present, and future scenarios. The model identified the main factors that limit the plant's range and mapped how suitable habitat may shift. Such maps help conservation planners choose reserves and decide where replanting efforts are most likely to succeed.
pmc-11532367:
Old age brings oral disease, and for tribal elders the burden can be heavy. The three authors surveyed 486 members of the Irula tribes of Tamil Nadu aged 65 and over, chosen by multistage sampling in the northern district. They used the Geriatric Oral Health Assessment Index to score oral health-related quality of life, alongside demographics, medical history, and oral complaints.

Most respondents were 65 to 69, three quarters were women, and two thirds could not read. Many reported trouble eating and speaking and oral discomfort. Education stood out: more schooling went with better oral quality of life scores, while arthritis went with worse ones. Other conditions showed no clear link. The authors call for targeted oral health programs and awareness drives in tribal communities, plus larger studies of elder oral health.
pmc-11535567:
Four researchers examine magnesium composite parts made by stir processing with added ultrasound, in a research paper from 2024. The base alloy gains strength from hard titanium carbide particles stirred into its surface. Ultrasound during stirring adds energy that may spread the particles better.

Parts made with vibration had no voids in the stirred zone and showed finer grains. The particles spread evenly and pinned the grain edges, raising dislocation counts. Hardness and tensile strength rose clearly over plain stir processing. The grain size shrank as well. The study shows vibration-assisted stirring as a route to tougher light-metal parts for transport use.
pmc-11536767:
Aboalsamh and co-authors tell of a rare in-gut loop post a one-cut kidney gift. Scope gift cuts took the place of open cuts from 1995 on. One-cut work trims four cuts to one for the gift pull. Known risks span blood hits, in-cut organ harm, and gut stalls. Rare snags past those have gone less probed in print. In-gut loops are one such rare snag in that set. They can block the gut, starve it, and kill its wall.

Their case is a through-web loop post the one-cut gift work. The host was sound in the main, with no grave past ills. One past mark stood out: an irate bowel call years prior. The team flags how such loops form post the cut.
pmc-11540067:
Xue-Feng Liang and co-authors measure how well flu shots in pregnancy prevented flu-like illness in Gansu, China, in this 2024 paper. Province records from the 2019 to 2021 seasons formed a large comparison group. Vaccinated and unvaccinated mothers were followed for illness rates.

Illness struck about four point seven percent of the vaccinated group and about six point nine percent of the unvaccinated. After adjustment, the vaccine's protection came to roughly twenty-two percent. Timing within pregnancy made no clear difference. The authors conclude the shot gave real, if modest, protection, and they report the finding for maternal health planning.
pmc-11575067:
Naghmeh Abbasi Kasbi and seven co-authors survey what patients believe triggered their multiple sclerosis in a 2024 study from Iran. The disease inflames and strips nerves in the brain and spinal cord. What sets off the first attack remains disputed among scientists.

A questionnaire went out through a hospital research center and social media channels. Patients reported stress events, infections, vaccines, pregnancy, head injury, surgery, and weight loss around onset. Answers split by whether diagnosis came before or during the COVID-19 pandemic. Comparing the eras shows whether pandemic conditions changed the trigger mix. Patient-reported patterns can guide deeper studies of true causes. The survey also captures how a crisis era reshaped illness experience.
pmc-11576967:
Léo-Paul Tricou and seven colleagues study how the germ Staphylococcus aureus gets inside bone cells, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The germ's usual door uses a bridge of proteins that ends at docking spots called beta-1 integrins. A membrane protein, caveolin-1, was known to slow entry in skin cells. The team asked what happens in bone cells when the usual door is missing.

Entry needed recycling of the docking spots plus three helper switches. To their surprise, germs still entered cells that lacked the usual door, as long as caveolin-1 was also gone. Backup docking spots then took over the bridge role. The work shows the cell's membrane order decides which door the germ can use.
pmc-11579267:
Muhammad Arif Asghar and four co-authors review infectious uveitis, a swelling inside the eye caused by germs, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites can all trigger it, and it harms sight worldwide. The team mapped trends over fifteen years and traced how the disease works at the molecular level.

They searched five databases for studies from twenty oh nine to twenty twenty-three, keeping ninety-seven. Reports rose over time, above all for viral cases. Viruses caused the largest share, then bacteria. Rates ran highest in poorer regions with more body-wide infections and fewer test tools. Network analysis of linked proteins flagged a few immune signals as hubs. The review ties germ types to immune pathways.
pmc-11588067:
Shravan Pradeep and five colleagues published a materials study in two thousand twenty-four on baseball's famous Rubbing Mud. For nearly a century, mud from a secret New Jersey river site has dulled new baseballs for Major League play. What makes it work was a mystery of soft matter physics.

Multi-scale tests of flow and friction revealed three mechanisms. The cohesive mud fills leather pores, evening the surface, thanks to strong shear thinning. Its residue doubles sticking contact on the ball. Sparse angular sand grains, glued on by clay, stud the surface and raise grip friction. The authors say the mix could inspire sustainable geomaterials. They also note lessons for mudslide modelling and moving through mud.
pmc-11590367:
Jane Foo and co-authors published this drug discovery study in 2024. Up to forty percent of patients with estrogen receptor positive breast cancer eventually resist standard hormone therapies. Resistance often comes from changes that keep the receptor switched on. Rather than block the usual hormone pocket, the team targeted a second site on the receptor called AF2. Partner proteins must dock there for the receptor to drive gene activity.

Using AI-guided deep docking, they screened over a billion small molecules in the computer. About 290 candidates went into cell-based and cell-free tests, ranked by how well they cut receptor activity and cancer cell growth. One lead compound, VPC-260724, worked at low doses. Tests confirmed it binds the AF2 site directly and breaks the receptor's grip on a key partner protein. It also slowed resistant cancer cells. The authors suggest pairing such a blocker with current treatments.
pmc-11592067:
Wenyi Tang and co-authors review two hormone families in a 2024 paper. Activins and inhibins were first known for opposed effects on a pituitary hormone. Wider roles across many tissues have since emerged. They signal mainly through a classic pathway, with other routes in play. Their action is complex and depends on context.

Recent work ties both families to heart and vessel disease. Signals from other organs also track with heart disease growth. The review sums biological roles, mechanisms, and heart findings in one place. Heart researchers get a map of two factors long filed under reproduction. Cross-system signals are easy to miss in organ-siloed research. If these factors drive part of heart disease, they offer fresh drug targets. The authors frame the field as young, with mechanism gaps still open.
pmc-11594467:
Grigorios Kyriakopoulos and three co-authors review farm pesticides, legal and banned, in a 2024 paper. Pesticides drive modern yields but are criticized for harming soil, water, and sometimes people, so greener options are in demand. Their review catalogs dozens of distinct chemicals, alone or in mixes and residues. Most target insects, with smaller groups against weeds, fungi, and mites.

They sorted the chemicals by structure into simulated marketable and banned pools and computed adjustment measures that grouped them into four clusters. Crystal analysis worked only for the marketable set. The authors frame the catalog as a base for judging which chemistries deserve replacement.
pmc-11595067:
Hikosaka-Kuniishi and a team of colleagues studied a signaling helper protein, TRAF5, in mouse immune responses in twenty twenty-four. Germinal centers are lymph node hubs where B cells refine antibodies. TRAF5 connects to CD40, a key switch in that process, but its exact role was unclear.

Mice lacking TRAF5 were immunized with a model antigen plus adjuvant. Their germinal center B cells formed poorly, and antigen-specific IgM and IgG1 antibodies fell sharply. Genes that CD40 normally switches on for center formation also dropped. In lab tests, TRAF5-free B cells made less antibody, grew less, and answered CD40 stimulation weakly. Giving a CD40 activator to deficient mice still failed to rescue center growth. The authors call TRAF5 crucial for CD40-driven, T-dependent immunity.
pmc-11595267:
Yuxin Chen and co-authors sequence stick insect genomes in a 2024 paper. Stick and leaf insects are famed for mimicry, but their family tree is still debated. Mitochondrial genomes offer markers to settle the branches.

The team sequenced five mitogenomes and built trees with two methods and two data sets. Their results place the leaf insect family at the base of a major group. Two subfamilies held together as single branches, while one family proved polyphyletic, drawn from mixed lines. A time tree put the origin of living stick insects in the Jurassic, with most lines splitting after the dinosaur-killing extinction.
pmc-11595967:
Georgy Lazorenko and four co-authors tested flax waste as a soil strengthener in a 2024 paper. Expansive soils swell and shrink as their moisture changes, which cracks roads and foundations. Usual fixes are costly and hard on the environment, so the team tried fibers left over from flax processing.

Mixed into clay soil, the flax tow raised strength by up to 29 percent at a dose of 0.6 percent. Cracking fell sharply at a slightly lower dose. Adding more fiber backfired, because the fibers clumped and gripped the soil less well. The authors present flax waste as a cheap, green way to steady problem soils.
pmc-11597267:
Elana Bosch, Jorg Sporri, and Johannes Scherr review genetic variants that affect iron handling in healthy adults. Their review came out in 2024. The goal is to support nutrition advice that is tailored to a person's genes.

The team searched three large databases for studies in English and German over a long span. Twenty-one papers met their rules, and all of the variants found affected iron measures. One gene showed the strongest link to iron levels. Two variants in another gene appeared to protect against low iron. Eleven other variants raised the risk of iron shortage, which suggests those carriers may gain from extra iron in the diet.
pmc-11597367:
Khursheda Parvin and co-authors present a 2024 study of a plant acid that helps tomato seedlings ride out drought. Water shortage cuts seedling growth, drains leaf water, and lets reactive molecules damage cells. The acid, a natural compound from plant cell walls, is known to tune stress responses.

Seedlings grown in water culture were pretreated with the acid for two days, then put under four days of drought stress, both by withholding water and with a drying agent. The team tracked growth, leaf water, green pigments, and the antioxidant defense system, plus a detox pathway for a harmful byproduct. Pretreated plants kept more growth and suffered less oxidative damage than untreated stressed plants.
pmc-11600867:
Tiina Savikangas and four co-authors published an aging study in twenty twenty-four on how mood and movement related during COVID restrictions in Finland. Two population cohorts, one around age sixty and one spanning the seventies and eighties, reported activity frequency, changes in activity, and three facets of mental well-being.

Feeling more positive affect tracked with moving more often in both cohorts, and with having increased activity in the younger one. Negative affect and depressive symptoms showed their own, separate associations, examined independently rather than as one mood score. The authors argue well-being's bright and dark sides are distinct levers on older adults' activity. Pandemic-era data make the snapshot historically specific.
pmc-11601067:
Catarina Cardoso and colleagues test for sleep apnea in patients whose lungs are scarring from interstitial disease other than the idiopathic kind, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Fifty patients took home sleep tests. The yield was striking: seventy-six percent had obstructive sleep apnea, a rate echoing the idiopathic fibrosis literature.

Two measures predicted it independently: lower total lung capacity and lower waking oxygen saturation. Twelve patients started positive airway pressure therapy. Within three months, over ninety percent were well controlled, sleepiness scores fell significantly, and night-time low oxygen was corrected in every patient. Emotional well-being trended upward. The authors argue for a low suspicion threshold in fibrotic lung clinics: ask, test, and treat, because the mask quietly fixes the nights of most who wear it.
pmc-11602067:
Zhendong Gao and six colleagues review whether social capital lifts student physical activity, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Students often move too little, harming health and grades. Social ties might push them toward exercise. The reviewers searched four databases under standard guidelines.

Ten studies covering twenty-seven hundred students qualified, mostly from North America and Europe. Study quality scored high across the set. Strong networks, family and friend support, and social cohesion all tracked with more activity. Emotional support, role modeling, and social norms were the proposed mechanisms. Most evidence was self-reported and cross-sectional, limiting causal claims. The authors still see social capital as a real lever. They urge objective measures and longitudinal designs next.
pmc-11602667:
Firoozeh Gerayeli and co-authors map airway cells one by one in a 2024 study of pulmonary long COVID. Some patients keep new or worsening breathing symptoms long after their first infection. The cell-level drivers of that lingering illness were unclear. The team built a single-cell gene map of the airway lining to find them.

Adults with and without long COVID were recruited around Greater Vancouver in Canada. The long COVID group had new or worse respiratory symptoms at least twelve weeks after infection. Bronchial brushings gathered cells from the airway wall, and each cell's gene activity was read on its own. The map shows which cell types shift in number or state in the sick group. Such shifts point to the pathways that keep lungs inflamed and suggest where treatment could aim.
pmc-11603067:
Zhiqiang Wang leads a team that tests a spine fusion setup in the lab. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with oblique lateral interbody fusion. The surgery treats lumbar degenerative diseases with small cuts.

A side plate adds stability in normal bone cases. Whether it works in weak bone was unclear. Calf spine samples were split by bone condition. Normal, thinned, and osteoporotic groups were compared. Loads were applied in many directions for the tests. A camera system tracked segment movement in three dimensions. States ran from intact spine to cage plus plate.
pmc-11604967:
Zong-jie Wang and Tian-hua Lin analyzed hospital data in 2024 on brain bleeding and sedation. The condition is subarachnoid hemorrhage, a sudden bleed around the brain. Sedative choice may affect how patients fare. The team drew cases from a large intensive care database. They compared three sedatives on predictive value. They then matched patients who got one drug, dexmedetomidine, with similar patients who did not. Later models weighed death and length of stay together.

Dexmedetomidine predicted outcomes better than the other two sedatives. After matching, the two groups were equal in size. Use of the drug tied to lower risk of death in hospital. A competing-risk model treated death as the rival outcome for stay length. In that model, the drug still protected against death. It showed no clear link to length of stay. The authors call the drug a promising sedative choice here.
pmc-11605067:
Guangpeng Xu and five colleagues published a computer vision study in two thousand twenty-four on finding tyre defects in X-ray images before tyres leave the factory. Tyre structure is complex and defects slender and varied, defeating manual inspection and older algorithms.

Their detector, built on the YOLOv5 model, adds a snake-like convolution that follows curved, thin features such as cord cracks and overlaps. New fusion modules blend image scales while attention blocks suppress busy backgrounds. A softer box-selection step sharpens final calls. Accuracy rose about six percentage points over the base model on standard measures. The authors claim it beats current mainstream detectors on this task.
pmc-11606167:
Zhu and four co-authors test an iron-cheat drug as a cure for gum rot in rats in this twenty twenty-four study. Gum rot eats the bone that holds teeth and is fed by swelling in the gum. The drug fakes low air in cells, a state known to curb such swelling.

Inside, cells dosed with the drug made far less of the scent marks that call swelling in. The drug also blocked a key swelling path by holding its switch out of the cell core. Bone-eat cells formed in far lower counts when the drug was on board first. Sick rats on the drug lost less jaw bone and had calmer gums. The team backs it for more cure work.
pmc-11607067:
Zheng Fang and co-authors weigh a hard trade-off in panda country: dogs living near giant panda habitat are vaccinated against canine distemper to protect the pandas, but the vaccine itself may spread. They tracked 69 dogs in panda areas, testing blood for virus defenses and swabs for virus shedding after shots.

Vaccinated dogs did shed virus, mostly starting around day nine. Unvaccinated dogs kept in shared kennels caught the virus from them, as family-tree tests of the virus confirmed. Dogs that started with stronger defenses shed less and for fewer days. Dog ranges also overlapped wild panda ranges in two reserves. The authors advise keeping vaccinated dogs restricted for at least three weeks, with local officials, reserve staff, and villagers managing shots together.
pmc-11607867:
Khadivi, Mirheidari, Saeidifar, Moradi, and Tunç measure in twenty twenty-four the shape diversity of tamarind trees grown in southeast Iran. Tamarind is a valued fruit tree across the tropics, but its local variation was poorly charted. The team scored fifty-five local types on dozens of leaf, fruit, and tree traits and analysed them with several statistical tools.

Most traits varied widely between types, which signals rich diversity for breeding. Leaf size tracked together, as did fruit length with fruit weight. The types fell into four clusters, and the team ranked the top twenty by trait performance. The authors offer the results as a resource for breeding tougher, better tamarind varieties.
pmc-11613967:
Junaid Zafar Sheikh and four co-authors describe a rare illness showing up in an even rarer place, in a case report published in twenty twenty-four. The illness, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, causes fever and swollen lymph nodes and usually fades on its own. It nearly always strikes the neck nodes; only two past cases involved chest nodes alone.

Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old Indian man with fever, mouth and skin sores, weight loss, and swollen chest nodes on a scan. Tests ruled out cancer, infection, and immune disease. A needle sample taken through the airways showed the dying node tissue typical of this illness. He was treated for symptoms and reassured. The authors stress that knowing this illness spares patients harsh care meant for look-alike diseases, and that long follow-up matters since it can pair with immune conditions.
pmc-11616267:
Mormone and co-authors compare two bone marrow sources for knee arthritis care, in work from 2024. Marrow holds rare stem cells and healing factors, and shots of it can ease joint pain. It is most often drawn from the hip crest, and rarely from the shin bone. The trial set both sources against platelet-rich plasma in thirty patients.

Half-year checks on half the patients showed hip marrow held far more key cells than shin marrow. Yet pain and function gains at six months were alike across all three arms. Hip marrow led on pain change, shin marrow on function change, but neither lead was firm. Full results are still to come.
pmc-11616867:
Luis Genaro and co-authors test ways to measure hand skill in dental students in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Fine finger control matters for cavity work, and schools want tests that predict who will struggle in preclinical training. Five assessment methods were compared in ninety-five fifth-year students.

Scores on real cavity and filling work served as the standard. A dentistry-specific dexterity test performed best, with clear significance and acceptable discrimination. Two classic pegboard and finger tests did not reach significance. The authors recommend the dental test for early screening, so students with motor difficulties can get targeted help sooner.
pmc-11618467: Melvin Lee Qiyu, Amna Ahmed, and Tom Dawson report a toddler whose scurvy fooled his doctors at first, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. The three-year-old boy could not bear weight for four weeks. Fine red spots marked his lower legs. Scans showed swollen bone and soft tissue, raising fears of worse disease. Blood tests and his picky diet pointed instead to vitamin C lack. Vitamin C and pain relief, plus diet and physio help, set him right.
pmc-11621567:
Xiangyu Ma and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four structural study of a receptor that keeps hearing working. The receptor, GPR156, lacks the large outer part most relatives carry. It stays unusually active even without a trigger.

Frozen-electron microscopy revealed the receptor alone and joined to its partner protein. A small loop region forms its outer face. Paired receptor units touch through a shared surface in both states. The tail of one unit both helps partner binding and blocks a second partner. The structures explain its constant activity and guide future hearing research.
pmc-11623267:
Michaela Kosticova and three co-authors report interviews in 2024 with teens about why they go to bed late on school nights. Late bedtimes cut sleep and harm health, yet most prior work did not ask teens for their own view. The team interviewed twenty four teens aged fourteen to seventeen, alone and in groups, as part of a wider school health study.

School demands and free time, in particular chatting with friends online, pushed bedtime later. Teens often saved both homework and leisure for late evening and put them ahead of sleep. Worry at bedtime also kept some awake. Teens said less homework, more activity, and parent set bedtimes would help them sleep earlier.
pmc-11627167:
Suzane Shiyun Chin recounts her stint on the science team of a family medicine conference in Malaysia, in a personal essay from two thousand twenty-four. She had just returned to work after a long break when her home state hosted the national meeting. It was her first time as an organizer rather than a guest.

Her team reviewed over two hundred research abstracts, shortlisted entries, and kept authors, judges, and vendors in loop. A highlight was briefing the health minister at the electronic poster board. Judging day talks showed her how experts weigh posters. She closes by hoping to stay in primary care research.
pmc-11628967:
Elliott-Sale leads a large team building a classification tool for ovarian hormone profiles in female athletes, in work from twenty twenty-four. Hormone profiles shape training response and health in athletes, yet they are rarely classified in a standard way. A fit for purpose tool was missing.

The study developed and evaluated step one of a two step process: classifying the ovarian hormone profile itself. Athletes from post puberty to perimenopause are the target group. Reliable classification is the base for later work linking profiles to performance, injury, and contraceptive use. Sports science has long under served female physiology, and tools like this help close the gap.
pmc-11634967:
Simon Hadjaje and colleagues studied how fruit fly wings unfold in 2024. A fly leaves its pupal case with folded wings. Within minutes, the wings open into stiff flight blades. Rising body pressure drives the change. Fluid then flows into the wing structure. The team imaged the wing inside and out. They filmed unfolding at the whole organ scale. They also tracked fluid flow during opening.

Opening proved to be more than simple unfolding. The wing also expands in area as it opens. Surface cells stretch, and the outer skin smooths its wrinkles. A computer model joined material measures into one account. The model predicted a working point for successful opening. It also matched the timing of the real process. The authors say flies exploit material quirks for speed. The lessons may inform soft deployable designs, they suggest.
pmc-11635167:
Michelangelo Certo and colleagues show that a little-known metabolic enzyme, CARKL, steers T-cell behavior by resetting metabolism. How immune cells use fuel decides how they work. The pentose phosphate pathway branches off glycolysis, giving molecules for defense against oxidants and for building. CARKL is a sedoheptulose kinase in that pathway, known to count in macrophages.

The study looks at CARKL in T cells, where its level shifts in a dynamic way as cells switch on. When CARKL was raised, big metabolic shifts came, hitting mitochondrial respiration, ATP production, and the mix of inflammatory cytokines. Changes to CARKL also shaped how T cells move, by guiding chemokine receptor levels. In one key case, CARKL cut the receptor CXCR3, hurting movement toward its chemokine signals. The finds set one enzyme as a dial for both what T cells give off and where they go. Such control points draw drug work.
pmc-11638367:
Lu Tian and colleagues hunt a vanishing fish by the DNA it sheds in river water, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The fish, Bangana tungting, is endangered and lives in a protected stretch of the Yuanshui River in Hunan, China. Net surveys can miss rare fish and harm them, so the team filtered water instead and read the traces left behind.

Over two years, the fish's DNA turned up at eight of sixty sites in the first survey and four of forty-four in the second, proving it still holds on there. Where it appeared, the water carried enough dissolved oxygen; below a clear threshold, it vanished. Sites near hydroelectric dams showed fewer traces, and more dams meant fewer finds. The authors say water testing gives rangers a gentle, sharp tool for tracking rare fish, and they urge cleaner, freer-flowing water in the reserve.
pmc-11639767:
Kuźnicki and co-authors review how macrophages, a type of immune cell, might be turned against cancer, in a review paper from 2024. Macrophages that gather in tumors can help or hinder growth, and the mix of their subtypes links to patient survival. The review sets out their traits and roles in tumor growth.

The authors explain how these cells affect the main treatments: immune therapy, radiation, and chemotherapy. New ideas include tiny particles that carry drugs to the cells and reshape the tumor setting. Lab-made receptor macrophages, called CAR-Ms, show early promise. The review also covers training the cells with magnetic fields, plasma, and electric pulses. It closes with prospects for pairing these cell-based plans with other care.
pmc-11640367:
Juanxiang Zhang and eleven co-authors, plus Maria Luisa Dettori, hunt for DNA markers that predict growth in Ashidan yaks. Two genes were the suspects: TXK, a signaling kinase, and PLCE1, an enzyme important for muscle cell development. Both had been tied to economically valuable traits in other animals.

A liquid microarray genotyped two hundred thirty-two yaks at one variant in each gene. Both variants correlated significantly with weight, height, length, and chest circumference at various ages. Animals carrying the CC form of the TXK variant, for example, grew significantly heavier than their herdmates. Such markers could let breeders select for growth genetically instead of waiting to measure each generation.
pmc-11640467:
Ivan Ramos-Martínez and colleagues pool studies from around the world to gauge how much flu circulates in dogs, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-four. Influenza A crosses between species, and dogs can catch strains named for other hosts. The team gathered every study that measured antibodies or active infection in dogs for three subtypes.

Past exposure ran at about eight percent for the horse strain H3N8 and seven percent for the dog strain H3N2, and about three percent for the pandemic H1N1 strain. Active infection told a split story: the horse strain was rare, while H3N2 showed in nearly a fifth of tested dogs in prevalence studies. The authors place dogs as a reservoir where human, swine, horse, and bird flu viruses can meet. That mixing is exactly why vets and doctors watch this species closely.
pmc-11640667:
Yi Xue and co-authors teach computers to tell goats apart by sight, in a 2024 study. Knowing each animal's identity is basic to careful farm management. Most past work used face photos only, leaving other views untried.

The team built a rig that photographs each goat from five angles: both sides of the face, the front, the back, and the side of the body. They tested four standard vision networks on 54 white goats. A single side-body view with one network reached over ninety-nine percent accuracy. Mixing two views beat any single view, and three views helped further. The results give farms a practical recipe: side shots and fused views identify goats with very few mistakes.
pmc-11641767:
Corneliu-George Coman and colleagues test chitosan nanofibre dressings carrying an antibiotic on burn healing in rats. Their 2024 study measures biochemical, oxidative, and immune effects of the wound coverings.

Two fibre formulations were spun with different antibiotic amounts, and some received a surface coating treatment. Burns were made with a heated steel rod on male rats. Dressings were compared against untreated controls and a standard commercial silver dressing using wound size, tissue analysis, and blood inflammation markers. Chitosan dressings significantly accelerated healing. The high-antibiotic coated group showed best wound closure and least inflammation, with higher protective enzyme levels and lower stress hormone levels than other groups.
pmc-11643367:
Arshad and six co-authors linked a brain-healthy diet to mood in this cohort study from twenty twenty-four. The MIND diet blends Mediterranean and blood-pressure eating patterns. Nearly five thousand British civil servants reported their diets in the early two thousands. Their depressive symptoms were then tracked across thirteen years of follow-ups.

About thirteen percent had symptoms return at least twice. Those eating closest to the MIND pattern had about a quarter lower odds of that recurrence. Three foods carried the signal on their own: leafy greens, other vegetables, and berries. The links held after accounting for income, habits, and prior health. The authors present diet as a plausible lever against repeat depression.
pmc-11644367:
Baoshan Kang and co-authors found a plant protein that helps a watermelon virus spread in a 2024 study. The virus causes yellow mosaic disease and cuts yields. One of its proteins, P3, plays roles in copying, moving, and harming the host, but its chemical job was unknown.

The team showed that P3 grips a watermelon protein with two cutting jobs, housed mostly in the leaf's green parts and outer skin. The grip sits at one end of P3. When the two met in tobacco leaves, they clumped as a pair. That plant protein boosts the infection, so blocking the grip could breed or spray for hardier melons.
pmc-11645467:
Alexander Tamalunas and eight co-authors survey what patients with lower urinary tract symptoms think about plant-based medicines. Their study came out in 2024. These symptoms, often tied to an enlarged prostate, are commonly treated with prescription drugs whose benefits are limited and side effects are common.

Three hundred patients at a specialist center answered the questionnaire. Most were taking prescription medication, led by one main drug class. Plant medicines were the second most common treatment, used by about four in ten of those on medication. Patients rated plant medicines as only modestly effective, but almost nine in ten praised how well tolerated they were. Two thirds thought health insurance should cover them. The authors say such medicines may keep patients on treatment where prescription drugs fail.
pmc-11647367:
Yuichi Iida and Mamoru Harada test a cell therapy that turns donor stem cells into beacons drawing immune fighters into tumors. Their study appeared in 2024. The stem cells are engineered to release CCL19, a signal that attracts dendritic cells and T cells. An earlier version used the host's own cells, which is slow to prepare for each patient. The new version uses cells from a donor line, ready off the shelf, and was tried in several mouse tumor models.

The donor cells shrank tumors strongly. Part of the effect came from the host reacting to the foreign cells themselves. The therapy packed tumors with a rare dendritic cell type that makes interleukin-12 and primes killer T cells, and it worked without the lymph nodes that such priming usually needs. The authors see a practical path toward ready-made immune cell therapy.
pmc-11647967:
Biao Qi and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on a magnetized string that turns pull into commands for wearable interfaces. Inspired by tendons, the device reads the string's natural vibration tone: stretch changes the pitch, and a coil picks the tone up electrically as a fading ringing signal. Each tone stands for one command, so many commands share a single channel.

Designers can tune the tone library by string size, material, or tension, and even retune one string mid-use by changing its stretched length. Demonstrations ran touch addressing, identity checks, and robot control. The authors offer the scheme as a simple, high-capacity wearable link.
pmc-11649767:
Franziska Stoller and co-authors published this neuroscience study in 2024. A European research project had linked social dysfunction across diagnoses to the integrity of the default mode network, a set of brain regions active at rest. The team tested cause and effect in mice by damaging the forceps minor, a fiber tract tying together the network's frontal hubs, using focal loss of myelin insulation.

Brain imaging confirmed the damage weakened the network's connectivity. The mice then interacted less socially and showed more anxiety in automated behavior tests. Strikingly, the effects reversed as the tract recovered. The authors present this as direct evidence that default mode integrity drives social behavior, not merely correlates with it. They argue the finding supports treatments aimed at network repair in precision psychiatry.
pmc-11650267:
George Wanjala, Lenox Omondi Pius, Péter Strausz, and Szilvia Kusza argue for advocacy to save farm animal diversity in East Africa. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, centers on Kenya and Tanzania. Local breeds carry genes that help livestock cope with heat and drought. That diversity is shrinking, which threatens future protein supply.

East Africa historically spread domesticated herds across the continent. The authors outline roles for advocacy and management groups. Their framework runs from farmers up to regional associations. Regional promotion, they argue, can sway national policy. Saving breed variety is pitched as climate insurance. The paper offers a structure others could adapt.
pmc-11652367:
Han Chen and colleagues published a data-driven study in 2024. They studied diabetic retinopathy, a serious eye complication of diabetes. The disease can badly damage vision over time. The team focused on a cell death process called PANoptosis. They hunted for related genes that change in the disease. Public gene datasets supplied the patient data. Gene databases supplied the PANoptosis gene lists. Several computer methods narrowed the candidates down.

Three machine learning methods selected key hub genes. The team built a diagnostic scoring chart from them. Lab tests then checked the chosen genes directly. Cell experiments tested what silencing two genes does. Blood vessel cells behaved differently after that silencing. Immune cell patterns in tissue were also analyzed. The work offers candidate markers for earlier detection. It also suggests targets for future treatment research.
pmc-11653767:
Nicola Farrar and colleagues studied how the way health professionals talk shapes patient choices about joining a clinical trial. Recruitment is a known weak point of randomized trials, and recruiters clearly sway decisions, but the mechanism was murky. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team embedded data collection in three British trials from different specialties. They recorded recruitment consultations and interviewed patients who had agreed or declined, linking the two sources for the same patient where possible, and analyzed the material thematically.

Professionals across the whole care pathway, not just recruiters, influenced how patients judged their need for and benefit from the treatments on offer, often by signaling a personal preference for one option. Patients still drew on family and other support and framed the final call as their own. Willingness to be randomized hinged on expected benefit and on access outside the trial.
pmc-11653967:
Santana Silver and co-authors ask when a new clinical practice stops being new and becomes the normal standard, in work from twenty twenty-four. Health groups need a clear way to tell that shift, so care stays in line with the best proof. The team spoke with leaders who run quality and change work.

Seventeen leaders from varied health settings took part in deep interviews. They named four signs of a settled practice: it fits the workflow, spans the whole unit, has staff buy in, and needs no watch to last. Plans that worked started slow, built staff ownership, and kept measuring progress. The findings can guide tools to track the change process in a firm way.
pmc-11656367:
Yuhan Jiang and six co-authors present a 2024 study on a drug-loaded gel meant to calm inflammation in cartilage implants. Implants for cartilage repair often fail through poor bonding, swelling, or infection. The team loaded a soft gel with soyasaponin Bb, a compound from traditional Chinese medicine. They tested the gel on human cartilage cells in the lab and in implants placed in rabbits.

The compound lowered levels of three swelling-related markers in cartilage cells stressed by an immune signal. It acted through a known control pathway inside the cells. The loaded gel did the same in lab tests. In rabbits, stained tissue showed the gel cut the local swelling response around implants. The authors conclude the gel is a promising aid for cartilage repair. It could help implants settle with less reaction from the body.
pmc-11656767:
Hazel Jenkins and seven co-authors studied imaging for low back pain in older adults in a 2024 paper. About a quarter of back pain patients in primary care are sent for scans, but older adults are often left out of the counts. The data come from an Australian cohort study of people aged 55 and over seeing chiropractors.

Of 217 patients with a new bout of back pain, about 61 percent got some form of imaging over twelve months. X-ray was the most common choice. The paper describes who was sent for imaging and what the images showed. The findings help clinicians weigh when scans are truly needed in older patients.
pmc-11656867:
Wenrui Zang and a large team study treatment resistance in a deadly brain tumor in a 2024 paper. The tumor, called glioblastoma, often stops responding to both drug therapy and radiation. The team created resistant tumor cells by exposing them to the standard drug over a long period, then checked resistance in lab and animal tests.

Gene activity checks pointed to amino acid handling as a key factor. A transporter protein called LAT4 rose after drug exposure and boosted use of the amino acid leucine. That in turn switched on a growth pathway and made cells resist radiation. Blocking the transporter, paired with radiation, improved outcomes in animals. The work names a target for future combination therapy.
pmc-11657567:
Changlong Hu and Lin Wang review tiny parcels shed by stem cells as a liver therapy, in work from 2024. The parcels, called exosomes, come from mesenchymal stem cells, which can also grow into liver cells and aid repair. Fresh proof casts the parcels as the main healing cargo the cells release.

The review explains how the parcels form and what they carry. It then walks through their roles in liver harms of many kinds, from scarring and organ failure to cancer, oxygen strain, and fat buildup. The parcels also join the regrowth process after injury. The authors weigh what must be solved before clinic use.
pmc-11657967:
Jingyang Li and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on sleep length and lung function in United States adults. The team drew on national survey data for 9,284 people aged 20 to 64, grouping sleep into four bands with seven hours as the reference. Breathing tests measured air volume, flow, and two kinds of impairment.

Both short and long sleep went with weaker lungs. Six hours or less, and eight hours, cut the main volume and flow measures; nine hours or more cut peak flow too. Short and long sleepers also faced higher odds of restrictive impairment. The links ran stronger in men. The authors place seven hours as the sweet spot.
pmc-11663667:
Sakina Abbas and co-authors published this wheat study in 2024. Stripe rust, a fungal disease, threatens wheat harvests worldwide, and the fungus keeps evolving past existing defenses. The team examined 349 wheat lines from Pakistan and southwest China. They screened them for thirteen known resistance genes using DNA markers. Field trials then measured how each line actually withstood current rust races.

Over sixty percent of the Chuanyu lines from China resisted, against half of Pakistan's recent varieties and a fifth of its historic ones. Some genes appeared everywhere, while one useful gene was missing entirely from the Chinese set. Certain historic genes still worked well against today's fungus. Four gene pairings stood out for strengthening resistance when combined. The authors urge breeders to stack such genes deliberately. Rotating and combining defenses should slow the fungus and protect yields longer in both regions.
pmc-11665267:
Andrey Frolov, Stuart Atwood, Miguel Guzman, and John Martin report an unusual brain malformation case in a 2024 medical article. Polymicrogyria, the most common malformation of cortical development, folds the brain's surface into many tiny gyri separated by shallow grooves. It usually surfaces early in life through developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, or language and motor trouble, with severity varying widely between patients.

Finding the condition in an elderly individual is rare, and the authors describe a distinctive polygenic background in their patient. Late-presenting cases stretch the known spectrum of the disorder and remind clinicians it can hide behind decades of milder symptoms.
pmc-11666567:
Jing Lu and co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-four, whether blood iron levels predict death in people with cardiovascular disease. Heart disease is a leading global killer, and iron may play a role, but data in patients were thin. The team used a national United States survey from nineteen ninety-nine to twenty eighteen, with mortality follow-up. The cohort held one thousand nine hundred three cardiovascular patients, mean age about sixty-four. Survival curves, adjusted hazard models, and flexible curve fits linked iron levels to all-cause and cardiovascular death. Subgroups split by age, sex, weight, blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking.

Survival differed clearly across iron quartiles. After adjustment, lower serum iron tied to higher risk of both death outcomes. The study flags iron status as a prognostic marker in this population.
pmc-11668167:
Sameh Msaad, Rim Khemakhem, and Dorra Abdelmouleh studied sleep apnea that lingers in children in a 2024 paper, written in French. In this disorder, a child's upper airway partly or fully closes again and again in sleep, cutting airflow despite effort to breathe. Removing the tonsils and adenoids is the standard first cure.

For some children the apnea stays or comes back after surgery. The team hunted for traits that forecast that poor result, so high-risk children can be watched or treated in other ways. Grades of the disorder rest on how many airway events strike per hour of sleep. Their findings guide follow-up care after the operation.
pmc-11672267:
Ai and co-authors review ways to switch diarylethene molecules with heat, acid, or electricity instead of light. These molecules are champion light switches, stable and hard to wear out. They serve in devices, data storage, smart materials, and imaging. Newer work drives their shape change with other triggers. A molecule that answers several triggers can do more jobs at once. Logic gates and denser storage are among the payoffs.

The review sorts advances by trigger type: acid, heat, and electric response. It stresses how molecular design makes each response possible. The flip and flip-back paths get close attention. The authors map a field moving past light-only control.
pmc-11672667:
Daniel Robertson and six co-authors describe a battery material that forms inside the cell as it first charges, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The starting oxide mixes vanadium and molybdenum. Once charged, it shifts into a disordered rock salt form that can store and release lithium fast. Such fast charging is prized for cars and grid storage.

Using X-ray tools that watch the cell as it works, the team saw the shift happen in a single step. Fine imaging showed the product forms thin, bent layers inside grains that stay fairly large. In spite of that size, the material charged fast and behaved like much finer powders. The work helps explain what lets these formed-in-place materials charge quickly.
pmc-11672967:
Karol Rycerz, Aleksandra Krawczyk, Jadwiga Jaworska-Adamu, and Marcin Arciszewski wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It shows that feeding rats monosodium glutamate, the flavor enhancer, switches on the star-shaped support cells of a deep brain movement center.

Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory messenger, but in excess it can poison neurons and their astrocyte partners. Fifteen rats got salt water or one of two glutamate doses for three days. Brain sections through the caudate nucleus were stained for two astrocyte marker proteins. Treated animals showed denser astrocytes and stronger staining for both markers, most clearly at the higher dose. The cells' process counts, though, stayed the same. The authors read the change as astrocytes reacting to a glutamate flood, an early response that could protect or harm. The work links a food additive's brain chemistry to glial behavior.
pmc-11673167:
Hong and co-authors test whether computer traits of bone marrow cells can spot abnormal blood cell growth, in a study from 2024. The condition, myelodysplastic syndrome, warps how marrow cells form and lowers blood counts. Digital pathology and pathomics turn cell images into hundreds of numbers per cell.

The team studied marrow smears from 24 patients and 21 healthy peers, sorting 12,360 cells into normal and warped types across three lineages. Each cell yielded 476 features of brightness, shape, and texture. Two classifier pairings sorted the cells with fair accuracy in cross-checks. Warped red cell and white cell precursors stood out with lower heat map values on key traits. The authors propose the traits as a helper marker, pending larger studies.
pmc-11674567:
Galvany-López and co-authors review dog-assisted therapy for children and teens with autism spectrum disorder. Animal therapies are used widely to lift quality of life. The team searched eight databases for studies on dogs with this group. The review plan was registered in advance. Nineteen papers met the bar for inclusion. Most, 84%, found gains in communication and social interaction.

Dogs often act as a bridge that draws the child's attention and rewards contact. Emotional gains also appeared across studies. The review weighs how feasible such programs are to run. Limits include small samples and varied methods. Still, the signal favors the dogs.
pmc-11674667:
Altrawy leads a large team reviewing gut microbes and breast cancer, in work from twenty twenty-four. Breast cancer is a major cause of death in women. Beyond genes and environment, gut bacteria now look like a real factor in how tumors grow.

Helpful and harmful gut species make small chemicals that affect hormones, immunity, and cell signals in breast tissue. An unbalanced gut mix has been linked to higher risk. The review maps how those microbial chemicals reprogram the tumor surroundings and may change treatment response. The authors argue that diet and microbe care deserve a place in future breast cancer plans.
pmc-11674767:
Amalia Făgărășan and co-authors ran a pilot study of heart function in children born with a bicuspid aortic valve, which has two leaflets instead of three. The usual pumping measure, ejection fraction, can look normal while the heart muscle already weakens. A speckle-tracking ultrasound method measures muscle stretch directly and is thought to catch trouble earlier.

The study followed seventy-three children with the defect and fifty-five healthy controls over one year at a Romanian referral center. Ejection fraction was normal in the patient group. Stretch analysis, though, showed reduced values in the heart's inferior and anterior segments and in one standard view, compared with controls. The authors ask whether these early dips predict later heart failure and whether spotting them early can cut illness.
pmc-11675967:
Charlotte Werndl and co-authors, writing in 2024, ask where the Boltzmann equation belongs in the foundations of statistical mechanics. The field is usually split into two camps, one following Boltzmann's line and one following Gibbs, and the famous equation fits awkwardly in both. The authors first restate the Boltzmann-style approach using local field variables to define the large-scale states of a system. On that restatement, the equation appears as a special case of the approach.

They then turn to the Gibbs-style side, working through a chain of linked equations. The version of the equation that drops out of that chain counts as Gibbsian only in a thin sense, they argue: it uses a steady measure over the whole system's state space. The paper sorts concepts rather than reporting data. Its claim is that a clearer statement of each camp dissolves much of the puzzle.
pmc-11676667:
Cristina Sempio and ten colleagues measured how the body processes an oral dose of a lesser-known cannabis compound. The compound, delta-8 tetrahydrocannabivarin, occurs in cannabis and may have useful drug properties. Its behavior in humans after dosing had never been studied. The twenty twenty-four analysis came from a two-phase, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial in healthy volunteers. Doses ran from 12.5 to 200 milligrams in an oil formulation.

Twenty-one participants completed sessions, and blood samples from fifteen were analyzed up to eight hours after dosing. A carboxy metabolite of the compound was the main breakdown product detected in plasma. Mapping these pharmacokinetics is basic groundwork for any future medical use. It tells researchers how fast the compound appears, converts, and clears in people.
pmc-11676967:
Hadi Darawsheh and co-authors study how skull variation shifts the position of the mandibular foramen, in an anatomy paper from 2024. The foramen is the entry point for the nerve that dentists block for lower jaw work. Its place varies with skull and face shape, so a one-size rule can miss the nerve.

The team measured one hundred six certified cadaver heads of both sexes. Skull, face, and jaw shapes were classified with standard indices. Foramen position was then compared across shapes. Key jaw indices tracked with foramen place in a significant way. The data support a personalized read of anatomy before nerve block and jaw surgery, rather than a fixed landmark rule.
pmc-11677867:
Tatiana Kekeeva and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on ovarian cancer tumors that share one trait but act in different ways. These tumors have a broken DNA repair system, which makes them sensitive to platinum drugs. The team asked whether the cause of the break splits patients into groups with different outlooks.

They tested three hundred fifty-two tumor samples for gene mutations, repair scores, and chemical silencing of repair genes. About two thirds had the repair defect. The group with true gene mutations responded best to platinum, gained most from a targeted drug, and lived longest without the disease returning. Splitting the patients this way can guide which drug each woman should get first.
pmc-11678067:
Jing Yin and seven co-authors warm a subalpine meadow at several altitudes in a 2024 paper. Mountain grasslands are sensitive to climate shifts, and most warming studies use one altitude. On a high mountain site, warming eased cold limits on grass, raising biomass, height, and coverage. Richer plant matter fed more soil carbon, which in turn reshaped the soil fungal community measured by gene sequencing.

Fungal diversity rose at low altitude under warming but fell higher up, as community assembly turned more deterministic. Nutrient-cycling fungi grew more common and better connected. Yet grass pathogens also increased, a risk the authors say needs long-term watching.
pmc-11678467:
Benjamin Tutolo and co-authors study two small alkaline lakes in British Columbia and what they say about early Earth. Such lakes are thought to help build the first blocks of life, since they can stock key feedstocks like phosphate. Yet the needs of key steps clash with each other, and with the needs of early cells. Past work had not traced how water and land shape the lakes over time.

Field tools, water tests, and models show what drives the pair, Last Chance Lake and Goodenough Lake. Strong loss of water to air is what lets phosphate build to high levels. The clash between salty lake water and fresh inflow stirs strong mixing. That mixing may let one lake both feed early reactions and shelter early life.
pmc-11678667:
Adina Andreea Mirea and co-authors examine, in a 2024 study, whether tooth and gum damage tracks with small-vessel harm in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes and gum disease feed each other: mouth infection and poor sugar control form a hard circle to break. The team asked whether worse dental lesions go with more vessel complications and weaker control.

The study enrolled 112 patients who had a dental exam. Half had deep, complicated lesions and half had shallow ones, matched by age and sex. The deep-lesion group showed higher blood sugar, higher long-term sugar marks, and more inflammation signals, along with worse kidney function. Nerve damage and eye damage from diabetes were both more common in that group. The authors built a score from these signs that predicted complicated lesions well.
pmc-11678767:
Sydney Chase and three co-authors tested how well an Apple Watch Series 9 reads energy use and heart rate, and whether skin tone changes the result, published in two thousand twenty-four. Thirty young, healthy adults were grouped by a standard skin tone scale. Each walked a ten-minute treadmill routine at mixed speeds and slopes while wearing the watch, a lab breathing mask setup, and a chest strap.

Energy use readings missed the lab values in every group. Heart rate readings drifted more for darker skin than for lighter skin, and drift grew and shrank with effort level. The authors warn that watch numbers should not be taken as exact, least of all for users with dark skin.
pmc-11678867:
Ignacio Diaz-Lorenzo and co-authors present a 2024 review of CT pulmonary angiography in lung clot care. The scan is the main test for pulmonary embolism, a clot that blocks lung arteries. The review covers clot burden scoring and death risk prediction. It also weighs new scan techniques and clot makeup reading. Artificial intelligence tools for the scan get a section.

One scan finding is firmly validated for prognosis so far. A right-to-left heart chamber width ratio above one links to far higher death risk. Other burden scores remain unproven by comparison. Radiologists get a disciplined account of what the scan can and cannot promise. Clot age reading from makeup could one day match treatment to clot stage. The review separates proven signs from hopeful ones, which busy clinicians need.
pmc-11679367:
Weny Rinawati, Abdulloh Machin, and Aryati Aryati test whether routine blood counts taken at admission can predict which stroke patients will develop an infection, in a 2024 study. Infections after a stroke worsen outcomes, and cheap early warnings would help wards act fast. The team reviewed records at a brain hospital in Jakarta, Indonesia.

The study covers 163 patients with a first ischemic stroke, admitted between October 2023 and March 2024, all with blood counts drawn within a day. Twenty-four patients developed an infection. Simple counts did best as predictors: total white cells, neutrophils, and monocytes each separated the groups with fair accuracy. Ratios built from those counts are also examined. The authors argue these everyday measures, read early, can flag patients who need closer watching for infection.
pmc-11690367:
Allen Glicksman and co-authors examine how birthplace and language shape older immigrants' use of formal health care, in a 2024 paper. Meeting the health system is hard for any older adult, and harder still for immigrants facing language gaps, cultural differences, and an unfamiliar system. The team studied service records for patients who spoke Chinese, Spanish, or Russian, comparing clinic visits, emergency department use, and hospital stays among people with similar insurance and diagnoses.

Chinese speakers stood out, above all for using emergency departments far less than other groups, including white and Black English speakers. The authors also warn about a data problem: health records usually capture the language spoken at the visit, not the patient's birthplace, which blurs exactly the differences researchers want to study. The paper calls for attention to both origin and encounter type in aging and migration research.
pmc-11690867:
Claudia von Bastian and co-authors present first findings, in a 2024 conference paper, from a large study of speed training across adult life. Speed training is one of the few brain training types that seems to lift untrained skills. Yet why it works is unclear, and the role of attention demands in the tasks is untested.

The study enrolled 476 healthy adults aged eighteen to eighty-five at sites in three countries. Groups trained on tasks with rising attention demands over ten sessions. Gains were checked right after training and three months later, across memory, reasoning, and daily thinking skills. Early results were shared in this talk, with close to four hundred adults finishing the study.
pmc-11691567:
Lillian Hung and seven co-authors published this study in 2024. It gathers staff views on virtual team-based care during one of care's riskiest handoffs: moving an older patient from hospital to long-term care. Video-linked teams promise coordination across sites, but the transition's success depends on the humans using the screens.

Fifty-two participants, clinicians, leaders, and patients with families, joined interviews, focus groups, and a policy review. Staff called the model acceptable, efficient, and cost-saving. Enablers were engaged teams, training and support, and access to equipment. Barriers were the mirror image: shaky infrastructure, scarce resources, and privacy worries. Families' involvement emerged as the pivot: their complex knowledge of the patient makes or breaks the plan, and virtual planning must include them. The authors ask for policies to standardize the practice. They frame virtual transition care as promising but unfinished, pending family-centered design.
pmc-11692167:
Jun Chu, Christine Mair, and Michel Boudreaux examine whether hearing trouble raises the risk of dementia among older adults living in the community in the United States. Their research article, published in twenty twenty-four, follows the question over time rather than at a single moment, using nationally representative survey data.

Drawing on the National Health and Aging Trends Study from twenty eleven through twenty twenty-two, the authors apply a Cox proportional hazards model. They adjust for demographics, chronic conditions, hearing aid use, and social isolation. Older adults with hearing trouble faced more than double the risk of developing dementia over eleven years. The link did not differ significantly by race or ethnicity. The authors suggest that policies promoting hearing tests and hearing aid use might help delay or prevent dementia.
pmc-11693067:
Jethro Raphael Suarez and co-authors test whether anxiety shifts how older adults sway, in work from 2024. Balance loss is a known harm of anxiety, but which sway path it drives was unclear. The team measured sway in one hundred seventy adults aged sixty-one to ninety-one with a simple board test, eyes closed, and sorted them by a short anxiety survey.

Adults with mid-to-high anxiety swayed more from side to side than calmer peers. Front-to-back sway did not differ by group. The authors note that past injury or low mood could sway the results too. They call for more work that weighs those factors in anxious older adults.
pmc-11693167:
Ruth Melo and seven co-authors follow frailty in Brazilian older adults over nine years. Their study came out in 2024. Frailty, a state of weakness and low reserve, predicts disability and death, but its long-term course in Latin America is little studied.

At follow-up, the share of frail participants had risen while the robust share fell by more than half. New frailty appeared in about a quarter of those at risk. Older age, cognitive impairment, illiteracy, male sex, and giving up advanced daily activities each predicted decline or death. Living alone, somewhat surprisingly, protected against frailty. The authors call for more long-term studies to pin down which risks can be changed.
pmc-11693267:
Woo Jang, Drew Krull, Seonhwa Lee, and Merril Silverstein wrote a 2024 paper mapping health care access for older people in Minnesota. The state's oldest group, those eighty-five and up, is set to more than double in thirty-five years. Rural counties will age even faster than cities. Yet clinics and hospitals are spread thin in rural areas.

Using 2020 census data and map-based methods, the team measured how social and money factors shape access for people sixty-five and older. Their maps show detailed patterns of where care is hard to reach. Naming those pockets helps the state plan clinics, transport, and home services before the wave of older residents arrives.
pmc-11696667:
Li and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on injecting a chemotherapy drug into the spinal fluid of lung cancer patients whose disease had spread to the membranes around the brain. That spread is hard to treat, since most drugs reach it poorly. The patients all had a mutation-driven form of lung cancer and had failed targeted pills. Fifty patients at one cancer hospital in Hunan received the spinal injections.

About two in three patients improved in nerve symptoms and function scores. Survival without growth inside the skull ran about five months, and overall survival about a year. Responders lived far longer than non-responders. Side effects were mainly lowered blood counts and liver strain, none fatal. The team calls the route a workable option after targeted pills fail.
pmc-11699567:
