Supawadee Patathananone and co-authors profile ripening karanda fruit to judge its promise as a functional food. The fruit carries plant chemicals with varied biological effects. The team extracted those chemicals at low temperature and measured the fruit's phenolic content, antioxidant strength, sugars, and vitamin C. They also checked whether the extracts harm human blood cells.

Repeated ultrasonic extraction worked best at four rounds. Extracts from fresh fruit and from freeze-dried powder both showed antioxidant activity. The extracts did not kill white blood cells at moderate doses, though they damaged red blood cells at higher ones. Fresh fruit extract held 0.27 percent total sugar and a small amount of vitamin C. Chemical analysis named the extract's main components. The authors say the profile supports developing supplement foods built on ripening karanda fruit, with dose care guided by the blood cell results.
pmc-11704867:
Yun and co-authors write a reply letter on drug resistance and the One Health approach, in a letter from 2024. The letter answers a commentary on their report about antibiotic use in Korean hospitals from 2018 to 2021. The authors agree that resistance is a grave threat to public health worldwide.

They note that resistance grows not only from drug use in care settings but also from farm chemicals, waste, and contact among livestock, wildlife, and people. That web of links is the heart of the One Health view. Still, their own data spoke only to hospital use, so their firm claims stay with stewardship in care facilities. They call for shared global data systems and joint work across human, animal, and environmental health.
pmc-11709567:
Mark Dubbelman and nine co-authors test a new digital way to check sense of time, place, and self in older adults with no thought loss. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. A chat tool asked about past events, places, and close ties, then posed short quiz items in each of the three areas. Scores mixed right replies with speed of reply.

Fifty-one adults took the test and also had brain scans for amyloid and tau. High amyloid linked to worse sense of place. Sense of time linked to amyloid plus tau in two brain areas. Sense of self showed no such link. The team sees place and time sense as early signs worth tracking.
pmc-11709867:
Jeanne Gallée and co-authors offer a 2025 conference abstract on language skills in subgroups of Alzheimer's disease. Some patients show clear language loss early, while others show no single weak area. The team asked whether a known language pattern, tied to a form of aphasia, shows up more often in the language-weak group.

The team studied 642 people from three long-running aging studies. They scored word understanding, naming, and phrase repetition, then sorted each person into one of eight language patterns. The patterns differed sharply between the two groups. The aphasia-like pattern appeared far more often in the language-weak group, as the team expected.
pmc-11710067:
Anil R Wadhwani and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on chemical marks on DNA in two tau conditions. Alzheimer's disease spreads tau tangles across the cortex, while a related condition, PART, keeps them near the hippocampus. The team asked whether methylation marks help explain why tangles spread in one and stall in the other.

The team profiled frontal cortex from 398 donors and checked the findings in a second cohort of 707. Marks tied to tangles did not overlap with marks tied to amyloid plaques in the first cohort. Shared marks in the second cohort pointed to T cell and transport genes, while tangle-only marks pointed to synapse genes.
pmc-11712067:
Arlene Astell and co-authors tour the homes of people living with dementia to log their technology in a 2025 study. Everyday devices already hold helpful tools, from stored phone numbers to calendar reminders. Nine people walked the researchers through their homes room by room, naming each device, its use, and how they got it.

Residents used far more than phones and tablets: televisions, stoves, mobility aids, and voice assistants all featured. They used tech to keep up valued activities, stay in touch, and stay independent. Ease of use and safety features mattered to them. Many wanted more from their devices but found learning new functions hard. The authors say the tours dispel myths about dementia and digital tools.
pmc-11712467:
Marina Ritchie and co-authors ask what helps people join early Alzheimer disease trials, in a research paper from 2025. New drugs are in tests, yet sign-up is slow. The team looks at how trial design shapes the choice to take part for people with mild memory loss and their families.

People rated sample trials on a scale of one to seven. The trials varied in drug type, scan result sharing, and whether a study partner had to attend in person. A risk of brain swelling was also varied. The results show which perks draw interest. Trial teams can use the findings to plan fair sign-up.
pmc-11712967:
Avi L Benitah and co-authors present a 2025 drug design study aimed at an enzyme called Lyn, which sits inside microglia, the brain's immune cells. Blocking the enzyme may switch these cells into a state that clears toxic amyloid from the brain. No strong, selective blocker that reaches the brain was available to test this idea.

The team screened known drugs, took one as a starting point, and reshaped it on a computer model of the enzyme. They built new compounds, tested how well each blocked the enzyme, and checked the best ones in cell tests. The work produced a new set of blockers ready for testing in animals.
pmc-11713467:
Fonov and co-authors map amyloid and tau build-up in living brains using PET scans, in this 2025 paper. In Alzheimer's disease these two proteins spread through the brain in known stage patterns. Past work matched the tau stages in living people using hand-drawn scan regions.

The team instead let the data speak, with no regions set in advance. Their scans came from young adults, healthy older adults, people with mild impairment, and patients with the disease, all seen at a Montreal aging center. Two tracers lit up amyloid and tau in turn. The joint patterns they found track disease progress and may help stage patients without guesswork.
pmc-11713767:
Johanne Stümpel, Marlena van Munster, Annika Dörrhöfer, and Björn Schmitz-Luhn explore what dementia patients and caregivers need in a 2025 paper. Alzheimer's cases may grow fourfold by the year 2050. Care often falls on families, and their views are key to good care design. The team worked with people who have Parkinson's disease, whose care needs overlap with dementia care.

Ten talks and group workshops were held with patients and caregivers. People picked cards about resources, tools, and human contact to picture their future care. The team compared what came up with past Alzheimer's research. Heavy feelings and upset daily routines stood out across the disease course. The themes can guide care plans that fit real family life.
pmc-11714067:
Taylor Kimberly tests a portable low power brain scanner for use in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. A scanner that can travel to the patient could open brain imaging to far more people. The trade off is a weaker signal and fuzzier images than standard hospital machines.

The team enrolled 45 clinic patients with mild loss or dementia, plus 23 controls from an emergency unit. Each had a scan on the portable machine, which runs at a fraction of standard strength. Smart software rebuilt the images and measured brain areas and scar spots. The same measures from standard scans matched closely, with whole brain size nearly exact. The author says the portable scans are sound enough for point of care use.
pmc-11716267:
Polina Shichkova and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on how aging changes proteins in blood and spinal fluid. Age is the top risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, yet healthy aging and disease aging are hard to tell apart.

The team took paired blood and spinal fluid samples from ninety-three people at Johns Hopkins clinics, both young adults and healthy older adults. A mass spectrometry method counted tens of thousands of protein pieces in each fluid. The reads covered paths tied to amyloid, tau, nerve harm, swelling, and iron damage. The team paid close heed to protein pieces cut or joined in ways that mark disease steps. Their map gives a base line of normal aging that later disease studies can measure against.
pmc-11727567:
Leónides Fernández and co-authors review the safety of probiotics for pregnant and nursing women in a 2024 paper. Probiotics are live germs sold to aid health, and many women use them for minor or major issues in pregnancy. Yet most products were never tested in this group, so claims of benefit and safety often rest on thin ground.

Trials in pregnant and nursing women mostly find the products well tolerated and safe, though side effects can occur. The authors say staff who care for these women should know what is being used and watch how it works. They urge that advice rest on solid proof. Only products made for the exact need, and tested in this group, should be advised.
pmc-11728467:
A research team reviewed what is known about hepatitis E infection in people with beta-thalassemia, in this 2024 paper. Thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder treated with frequent transfusions, which can carry the hepatitis E virus. For most people the infection passes, but in thalassemia patients it can turn chronic and dangerous.

Reported infection rates vary widely by country. Risk climbs with age, with where a patient lives, and with the total volume of blood received over years of care. Several countries now screen donated blood for the virus, either for everyone or for high-risk groups. The authors call for close watching of thalassemia patients and antibody checks, so infections are caught and treated early.
pmc-11748067:
Christoph Schindler and colleagues run a first-in-human phase one study of a multi-target gene therapy for diabetic foot ulcers. Their 2024 open-label dose-finding study uses bacteria engineered to produce three healing factors.

Sixteen patients aged in their fifties to eighties with non-healing ulcers joined four dose cohorts. Treatment ranged from a single low dose to repeated higher doses three times weekly for six weeks. A standard dose-escalation scheme monitored safety, tolerability, and efficacy in each cohort. The therapy demonstrated a favourable early profile in the reported results. The study aimed to judge safety, wound healing, quality of life, and to select a recommended dose for phase two testing.
pmc-11790667:
Shuiping Ni leads a team that improves a light net for tomato leaf disease. Their work deals with ShuffleNetV2, a small deep learning model. Fast, true disease spotting is key for tomato yield.

Large models are sharp but too heavy for edge devices. Their trick builds many shallow models at varied depths. A joined feature map blends maps from all those models. A light convolution layer then pulls more useful traits. The joined model teaches the small model in a dynamic way. That keeps key traits while the model stays light.
pmc-11801267:
Judit Tomsen-Melero leads a large team packaging a missing enzyme into targeted nanoliposomes for Fabry disease. Patients lack working alpha-galactosidase A, so fatty material accumulates across organs, and standard enzyme infusions distribute poorly and never reach the brain. Their formulation aims a recombinant enzyme at the tissues that need it.

In a Fabry mouse model, the nanoformulation cleared more of the stored material than free enzyme at the same task, including deposits in the brain. That reach into the central nervous system addresses one of replacement therapy's biggest blind spots. European regulators have granted the product orphan drug designation. The authors present it as a platform for other lysosomal storage disorders with brain involvement.
pmc-11847667:
Wabi Temesgen Atinafu and Kefyalew Naniye Tilahun survey diet adherence among diabetic patients in Addis Ababa in this paper, published in 2024. Diet control is central to type 2 diabetes care, yet adherence in Ethiopia is poorly documented. Four hospitals joined the study in mid 2024. Systematic sampling recruited 420 patients.

Questionnaires measured how closely patients followed dietary advice. Analysis searched for traits linked with good or poor adherence. Results were summarized with standard statistical reporting and odds ratios. Income, education, and support often decide whether advice is followable. Hospital based data miss patients who never reach care, a limit to keep in mind. The findings guide counseling and food support in urban clinics.
pmc-12171967:
Amirhossein Alirezaie, Habibeh Ahmadipour, and Mina Mobasher grade a medical ethics course through students' eyes, in a 2024 study. Ethics teaching aims to keep the human side of medicine alive as schools try varied formats. The authors use a four-part evaluation model that judges a program's setting, inputs, delivery, and results.

They surveyed 136 senior medical students at an Iranian university with a tailored questionnaire. Results scored highest: students felt the course conveyed ethical ideas and deepened understanding. Inputs scored lowest, pointing at materials and resources. The authors urge better alignment with cultural norms and stronger support for student engagement. The study gives curriculum committees a map of where a valued course still leaks.
pmc-12331167:
Torres and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a lab study of debris pushed out of tooth roots during root canal work. Material extruded past the root tip can cause pain and slow healing. Before shaping a canal, dentists carve a glide path with a starter file. The team compared three glide path files in curved molar roots. Twenty-four extracted human roots were split into three groups. Roots sat in gel-filled tubes that were weighed before and after.

All three files extruded some debris through the root tip. The WaveOne Gold Glider extruded the least by a clear margin. The R-Pilot file came next, and the hand file extruded most. Differences between groups were statistically significant in their tests. The authors suggest powered glider files may reduce postoperative problems. The bench setup cannot prove clinical benefit, but it ranks the tools.
pmc-12381767:
Neri Niccolai, Edoardo Morandi, and Andrea Bernini published a simulation study in two thousand twenty-four on long-range electric effects inside proteins. Proteins must find their partners in crowded cells without random luck. The authors propose that surface charges, arranged in clusters, broadcast electromagnetic signals.

Molecular dynamics simulations on two very different proteins, small human ubiquitin and a large insect enzyme, tracked charged side chains moving in concert. Their motions create charge proximities that could guide recognition at a distance. The authors frame protein electrodynamics as a lens on long-range interaction. They suggest the findings could steer design of proteins with programmed recognition patterns.
pmc-12384267:
Suicide attempts among older adults are a grave concern in South Korea. Hye Jung Jun and Jun Hee Jang dig into a national health survey from twenty twenty-one to find what raises the risk. Their sample covered seventy-three thousand three hundred and twenty-six older adults living in the community. About zero point three percent reported a suicide attempt.

Thoughts of suicide stood out as the strongest factor, raising the odds more than fifteen-fold. Depression raised them about three-fold, and low life satisfaction about two-fold. Schooling and region mattered too, with more schooling linked to lower odds. The authors call for screening that catches depression and suicidal thoughts early, plus nursing care that lifts life satisfaction in older adults.
pmc-12453567:
Kiersten Fullem and seven co-authors describe two new bacterial species found on watermelon leaves in Florida that showed leaf spot disease. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Three fluorescent strains were isolated from the sick foliage. Sorting them took a full battery of lab and genome tests.

Phenotype checks covered classic biochemical traits and whether the strains sicken watermelon and squash seedlings. Genome trees placed the isolates in two separate branches of the Pseudomonas genus. Similarity scores against all known relatives fell well below the species cutoff. Other ID systems, from chemical profiling to mass spectra, also failed to name them. The combined evidence says the strains are two species new to science. They are named for Florida and for their watermelon host.
pmc-12660867:
Dalia Sanchez, Analí Sulca, and Liz Pacheco-Pumaleque test whether strong leadership pushes firms toward greener, more digital business models, in a 2025 study. Companies face twin pressures: cut waste through circular practices and adopt new technology such as artificial intelligence. The authors ask if the person at the top is the lever.

They surveyed 146 companies in metropolitan Lima and modeled the answers statistically. Leadership, defined as mobilizing a firm toward strategic change, promoted the adoption of circular practices. It also drove uptake of AI solutions by fostering adaptability and openness. Decisiveness, a shared vision, and skill at handling resistance stood out. The findings argue that model change starts with who leads, not just with budgets or rules.
pmc-12661767:
Mengting Wang and co-authors rank immune drugs for advanced stomach cancer in a 2025 analysis. The drugs block a brake on immune cells called PD-1, freeing them to attack the tumor. Several such drugs are used for stomach and junction cancers that cannot be cut out or have come back. No trial has tested them against each other directly.

The team pooled nineteen trials with close to ninety-five hundred patients, using a network method that links drugs through shared rivals. One drug alone, nivolumab, ranked first for survival and tumor response, but worst for severe side effects. Drug plus chemo pairs beat control care and did not raise severe harm. A distinct drug alone proved safest but weakest. The authors advise chemo plus immune therapy first, with nivolumab pairs giving the best balance.
pmc-12663267:
Clare Webster and co-authors published this data paper in 2025. It presents SwissRad10, a set of maps that give the light reaching the ground across Switzerland, hour by hour for a full year. Each cell of the map spans ten meters. The maps count both direct sun and soft sky light, and they are built from laser scans so fine that the shade of each tree is cast.

Forest plots come in two forms, with leaves on and with leaves off, and bare-ground values are given as well. Light at ground level shapes where plants and animals can live, how snow melts, and how forests trade carbon and water. The team offers the set as a base for ecology and land work across the country.
pmc-12663367:
Tan and seven co-authors ferment pumpkin juice with a mix of yeast and bacteria to boost its health value, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Pumpkin juice is rich but plain, with room to improve flavor and nutrients. The mix pairs one yeast with two milk bacteria used in yogurt. Together they turn sugars into new acids, scents, and active compounds.

The fermented juice held high counts of live microbes after brewing. Vitamin C, plant pigments, and protective compounds all rose versus plain juice. New fruity and floral scent compounds gave it a richer aroma. Color stayed nearly the same, and texture pleased tasters most among test batches. Sensory panels gave the mixed ferment the top score overall.
pmc-12663567:
Sebastiano Vaccarella and co-authors build tumor organoids from womb cancer patients to test drug response, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Womb cancer rates and deaths have climbed over the last decade. The mini-tumors grown in the lab matched their source cancers in looks, gene faults, and activity patterns.

Organoid responses to standard and targeted drugs matched the patients' own responses, guided by each tumor's drug-sensitive gene faults. Matched support cells from the tumor's surroundings were also grown and profiled. Unlike the organoids, those support cells barely responded and aged into an inflamed state under standard drugs. The platform pre-tests therapy on tumor and surroundings alike.
pmc-12664267:
Dai reports fast relief of depression with extra potassium in a single patient, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. Most drugs for depression act slowly, and they do not work the same way for all. A woman of thirty-two has mild anxiety that came on not long ago, and severe depression. She is given potassium ions, based on the idea that her body holds too little of them for its needs.

Her signs of illness clear fast and in full once the extra potassium starts. The report looks at how low potassium might link to depression. Too little of the ion, for the body's needs, may play a part in the core of the illness. One case cannot prove a treatment, no matter how good it looks. More care notes and group studies are needed to test the claim.
pmc-12693867:
Yejin Kang, Katherine Dillon, Danielle Levitt, and Arturo Figueroa test an amino acid supplement in people with type 2 diabetes in a 2025 trial. High blood sugar, both steady and spiking, stiffens arteries and harms their lining, raising heart risk. Sixteen middle aged and older patients took either the supplement, citrulline, or a placebo daily for four weeks.

The supplement group improved artery dilation, leg artery stiffness, aorta pressure, and fasting glucose compared with placebo. After a glucose drink, the same advantages appeared: better dilation, softer arteries, lower pressure and sugar. The authors conclude citrulline helps vessel function and glucose control in both chronic and acute high sugar states in this group.
pmc-12697267:
Wei Feng, Pingping He, Zhimin Wang, and Weishuai Li review ultrasound-burst microbubbles to treat heart reperfusion harm. Their review from twenty twenty-five covers a way to carry drugs to the heart. When blood flow comes back after a heart attack, it can harm the muscle yet more. Oxygen stress, inflammation, and failure of cell power units drive that harm.

Sound waves pop aimed microbubbles right at the heart. The pop, called cavitation, pushes drugs past walls of tiny vessels. Aim grows exact and more of each drug gets through. One path this way grows new blood vessels. A second calms a key alarm knot for inflammation. Drugs in use stay narrow in reach and raise safety doubts. This way aims for exact hits, not brute dose size.
pmc-12700367:
Lingling Wu, Weiwei Cai, Fei Wang, Yazhuo Wang, and Chang Wang surveyed obstetric nurses in China in two thousand twenty-five. The nurses care for women in pregnancy and birth, and many now also offer care through online services. The authors asked how a strong sense of work identity links to quality of work life.

Nurses came from thirty-three large hospitals in Anhui Province that run such online services. The study found that mental resilience, the ability to cope with strain, helped carry the link from identity to work life. Willingness to join the online services also shaped that path. The authors urge managers to support both resilience and willing participation.
pmc-12700767:
Xiaohui Xie and co-authors report, in a 2025 case study, a rare thymus tumor that first showed up as swollen neck glands. Tumors of this type arise from hormone-like cells in the thymus and are uncommon. The patient presented with neck lymph node swelling as the main sign, which can point to many other causes first.

The authors stress that early notice and a team-based diagnostic path were key to finding the true source. Correctly locating the tumor opened the way to full surgical removal, the main hope of cure. The case adds a warning for doctors who see lone neck gland swelling: rare chest tumors belong on the list of possible causes.
pmc-12700967:
Robert Biney and seven co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-five. It is about stigmasterol, a plant sterol found in every vegetable oil. They test it as a candidate antidepressant. Computational network analysis first mapped forty genes. At those genes, the compound's predicted targets meet the genes of depression. A handful of hubs stood out. They include AKT1 and the monoamine enzymes.

Docking simulations checked the fit of the compound. Then came the animal work. Mice given stigmasterol struggled less in two tests. Those were the standard swim and suspension despair tests. When the team blocked monoamine production or storage, the effect went away. That confirmed the predicted mechanism in an experimental way. The pipeline is the template here. Computation proposes, and animals dispose. The authors present a dietary molecule with a traced, testable antidepressant pathway.
pmc-12701067:
Xiren Zhou and co-authors present a computer model for finding hidden flaws under city roads, in a study published in 2025. Ground radar can picture what lies below the surface, but cracks and cavities are hard to mark: labels are scarce and edges are fuzzy. Radar traces also carry wave patterns that plain image tools ignore.

Their model extends a well-known image-cutting tool with a memory-like step that studies how waves change near a suspect spot. It first flags likely flaw areas by sight, then refines them using the wave evidence. In real-world tests it beat older methods, scoring above eighty-five percent, while needing very little training data. The system can run on its own or with light human guidance, cutting the effort of road checks.
pmc-12701867:
Denis Laloë and a large team compare the fluid left behind by cow embryos grown in the lab with fluid from embryos grown inside the cow, in a twenty twenty-five study. Lab-grown embryos are now more common than natural ones in cattle breeding, but their quality lags. The fluid an embryo grows in can hint at its health and sex. The team wanted to know what drives the mix of small chemicals in that fluid.

Embryos grown in the lab showed far less spread in their fluid chemistry than those grown in the cow. Stage and grade explained a fair share of the spread for natural embryos but almost none for lab ones. The authors say lab growth flattens the very differences that might help pick the best embryos.
pmc-12702267:
Jun Wu and eight co-authors profile blood chemistry in narcolepsy type one, a sleep disorder, focusing on its link with unhealthy blood fats. Their multi-center study was published in twenty twenty-five.

Forty-four patients and forty-four matched comparisons took sleep lab tests overnight and a nap test by day. Fasting blood was checked for the main fats and scanned broadly for small molecules. Patients showed higher total and harmful cholesterol and lower protective cholesterol than comparisons, even after adjustments. Certain chemical pathways, above all those around the amino acid arginine, differed between groups. The team split samples into discovery and validation sets to firm up the pattern. The signatures may help explain why this sleep disorder strains the heart.
pmc-12703267:
Canty, Gartner, Hoek, and Hefler scan in twenty twenty-five how countries regulate shops that sell smoked tobacco. Shop density and closeness to schools run higher in poorer areas, and easy access normalises smoking and undermines quitting. The team gathered laws, reports, and expert leads from every world health region to map what rules exist.

Many places set a minimum buying age and limit shop-window promotion, but few attack availability head-on. Some use licences with fees, caps on licence counts, or rules on shop type and distance from youth spaces. A very few places have ended tobacco retail outright. The authors urge licensing, caps, and distance limits at minimum, backed by monitoring and enforcement.
pmc-12705767:
Lukas Urbanschitz and four co-authors ask whether surgical residents can learn to place spinal screws inside virtual reality as well as on plastic bones. Four neurosurgery residents with under a year of spine experience each placed screws from the first lumbar to the first sacral vertebra in three rounds. Everyone started after self-instruction alone.

Before round two, one pair trained conventionally on a synthetic bone model and the other in VR; for round three everyone had both. After self-instruction, forty-four percent of screws were misplaced, worst in the VR-bound pair. After training, errors collapsed: one misplaced screw in the VR group and none in the conventional group. The pilot suggests VR training is a legitimate alternative for this skill.
pmc-12708867:
He and a large team dope perovskite crystals with lanthanide ions to pin phase separation and enable dual-color lasing, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Mixed-halide perovskites can split into domains with different band gaps. Uncontrolled splitting harms devices, but pinned splitting may be useful. Vapor growth yields high-quality microplates across halogen pairs.

Each plate emits two stable light bands under steady excitation. Pairwise halogen mixes cover red, green, and blue regions together. Dual-wavelength lasers with high performance result from the plates. Domains are tens of nanometers wide with sharp boundaries. Calculations show doping drives splitting, then blocks ion drift to pin it. Stability and tuning improve at once.
pmc-12712067:
Jinjing Ma and four co-authors published a computer vision study in twenty twenty-five on reading facial expressions in real time without heavy computation. Existing recognizers are expensive to run and miss the subtle features that separate expressions. Their network, SPAYOLO, rebuilds the YOLOv8 detector around a new module mixing space and frequency information.

Three paths work together: multi-scale convolutions catch fine and mid-level facial changes, a Fourier path extracts high-frequency texture and micro-expression cues, and a gated attention step fuses the streams. Accuracy reached about seventy-one percent on one standard dataset and sixty-eight on another, at real-time cost. The authors pitch the design for live affective computing.
pmc-12714767:
Yumi C Del Rey and co-authors test a new surface for dental implants in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Titanium implants are strong and safe, but germs stick to them more easily than to ceramic, and infection is a main cause of implant failure. The team made a titanium surface coated with zirconium using an electric process that leaves tiny pores.

They compared the new surface with plain and acid-treated titanium worn in the mouth. The coated surface had moderate roughness, lower surface energy, and less wetting. Films of mouth germs grown on it held far fewer germs in total, with fewer harmful types and more harmless ones. The authors say such coatings could cut implant infection.
pmc-12717167:
Vallely, Weadick, Treacy, and O'Reilly surveyed sleep in breast cancer patients for this short report from twenty twenty-five. Earlier Irish work found insomnia twice as common in cancer patients as in the general public. Breast cancer itself predicted clinical insomnia. The team widened the lens to a larger group of patients with early-stage disease.

Three hundred fifteen patients completed a forty-item questionnaire. Over half said their sleep had changed since diagnosis. More than half met the bar for near-clinical or clinical insomnia. Two thirds agreed sleep should be part of cancer assessment. Yet only a third recalled ever being asked about sleep, and about a quarter felt their problems were handled well. The authors call the gap a target for care.
pmc-12718267:
Haoyun Mao and colleagues published a 2025 study asking whether low blood oxygen worsens kidney injury in sepsis. Sepsis often damages the kidneys. Low oxygen is common in these patients too. The team analyzed thousands of intensive care records. Mice experiments tested the mechanism directly.

Patients with lower oxygen looked sicker at first glance. Careful adjustment removed the independent link. Kidney markers matched that pattern. Mouse groups combined sepsis, low oxygen, or both. Tissue and protein measures tracked the injury. The combined evidence argues low oxygen is a warning sign. It may not itself drive the kidney damage.
pmc-12721367:
Qianqian Chen and co-authors wrote a 2025 set of clinical guidelines from China on a gentler way to treat tumors of the digestive tract. Standard surgery removes whole organs or key valves in the gut, which cures the tumor but often leaves patients with lasting problems like reflux or poor digestion. The new approach aims to cure the disease while keeping the body's normal layout.

The method, called super minimally invasive surgery, works through scopes passed into the body rather than large cuts. The guidelines describe its routes and the cases each route suits. They come from China's digestive endoscopy society with an international committee. Shared standards help more hospitals adopt the approach safely and train surgeons the same way.
pmc-12722167:
Eight clinicians report an unusual rescue for severe bleeding during fibroid surgery in a case report from 2025. The patient was a woman with a two-year history of symptomatic uterine fibroids. During removal of a fibroid, heavy bleeding began deep in the pelvis from low-pressure vessels. Standard methods could not stop it, and the loss threatened her life.

The team packed the pelvis with surgical mops through the vagina, cutting bleeding sharply. A further mop pressed from the abdomen stopped it fully. The packs were removed after forty-eight hours, and she recovered without further problems. The authors present combined packing as a life-saving option for deep pelvic bleeding.
pmc-12722467:
Leyna Díaz and co-authors published this genomics study in 2025. Malassezia yeasts live on the skin of warm-blooded animals and cannot make their own long-chain fatty acids, so they normally need fats supplied. One species, common on pets, usually manages to grow on standard lab agar anyway. A few odd strains cannot. The team sequenced three of those atypical, fat-demanding strains and compared them with the reference genome.

They found 397 small genetic changes with likely effects on proteins, concentrated in fat-handling genes. Twelve of the thirteen genes for secreted lipases, enzymes that harvest fats from the surroundings, carried changes. So did a gene unique to this species in its genus. The pattern suggests the atypical strains have a blunted ability to scavenge fats, forcing them to demand richer food. The authors link the variants to how flexibly the yeast adapts to different environments.
pmc-12723867:
Jianlin Xu and seven colleagues published a real-world analysis in two thousand twenty-five on lung cancer after targeted drugs fail. A mutation called C797S commonly defeats third-generation EGFR inhibitors. What to give next was guided by little evidence.

Forty-four patients with the mutation and full records were compared across follow-up regimens. Chemotherapy-based care beat non-chemotherapy care on time without progression, five point five versus three point four months. Adding a blood-vessel blocker to chemotherapy did best. Subgroup patterns differed by whether a second mutation coexisted; one subgroup fared better on targeted drugs. The authors conclude chemotherapy remains the backbone for most of these patients.
pmc-12725567:
Alex Bhattacharya and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, phone and digital tools meant to raise childhood vaccine uptake in nineteen African countries set to roll out new malaria vaccines. Multi-dose vaccines only work if families return on time, so reminders and records matter. The team searched eight databases plus grey sources for trials of such tools.

Fourteen studies met the bar, but they covered only four of the nineteen countries. All tested appointment reminders in some form. Evidence strength and bias were graded with standard tools. The patchy map shows where proof exists and where it does not. Digital reminders help, the authors suggest, but most target countries still lack direct trials.
pmc-12728067:
Fei Li and co-authors test whether immune drugs can work a second time in advanced stomach cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Most patients worsen after first immune-plus-chemo care. Records covered eighty-three patients at one Chinese hospital who moved to second-line care.

About half got the immune drugs again, and the rest got chemo alone. The immune group responded far more often and lived longer on median. Grave side effects were less common in the immune group. A marker of immune activity split the gain: those above the cut gained, those below did not. The authors see real promise in the second try.
pmc-12729567:
Bingqing Gao and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether the alkaloid part of a traditional Chinese herb can fight ovarian cancer, and how. The herb has broad reported effects, but its alkaloid share was unmapped. Chemical scans found thirty-eight nitrogen-bearing compounds in the fraction. Lab assays then tracked cancer cell growth, movement, and death.

The fraction slowed cell growth and spread in a dose-wise way and pushed cells into programmed death. A stress and guardian protein pathway sat at the center of the effect. In mice carrying human tumors, the fraction repeated its good showing. Tissue and blood checks backed the lab story. The authors pitch the fraction as a lead for new ovarian drugs.
pmc-12731067:
Rodrigo Vargas and co-authors published a 2025 study on the genetics of tuco-tucos, burrowing rodents of the Andes in Chile. These rodents are famous for how much their chromosome counts vary between species. Much of that variety comes from repeated DNA stretches being gained, lost, or moved. The team focused on two closely related forms living side by side.

One form has twenty-six chromosomes and the other twenty-eight. Using several lab methods that light up repeated DNA, they mapped where those repeats sit in each form. One form lacked rich repeat blocks on four chromosome pairs; the other lacked them on nine. Neither form showed a fresh burst of its own repeats. A family tree built from a gene sequence dated their split to the late ice age period. The authors argue that repeat loss, tied to chromosome splitting, drove the change in chromosome number.
pmc-12731367:
Yunxiao Wang and four co-authors test robot help for dental implants in a lab study from 2025. They printed jaw models with two sites: a fresh socket after tooth removal and a healed site. A robot drilled the sites and placed implants under two levels of guidance, with or without an extra thread step.

Healed sites gave more exact placement and lower drill forces than fresh sites. In fresh sites, the extra thread step and full guidance each cut placement error a great deal. In healed sites, full guidance helped less. The findings guide how dentists should plan robot work by site type.  Force on the drill was logged by a sensor on the robot arm during each placement.
pmc-12731667:
Eleni Geladari and co-authors review liver injury in sepsis in a 2025 paper. Sepsis can damage the liver early, in a pattern called sepsis-associated liver injury. The injury unfolds in two phases: a fierce inflammatory phase and a later immune-suppressed phase.

In the first phase, signaling storms harm liver cells and track with worse survival. Immune cells in the liver add to the damage with harsh chemicals. In the second phase, weak defenses invite new infections and slow repair. Liver cells also lose their normal fat-burning program. The review frames these phases as a base for immune treatments tailored to each patient.
pmc-12731867:
Xanthan gum is a thickener used in foods and industry, but the powder dissolves poorly and its texture is hard to control. Lei Zhang and co-authors studied how ultrasound travels through xanthan solutions and changes them. They compared single frequency ultrasound with dual and triple frequency setups, using a curved flat plate device. In thick solutions the single frequency field faded fast, while the combined frequencies kept a stronger, more even field across a wider range of concentrations.

The treatment paid off. Dissolved share rose from about sixty-three percent untreated to nearly eighty-six percent under the dual frequency setting. The solutions also grew less viscous, their surface tension fell, and their chains moved more freely. Microscope images showed broken fibers and a porous network, most clearly after multi-frequency treatment. The authors conclude that keeping sound energy alive in thick fluids is the key to the improvements.
pmc-12732267:
Krisztina Martha and colleagues study how infant feeding links to tooth decay in young children, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Early childhood decay is one of the most common long-term conditions in preschool children. Feeding in the first months shapes the germs that settle in the mouth. The team examined 103 children aged three to five and asked parents how each child was fed as a baby.

Children fed only formula had the worst decay scores, and breastfed children had the lowest. Mixed-fed children fell in between. Decay was also tied to feeding type in group tests. The authors say early feeding habits leave a mark on teeth years later, so guidance for new parents should cover oral health too.
pmc-12735467:
Moswane and colleagues read the full genomes in twenty twenty-five of vaccine-strain bacteria that caused disease in patients. The TB vaccine is made from a weakened cattle strain, but decades of uncontrolled growing split it into many gene variants. In rare cases the vaccine strain itself makes people ill, and telling it apart from true TB matters for care.

The team sequenced seven samples from a national TB lab and compared them with reference strains. The samples differed widely from each other and from the references. One sat close to a standard vaccine strain, and one near a TB strain, hinting at a wrong first diagnosis. Two samples showed possible resistance to a TB drug. The authors urge routine gene testing in such cases.
pmc-12736167:
Qian Zou, Rafael Ogaz-González, Gerton Lunter, Eva Corpeleijn, and Christian Ritz link lifestyle patterns to chronic disease in this two thousand twenty-five prospective cohort study. Lifestyle factors interact in tangled ways, so the authors derived patterns from baseline self-reports in the Dutch Lifelines cohort. Diet, activity, substance use, sleep, stress, and social ties were each graded healthy, middling, or unhealthy, then combined into patterns and summation scores. Disease-free adults were followed a median of eight years.

The analysis covered over one hundred thousand people per disease, with thousands of cases of diabetes, cancer, respiratory disease, and cardiovascular disease. Against the unhealthy pattern, both a balanced healthy pattern and a healthy-but-inactive pattern were protective. One pattern, unhealthy overall but without substance use, raised diabetes risk while lowering cancer risk. The study shows whole-lifestyle patterns predict disease in ways single habits cannot.
pmc-12736467:
Mateus Pena and co-authors present a 2025 study on how cannabis plants handle drought. Dry conditions limit yield of both plant material and the active compounds people harvest. The team compared two contrasting types: one rich in THC and one rich in CBD, the two best-known compounds in the plant.

Plants were grown in a greenhouse, and water was cut at early flowering. The CBD plants built more biomass but did not photosynthesize faster when water was plentiful. Under drought, the THC plants mainly closed their leaf pores to save water. The CBD plants showed deeper internal limits and a stronger drop in photosynthesis. Both types ended with similar cell damage, so sun-protection tricks did not explain the gap.
pmc-12736767:
Yessenia Ibeth Paucar and colleagues map out how to print graphene strain sensors with a cheap diode laser. Laser-induced graphene, formed by irradiating polyimide film, promises low-cost flexible sensors. The team varied laser power, focal length, and number of passes using a blue diode laser. They then evaluated the resulting sensors in three-point bending tests.

Shape checks, Raman spectroscopy, and electrical measurements gauged conductivity, bending stability, and sensitivity. Laser power proved the key factor for graphene quality and sensor performance. Focal length had almost no effect. Extra passes in fact reduced material quality and sensitivity. That is a useful negative result against the gut sense that more processing helps. The work shows working, low-cost graphene strain sensors from a commercial diode laser. It offers a route to make them at scale, cheaply.
pmc-12738067:
Basil Baby Mattamana and co-authors tuned a prep method for cell culture fluid in a 2025 paper. The fluid cells grow in holds the proteins they shed, a rich source of disease marks and signals. Big volumes, over five milliliters, defeat standard prep: proteins are scarce, serum floods the mix, and losses mount.

Their workflow stacks three steps: a fine filter that keeps the mid-size proteins, a column that pulls out the flood proteins, and a solvent crash that gathers the rest. The stack keeps both rare and common shed proteins for the mass spectrometer. Labs can scale it to large culture runs.
pmc-12738767:
Jiali Shou and co-authors present a 2025 study on using ultrasound to detect muscle loss in heart patients. Sarcopenia weakens people with cardiovascular disease, but standard checks of mass and strength can be slow. The team tested whether standard ultrasound plus a stiffness method, shear wave elastography, could flag the condition.

They enrolled 114 patients with heart disease or stroke. Thirty-six had sarcopenia by the standard measures of mass, grip, and walking speed. Ultrasound features of the front thigh muscle were taken at rest and stretched. The muscle loss group showed thinner fat and muscle layers and smaller muscle area. Correlation checks and a combined model then weighed which scan features predict sarcopenia on their own.
pmc-12740967:
Oveys Ziya, Laxmi Sushama, and Husham Almansour present a 2025 study of flood loads on road overpasses in Montreal. A warmer climate can bring more short, intense rain bursts. Such bursts cause flash floods that can strain city structures, yet overpasses have been little studied in this regard.

The team paired fine scale climate runs with a two dimensional water flow model of the city. They built design storms for current and future climates under several paths for gas emissions. The storms matched the kind of rain expected once in a hundred years. Then they weighed the push, drag, and debris hit loads that flood water would place on overpasses.
pmc-12741067:
Liang and ten co-authors show a medicinal chrysanthemum extract protects skin from ultraviolet A damage, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Sunlight's UVA triggers stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment, causing cell death. The plant, Coreopsis tinctoria, is rich in antioxidant flavonoids. Over twelve hundred metabolites are profiled in the extract.

In human skin cells, the extract cuts death, inflammation, and reactive oxygen. All three stress branches are suppressed while Nrf2 defenses activate. Removing Nrf2 abolishes the protection, proving its central role. Topical use also protects UVA-exposed mouse skin in tests. A natural photoprotective agent candidate emerges.
pmc-12742167:
Chiara Bernardi and thirteen co-authors present a 2025 study asking whether the time of day a stem cell graft is given changes transplant results. The body clock shapes blood formation and immune control. An earlier study had linked afternoon grafts with more graft versus host disease and worse survival.

The team checked that claim in their own center's records. They reviewed 368 patients who got donor stem cell transplants in Geneva from 2015 to 2024. Timing patterns at their center differed from the earlier report, which gave a clean test of the link. The study weighs disease rates and survival by infusion time.
pmc-12742767:
Linen Li, Hao Chen, Feng Zhou, and Yanqing Shi sort, in a 2025 study, stomach cancers into immune subtypes using two genes from a cancer-testis family. The immune surroundings of a tumor decide much of its course and its answer to immunotherapy, but epithelial genes that flag those surroundings were poorly mapped. The team crossed single-cell data with a large tumor atlas to find such genes.

Two genes, MAGEA3 and MAGEA6, split the tumors cleanly. Cancers high in both were immune cold, thinly infiltrated by immune cells, while cancers low in both were immune hot. Two further genes, BCL11B and PAEP, tracked closely with infiltration and immune regulation, marking them as candidate levers. The authors propose the pair as a simple subtyping test for stomach cancer, and the extra genes as targets worth probing for therapy.
pmc-12743267:
Jialei Zhang and ten co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a rare gut illness tied to the IgG4 disease family. The illness scars and thickens the mesentery, the fold that holds the gut. It is little known and may be missed. The team drew on a large cohort at a Beijing hospital, with close to thirty such cases, plus cases from past reports.

Cases skewed to older men with more organs hit and higher disease scores than kin cases with no gut form. Scans showed a range from misty haze to soft masses in the mesentery. Their cohort had less belly pain but more gland swell than past reports. Drug care in the cohort matched surgery in past cases on relapse rates.
pmc-12744867:
Gu and four colleagues track the global burden of psoriasis from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one in a twenty twenty-five study. Psoriasis is a long term skin disease marked by inflammation. The team drew rates of new cases, total cases, and years lost to disability from a global disease database. They also forecast trends for the next fifteen years.

Rates of new cases rose over the study period, and total case rates rose as well. Rates were higher in men than in women. In twenty twenty-one, new case rates peaked in the fifty-five to sixty-nine age group. Rates were highest in wealthy regions, in Western Europe, and in Germany. The forecast sees rates rising further, so the authors urge plans aimed at high risk groups.
pmc-12745967:
Sanjiao Liu and five co-authors present a summary from twenty twenty-five of best care before pregnancy for women with rheumatoid arthritis. The disease often starts in the childbearing years. Its chronic inflammation plus drug effects raise the risk of poor pregnancy outcomes. Yet the evidence for care before conception is scattered across many sources. The team hunts it down in a set order.

Eleven sources made the cut: guidelines, expert accords, and reviews. From them came a set of best practice points in seven areas. Areas span fertility risk checks, screening, drug tweaks, fertility saving, weight and food, and mind support. Most points won a strong backing grade. The set is meant as a bench guide for nurses.
pmc-12748367:
Satoshi Naruse and co-authors report an emergency caesarean delivery in a pregnant woman with uncorrected diabetic ketoacidosis, in work published in 2025. The condition, where blood turns acidic from uncontrolled diabetes, is rare in pregnancy but often fatal for the baby. Standard care stabilises the mother first, yet the baby's distress can force immediate delivery.

The patient was a 24-year-old first-time mother at thirty-five weeks with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Her baby showed a worrying heart pattern, so surgery went ahead before her blood chemistry was fixed. A combined spinal-epidural block was used, with insulin and glucose therapy running and blood gases checked through an arterial line. Both mother and baby recovered and went home without complications. The case shows a coordinated path for this rare emergency.
pmc-12748867:
Jolanta Nowak and six co-authors published a muscle biology study in twenty twenty-five on myosin VI, an unconventional motor protein, at the junction where nerves meet muscle. The protein already had known roles in muscle building and heart function. Its job at the neuromuscular junction, the synapse that triggers contraction, had never been examined.

The protein concentrates at the junction's receiving side in young and adult animals. Mice lacking it showed delayed junction maturation in both fast and slow muscles, and smaller junctions in the soleus. The normal pruning of extra nerve inputs, though, proceeded on schedule. Grip strength suffered in both sexes. The authors conclude myosin VI is a genuine regulator of junction size and timing.
pmc-12751867:
Tianlin Wang and colleagues test a head-start training plan for new clinical pharmacists in China, in this trial from twenty twenty-five. Standard training lasts a year and leans on drug knowledge, but new hires without a clinical pharmacy degree often lack job readiness and soft skills. The team's plan adds three months of adaptability training before the standard year.

Twenty new pharmacists were split at random into two groups. One group took the extra training, covering career awareness, teamwork, clear thinking, and coping with stress, and the other did not. After the shared year of training, expert panels rated both groups. The head-start group scored higher on career awareness, fitting in with ward demands, reasoning through cases, and working across fields. It also won praise for sound analysis and care for patients. The authors urge wider use of the plan.
pmc-12751967:
Andrea Duarte-Díaz and colleagues pooled dementia therapy trials in 2025. Dementia brings fading memory and heavy emotional strain. Emotion-oriented care targets feelings and psychological needs directly. Such care skips drugs entirely. Forms include supportive talk therapy and reminiscence work. Sensory programs and simulated family presence also count. The team searched seven databases for randomized trials. Thirty-four trials entered the combined analysis. Bias checks used standard Cochrane tools.

Treated patients improved on several fronts. Thinking scores and depressive symptoms both got better. Life quality and daily function also improved. Gains looked largest where few other options existed. Results varied against active comparison therapies, though. The specific method and setting shaped the effect. The authors call these therapies a valuable complement. Low-resource settings may gain the most from them. More work must set long-term value and delivery rules.
pmc-12752967:
Cecere and co-authors share a protocol for moving a standard genetic tool into wild strains of a glowing marine bacterium. The bacterium, Vibrio fischeri, lives in symbiosis with the Hawaiian bobtail squid. Tools built for the lab strain often fail in its wild relatives.

Their workaround first inserts the desired DNA into the lab strain at the usual landing site. DNA from that strain then transforms the target strain, whose natural uptake is switched on. As proof, they restored a broken gene in another strain using an inducible copy. The authors offer the method to anyone studying symbiosis genes in hard-to-edit strains.
pmc-12754467:
Six researchers pool studies on shockwave therapy after knee ligament surgery in a review from 2025. The surgery rebuilds the anterior cruciate ligament, a key knee stabilizer. Recovery is often slow even with standard rehabilitation. Shockwave therapy sends pressure pulses into tissue and may speed healing. The team gathered six studies, five of them randomized trials, comparing added shockwaves with rehab alone.

One knee function score improved modestly with shockwaves, though studies varied widely. Focused shockwaves looked better than radial ones. Other scores, including pain and knee looseness, showed no clear gain. The authors note signs of publication bias. They call for larger, placebo-controlled trials with standard methods.
pmc-12757967:
Bárbara dos Santos and co-authors test denture materials in this 2025 study. Full dentures can be relined with hard acrylic to restore their fit. Many wearers also use adhesives to keep dentures in place. The team asked how adhesives and aging change the reliners' color, hardness, and surface roughness.

They tested three reliner brands with three adhesives on 120 samples. Samples were checked fresh, after two months, and after heat-cycle aging. Time changed every property, with hardness and roughness rising. One brand held its color and hardness best, a trait tied to elements in its makeup. Its surface, though, grew roughest. The results help dentists weigh looks and durability by brand.
pmc-12770067:
Mobina Nakhaei Shamahmood and co-authors review the diabetes drug metformin as a partner drug against acute myeloid leukemia, in this 2025 paper. The leukemia kills many patients through relapse and drug resistance. Metformin alone does little, but studies hint it sharpens other drugs. The team sifted over a hundred papers down to thirty-two that tested real combinations.

Partners ranged from targeted agents to classic chemotherapy. Across studies the pairs drained cell energy, stalled growth cycles, and pushed leukemia cells into death, trimming disease burden and lengthening survival in models. Effects like blocked sugar burning and lowered power output recurred. The authors conclude metformin can add real synergy to leukemia regimens. They call for clinical testing to sort which pairs deserve patients first.
pmc-12771067:
Raviprakash T. Sitaram and Börje Ljungberg reported a tissue study in 2025 on the most common form of kidney cancer. A protein that normally keeps oxygen sensing in check is often lost in these tumors. Losing it frees oxygen-response proteins and may weaken a protein that helps cells stick together. The team measured all three in tumors from many patients, alongside normal kidney tissue, and linked the patterns to stage, size, and survival.

The control protein was lower in tumors than in normal tissue. One oxygen-response protein rose in the most advanced tumors, while another rose with tumor size. The sticking protein fell in tumors, above all in larger and later-stage ones. Higher levels of that protein tracked with better survival only when the control protein stayed high. The authors read the chain as a driver of tumor growth and a possible source of drug targets.
pmc-12781267:
Alvin Chai and co-authors review lymphoma care outcomes at a Malaysian tertiary hospital. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma in Malaysia and worldwide. Records covered 202 patients treated from 2015 to 2020 with the R-CHOP drug mix. Median age was fifty-eight, and most patients were men.

Complete response came for about fifty-eight percent of patients. Three-year survival sat near sixty-one percent, with progression-free survival close behind. High prognostic index scores and B symptoms both marked worse paths. Low blood albumin stood alone as an independent death risk in deep analysis. The authors call for bigger prospective trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-12784867:
Junnan Ding, Yingjian Wang, and Shaopeng Yu study how microbe communities change as salty, alkaline wetlands break down, in a 2025 paper. They sampled four habitats, from untouched wetland to converted farmland. As wetlands degrade, soil dries out, nutrients fall, and salt stress grows, but bacteria and fungi may not respond in the same way.

Soil water and nutrients were highest in the untouched wetland and lowest in the harshest habitat. Bacteria were ruled more strongly by soil traits such as acidity, carbon, and moisture. Under stress, bacterial grouping followed set rules driven by selection. Fungal grouping stayed mostly random, and fungal networks held up better under extreme damage. The split shows the two groups follow different rules during wetland loss.
pmc-12786567:
Tianyi Feng and co-authors study how iron and silicon impurities shape the strength of aluminum-copper-lithium alloys, metals prized for aircraft. Trace iron and silicon sneak in, above all when scrap is recycled. The team made five alloy mixes with iron and silicon each held between 0.03 and 0.12 percent by weight. All went through the same chain of heating, extrusion, solution treatment, and aging.

Iron pushed the growth of coarse, skeletal iron-bearing crystals. Silicon favored blocky iron-silicon phases and plain silicon grains. More iron cut strength, ductility, and fracture toughness. The harm runs two ways: the iron phases persist, act as stress points, and start cracks; and iron eats up copper that would otherwise form the key strengthening particles. Silicon hurt less. For makers of recycled alloys: control iron tightly; silicon is the lever to trade for lower cost.
pmc-12787167:
Barr and four co-authors test treated dietary protein in mice on high fat diets, in work from twenty twenty-five. Fatty liver disease linked to metabolism is rising, and diet change is hard to sustain. A protein treatment with ammonium hydroxide may soften liver harm without strict dieting.

Mice ate high fat diets built on beef or casein protein, with or without the treatment. Liver metabolism signaling was tracked by sex and age. Effects differed between males and females and across ages. Molecular evidence like this is an early step; it does not yet show the approach works in people.
pmc-12787967:
Giulia Moretto and co-authors study a lemon verbena leaf extract for its power to block harmful sugar-protein reactions, in work published in 2025. Those reactions build up products called AGEs in the body, which are linked to ageing and degenerative disease. Plant compounds can interfere with the chemistry at several steps.

The extract proved rich in several families of plant metabolites. In lab tests, it strongly blocked AGE formation at the middle and end steps of the reaction, and it trapped two reactive sugar fragments at high rates. Computer docking suggested the compounds can bind the receptor that AGEs activate. Simulated digestion broke down much of the extract, leaving about forty percent accessible. The bioaccessible part kept some protective activity. The work weighs promise against losses in digestion.
pmc-12788267:
Qinghua Zhang, Zhenxing Liu, Jianbo Wu, Ping Sun, and Hanwen Zhang design a flexible pressure sensor with a graded porous layer, in a research paper from 2025. Pressure sensors usually trade sensitivity against range: keen sensors saturate early. The team aimed to keep both wide range and sharp response.

The sensing film mixes plastic with carbon nanotubes over printed silver electrodes. Mixed sugar grains of two sizes form uneven pores when washed away, building the graded structure. Tests showed near-perfect linearity and high sensitivity across a wide pressure span. The sensor answered in fifty milliseconds and survived over five hundred cycles with little drift.
pmc-12800067:
Tomoyo Sawada leads a large team studying a gene tied to schizophrenia in this twenty twenty-five paper. Rare broken copies of the gene raise the risk of the illness. What the working gene does in the brain, and why its loss matters, were unclear. Its role for patients without the rare change was also unknown.

Working with human fetal brain tissue and lab-grown nerve cells, the team mapped where the gene's protein binds and which genes it controls. It favored the start sites of genes tied to mental illness risk, DNA repair, and nerve signaling. The results link one rare cause to pathways shared by the wider illness.
pmc-12806567:
Baloch, Javed, and Grosu audit tool-assisted births at Bedford Hospital. Forceps and vacuum cups help when labor stalls or the baby is at risk. Rates have fallen worldwide, yet the skill stays vital. Good notes and rule-based care guard mother and baby.

The audit covered all 62 attempted tool births in late 2024. Records came from electronic maternity files and a data hub. The team checked tool type, success rate, and time to birth. Consent and note quality were also graded in full. Care was weighed against national and local rule sets. Gaps point to training and form fixes.
pmc-12808167:
Chengfei Zhang and eleven co-authors show a growth part, PRAS40, feeds colon cancer stem traits by way of sugar burn. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Stem-like cells drive this cancer's growth and cure shrug. The part ran high in tumor cuts and tied to short life. Its cut-out curbed tumor birth in mice.

With the part, cells made more balls, bore more stem marks, and seeded tumors with ease. It binds and wakes a sugar burn step and draws in a tag crew that tags that step, which fires the burn. Block of the tag step cut stem traits and tumor birth in tests.
pmc-12815767:
Peiqin Li and colleagues test a traditional Chinese herbal mix against lung cancer in mice, in this study published in twenty twenty-five. The mix, called Jinfu'an decoction, is already used to treat lung cancer and has shown anti-tumor effects in past work. Here the team asks how it works, by joining two tools: body chemistry profiling and gut microbe analysis.

The team grew human lung tumor cells under the skin of mice, then split them into groups. Three groups got low, medium, or high doses of the mix by tube feeding for twenty-one days, next to an untreated tumor group and a healthy group. By tracking tumor growth along with blood and tissue chemistry and gut microbes, the study maps the paths through which the mix may slow tumors. The design gives later work a base for testing single active parts.
pmc-12817767:
Zewditu Denu and thirteen colleagues measured whether mothers in Ethiopia give birth with skilled help at hand, and whether that care works in fact. Skilled help at birth cuts deaths of mothers and newborns, but only when sites are ready and care is good. The study covered the population. It used a cascade with four steps toward coverage adjusted for quality. Site readiness came from a 2019 check of services. The final figure was built step by step: attendance, readiness, care given, quality of process.

Crude coverage for skilled delivery stood at fifty-four percent. Each cascade step then cut that figure down toward true coverage that works. The gap between contact and quality is the heart of the story: many women reach a site that lacks key supplies or skills. For planners in Ethiopia, the 2025 numbers show where the chain breaks, supplies, skills, or follow-through.
pmc-12819167:
Xiang Han proposes a graph-based offline learning method for robot path planning. His study from twenty twenty-six tackles long-horizon navigation. Sparse rewards make ordinary reinforcement learning inefficient here. Hierarchical methods split the job into subgoals and steps.

Earlier latent-space subgoal methods search a continuous space wastefully. Training instability and slow convergence follow from that search. Han's design places subgoals on a learned latent graph instead. A proven policy algorithm runs at both hierarchy levels. Offline training uses logged data rather than live trials. Structured subgoal spaces should stabilise the learning process. Warehouse and service robots need exactly this reliability.
pmc-12820167:
Qiu and coauthors build a stiff scope frame that stops drift in fine imaging. Single-molecule imaging can locate points at nanometer scale. Sample drift during shots blurs that sharp result. Most fixes correct drift after shots or add marker beads.

Their frame stops drift at its source in the hardware. Holed parts linked by tungsten steel rods form the cage. Bench tests showed lateral drift near five nanometers in two hours. Single-molecule runs held drift to a narrow band in 15 minutes. No axial drift could be measured in those runs. The design may ease super-fine imaging in plain labs.
pmc-12821867:
Shun Yoshida and nine co-authors hunt what drives early grave infection in old folks with a vessel flare ill tied to MPO-ANCA. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Drugs that calm the immune set have lifted life odds in this ill, yet infections early in care stay a top risk in the old. Fifty patients aged past seventy-five at one hub were checked, all with the small-vessel form.

Grave infections hit one third of them in six months of care start. A drug pair used to guard lungs, TMP-SMX, tied to a sharp drop in infection risk, and held past checks for sex. The team pitch lung guard use for high-risk old folks, with care for the watch-only design.
pmc-12826567:
Giovani Burgos and Alex Trillo study how discrimination is measured in Latino health research, in a paper from 2025. Feeling discriminated against is tied to worse health. Most studies, though, flatten Latino groups into one bloc and use a single score. That habit can hide real gaps and bend the results.

Using a national survey of Latino and Asian Americans, they test a common discrimination scale group by group. The scale split cleanly into two sides: subtle slights and overt acts. That two-sided form fit every Latino group in the data. When the scale was modeled that way, its link to depression and chronic illness grew stronger. The authors say finer scales give truer answers. Splitting the bloc also reveals how each group fares on its own.
pmc-12827567:
Paola Gobbi and co-authors update the genetic map of small ruminant lentiviruses in Italy, in a study first shared in 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. These retroviruses infect sheep and goats and vary a great deal. They cause a range of slow illnesses and cross between the two hosts with ease. Samples came from routine watch work in sixteen of Italy's twenty regions.

Family tree analysis of samples from 2019 to 2024 showed wide variety across the country. Some virus clusters stayed locked to single regions. The clusters did not match the current naming scheme for subtypes. That mismatch suggests the scheme needs an update. The authors call for steady watch work with full gene reads. A fresh classification would help vets track how these viruses spread and change.
pmc-12830667:
Zaagan and three co-authors improve a process control chart with machine learning in a paper from 2025. Control charts watch a factory process and flag shifts, but charts that trim extreme values can miss real changes, while classic charts assume tidy data. Their hybrid chart lets an anomaly model weigh each new reading before it enters the running average.

Simulations across dirty-data settings and shift sizes showed the hybrid kept false alarms lower than classic charts. It also caught moderate shifts faster. A case study on real contaminated process data backed the lab results. The authors offer the chart for robust monitoring where outliers are common.
pmc-12831267:
Rashid Nasr and a team of colleagues published a headache survey in two thousand twenty-five among Sudanese health sciences students. Migraine and tension headaches are common in students and hurt study performance. Data from Sudan were scarce.

The questionnaire reached nearly one thousand eight hundred medical, dental, and pharmacy students. About forty-two percent reported recurring headaches. Migraine made up about twenty-four percent and tension headache about eighteen percent. Light sensitivity came with most migraines. Stress and lost sleep were the top triggers. Nine in ten students treated themselves with shop-bought painkillers, and few saw a doctor. About a fifth had missed classes or exams because of headaches.
pmc-12836867:
Wang-Sheng Lin and five co-authors tracked fitness trends in older adults who live at home in Taiwan. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, starts from the worth of fitness for free life in old age. Long term proof on many sides of fitness in Asian elders was thin. The group held four hundred three adults of age sixty-five and up. They joined a community health drive and took the same tests at three points in time.

Tests spanned grip strength, arm curls, chair stands, balance on one leg, timed up and go, step and walk endurance, and reach and stretch marks. The team read which way each trait moved and what traits pushed the change. Readers in elder health get a rare long view of fitness drift.
pmc-12836967:
Yang and coauthors study a gene that may drive heart harm in sepsis. The gene, called JunB, was high in hurt heart tissue. Its role in sepsis heart harm had not been probed yet. The team built cell and mouse models of that harm.

Toxin-treated heart cells and septic mice both served as models. The team lowered JunB in each model and tracked results. Cell death, swelling signals, and stress marks all fell. A growth path in cells switched on as JunB fell. A blocker of that path erased the gains in cells. The work names JunB as a drug target worth study.
pmc-12838067:
Shuguang Yang and seven co-authors built risk models in a 2025 study of patients admitted to intensive care with suspected infection. Such patients can slide into sepsis, and drug-proof infections raise the danger further. The team took data from 2,963 patients in 67 hospitals across China. They trained several machine learning models to flag, at admission, who might die or carry a drug-proof infection.

A simple model beat the fancier methods, scoring 0.87 for death and 0.86 for resistant infection. Recent surgery, a severity score, and blood infection flagged the risk of death. Certain bacteria, above all two hardy kinds, flagged resistant infection. Lung infection was the most common site, and deaths ran near 11 percent overall. The models could help units act sooner on the riskiest patients.
pmc-12840467:
Rodrigo de Miguel uses a simple grid model to teach the ideal gas law in a paper from 2025. The law links the pressure, volume, and warmth of a gas. Textbooks often derive it by assuming a huge system at low density. De Miguel instead places free particles on a grid with a set number of boxes.

The analysis shows the gas law emerging as the gas settles into balance with its surroundings. No extra assumptions about size or density are needed. A second version treats volume as split into small steps and reaches the same result. The paper aims to give students a clearer view of what the law assumes.
pmc-12844967:
Elshafie, Kattoor, Kelly, and Wilkes adapted this test panel in twenty twenty-five for disease watch in wild meat-eating animals. Standard tests each hunt one germ at a time and can miss mixed infections. The team moved a targeted sequencing panel onto a small portable sequencer, the MinION. They merged it with a full-genome test for the virus behind COVID-19.

Spiked samples showed the panel could find the virus at low levels and read nearly its whole genome. It also spotted other pathogens in the same run. Accuracy tests gave high marks for both finding true cases and clearing true negatives. All one hundred sixty-one real wildlife samples tested negative. The authors offer the workflow as a cheap, flexible tool for wildlife surveillance.
pmc-12847467:
Shihao Huang and five colleagues study a gene called CTHRC1 in mouth cancer and its link to a rust-like cell death, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The gene is overactive in many cancers, including oral squamous cell carcinoma. The team measured it in three cancer cell lines and then silenced it. They tracked growth, cell death, and iron-driven damage markers.

Silencing the gene slowed growth and pushed cells toward both normal suicide and the rust-like death, ferroptosis. It also quieted a growth pathway called TGF-beta Smad. A drug that wakes that pathway reversed the death effect. The authors name this gene axis as a possible treatment target.
pmc-12849167:
Stefanie Braig and co-authors present a 2025 study of work ability two years after a COVID-19 infection in Germany. Lingering symptoms after the illness can cut work capacity and stretch sick leave. The link is tangled, since symptoms vary widely and work ability has many sides.

The study followed 5,422 adults aged eighteen to sixty five in the southwest of the country. All had a confirmed infection. The team tracked self rated work ability and sick leave at six to twelve months and again at twenty four months. About 1.1 percent stayed on sick leave from the first infection onward, they report.
pmc-12853067:
Bhagvat Maheta and co-authors studied which numbers on a residency application best predict matching in a 2025 study. The match weighs many factors, but scores and counts are the most objective and consistently reported. The team asked which quantitative variables track match success most strongly.

They used national data on residents from 2013 to 2021 across all approved fields. Candidate predictors included licensing exam scores, research experiences, publications and presentations, and volunteer and work histories. Tracking these over time and by field shows which credentials actually move the needle. Such evidence helps students spend effort where it counts instead of padding every line.
pmc-12855267:
Yanan Wang and colleagues follow what happens when prenatal testing finds a genetic variant nobody can classify, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Copy number variants of unknown significance turn up in amniotic fluid tests and leave parents in limbo. The team tracked one hundred thirty-two such findings from over three thousand six hundred samples.

Most parents, nearly nine in ten, chose to continue the pregnancy, and even brand-new variants rarely led to termination. Of one hundred fifteen live births, three babies had abnormalities, none provably tied to the variant. Checking whether a variant came from a parent helped counsel families. The authors conclude that most such variants end in healthy babies. They recommend a shared database and steady follow-up of these children, so tomorrow's parents get evidence instead of a shrug.
pmc-12859967:
Nasim Sadeghi and co-authors test probiotics in smokers in a randomized trial from 2025. Smoking links to metabolic problems and to poor mental health. Gut microbes may play a role in both, so live microbe capsules might ease nicotine dependence, anxiety, and low mood while improving blood markers.

Seventy-four adult smokers in Kashan, Iran, took probiotic or placebo capsules for twelve weeks. The active capsules held four Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. Standard scales tracked mood, anxiety, and dependence. After twelve weeks, the probiotic group showed drops in fasting blood sugar, triglycerides, and an inflammation marker, among other shifts. The trial tests a gut route to smoker health.
pmc-12860467:
Ling Sun, Xin Feng, Xingru Li, and a wider team wrote this meta-analysis, published in 2025. It pools studies of a surgical trick for dialysis patients: inflating a balloon inside a narrow wrist artery before sewing it to a vein, so the access port survives longer.

Dialysis needs a durable port, and a self-made vein fistula is preferred, but thin arteries make fistulas fail often. The review gathered twenty-five studies covering 2,450 patients. Balloon-assisted fistulas stayed open without help in about eighty-eight percent of cases at six months and seventy-five percent at twelve months. The pooled rates beat traditional surgery, and the review also tracked procedural success, ripening of the fistula, and complications.
