The authors say widening the artery first is an effective and safe way to rescue an otherwise doomed access.
pmc-12872167:
Plant psychedelics like ayahuasca and huachuma, the San Pedro cactus, are studied for mental health, yet their link with the gut microbiome is barely studied. The seven authors present a single-patient case study. A thirty-five-year-old woman who had used them before took part in two ceremonies, one per plant. Stool samples came before and after each, plus depression and connectedness scales and talks with the team.

Both sessions cut the depression scores sharply, from eighteen to six after ayahuasca and from twelve to two after huachuma. Scores for feeling close to others climbed. Each plant shifted gut microbes in its own way, but both trimmed pro-inflammatory species and boosted butyrate producers. The authors frame the case as a source of ideas for later tests: shifts in gut microbes may help explain the mood lift, through the gut-brain axis.
pmc-12872867:
Tian and co-authors report a rare soft tumor inside a jaw muscle. The patient had a painless lump under the jaw. A CT scan showed a cyst-like lesion in that area. The growth came from the mylohyoid muscle under the tongue. Lab review of the removed tissue confirmed an intramuscular myxoma.

Such tumors are benign but rare, at about one case per million people per year. Growths in the jaw muscles are rarer still and can mimic gland cysts. Scans alone can mislead, so tissue review stays the sure test. Full removal is the standard cure for this tumor type. The patient healed well after surgery, and outlook is good.
pmc-12896067:
Lucía Pérez Rodríguez and eight colleagues test a quick infrared tool for typing a hospital germ group, in a twenty twenty-five study. Typing tells staff whether infections share one source, but classic methods are slow and costly. The team checked the IR Biotyper on seventy-two drug-resistant strains of the Enterobacter cloacae complex. They compared its groupings with two gene-based methods.

The infrared tool sorted strains at least as sharply as the older gel method and near the level of full gene reading. Its groupings matched both methods closely. Results came in under three hours at low cost. The tool also performed well in a real outbreak check, backing its use in routine hospital labs.
pmc-12913167:
Liba Sokolovska and thirteen colleagues published a cancer study in two thousand twenty-five on the viruses behind cervical disease in Latvia. Latvia has some of Europe's highest cervical cancer rates. The team typed the high-risk human papillomaviruses in tissue samples spanning two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty-four.

They tested one hundred forty-five samples from precancer and cancer cases. Nearly all carried at least one high-risk virus type, and many carried several. Type sixteen stayed the most common across the years. Type eighteen fell sharply over the period. Several other types became more common instead. Worse disease stages carried heavier virus loads and more types. The authors say these shifts matter for screening and vaccine planning in Latvia.
pmc-12922367:
Senjeet Sreekissoon and eleven co-authors study a mouth cancer that comes with a scarring condition of the mouth lining, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Both are common where betel nut is chewed, in parts of Asia. Whether cancer with the scarring behaves worse than cancer without it was debated.

The team followed patients treated at a dental hospital in China over about a decade, sorted by whether they had the scarring. Checks every three months tracked return of disease and problems after care. The study also probed immune cells and checkpoints around the tumors, which seemed to form a suppressive shield. The findings may guide how these patients are watched.
pmc-12930467:
Silvia Camporesi and four colleagues published a critical essay in two thousand twenty-five on sex testing in women's sport. For decades, all women athletes faced forced sex tests, a practice that ended in the nineteen nineties after strong objections. The essay examines a two thousand twenty-five policy shift by World Athletics.

The new rules bring back blanket screening of elite women runners for a single gene. The authors note the rules call women's events female events, putting biology ahead of gender. They also merge rules for women with sex variations and transgender women into one set. The authors argue these choices repeat past harms flagged by medical, ethics, and human rights experts. They warn today's athletes face the same risks.
pmc-13135567:
Dániel Keliger and Illés Horváth explain a puzzle in epidemic modeling: the curve is easier to predict than the network behind it. Their 2026 paper studies a standard model where people cycle between susceptible and infected states on a weighted contact graph. Earlier work showed a learned stand-in network can forecast the curve well even when it looks nothing like the true network.

The pair give a rigorous account of that odd fact. For large networks, curve prediction is robust, while rebuilding the true network from the same data is ill-conditioned. They also give an explicit formula for the network in cases where rebuilding is possible. Their proof leans on a classic regularity result from graph theory. The lesson guides modelers to trust forecasts while doubting reverse-engineered contact maps.
pmc-13139767:
Edward Gilbert and co-authors track what sets telomere length in a Canary Islands lizard, and find drought years leave a mark. Their study appeared in 2026. Telomeres, the caps on chromosomes, signal aging and population health. The team measured them in the western Canaries lizard across varied habitats over ten years. Built-in traits dominated: males carried shorter telomeres than females, and larger females had shorter ones than smaller females.

Weather and habitat factors mattered less, but dry years lined up with shorter telomeres across the population. The authors read this as a cumulative burden from harsh conditions, laid on top of each animal's own baseline. The work warns that climate stress may quietly age wild populations even when individuals look healthy.
pmc-13144967:
Isabella Püschel and eight colleagues report the LUMOS study, a conference abstract on skin blood flow after acute ischemic stroke. Working at a German tertiary stroke center, the team asked whether weakened limbs show worse small-vessel circulation than the other side. They also asked whether that weakness predicts recovery.

Sixty-six patients had laser Doppler imaging of both forearms at admission and again on day three. Blood flow was lower in the weakened limbs, and it fell over time on both sides. Early impairment did not predict function at ninety days, however. The authors suggest the pattern points to body-wide autonomic disturbance, and that bedside imaging could help monitor it.
pmc-13147967:
Zaid Akram Thabit and co-authors read the full genome of a gut germ found on fresh vegetables in Baghdad, in work published in 2026. Raw greens are a healthy plate staple, yet outbreaks tied to fresh produce have grown, with Escherichia coli the top cause. The team tested fifty market vegetable samples for the germ.

Three samples, two cucumbers and one celery, carried it. The genomes ran near five million letters with a balanced letter mix. Two strain types turned up, kin to a known outbreak strain. The germs held many drug-proof tricks, from pumps to gene tweaks. The authors urge steady genome watch on produce germs.
pmc-13148467:
Marcela Xiomara Rivera Pineda, Jaakko Lehtimaki, and Guillaume Jacquemet present a customisable three-dimensional printed mould for orienting zebrafish larvae during live imaging. Their 2026 methods article improves on standard agarose mounting, which makes precise orientation difficult.

The mould is printed by fused deposition modelling and coated with resin for a smoother surface. It creates consistent larva-shaped wells that hold larvae in a belly-to-back orientation. Designed for standard glass-bottom dishes, the moulds are cheap to print on desktop machines. Open design files let users adapt them to different imaging setups. The approach enables reliable long-term imaging of multiple larvae, extending low-cost manufacturing in zebrafish workflows.
pmc-13148967:
Gani Oruqaj and co-authors published a 2026 study of a freezing-cut way to take tissue samples from chest lymph nodes, set against the standard suction-needle way. The needle way is the norm for such nodes. It can fall short on rare tumors, benign diseases, and blood disorders, and for detailed cell analyses. The freezing way takes a bigger, intact sample.

Ninety patients had both ways done in the same node, one after the other. Two tunnel paths were used, with two needle sizes. The freezing way found the diagnosis in over nine of ten cases, for both tunnel paths. The needle way found it in nearly seven of ten for one path, and over three in four for the other. Procedure times and sample sizes were nearly the same for both tunnels. The advantage of the freezing way was firm in statistical checks.
pmc-13151167:
El Ghoul and colleagues review care at a trauma stop point in Khan Younis, Gaza, in twenty twenty-six, using records from early twenty twenty-four. Such stop points, borrowed from army practice, give fast first care and sorting close to where people are hurt. Civil systems in war zones often lack that speed, so the model was brought in to fill the gap.

Nearly two thousand patients were logged over about ten weeks. Just over half came with non-injury problems, and most arrived stable. Care was mostly basic, such as stitching wounds and giving fever drugs. Four in five patients went home the same day, while one in five moved to a working hospital. The authors say the site eased pressure on hospitals and ambulances.
pmc-13152167:
Qian He and Xu Huang study a blood marker for immune shutdown in sepsis in a 2026 paper. Sepsis can leave the immune system too weak to fight later infections, a state tied to many deaths. A blood enzyme called cholinesterase drops in sepsis, but its tie to immune weakness was not well mapped.

The team combined patient data, gene data mining, and mouse experiments. Low enzyme levels went with worse severity scores and fewer key immune cells. Their gene work singled out RORA as a hub gene linking the enzyme, sepsis, and immunity, and mouse data matched the pattern. The authors propose the enzyme level as a handy marker for tracking immune state in sepsis care.
pmc-13155667:
Ida Sutrisni leads a large team on COVID vaccine uptake in three Asian lands. Their study from twenty twenty-six covers Indonesia, Nepal, and Vietnam. Vaccine doubt is a top world health threat, WHO says.

Talks with folks in town and rural zones were held. Themes were risk sense, trust, logistics, and social norms. Each theme was shaped by local context and changed with time. Rollout tales give clear lessons for new vaccine work. Trust should be built as early as one can. Local norms must be embraced, not fought.  The study ran as part of mixed methods work.
pmc-13158367:
Motlagomang Khantsi and Olubukola Babalola wrote a review from 2026 on how cowpea plants shape the bacteria that live around their roots. Cowpea is a key food crop in much of Africa south of the Sahara. Its roots host a rich mix of germs. Some fix nitrogen from the air, some free up phosphorus, and some break down dead matter, all of which feed the plant and build the soil.

The review gathers what is known about this root zone. Soil traits such as acidity, salt, and food levels steer which germs thrive. Studies do not yet agree on how acidity alone shapes the mix. New gene-based tools have shown both common and rare germs at work near the roots. The authors say gaps remain on how the mix shifts under stress, and they call for joined studies that read genes, proteins, and small chemicals at once.
pmc-13162967:
Zhang and co-authors silence a sex gene in swimming crabs to watch growth and gonads. The IAG gene guides sexual development in decapod crustaceans. The team mapped the gene in Portunus trituberculatus first. Its build matched the standard B-C-A pattern of its family. Gene activity showed as early as the zygote stage.

Long silencing did not flip sex in either males or females. Body weight fell and gonad growth lagged in both sexes. A binding protein gene dropped sharply after silencing. The insulin receptor gene fell in males but was absent in the ovary. The authors call IAG a broad growth and maturation coordinator.
pmc-13164167:
Kazuyuki Yusa and co-authors ask, in a 2026 pilot study, whether scans taken before jaw surgery can predict how long the operation will take. The surgery splits and resets the lower jaw on both sides. The team reviewed forty-six patients treated over seven years at one hospital.

Body weight and bone density in the jaw's upright part, read from scans, both rose with operating time. Men also had longer operations on average. Once other factors were accounted for, bone density kept its link with time. Denser bone likely resists the cut more, which slows the work. Scan readings could help teams plan theater time and staffing.
pmc-13165267:
Muhammad Rao and a large team compare wild and farmed strawberries in a 2026 study of health related compounds. Phenolic compounds give fruit much of its protective value, yet breeding for yield and looks has often thinned their variety. The team paired chemical profiling with gene activity data for one wild type and three farmed varieties.

The wild fruit had stronger antioxidant activity and a far richer mix of these compounds, including forms largely missing in farmed fruit. Each farmed variety kept a narrower, specialized profile. Gene checks found a family of control genes more active in the wild type, tied to key compounds. The authors say wild stock is a valuable source for breeding healthier fruit.
pmc-13175267:
Jie Li and nine co-authors trace how an unusually small vertebral artery raises stroke risk over twenty years, in a two thousand twenty-six neurology cohort study. The artery variation was suspected to act partly by bending the basilar artery it feeds.

The retrospective study followed fourteen hundred sixty-four people from two thousand four to two thousand twenty-four, five hundred forty-seven with the hypoplastic artery. Ninety-one developed posterior circulation infarctions. Both the artery variation and worsening basilar bending independently raised the odds of infarction. Mediation analysis attributed about half of the variation's effect to the bending progression. The result identifies a measurable intermediate step on the path to posterior stroke.
pmc-13176167:
Pengfei Chen, Denian Miao, and seven co-authors test a new vaccine for a pig virus. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, targets the 2d strain of porcine circovirus type 2. This virus causes one of the costliest diseases in pig farming worldwide. The 2d strain is now the most common, which raises doubts about older vaccines.

Their shot uses hollow shells built from the virus coat protein. Pigs that got the shot and then the live virus fared far better. They ran lower fevers and kept gaining weight. Virus levels in blood and organs dropped sharply. Strong antibody levels show the shot fired up the immune system well.
pmc-13177867:
Emre Demirsoy and co-authors test AI-found germ-killing peptides as a stand-in for antibiotics in broiler chickens, in a study from 2026. Heavy antibiotic use in farming breeds resistant bacteria, which drives the hunt for new options. Peptides are short protein chains that can kill germs and calm immune overreaction. A machine learning screen had picked candidates from hundreds of options.

Three lead peptides went into egg and pen trials. Infected chicks given one peptide showed fewer germ-positive organs and gained far more weight. In farm-scale pens, two peptides raised survival rates by day thirty-five. Growth and feed use stayed normal across the trials. One peptide also tamed a fierce immune signal in lab cells. The authors call the pair promising for poultry use.
pmc-13181367:
Sui-Lung Su and seven co-authors report a 2026 study of air pollution and early memory loss in older adults in Taiwan. Mild memory and thinking problems often come before dementia, and they are hard to reverse once set. Dirty air has been named as a risk, but large national studies were lacking.

The team used data from the Taiwan Biobank for people over sixty, gathered between 2008 and 2021. Thinking was checked with a standard short test, and cut scores for problems varied by schooling level. Home sites were mapped so that each person could be matched with local air measures. The study then looked for links between the air measures and test scores.
pmc-13191367:
Yanting Zhang and colleagues review the measurement traits of the revised Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire, a tool to assess sleep in intensive care patients. Sleep in such care is known to be poor and counts for health, so the quality of the tool matters. The review used standard guidelines, and graded studies with the COSMIN risk-of-bias checklist and mate quality rules.

Fourteen studies were taken in, covering eight language versions of the revised questionnaire, most from Asian countries. Samples went past intensive care to older inpatients, orthopedic patients around surgery, and acute stroke patients. Scores held up well inside most versions, but content validity, structural validity, and validity across cultures were thin, as was measurement error. The quality of methods showed some risk of bias. Proof across versions did not line up well.
pmc-13191767:
Wittaya Chaiwangyen and a team of co-authors test a plant extract for shielding placenta cells from stress, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The plant, Elsholtzia kachinensis, is rich in rosmarinic acid. One extract fraction showed the strongest antioxidant power and the richest store of plant chemicals. The team treated human trophoblast cells, which form the placenta's outer layer, with a bacterial toxin plus the extract.

The extract saved cell growth, movement, and invasion that the toxin had harmed. It cut cell suicide, oxygen waste, and swelling signals. It worked by lowering a small RNA that the toxin raises and restoring its target gene. The authors see a lead for guarding pregnancy health.
pmc-13194467:
Wen He and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma that masqueraded as squamous lung cancer. Some of these tumours switch off their usual marker proteins. Their squared shape then misleads pathologists toward a different diagnosis and treatment.

Biopsies from lung and liver showed poorly differentiated tumour with all classic neuroendocrine markers negative. Rapid liver spread, a soaring marker enzyme, and fierce growth rate contradicted the first diagnosis. A ninety-gene expression test reclassified the tumour. The case warns that marker-negative results demand molecular backup when behaviour disagrees.
pmc-13195267:
Ning Tian and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six comparing stool chemistry in children with and without migraine. Most gut research on migraine covers adults, leaving children's metabolic patterns largely unmapped. The team used targeted chemical profiling to look for a signature tied to the childhood form of the disease.

They enrolled thirty children with migraine and thirty healthy peers, aged five to fourteen, in Hebei Province, China. Eight amino acid compounds ran higher in the migraine group, including valine, leucine, and phenylalanine. Those changes clustered in pathways that build and break down key amino acids. Short-chain fatty acids differed too, though most single comparisons fell short of clear significance. The authors call the work exploratory.
pmc-13197767:
Yu'e Sun and co-authors take stock of the live monitoring that guards the nervous system during brain and spine surgery. Electrodes watch motor and sensory signals while the surgeon works, warning when a cut threatens movement or feeling. The review weighs what is settled practice, what is still argued, and where the field is heading.

Good results rest on two pillars, they say: combined signal monitoring and an anesthesia style built on intravenous drugs with careful muscle relaxation. The method cuts nerve damage in spine deformity, tumor, and hearing-nerve surgeries. Yet alarms are often false, and turning a signal dip into the right action stays hard. The authors look ahead to artificial intelligence dashboards that predict trouble instead of merely reporting it, while urging common standards and team-wide training.
pmc-13197867:
Pishoy Gouda and co-authors run a randomized trial on how to recruit people into research by message, in a paper from 2026. Recruitment shapes who joins a study and how far its results apply. Digital invites are now common, but proof on the best channel and wording was thin.

The trial sat inside a larger heart disease prevention study at one large academic health system. Invites were sent either by email or through a patient portal. The message text appealed either to helping others or to personal gain. The main measure was interest, shown by logging on to the study site. The design lets each factor be judged on its own and in combination. The authors frame the work as evidence for a routine but understudied step in research.
pmc-13198067: Federica Vernacchia and four co-authors present a 2026 case report on a heart tracing that seemed to show a block but did not. A sixty-five-year-old man came to hospital with fever, belly pain, and tiredness and was treated for abdominal sepsis. He had no heart symptoms and stayed stable. His electrocardiogram, though, showed odd conduction patterns. Review found the machine's signal had briefly saturated, faking a pattern that mimicked advanced atrioventricular block. The authors stress checking a tracing's internal agreement before diagnosing a heart wiring fault.
pmc-13198467:
Kirsi Manz and colleagues tested a new iron marker in blood cancers in a 2026 study. Myeloproliferative neoplasms are cancers where the marrow makes too many blood cells. Inflammation and anemia blur standard iron tests there, so the team checked zinc protoporphyrin, a marker that rises when red cells lack iron.

They studied 445 patients and compared them with a large general cohort. Standard iron patterns flipped in cancer patients: higher stored iron went with lower blood counts, the reverse of healthy people. About twenty-eight percent had high marker values showing true iron shortage. Values varied by cancer subtype and tied to blood counts more than to stored iron. The marker may sharpen iron checks in these cancers.
pmc-13199067:
Kenjiro Kaneko and colleagues review balloons and stents for leg artery disease in a 2026 article, translated from a 2024 Japanese journal paper. Endovascular therapy treats narrowed leg arteries from inside the vessel. Better balloons and stents have widened who can be treated and improved results.

The review covers basic device topics for daily practice. Balloon catheters vary by wire size, length, and how they ride the guidewire. Choice depends on vessel width, lesion length, and access route. Stents prop vessels open after balloon widening. With device variety growing, selection has grown more complex. The authors lay out core traits to guide sound picks for each lesion.
pmc-13200567:
Ulcerative colitis can be controlled with modern drugs for many patients, but some still lose their colon to surgery. Sandro Ferreira and co-authors reviewed two hundred thirty-two patients at a Brazilian referral center to learn who ends up needing a colectomy. About one in five had the operation. The leading reasons were disease that no longer answered to medicine, and sudden severe flares.

Longer disease duration raised the odds of surgery. So did inflammation spanning the whole colon, compared with disease limited to the rectum, and severe findings on endoscopy at diagnosis. Patients who started on biological drugs early also went to surgery more often, most likely because their disease was the most aggressive from the start. Sex, race, smoking, and steroid use showed no link. The authors conclude that wide and severe disease at diagnosis marks the patients most likely to need surgery later.
pmc-13200667:
Jae Hyun Park examines how white hair makes scalps look thinner in a 2026 clinical article. White hair lacks pigment, so it contrasts weakly with the scalp and can look translucent under magnification. The scalp then seems exposed even when hair density and thickness are unchanged, a visual illusion with real clinic effects.

The article lays out the optics of scalp show-through and its non-linear rise as white share grows. Misreading it can lead to overtreatment for hair loss that is not progressing. Transplant work also suffers: pale hairs complicate strip dissection and graft harvest and placement. Five dyeing principles for white-haired patients close the piece. The claims rest on clinical experience, not yet on measured trials.
pmc-13202167:
Premature babies often need repeated blood transfusions, and a 2026 retrospective study authored by Malavika Krishnakumar builds a tool to predict that need from two simple measures. The research article analyzes transfusion patterns in a South Indian neonatal intensive care unit and models requirements from gestational age and birth weight.

The study covered preterm babies born at twenty-three to thirty-two weeks who received at least one transfusion during 2023. In total, 422 transfusions went to 118 babies, with smaller and earlier babies needing the most blood and the most donors. A Bayesian model using the two birth measures reduced projected multi-donor exposure, offering better planning for blood banks.
pmc-13203067:
Matthew D Galsky and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six trial design paper for bladder and urinary tract cancer that has advanced after standard therapy. A leading first-line drug pair now sets the standard. What to give after it stops working lacks randomized guidance.

The global trial tests an antibody-drug conjugate plus platinum chemotherapy against a standard pairing. A first phase picks between two doses in a small group. A larger phase then compares the chosen dose head-to-head in hundreds of patients. The design aims to settle post-progression treatment with solid evidence.
pmc-13204567:
Laura Del Gaudio, Stefano Lattanzio, Roberta Di Pietro, and Silvia Sancilio review how engineered materials coax the body to regrow tissue. Their review appeared in 2026. A good scaffold must invite cells to settle, grow, and specialize, and its chemistry, stiffness, and surface all matter. The authors survey natural and synthetic options, how the body answers them, and the tricks used to tune their surfaces.

Special weight goes to cold atmospheric plasma, which rewrites just the topmost layer of a material, making it wetter, stickier for proteins, and better at holding drugs. Stem cell behavior on these materials and AI tools that predict performance close the survey. The authors see design and surface treatment converging.
pmc-13208367:
Jin, Feng, Tong, Li, Huang, and Peng test in twenty twenty-six how welding heat changes joints between two different magnesium alloys. Welding helps these light alloys reach wider engineering use. But fast heating and cooling can coarsen grains near the weld, making that zone the weak point where joints fail.

The team welded thin sheets at several heat levels and checked strength and structure. One mid-level heat gave the best overall result, with the finest, most even spread of hard particles near the weld. All breaks still occurred on the same side's heat-affected zone. The findings give welders a target heat for strong, sound joints in such mixed alloys.
pmc-13210267:
Star ratings hide how hard a product is to live with, and a 2026 study headed by Shoukat Ullah builds a model that reads reviews for complexity instead. The research article pairs a transformer language model with a recurrent network to judge Amazon reviews along two appraisal dimensions: user-friendliness and judged effectiveness.

Human annotators first labeled reviews by perceived complexity, and an explanation method cross-checked those labels for consistency. The hybrid model then learned both context and word order, reaching higher cross-validated accuracy than the forest, transformer-only, and large language model baselines cited. Built-in explanations show which words drive each judgment, making the scores auditable for shoppers and sellers.
pmc-13211767:
Doris Chirinos-Peinado and colleagues assess lead and cadmium risk in raw milk from Peruvian Andes farms. Their risk study from twenty twenty-six covers small-scale dairy systems. Milk nourishes children, but mining pollution can taint it. Metal transfer into the food chain needs local measurement.

Forty-five milk samples were tested with emission spectrometry. Average metal levels stayed below legal limits overall. Hotspots near smelters showed much higher lead levels, though. Risk was modelled for ages from toddlers to the elderly. Three consumption levels covered light to heavy milk drinkers. The findings separate general safety from localised danger. Targeted monitoring near industry protects families best.
pmc-13211867:
Remote monitoring only works if patients can and will use it, and a 2026 qualitative study headed by Syed Mustafa Ali listens to a group often missed by such research. Seventeen Pakistani adults in the United Kingdom with rheumatoid or early inflammatory arthritis, none with English as a first language, joined interviews or a focus group about monitoring technology.

None had used remote monitoring before, yet many saw value in it, especially where current services dissatisfied them. Needs split by generation: first-generation immigrants leaned more on family and community help with technology than later generations did. Language support and relatives' involvement emerged as design requirements, not afterthoughts, for equitable rollout.
pmc-13212367:
John J. Tyson published a 2026 correction to his paper revisiting Alan Turing's chemical theory of pattern formation in development. The notice repairs formatting faults that crept in during production and distorted several mathematical statements in the published version.

Readers are shown the faulty lines beside their repaired forms for three places in the paper, covering a steady-state condition, a matrix equation, and a set of inequalities. The equations render poorly in print, with markup and stray characters mixed into the maths. Even so, the notice lets anyone checking the model use the intended symbols rather than the corrupted print.
pmc-13212767:
Anisha and colleagues explore in 2026 whether future electron-positron colliders could detect signs of a violent early-universe transition involving two Higgs fields. Such a transition might explain why matter outnumbers antimatter today, a puzzle the standard model cannot solve.

The team checked model settings that allow a strong first-order transition against expected precision from planned machines in Europe and China. Even when current collider data look standard, the rate of Higgs production alongside a Z boson should shift by more than the planned machines' tiny measurement error. Precision Higgs measurements could therefore expose hidden physics indirectly, long before any new particle appears directly.
pmc-13212867:
Enhui He and colleagues review in 2026 how nanotechnology is reshaping neuroprostheses, devices that restore lost senses or movement by linking electronics to the nervous system. The weak point remains the junction where hard electronics meet soft living tissue.

The review covers six device classes, from motor and visual systems to memory and smell, and proposes an architecture built around two key interfaces. New materials promise gentler, sharper electrodes and better sensors, while brain-inspired computing could process signals on the device itself. The authors look toward two-way, adaptive systems that adjust in a closed loop, aiming for a far more natural fit between machine and nerve.
pmc-13213167:
Hiroko Otake and co-authors test in 2026 whether adding a moisture-holding polymer to glaucoma eye drops helps the drug work longer. Timolol lowers eye pressure, but tears wash drops away quickly, so keeping the drug on the eye surface could improve its effect.

In rats and rabbits, the polymer additive formed tiny particles in a clear, stable drop and caused no damage with repeated use. More timolol stayed on the eye, crossed the cornea, and reached the inner fluid than with ordinary drops. In rabbits with raised pressure, the combined drop lowered pressure more strongly and for longer. The additive looks like a safe route to longer-acting glaucoma treatment.
pmc-13215167:
Suqin Q. Duan and co-authors examine in 2026 the statistics of extreme rain across the world's weather systems, asking whether the worst downpours follow one pattern. Models struggle with these events, which drive floods and infrastructure damage.

Using high-resolution hourly observations split by system type, they found the intense tails of rain distributions share a typical shape set mainly by storm dynamics. Heat and moisture conditions scale how big the tail gets. Because dominant storm types share similar environments, overall extremes largely inherit their shape. Exceptions appear where intense tropical lows or overlapping storm clusters stack the odds. Risk assessors, the authors say, can often skip fine weather typing.
pmc-13215467:
Tsebaot Tesfaye and co-authors report a balloon procedure that relieved a narrowed pulmonary valve in a woman whose rheumatic disease had touched all four heart valves, in this 2026 case report. She had already received two replacement valves and one repair, so another open operation carried high risk. Scans showed the pulmonary valve squeezed tight, with pressure across it near 97 millimeters of mercury.

Guided by X-ray imaging, the team inflated a balloon inside the valve and stretched it open. The pressure gap fell to about 35 at once, and her breathlessness eased. Three months on she stayed symptom-free with the gain holding. The authors present the balloon route as a safer stand-in for repeat surgery in well-chosen patients.
pmc-13215667:
Roy van den Heuvel and co-authors present a 2026 mixed methods study of an app that helps people with diabetes check their own feet for ulcer risk. Foot ulcers are a serious diabetes complication, and podiatry services face rising demand.

Twenty-four patients with type 2 diabetes used the Feetchecker app for three months, logging 393 checks and sending nine photos that all prompted podiatrist follow-up calls. Patients rated the app positively and valued how easily a photo could reach a professional. Engagement fell into steady, frequent, and minimal patterns, shaped by ease of use, social support, and digital skills. Podiatrists liked the faster reporting but found promoting the app in consultations difficult.
pmc-13216167:
Toru Nakai and co-authors present a 2026 case report, with a literature review, on treating a ruptured aneurysm of a tiny perforating branch of the basilar artery. These aneurysms cause bleeding around the brainstem and are notoriously hard to even see on first scans.

Their patient, a 75-year-old woman, showed no clear aneurysm on day one; repeat angiography on day four revealed a small saccular bulge that later grew. On day sixteen the team threaded in two overlapping LVIS Blue stents to divert flow while keeping the perforator open. She recovered without symptoms, and imaging at one month showed the aneurysm completely closed. The authors argue the overlapping stent approach suits aneurysms arising from the basilar trunk.
pmc-13218167:
Kavindhaya Karunarathna and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a qualitative systematic review of family caregiving in cancer palliative care across countries. In low-income and lower-middle-income countries, formal palliative services are scarce, so relatives deliver most care for adults with advanced cancer. Their experience is the foundation the system rests on, yet it is rarely gathered together.

The review will search PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO with no language or date limits, plus an open repository for grey literature. Studies of family caregivers of adults receiving end-of-life cancer care in these countries will be appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Findings will be combined through meta-aggregation, or narratively if pooling proves unworkable, and reported under the ENTREQ framework. No ethics approval is needed for published data. The team will publish openly and carry the recommendations to policymakers and organizations that run palliative services.
pmc-13219667:
C. C. Loeff and colleagues track how the Netherlands adopted MRI scanning before prostate biopsy in a 2026 study. Guidelines recommend the scan first, because it can spare men biopsies and target sampling better, but uptake had never been measured nationwide. The Netherlands Cancer Registry supplied the data.

The cohort held 50,987 men diagnosed with biopsy-proven prostate cancer between 2019 and 2023, with a historical cohort from 2015 and 2016. Use of pre-biopsy MRI climbed from seventeen percent at the start of the period to seventy-four percent by 2023. Men over seventy, men with high PSA values, and men with signs of advanced disease were less likely to be scanned first, which matches guideline logic. Hospitals differed early on, with rates spanning ten to eighty-six percent, but by the post-implementation years the spread had narrowed to the sixties through eighties. The authors read this as implementation maturing into consistent, targeted practice.
pmc-13219867:
Pallavi V. Menon and colleagues describe a forty-five-minute session that asks students to name their purpose, in a 2026 report. Medical training front-loads skill and leaves professional identity, the process of becoming a doctor in one's own values, to chance. The Finding Your North Star session was built to give that identity an anchor.

One hundred thirty first-year students discussed values in groups led by senior students and deans, reflected with guidance, and wrote purpose statements printed on cards decorated with artwork. Of the 101 students who answered the survey, eighty-five percent said the session deepened their grasp of purpose in medicine. Over ninety percent valued hearing senior students' reflections and sharing their values with peers. Students asked for more discussion time and more voices, such as alumni and physicians. The authors present the exercise as insurance against the disorientation and burnout that stalk training.
pmc-13221167:
Lara de Souza Cruz Lizardo and co-authors study tooth loss among Brazilian adolescents in a 2026 multilevel analysis of a national oral health survey. Their dataset covered 8,053 teenagers aged fifteen and nineteen from the SB Brasil 2023 survey. Factors were examined at individual, municipal, and state levels together.

About one in seven adolescents had lost a tooth. Risk rose with age, toothache, use of public dental services, and receiving social program benefits. Wider primary care oral health coverage and richer, more developed areas showed lower rates. The authors argue that prevention and fairer access matter more than the mostly curative care many teenagers currently receive, especially for vulnerable groups.
pmc-13221767:
Mohamed Abdelgalil presents a 2026 case of heart valve infection caused by Achromobacter xylosoxidans, paired with a literature review. The patient was a 69-year-old woman with heart surgery history, kidney failure on dialysis, chronic breathing failure, and a persistent vegetative state after cardiac arrest. She was staying in a long-term acute care unit.

Blood cultures kept growing the bacterium despite targeted antibiotics and catheter exchange. Heart imaging first showed a small growth on the mitral valve, then new aortic valve involvement a month later. Surgery was judged too risky given her frailty. She later developed resistant pneumonia, septic shock, and a fatal arrest, illustrating how stubborn this rare infection can be.
pmc-13222167:
Jonas Korb and co-authors raise production of aurachin D, a promising antibiotic compound, in engineered Escherichia coli, in a 2026 biotechnology study. The compound comes from myxobacteria and also acts against protozoa. A membrane enzyme performs the final building step, and an earlier engineered strain made only small amounts.

Switching to a glycerol-based minimal medium and tuning the starting material lifted output roughly sevenfold in a microbioreactor. Glycerol did not mainly help growth or dissolve the substrate better. Instead it increased the supply of correctly folded enzyme, until osmotic stress began hurting the host. Medium design, not new genes, delivered the gain.
pmc-13222767:
Yubo Zhang and co-authors shorten a uterine fibroid symptom and quality-of-life questionnaire, in a 2026 validation study across twenty Chinese centers. The cohort held 1,939 premenopausal women with symptomatic fibroids facing surgery or focused ultrasound treatment, split into development and validation halves. Classical and modern test theory together chose which items survived.

The result, an eleven-item form, cut administration burden by seventy percent from the original thirty-seven items. One whole subscale was dropped, and sexual functioning kept a single item. Scores correlated strongly with the full form in every domain, with comparable sensitivity to health changes. Reliability was excellent. The short form promises faster assessment in clinics and trials, pending checks in new populations.
pmc-13223167:
Dorey Glenn and thirteen co-authors study how well COVID-19 vaccination works in people whose immune systems are medically suppressed, in a two thousand twenty-six immunology paper. Patients with immune-mediated diseases take drugs that can blunt vaccine responses, and their protection was poorly characterized.

The study measures both arms of vaccine immunity in this population: antibodies, the humoral response, and T-cell based cellular responses against SARS-CoV-2. Healthy people mount responses that protect against severe disease, but whether patients on immunosuppressants reach similar levels, and which drug regimens interfere most, needed direct evidence. The authors set out to supply that evidence for clinicians advising some of the most vulnerable vaccine recipients.
pmc-13223967:
Eleonora Pero and colleagues report a 2026 study of red blood cells in cystic fibrosis, a genetic illness caused by faults in the CFTR chloride channel. Although CFTR is usually studied in airway and gut tissue, it also appears in red blood cells at lower levels in patients. Whether that reduction changes how the cells bend and squeeze through small vessels was unknown.

pmc-13232567:

pmc-13238267:

pmc-13239367:

pmc-13239867:

pmc-13252767:

pmc-13253867:

pmc-13255067:

pmc-13255167:

pmc-13255667:

pmc-13255767:

pmc-13256067:

pmc-13256767:

pmc-13256867:

pmc-13257067:

pmc-13258167:

pmc-13258567:

Engineers weighing food waste treatment options get a combined risk and cost view of the concept.
pmc-13258767:

pmc-13258867:

pmc-13259167:

pmc-13259767:

pmc-13260067:

pmc-13260567:

pmc-13262167:

pmc-13262367:

pmc-13262567:

pmc-13262667:

pmc-13263367:

pmc-13263567:

pmc-13263867:

pmc-13266067:

pmc-13266367:

pmc-13266567:

pmc-13266767:

pmc-13266967:

pmc-13268167:

pmc-13268767:

pmc-13269167:

pmc-13269467:

pmc-13269567:

pmc-13269767:
Giulia Notini and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Trop2, a surface protein targeted by a class of cancer drugs that carry a poison payload into tumor cells. They combined gene activity data from over 20,000 samples across cancers and healthy tissues. The aim was to learn what controls the target's presence.

The protein's gene was confined to surface-lining tissues, enriched in many tumors, and present in some healthy ones. Gene faults were rare, while a chemical silencing mark tracked strongly and inversely with activity, pointing to that mark as the main control. Activity linked to barrier programs and varied immune contacts. The authors warn that target amount alone cannot predict drug benefit or harm.
pmc-13269967:
Nor Islafatun and Moh Heri Kurniawan published a perspective article in 2026 giving a family caregiver's first-person account of caring for an 85-year-old mother after a left upper limb fracture. The arm was set in a cast, and long recovery at home fell to the family. The piece examines what happened after hospital discharge.

Families were left to interpret symptoms, watch for decline, and handle new complications without structured guidance. The authors recommend a stronger clinical role for primary care after discharge. pmc-13270067:
Shailendra Upadhyay and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on treating a fast heart rhythm disorder in patients aged 21 and under without any X-ray guidance. The disorder, AVNRT, is a common rapid rhythm in children, treated by modifying a slow electrical path in the heart. A 3D mapping system replaced X-ray imaging.

The cohort held 125 patients with a median age of 14.9 years, treated from 2016 to 2025. Fluoroscopy time was zero minutes in every case. Acute success was complete, with no procedural complications, and procedures took a median of 121 minutes. Among 117 patients followed for a median of 36 months, the rhythm never returned. The authors support the X-ray-free approach at experienced centers.
pmc-13270467:
Till Joscha Demal and a large team ask in 2026 whether routine pre-surgery blood tests can sharpen risk prediction for aortic valve operations. Their registry followed 492 patients who had surgical valve replacement or repair between 2018 and 2022. Nine blood markers were measured before surgery and tested against a standard European risk score for predicting death within thirty days.

Models that merged the blood panel with the standard score beat either one alone by standard fit measures. The authors suggest heart teams use the combined estimate when weighing surgery against catheter-based valve replacement for each patient.
pmc-13270667:

The team built a two-step method: each centre first gathered and summarised its own data locally, then a central team pooled the summaries. In the end the pipeline covered ten centres, nearly 800,000 hospital encounters, and about 500,000 patients.
pmc-13270767:
Gamal M. Abdalla led a 2026 prospective randomized trial on cutting early bleeding after sleeve gastrectomy, a weight-loss operation that removes part of the stomach. The trial tested rinsing the staple line with warm salt water before a standard stitching step, against the usual room-temperature rinse.

Between December 2024 and June 2025, 200 adults were split evenly between warm rinse, at body-like warmth, and the cooler rinse. The combined bleeding outcome occurred in 5 percent of the warm group versus 15 percent of controls. pmc-13270867:
Mom Ean is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on discussion and interviews, on engaging young people in health and research in rural Cambodia. Since 2021, school students in Siem Pang have worked with a tropical medicine research unit through a youth advisory group called YAGHRE.

Thirty-five people took part, including 14 youth group members, teachers, health staff, other students, and family members. Members were seen as a bridge between researchers and the community. Taking part seemed to build their confidence, speaking skills, computer skills, and leadership, and the knowledge spread to families and peers. The authors present the group as a model for community-based research partnerships.
pmc-13272167:
Minghao Li and coauthors review in 2026 animal models of chronic rhinosinusitis across several species and how to choose among them. This long-lasting sinus inflammation burdens quality of life, and treatment progress lags behind the disease's immune complexity. Mice dominate the lab, yet their sinuses differ greatly from human ones.

Sheep drain their sinuses in ways closer to humans, while pigs mirror stubborn tissue remodeling in severe disease. The review judges each model against human disease types, from allergy-driven type 2 inflammation to other forms. A decision framework steers researchers toward the model that fits their question rather than the most convenient one.
pmc-13272267:
Rithvik Gundlapalli is lead author of a 2026 systematic review on radiomics for vestibular schwannoma. That is a tumour on the balance nerve. It is hard to reach, grows unpredictably, and threatens key nerve functions. Radiomics extracts large numbers of quantitative features from scans, beyond what the eye can see, and might predict outcomes and treatment response.

pmc-13272367:
Atefe Yadollahi Khales and coauthors test in 2026 a two-signal blood signature of long non-coding RNAs for Alzheimer's disease. Each RNA alone separated the groups with good accuracy, and their expression levels correlated with standard mental test scores. Network analysis suggested how the pair might regulate disease genes through shared microRNA partners.
pmc-13272467:
Iryna Vasyliv and coauthors test in 2026 whether a computer-aided tool speeds the staging of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma without losing accuracy, and how reader experience changes that benefit. Staging whole-body PET scans by eye is slow and varies between readers. Fifty-six children's scans were split into two matched groups for the comparison.

One group was staged traditionally and the other with a new web-based tool, by readers ranging from a resident to senior specialists. A joint expert reading set the reference standard, and agreement statistics measured accuracy in both arms. Timing results are reported by experience level, showing where the tool saves the most effort.
pmc-13272567:
Andreas Gold and Kayvan Bozorgmehr wrote a 2026 comment on how Germany now shares out European asylum and integration funds. The fund is a main European tool for reception and integration, worth 10.94 billion euros for 2021 to 2027. Germany runs its share through its federal office for migration and refugees.

They argue the revised German plan favors return advice and buildings, while people with pending claims get mainly short orientation courses. They also fault awarding funds first come, first served, noting that one call was oversubscribed by 30 percent in 27 hours. A minimum open period, a lottery among fit bids, or quality-based awards would be fairer, they say.
pmc-13273067: Correction notice from Samar El Achy and co-authors. It concerns a study of gold particles loaded with a small RNA against liver cancer cells. Figure 7 had an error when first published. The microscope images in panel A were a copy of those in panel C. The original figure and its legend are shown in the notice. The paper has now been corrected.
pmc-13273367:
Yi-Hsuan Li and a large team tested a plant extract against a honey bee parasite in a 2026 study. Nosema ceranae is a spore forming parasite that lives inside bees and causes the disease nosemosis. The extract came from Bidens pilosa, a plant used in traditional remedies.

Gene reads from the parasite inside bee guts showed wide gene shutdown early in infection, including a key energy pathway. Knocking down that pathway in a separate test also lowered parasite load somewhat. The authors say the extract reshapes parasite activity in a stage dependent way.
pmc-13273467:
Ruoyan Cao leads a 2026 multi-omics study of the genetic mechanisms behind periodontitis, a chronic gum disease driven by immune dysregulation. The team joined genome-wide data from two large cohorts with single-cell and spatial gene maps of tissues. Genetic signals for gum disease were enriched not only in jawbone and teeth, but also in brain and kidney cortex, which may explain links to body-wide illness. Monocytes and natural killer cells emerged as key immune subsets, and 23 genes linked causally to the disease. One gene, GNLY, was prioritized, and five candidate compounds bound it well in simulations.
pmc-13273567:
Charlotte Cresens and co-authors gave a protocol in 2026 for making polyacrylamide hydrogels of tuned stiffness for cell culture. Cells respond to how stiff their surroundings feel, so labs need gels that mimic tissues from soft brain to firm muscle. This gel system is cheap, and its stiffness is set by recipe.

The protocol makes large round gels that sit unattached, in custom shapes and sizes, and explains how to measure their stiffness by rheology. Mixing more or less of the two building chemicals sweeps stiffness across the range found in healthy and diseased tissue. The authors also cover using the gels for cell culture, collecting what cells secrete, and imaging proteins by fluorescence. Full detail points back to their earlier methods paper.
pmc-13273667:
Zheng-Kai Teng and five co-authors present a 2026 study of an adaptor protein that keeps a key immune signal alive in killer cells. The signal, interleukin-2, tells natural killer cells to survive and fight. When the signal is scarce, those cells die off unless something sustains the message.

Without kindlin-3, the receptor slips away and the survival signal fades. The study details the direct binding behind the link and its effect on cell survival.
pmc-13273967:
Karen Kolmodin MacDonell and co-authors price a tailored training program that brings youth HIV clinic staff to solid motivational interviewing skill. Their 2026 study starts from a delivery gap: brief workshops expose providers to the counseling method but rarely build real competence. Their program layers targeted support strategies onto the training, tuned for adolescent HIV care.

Working backward from training and personnel records, the team costed the path from beginner to intermediate or expert level. The base estimate lands near sixty-three hundred dollars per staff member. Sensitivity checks tested how the figure moves with assumptions. The authors find the cost in line with other serious training models, which supports the program's case for wider adoption in youth clinics.
pmc-13274567:
Gyujoon Hwang and a large team present a 2026 study protocol for brain imaging research on grief in older adults. Most bereaved people move from sharp early grief to an integrated, livable grief, but some develop prolonged grief disorder. Why paths diverge is unclear, and faulty emotion control is a leading suspect.

The single-site study plans to follow 170 adults aged fifty to eighty-nine for one year, 115 recently bereaved and 55 matched non-bereaved volunteers. Brain scans at start and twelve months include rest imaging, a face-matching task for emotion, and a stop-signal task for self-control. So far 103 bereaved and forty comparison participants are enrolled and matched, with good-quality scan data collected.
pmc-13274867:
Debiao Luo and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on spotting abnormal network traffic, an early sign of cyberattack. Their pipeline first cleans the traffic signal by splitting it into simpler waves, a step called empirical mode decomposition. A hybrid neural network then reads the cleaned signal, pairing an attention-based transformer with a memory network that reads sequences both ways.

Tuning such a network by hand is fiddly, so a firefly algorithm, a search method mimicking flashing insects, tuned its settings automatically. On benchmark data sets, the authors report their combined model beat rival and baseline systems on every metric they tested. The gains in prediction error and in the F1 score for catching anomalies were statistically significant.
pmc-13274967:
Tianqing Fan and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study asking whether internet addiction predicts new self-injury in Chinese middle school students. Cross-sectional links were known, but direction over time was not. The team recruited 1,315 students with no history of nonsuicidal self-injury, and 704 completed the six-month follow-up.

Among those followed, 9.8 percent began self-injuring within six months. Risk rose in a straight line with the severity of internet addiction at baseline. After full adjustment, addicted students had about double the odds of starting self-injury. The link was significant in girls, with roughly triple the odds, and in a middle 'internet-dependent' state, but not in boys. The authors urge sex-aware prevention.
pmc-13275767:
Alessandro Antonelli and co-authors report a 2026 clinical trial on removing stuck lower wisdom teeth. Such surgery often leaves patients with swelling, pain, and trouble opening the mouth. The trial tested piezosurgery, which cuts bone with fine sound vibrations, against the usual spinning drill tools.

Forty-seven healthy adults had one side treated each way, giving ninety-four extractions in total. Three-dimensional face scans measured swelling two and seven days after surgery. The vibration method left less swelling and less jaw stiffness at day two. Pain was lower at every check, and the drill side bled more and needed more painkillers. The new method took longer in surgery, but patients reported less disruption to daily life and higher satisfaction.
pmc-13275967:
Grigorios Avdikos and Stephen Smith wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about heart attacks caused by a fully blocked artery. Some of these attacks never show the classic pattern on an electrocardiogram, the heart tracing called an ECG. The letter comments on a report of three such cases that got delayed artery-opening treatment.

The authors argue the first patient's tracing actually pointed to a different artery than the report claimed. They explain how a common tracing quirk can hide or mimic warning signs in the second case, which they say was very high risk. They close by noting that the usual split between two heart attack types misses many blockages. A newer approach, focused on blocked arteries themselves, could speed up life-saving treatment, they argue.
pmc-13276467:

Most people with Parkinson disease struggle with balance and walking, raising fall risk and lowering quality of life. The programme, called MY-PACE, blends mindfulness, yoga, and mindful walking.

The randomised trial enrolled 132 people with Parkinson disease and balance problems, split evenly between groups. One group follows a twelve-week programme delivered by video call at home. The other receives usual outpatient care first and gets the programme after the study ends. Balance is the main outcome, with walking, mood, thinking, and falls also tracked over six months.
pmc-13276567:
Ramamurthy Shanmugapriya and co-authors report a 2026 randomized study on a moringa leaf gel as an add-on to standard gum disease care. Deep cleaning below the gumline is the main non-surgical treatment for advanced periodontitis. Plant-based adjuncts could help, since moringa is rich in protective compounds.

The authors rate the gel comparable to antibiotic fibers and want larger, longer trials.
pmc-13276767:
Lilla Markel and colleagues evaluate routine follow-up phone calls after gynaecologic cancer surgery, in a 2026 study. The programme ran at an urban safety-net hospital, where patients face complex medical and social needs. Four months before and after the launch supplied 466 patients for comparison, about half called. Called patients attended follow-up visits more often and had more complications managed without hospital care. Emergency visits and readmissions were similar, though repeat readmissions fell among called patients. Two in five called patients raised concerns, most often pain, constipation, or vague symptoms needing advice.
pmc-13276867:
Takashi Watanabe writes a 2026 letter critiquing a recent paper on so-called neuromelanin-sensitive MRI. The scan is used to study the substantia nigra, a brain area that degenerates in Parkinson disease. White matter and grey matter differ in water content, which sets their basic signal behaviour. Off-resonance pulses saturate bound water in proportion to T1 shortening, the letter explains. Magnetisation transfer then cancels much of the T1 contrast, leaving mostly proton-density contrast. pmc-13277767: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2025 article comparing the chemistry and biological activity of leaf extracts from spinach and a related plant, Basella rubra. pmc-13278467:

Broad measures matched older findings: more inflammation travelled with more precancers, scarring, and loss of enzyme-making tissue, hinting at blocked ducts. pmc-13278767:

pmc-13279167:

pmc-13279367:

pmc-13279567:

Most trials hinted at gains: smaller wound area, better wound bed and more blood flow, most in diabetic foot ulcers. One trial at the highest dose showed no gain. pmc-13279767:

pmc-13279967:

pmc-13280267:

pmc-13280767:

pmc-13280867:

The team then weighed sleep length and weekly activity, alone and paired.

pmc-13280967:

pmc-13281467:

pmc-13281767:

pmc-13281867:
Shengbo Yang and colleagues studied a Chinese herbal brew for liver cancer in a 2026 paper. The brew blends thirteen herbs and is used beside standard care. Its workings are poorly mapped. pmc-13282067:

The pressure-drop problem struck about a quarter of each group, with no real gap after adjustments. Early graft failure, kidney injury, rejection, and bile or vessel problems also looked similar. The authors say the approach appears safe in the short term and can widen the donor pool.
pmc-13282267:

pmc-13282367:

pmc-13282467:

pmc-13282867:
