Some rules, such as dose checks for pain drugs in kidney disease and blood sugar checks on steroids, are rare in foreign sets. The authors offer the rules for safer local prescribing.
pmc-13356267:
Markus D Moore and co-authors present a 2026 case of air leaking into the chest center in a 27-year-old man who vaped. Vaping heats a liquid into an aerosol that is breathed in, and heavy use can injure the lungs, a condition called EVALI. The man came in with two days of growing breathlessness, wheezing, and a cough that brought up mucus.

His history included asthma, anxiety, high blood pressure, vaping, and marijuana use, and blood tests showed raised white cell counts. The case centers on pneumomediastinum, air trapped around the heart and central chest, plus air under the skin, arising in the setting of vaping lung injury. The authors urge clinicians to watch for this problem in long-term vapers.
pmc-13356667:
Sian Seaman and others studied how intestinal sirtuin 1 controls liver regeneration in mice, in 2026. The gut-liver axis is thought to influence regeneration, but its ways remain poorly known. Better grasp could yield new care for liver disease and transplantation.

Mice lacking intestinal sirtuin 1 underwent partial hepatectomy with wild-type littermates, and regeneration was matched using immunostaining and related tests. The study defines how the intestinal farnesoid X target and fibroblast growth factor 15 pathway links gut signals to liver regrowth. Teams gain a mechanistic target for boosting regeneration after liver injury or surgery.
pmc-13356767:
Ronak Mahatme and co-authors ask whether hormone therapy before joint surgery raises the risk of blood clots. Hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, has been linked to clots in some groups of patients. The worry carries into bone and joint surgery, where clots are a known risk. The team used a large health records network to study adults aged forty to seventy-five.

They matched patients who used HRT before scope surgery of a joint to like patients who did not. Each group held 3,868 patients, and clots were tracked for ninety days. Clot rates were low and alike in both groups, as were return visits and infections. The authors call the results calming but early, not a final rule for care around surgery.
pmc-13358967:
Mohammad Jafari-Mohsen-Abad and co-authors compare two ways to turn biogas into methanol in a 2026 study. Biogas from waste holds methane and carbon dioxide; methanol made from it is a useful chemical and fuel. Both designs burn part of the gas for heat and power, then add hydrogen made by splitting water. They differ in the splitting machine used.

One design uses solid oxide cells, the other alkaline cells, for a plant fed 2,000 cubic meters of biogas per hour. The alkaline route converted more carbon and made more methanol, while the solid oxide route used less power per ton. Neither paid for itself under Italian prices, a sober guide for investors.
pmc-13359867:
Pei Zhang and co-authors profile a virus-caused sheep lung tumor in a 2026 study. Ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma is an infectious lung cancer of sheep that costs the industry heavily and mirrors human lung adenocarcinoma closely. A virus called JSRV drives it. Gene-level studies exist, but protein and metabolite maps were missing. The team built both and read them together.

Comparing tumor tissue with healthy lung, they found the virus rewires the tissue's proteins and chemistry on a wide scale. Three programs stood out: changed cell adhesion, stress in the protein-folding compartment, and reprogrammed metabolism with immune activation. These joint maps sharpen the picture of how the virus builds a tumor.
pmc-13360067:
Alakananda Basu wrote a 2026 review on how two cell processes, autophagy and senescence, affect each other. Autophagy is the cell's way of clearing out worn parts to stay alive under stress. Senescence is when a cell stops dividing for good, which can help block tumors. Basu focuses on kinases, proteins that switch other proteins on and off.

The review pulls together old and new studies on how kinases steer both processes at once. It covers harm to cell power plants and waste sacs, stress from reactive oxygen, and signals aged cells send to nearby tissue. Because kinases are common drug targets, the author argues that learning how they run both processes could lead to better treatments for aging and cancer.
pmc-13360467:
Smita Kumari and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of antibody-drug conjugates, a fast-growing class of cancer treatment. These drugs join an antibody, which homes in on cancer cells, to a cell-killing drug it carries along. The review traces how the field has moved from early proofs of concept to drugs in routine use. It focuses on how each part of the design has improved.

Better targets, antibody building, linkers, drug payloads, and joining methods have all raised how well these drugs work and how safe they are. The authors also weigh open problems: side effects, drug resistance, and hard manufacturing. Computer and AI methods now help guide design choices. The review offers a clear frame for building the next wave of these targeted drugs.
pmc-13360567:
Jinkimoni Singha and co-authors report a 2026 case of a sinus growth that looked like a tooth-root cyst. The patient was a 38-year-old man with pain and swelling at the back of his upper jaw. The true cause was a mucopyocele, a rare mucus-filled growth in the maxillary sinus that had become infected. Such growths expand slowly and can wear away bone over time.

The case shows how closely a sinus mucopyocele can copy a cyst that starts from a tooth. The team reached the right answer by combining the man's symptoms, a hands-on exam, scans, surgery, and tissue study. Their report warns dentists and surgeons to keep sinus causes in mind when jaw swellings appear. A full workup guards against treating the wrong disease.
pmc-13362767:
Md Sofiqul Islam and colleagues report a 2026 lab study on universal-shade dental fillings, the one-shade resins that promise to match any tooth and save chair time. They compared five such products with one classic multi-shade resin, testing hardness, stiffness, slow bending under load, color, and gloss after a day in water and after a simulated year of aging.

The classic resin stayed harder and stiffer and crept less than every one-shade rival. Yet the one-shade products matched it on color stability, and some kept a better gloss after aging. The authors advise picking by need: the classic for heavy-load spots, and one-shade products where looks and speed matter most, since quality varies by brand.
pmc-13363467:
Renfei Gao and colleagues report a 2026 study on toughening geopolymer mortar, a low-carbon stand-in for cement, with basalt fibers. The binder blends metakaolin, slag, and fly ash, but plain geopolymer cracks easily. The team dosed basalt fiber from zero to just over one percent and tracked flow, bending and crushing strength, and crack growth live with a camera method that maps surface strain.

A mid dose, half a percent, gave the best bending strength and slowed cracks the most, while squeezing strength peaked at a lower dose and faded past the mid dose. More fiber always hurt flow. Microscopy showed good grip between fiber and binder at the sweet spots. The authors mark the mid range as the practical window for tougher, greener mortar.
pmc-13364067:
Zhonghui Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 study on steering antenna beams when only the signal phase can be set and the noise picture is skewed. Real arrays estimate their interference map from few snapshots, which corrupts the math behind classic beamforming. Their cascaded network first runs the faulty map through a denoising autoencoder. That rebuilds a clean version and squeezes it into compact features. Then a residual network turns those features into phase settings directly.

Splitting the job this way skips the slow repeated optimization of older robust methods at run time. Tests under short snapshot counts and noisy estimates showed stronger tolerance of map mismatch and output quality that rivaled the classic approaches. The authors aim the method at radar and wireless arrays on tight budgets.
pmc-13364367:
Ayesha Mariam and co-workers review the 2026 state of knowledge on Firmiana colorata, a drug tree of South Asia. Old healers use it, yet its plant facts and drug traits had not been drawn into one place. The review pulls its naming, range, form, genes, and plant compounds into one account.

Lab work hints at use for pain, swelling, germs, and cell growth ills, but most tests use crude plant draws and weak dose proof. Safe use data are thin. The team calls for set plant standards, firm dose work, and harm checks before any clinic use.
pmc-13365067:

Culture problems may control vesicle output.

pmc-13365967:

Honghui Yu, Lin Cheng, and Hongbo Zheng report sleep care in a child heart surgery. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a girl of nine. She had a thick heart muscle that blocked blood flow.

pmc-13367967:

pmc-13369767:

pmc-13369967:

pmc-13370867:

pmc-13371267:
Petr Birke and colleagues describe parvovirus B19 crises in Czech children with hereditary spherocytosis in a 2026 study. In this inherited anaemia, red cells are sphere-shaped and break down early, and parvovirus B19 can halt red cell production, causing a sudden aplastic crisis. pmc-13372067:

pmc-13373267:
Abiodun O Adewuya and co-authors mapped faith leads as mind care gate staff in Nigeria in a 2026 study. Few Nigerians who need mind care get it from clinics. Pastors and imams are, in truth, the first port of call for most homes.

pmc-13375267:

pmc-13376167:
Daniela Münch and eight colleagues published a 2026 study on how zebrafish regrow sense organs. Fish can replace lost hair cells in their lateral line, a sense organ along the body. Regrowth starts after cells die, but deaths can happen in more than one way.

pmc-13376567:

pmc-13378367:

pmc-13379467:
Giulia D'Arcangelo and colleagues discuss a 2026 review on getting the treatment balance right for children with inflammatory bowel disease. Treating too weakly can let severe disease cause lasting damage before effective therapy starts. The review weighs both risks and argues for judging each child's likely course early. Its aim is care sized to the child, not to the average patient.
pmc-13379867:
Maulik A Patel and colleagues present a 2026 study of more than a thousand tunnelled dialysis catheter placements at one centre over four years. The study compared four entry sites, most often the large veins on either side of the neck. The comparison helps clinicians weigh which site serves patients best.
pmc-13380167:
Tang and colleagues examine whether blood in the urine, tracked over time, predicts kidney decline in IgA nephropathy, in 2026 nephrology research. In patients with proteinuria, moderate levels, 20 to under 100 cells, carried a hazard ratio of 1.89 in subgroup analysis. Tang argues repeated checks, not one-off readings, carry the prognostic signal.
pmc-13381367:
Ayushi Singh and co-authors report a 2026 study of two tissue stains that help diagnose prostate cancer and judge its behaviour. One stain highlights the basal cell layer that cancer usually lacks. The other, called NKX3.1, is found almost only in prostate tissue and marks cancer cells directly.

The team then checked whether stronger staining tracked with adverse features of the cancer, using blood PSA values where available. Combining both stains may sharpen diagnosis in difficult prostate samples.
pmc-13382067:
Muhammad Adeel Zafar and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study from Pakistan on high blood pressure medicines. Results can guide clinics toward the adherence problems that matter most.
pmc-13382967:
Zhenzhen Lin and a large team present DFA-YOLO, an image system that finds maize leaf stomata at any angle, in 2026 work. pmc-13383067:
Tengyu Liu's team reports a photocatalyst that turns biomass-derived oxalic acid fully into carbon monoxide, in a 2026 study. Mechanistic work showed shell and yolk cooperating through hydroxyl radicals and carbon dioxide radical anions protonated in place. The route upgrades a biomass waste stream into a useful chemical feedstock.
pmc-13385367:
Hulda Ingvarsdottir's team tracked five-year stability of blood proteins in older adults, in a 2026 study. pmc-13385967:
Catarina Pereira's team built trainable spin hardware that learns on-device, in a 2026 study. pmc-13386467:

pmc-13386867:
Shea A. Lowery and co-authors review knotted DNA structures inside herpesviruses in a 2026 article. G-quadruplexes form when guanine-rich DNA folds into stacked blocks instead of a helix. These folds can steer both active replication and the latent state that lets herpesviruses persist for life. Their shifting shapes in living cells make them hard to pin down and harder to drug, the authors note. The review gathers conserved roles across viruses and lists what tools the field needs next.
pmc-13389067:
Valdés Olmos and colleagues review how nuclear medicine guides surgeons in the operating room. Their 2026 paper traces radioguided surgery from the sentinel node procedure, developed over three decades ago. That procedure combined pre-operative scans, a hand-held gamma probe, and blue dye. Together they find the first lymph node draining a tumour. That procedure became standard in melanoma and breast cancer and founded interventional nuclear medicine.

Modern scanners such as SPECT/CT and PET/CT now give surgeons precise roadmaps before the operation. The review describes expansion into gynaecological, urological, head and neck, and gastrointestinal cancers, plus robot-assisted procedures targeting sentinel nodes and small clusters of metastases. Hybrid tracers that are both radioactive and fluorescent are highlighted as the coming step. The authors comprehensively assess current applications and the technology's trajectory.
pmc-13390367:
Qiang Gao's team presents ProtSeqGen, a deep-learning model for the protein inverse folding problem: designing an amino acid sequence that folds into a specified backbone shape. Existing methods struggle to optimise hit rate, stability, efficiency, and generalisation together across diverse folds.

ProtSeqGen encodes shapes as local geometric graphs, models residue interactions with a message-passing network, and predicts amino acids with a multilayer perceptron. Trained on the CATH 4.2 data set, it beat state-of-the-art methods on sequence recovery and made accurate, designable sequences for nine shape-diverse proteins, establishing a robust, scalable tool for de novo protein design.
pmc-13391367:
Andrii Bugai and a large team uncover, in 2026, how the cell nucleus decides which newly made RNAs to export and which to destroy. Cells produce many polyadenylated RNAs, packaged with proteins, but only functional packages should reach the cytoplasm while faulty ones are degraded in the nucleus.

The study centres on UAP56, also called DDX39B, a core part of functional RNA packages that docks them to a pore-linked export machine. The team traces how that docking hands the transcript over for release and export. Molecular biologists gain the missing decision step in RNA quality control, explaining how faithful gene expression is protected from a flood of defective transcripts.
pmc-13391467:
Sérgio Cavalheiro's team used a working drug-response assay to guide treatment for a four-year-old with repeat spread clival chordoma, a rare, locally fast-moving tumour considered chemotherapy-stubborn in children. Tumour cell balls were tested ex vivo on the Bioverso rig.

The assay showed broad resistance with relative response to irinotecan, and an irinotecan course made marked medical and scan shrinkage of brain and lung lesions after three cycles, without severe harm. Response held for fourteen months, illustrating working exact cancer care for rare, stubborn child tumours where gene targets are scarce.
pmc-13391767:
I. S. Alam's team weighed open, keyhole, and robotic total belly colon removal with end ileum opening for immune bowel disease, using matched national records data from 2022. Lightly cutting techniques have better bowel results, but head-to-head evidence for this extensive operation was limited.

Among 581 matched patients, eighty-three robotic, four hundred fifteen keyhole, and eighty-three open, overall thirty-day illness did not differ clearly. Robotic surgery took clearly longer than keyhole surgery, and secondary results including stay, return stays, and exact complications round out a comparison surgeons can weigh against surgery time.
pmc-13392367:
Ziling Liu's team built a sound time crystal from ringing meta-atoms in a one-axis acoustic wave guide, creating a time-varying meta-stuff that boosts sound at motion band gaps. Selectively harnessing Floquet band structure and opening multiple gaps had challenged experiment.

Dynamic squeeze swing made boosted passage and strong output boost for a compact Floquet slab at the gap rate. A time super-cell design then bent motion bands to create multiple gaps, yielding two boosted passage ranges near half and quarter of the original swing rate, opening routes to higher-axis time crystals.
pmc-13392467:
Connor Prosty, Mark Sorin, Emily G McDonald, and Todd C Lee pooled the trial evidence on giving vancomycin by mouth to stop Clostridioides difficile infection coming back. The risk returns whenever a past patient needs antibiotics again. A past bout of this gut infection makes a repeat episode much more likely during later antibiotic courses. Their review updated a search of MEDLINE and Embase to March 2026.

Only two randomised trials qualified, covering 102 patients in total, both judged at low risk of bias. Pooling them gave odds of recurrence modestly below the control level, with an eighty-eight percent chance of some benefit on the authors' Bayesian reading. Uncertainty stays wide, though, and the pair of small trials cannot settle the question, so larger studies are called for.
pmc-13392867:
Ya-Wen Lu and five colleagues asked whether a simple skin test of tiny blood vessels can forecast heart trouble after stenting for blocked coronary arteries. The test briefly squeezes off blood flow, then measures how strongly the skin flushes when pressure releases, a response called post-occlusive reactive hyperemia. Records covered one hundred ninety-seven patients followed for up to five years after their procedure.

Patients with a weak flush carried more metabolic risk factors and went on to suffer notably more combined heart events. A stronger flush independently lined up with lower event risk, at under half the rate in adjusted models, and the link survived a matched comparison designed to balance the groups. The authors suggest the painless skin check could sharpen risk sorting after stenting, while calling for bigger forward-looking studies to confirm it.
pmc-13393267:
Zhenxin Wang and twelve colleagues engineered a zinc single-atom nanozyme aimed at osteosarcoma, a bone cancer that spreads aggressively and resists standard therapy. Their starting insight links a lysosomal channel, TRPML1, through the oxygen sensor HIF-1-alpha and the glucose gate GLUT1, tying zinc handling inside cell recycling compartments to sugar metabolism. The platform carries dense zinc sites plus a glucose-burning enzyme, all drawn into those compartments.

Once inside, the particle devours glucose and acidifies its surroundings while its zinc sites generate corrosive oxygen species, jointly crushing the cell's reducing defences and triggering a sulfur-linked death programme. Zinc flooding and oxidative damage also rupture compartment membranes, firing an inflammatory death pathway. The double killing made tumour deaths more visible to the immune system and loosened the cancer's immune suppression in models.
pmc-13393667:
Anuran Bhattacharya and five colleagues show that breast tumours ship a misfolded blood protein to distant organs inside exosomes, priming those tissues for later metastasis. The cargo, a warped form of alpha-1 antitrypsin, was found in vesicles from mouse mammary tumour cells and confirmed in patient blood serum. Healthy lung, liver, and bone marrow cells, the classic landing sites for breast cancer spread, took up the delivery.

On arrival the misfolded protein partners with a stress chaperone in the cell interior. The pairing fires a survival-flavoured stress response. That response boosts growth and inflammation while suppressing cell death, in dishes and in animals. Stripping the cargo from vesicles blunted all of it. The authors propose the misfolded protein as both a warning marker and a target for cutting off metastatic preparation before tumour cells ever arrive.
pmc-13393867:
Ozkan Ozdemir reports a prostate inflammation case that mimicked advanced cancer on MRI in a 2026 case report. Multiparametric MRI guides prostate cancer detection and staging, and features like strong diffusion restriction and apparent spread beyond the gland usually signal aggressive malignancy.

A 49-year-old man with urinary symptoms and a modest PSA of 2.7 had a large peripheral zone lesion scored PI-RADS 5, suggesting locally advanced cancer. Systematic biopsy instead showed chronic prostatitis without cancer, and antibiotics led to marked lesion regression on repeat MRI. The case cautions against overstaging based on imaging alone.
pmc-13394467:
Sheng Gong and colleagues show, in 2026, a shortcut by which dopamine receptors tune learning in the brain. They studied D2 receptors in the nucleus accumbens, a hub for reward and dislike. With tools that break one link while sparing normal signals, they found D2 receptors bind a partner on NMDA receptors. That direct grip weakens NMDA action without the usual chain of messengers.

The effect showed at inputs from the thalamus, but not from the cortex. It also curbed lasting strengthening of synapses and helped mice learn to avoid harm. The authors argue that dopamine can gate single inputs by touch, not just by broad chemical signals. Such gating may matter in addiction and mental illness.
pmc-13394667:
Yijia Wang leads a 2026 study of chrysin, a plant compound, as a guard for hearts under pressure strain. Strain from a narrowed aorta makes heart walls thicken and scar in mice. The team gave chrysin to such mice and to heart cells pushed to swell by a hormone. They tracked survival, heart function, swelling, and scarring.

Treated mice lived better and kept stronger hearts. Swelling, scarring, and cell death all eased, and swelling signals fell. Chrysin also raised shield enzymes by waking a master switch named NRF2. A pathway named PI3K and AKT sat behind the effect. The authors pitch chrysin as a hopeful drug lead for strain-based heart disease.
pmc-13395967:
Mateusz Garus and colleagues review breathlessness in heart failure in a 2026 article, treating it as far more than fluid in the lungs. Breathlessness is the symptom that most often sends heart failure patients to hospital, especially in sudden episodes.

The authors trace it to raised pressures inside the heart, shifted blood volume, poor gas exchange, and sensors in muscles and blood vessels that misread the body's state. Hormone systems switched on by a weak heart add to the strain. Illnesses that often travel with heart failure, such as lung disease, obesity, anemia, and kidney trouble, lower the point at which breathlessness strikes. Trial evidence on easing it is covered as well.
pmc-13396667:
Zhu and co-authors attack, in 2026, one of drug design's hardest targets. It is the intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain of the androgen receptor, a prostate cancer driver with no stable shape to grip. They built a computational workflow built on enhanced sampling with machine learning collective variables. Using the known modulator EPI-002 as a probe, they mapped the Tau-5 region of the domain in detail.

The simulations mapped nine metastable states of Tau-5. They showed ligand recognition runs on pi-pi stacking plus hydrogen bonds, mediated by structured water molecules trapped at the interface. Screening compound libraries against the druggable shapes they found yielded K53, a designed blocker that binds the domain directly and shuts down androgen receptor transcription. K53 showed potent activity against enzalutamide-resistant prostate cancer cells, sparing normal cells, a relevant advance since receptor variants appear in nearly 40 percent of castration-resistant cases.
pmc-13396867:
Julia Sellin and co-authors test two blood markers side by side in ALS, asking whether each captures a different face of the disease. Their 2026 study pairs neurofilament light chain, a protein leaked by stressed nerve fibers, with troponin T, a heart protein that may instead reflect damage where nerves meet muscle.

Levels from a discovery group of 433 patients in Essen were checked against a second group of 185 in Bonn. Both were read through the D50 model, which splits each patient's course into how aggressive the disease is and how much of it has accumulated so far. Troponin T bound tightly to those measures, supporting the pair as complementary.
pmc-13397667:
Malene Eiberg Holm and colleagues revisit interviews with people who took part in unmoderated online groups centred on self-harm and suicidal behaviour. Their 2026 study asks how such spaces shape personal recovery, for better or worse. Past work looked at peer support inside these groups, but their role in a longer recovery path was less clear.

Thirteen people (twelve women and one non-binary person, aged 21 to 49) from all five Danish regions had given interviews for an earlier study. The new analysis reads those talks through the CHIME-D lens, covering connection, hope, identity, meaning, empowerment and difficulties. Findings show support and harm can sit side by side in the same community.
pmc-13397767:
Junko Niimura and others gauge trauma-informed care training for a community team serving young pregnant women in a 2026 longitudinal study. Young maternal age, at or below 24 years, is a documented risk factor for child maltreatment, and young mothers more often carry childhood trauma that perinatal care can re-trigger.

Since favorable staff views are critical for adopting and sustaining trauma-informed care, the team built and tested a training program's effects on community maternity staff views in the Tokyo metropolitan area. Rollout and testing of such training in community perinatal settings had been thin. Services gain proof for preparing staff to care for young mothers without re-traumatizing them.
pmc-13397867:
Giulia De Marco and co-authors describe a man whose rare glomus tumours kept appearing in his leg over many years. Their 2026 case report and literature review starts in October 2022, when the 64-year-old arrived with a painful lump in the lower third of his right thigh. Glomus tumours are benign growths that usually sit singly under a fingernail, where pain, cold sensitivity and pinpoint tenderness make them easy to spot.

Scans showed a solid thigh lesion, and a needle sample confirmed glomus tumour tissue before surgeons removed it in January 2023. The man's history held an earlier high-grade sarcoma treated in 1994 with wide surgery and chemotherapy, sharpening the need for proof. Away from the fingers, these tumours often stay silent or odd, which the review shows delays their naming.
pmc-13397967:
Chengcheng Duan and team looked at how age and thyroid immune markers relate to lymph node spread in thyroid cancer with Hashimoto disease. Their 2026 work covers 540 people who had both papillary thyroid cancer, the most common thyroid cancer, and Hashimoto disease, an immune attack on the thyroid. Whether age and immune marker levels predict spread to central neck nodes in this combined group had stayed contested.

After adjustment, age under 45 and a positive thyroglobulin immune marker raised the risk of central node spread, while a positive thyroid peroxidase marker seemed protective. Risk peaked when younger age joined with thyroglobulin positivity, and also when younger age joined with a negative peroxidase result. The findings give surgeons and hormone doctors a sharper risk picture for neck surgery planning, though past records cannot settle cause.
pmc-13398367:
Toby Lowe and co-authors describe a multilingual phone app that prepares breast radiotherapy patients to hold their breath on cue. Their 2026 report tackles a practical snag: breath-hold methods shield the heart during treatment, but many patients fail the rehearsal, often anxious and briefed just 20 minutes before. Patients from varied language backgrounds face the steepest climb.

Swapping pamphlets for interactive videos, visual guides and live translation in seven languages lets patients practise at home before their planning scan. Early teaching, the team argues, should cut failure rates and calm nerves while keeping tumour targeting exact. The project frames language access as a safety feature of radiotherapy, not a courtesy extra.
pmc-13398867:
Paulo César B Veiga Jardim writes a 2026 editorial, in Portuguese, praising fresh proof that cutting dietary salt lowers blood pressure, and lamenting how rarely the advice is followed. The piece salutes a systematic review and meta-analysis by Kelly and colleagues, judged careful in method. Its pooled result, as the editorial relays it, puts sodium reduction's effect on pressure on a par with a standard blood pressure drug.

History supports the link: communities eating little salt showed low pressure as far back as the mid-twentieth century, and migrants who moved to saltier diets saw pressure climb. No study, the editorial notes, has ever shown the reverse. The puzzle it leaves is practical, not scientific: a cheap, proven fix that health systems still fail to deliver.
pmc-13399367:
Ana Lúcia Ribeiro Valadares leads a panel of Brazilian gynecology specialists in this 2026 guidance document on unexpected bleeding in women using menopausal hormone therapy. Unscheduled bleeding is one of the main reasons women abandon such therapy. The document, numbered 8 in its series, lays out when bleeding is expected, when it signals a need for investigation, and how to manage it step by step.

Bleeding in the first months of therapy is common and usually settles, especially on continuous regimens. Bleeding that persists past six months, or returns after a bleed-free interval, needs workup. The panel sets a risk scheme for endometrial cancer. One major factor, such as a body mass index of 40 or more, or two minor factors, triggers investigation, with transvaginal ultrasound the usual first test. Management proceeds in phases, from adjusting dose or progestogen type to a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device when needed.
pmc-13400167:
Zhe Dai and colleagues built a colorectal cancer model on a microfluidic chip whose tumor organoids grow their own tumor-style blood vessels, in a 2026 study. The team's approach educates those vessel cells within the chip environment so they self-assemble into tumor-associated vasculature under stable perfusion. That mimics the environment that shapes drug response in patients.

Validation came from drug testing. Tumoroid chips grown from different patients responded differently to the standard FOLFOX chemotherapy combination plus bevacizumab, the anti-vascular antibody, exactly the inter-patient variation clinicians see and need to predict. The authors argue the model closes a realism gap. Because anti-vessel therapy is central to colorectal cancer care, a test bed whose vessels behave like tumor vessels should forecast patient responses better. They present the work as preliminary evidence for the chip's reliability and a step toward genuinely personalized drug selection.
pmc-13400467:
Hannah J Roeder and Enrique C Leira review, in 2026, how menopause interacts with brain and nerve health. Menopause is a hormone transition, not just the end of periods. Shifting hormones can change the course of several conditions that affect the central nervous system.

The review covers stroke, migraine, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease. Around menopause, hormone swings may worsen migraines and seizures in women prone to them, and the stage may mark a turning point for vessel injury and decline. Estrogen therapy effects differ by timing and age, helping in early ovarian failure yet raising stroke risk in older women. Care, the authors stress, must be tailored case by case.
pmc-13400867:
Yaohua Li and a team study, in 2026, a long non-coding RNA in chickens as a possible marker for breeding better meat birds. Such RNAs regulate muscle growth in mammals, but their use in poultry breeding is little explored. Breast muscle weight and body weight carry real economic value.

The RNA, called LOC416755, was most active in breast muscle, sat in the nucleus of muscle precursor cells and rose as those cells matured. Nine variants were found in the gene. Five linked significantly to traits including body weight, breast muscle weight, shank length and abdominal fat. Birds with mixed gene copies often scored best, which the authors flag for marker-assisted selection.
pmc-13401167:
Boyoung Kang and colleagues present a 2026 mixed methods pilot study of EvaluationPlus, a decision support framework for improving therapeutic artificial intelligence systems such as mental health chatbots. Most chatbot evaluations only diagnose problems, the authors note, without a clear path to fixing them.

The team ran three improvement cycles on Dr. CareSam, a bilingual chatbot built on GPT 4.0. Two licensed clinical psychologists used think-aloud reviews to find skill gaps against a seven-dimension competency rubric. Three large language models, GPT 4.0, Claude 4.0 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, then proposed targeted fixes for each gap. A blinded within-subject A/B validation checked whether the enhanced chatbot actually performed better.
pmc-13401267:
Natalie Van Pelt and co-authors wrote a 2026 synthesis on the blue orchard bee, Osmia lignaria, a solitary North American bee used to pollinate crops. On what it can teach both farming and ecology. With honey bee losses mounting, alternative pollinators draw growing attention, and most bee species are in fact solitary.

The authors review what is known about the bee's developmental flexibility, nesting behaviour, foraging strategies, pollination services, and main stressors. They stress how weather, habitat conditions, and management choices shape its performance in orchards and fields. Because solitary bees remain underused as model systems, the bee offers a bridge between behavioural ecology and real pollination function, with lessons for conservation and farm management alike.
pmc-13401567:
Naga Pradyumna Kothapalli and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of tumours found in people with aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. In that disease the immune system attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord. Tumour production of aquaporin-4 has been proposed as a trigger for such cases arising with cancer, but earlier reports conflict.

The team searched their database of 400 antibody-positive patients for coexisting tumours that were not confined to one organ. There was no time limit between tumour and disease onset. The data gathered covered demographic, clinical, imaging, and treatment details. Their goal was to measure how often the tumours themselves express aquaporin-4 and in what patterns. Expression of the protein varies dynamically within tumours, the authors argue, which can obscure any paraneoplastic link and explain why some earlier studies found none at all.
pmc-13401667:
Irina V Wang and a large group of co-authors wrote a 2026 white paper on the drug information system for new medicines, the tangled flow of evidence about them. Information on newly cleared drugs has grown complex and fragmented, and each audience needs something different from it.

Clinicians want short, usable guidance on prescribing, while patients want to weigh benefits against harms against their own goals. Payers need head-to-head effectiveness data to make coverage decisions. Poor communication often makes benefits look bigger and shrinks perceived harms. The authors trace how drug information is made, spread, and read, with a focus on set channels such as labels, drug guides, and trial snapshots. Regulators anchor the system by setting evidence standards, and other information sources get a look as well.
pmc-13401767:
Sara Almaradweh and Zonaira Gul present a 2026 case of lung cryptococcosis, a fungal infection, in a man whose sarcoidosis had already weakened his immune defences. He was 50 years old, with a fifteen-year history of pulmonary sarcoidosis and low CD4 immune cell counts.

His illness raised fears the fungus had reached his brain: neck stiffness, light sensitivity, headaches. Slowed thinking all pointed that way, and a blood test for cryptococcal antigen was positive while airway sampling confirmed Cryptococcus species. Spinal fluid culture grew nothing, but antifungal treatment had already begun, so brain involvement stayed suspected rather than proven. He had stopped his antifungal therapy himself, and recurrent shingles further signalled failing cell-mediated immunity. Treatment was complicated by kidney injury linked partly to the antifungal drug amphotericin B.
pmc-13401967:
Chaymae Cherrabi and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 12-year-old boy whose lymphoma care was complicated by a clot in the veins of the brain. The boy carried ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma and had just started chemotherapy. A brief spell of limb heaviness and slurred speech then cleared on its own, at first looking like a small, passing stroke.

Magnetic resonance venography showed wide clotting across the cerebral venous sinuses rather than a blocked artery. Doctors treated him with low-molecular-weight heparin, later switching to rivaroxaban, while chemotherapy continued under close watch. Repeat imaging at nine months showed the veins fully open again, and he was left with no lasting nerve damage. Clinicians reading the report take away a warning to image early when a child on cancer treatment shows odd, short-lived nerve symptoms.
pmc-13402267:
Claudia D’Anna and fellow authors review how epigenetic change, chemical marks that tune genes without rewriting DNA, feeds long-term airway disease such as asthma and COPD. Both illnesses share chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and slow reshaping of the airway walls. Lungs meet smoke, pollution, and germs daily, and that contact can leave marks that alter how immune and lung cells behave.

The review covers three mark systems: DNA methylation, histone changes, and non-coding RNAs that adjust gene output. Together they help explain lasting inflammation, airway remodeling, and why patients answer the same drugs so differently. New marks also promise sharper diagnosis, since some patterns flag disease or risk before symptoms peak. The authors point to fresh biomarkers and drug targets, while noting that turning mark readings into proven treatments still needs careful testing.
pmc-13402967:
Wen-Jie Hou and co-authors review machine learning tools that sort pleural effusion, fluid around the lungs, by its cause using routine biochemistry rather than invasive sampling. Fluid and blood chemical tests are quick, objective, and easy to get, yet each marker alone sorts poorly; culture and cell studies, the gold standards, are slow, subjective, and often insensitive. Learning algorithms promise to squeeze more signal from panels of ordinary tests.

Surveying the studies so far, the authors find early accuracy gains when algorithms combine multiple biochemical parameters, but they also catalog the field limits: small datasets, uneven methods, and little outside validation. Their recommendations push for larger shared cohorts and stricter testing before any model guides a needle or a diagnosis. The review maps a practical road from promising code to clinic-ready triage.
pmc-13403367:
Yu Zou and co-authors wrote a 2026 review arguing that eye damage from diabetes goes well beyond high blood sugar alone. The condition harms small blood vessels in the retina and can blind working-age adults. The authors set out its spread, its causes, and signs that may flag it early.

Several linked paths drive the damage, among them growth signals for blood vessels and stress from sugar by-products. Nerve cells in the retina also break down, aided by active immune cells and Wnt signals. Readers get a guide to screening, early markers, and treatment plans that aim to catch harm before sight is lost.
pmc-13403567:
Abbas Godian and co-authors described in 2026 a young woman in sub-Saharan Africa whose bone marrow failure took months to explain. The 26-year-old needed repeated blood transfusions, and her first marrow test came back dry. Money limits slowed further testing at the local center.

Seven months on, fever, a cheek rash, low blood counts, and fluid near a lung pointed to lupus. Standard rule sets for that immune disease were now met. Steroids plus a lupus drug freed her from transfusions for over five months. The case shows how steady suspicion can beat scarce test access.
pmc-13404367:
Shiori Kinoshita, Yu Miyawaki, Michihiro Osumi, and Akihiko Murai asked in 2026 why virtual reality feedback eases nerve-loss pain well for some people and barely for others. Ten patients with such pain took part, alongside 23 healthy adults for comparison. Brain waves at rest were recorded before and after the virtual sessions.

Relief levels varied widely across patients, as the team expected. The size of the relief tracked with web traits in one brain wave band, most of all in front brain areas. Patients showed tighter front-area webbing than healthy adults. Front-to-attention network links also ran stronger in patients. Those traits may mark who senses body feedback most keenly.
pmc-13404567:
Hafiz Muhammad Safwan and team found that hair testing beats blood testing for spotting Leishmania DNA in sick dogs. Their 2026 work takes on canine leishmaniosis, a zoonotic disease caused by Leishmania infantum, where early true diagnosis steers care and control. Hair sampling is painless, yet its worth across infection states had been little probed.

Among 134 Spanish dogs, hair quantitative PCR showed 74 percent sensitivity in clinically sick dogs versus 36 percent for blood PCR, a clear gap, while no gap showed in healthy seropositive dogs. Interferon-gamma output did not track with hair positivity, but medium or high antibody levels did. The work backs hair testing as a handy diagnostic tool for sick dogs, with larger studies needed across regions and stages.
pmc-13405367:
Akiko Hashiguchi and Satoru Takahashi study how a researcher's own habits shape grant success in Japan, in a 2026 report. Grants pile up in few hands, which deepens unfair gaps between scholars. Which habits help, and when in a career, could make staff reviews fairer.

Data come from Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research, the largest grant scheme in the country. The pair sorted 1,152 professors by their grant records over a whole career. Habit measures cover the fame of a mentor, place in author lists, paper quality and team shape. Tests check if these traits predict grant strength in the same way across fields and career stages.
pmc-13406767:
Ayşe Nur Coşkun and Haluk Topaloğlu profile boys diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy before age three, in a 2026 record review. The X-linked disease usually surfaces later, so early cases reveal how diagnosis begins without newborn screening. Records cover 198 children diagnosed between January 2020 and July 2025.

Over ninety percent were found incidentally through high creatine kinase blood results, the authors report. Nearly a third showed early language delay, widening the picture beyond muscles. Genetic testing confirmed almost every case, with one percent proven by muscle biopsy. The authors urge kinase checks for infants with non-motor delays and routine developmental surveillance alongside muscle monitoring.
pmc-13407167:
George Sharbeen and a large team report, in 2026, on HSP47, a helper protein that matures collagen, as a possible drug target in pancreatic cancer. This cancer kills most patients within years, partly because dense fibrous tissue laid down by support cells blocks drugs and aids spread, and collagen cannot form properly without HSP47.

Silencing HSP47 slowed growth of both cancer cells and their fibrous support cells in dishes. In mice carrying implanted tumours, treatment shrank internal fibrosis and opened tumour blood vessels, while silencing the protein only in support cells also slowed tumour growth. Patient tissue showed heavy presence in over 80 percent of cases, with survival links in the tumour compartment itself. Tests in living human tumour fragments backed the dual-target idea.
pmc-13407567:
Rachel M. Wood and co-authors test, in 2026, a multivariate method for reading metabolic fingerprints after weight-loss surgery. High-throughput metabolomics measures hundreds of small molecules at once, yet simple one-at-a-time tests miss how those molecules move together, so the team tried a relational approach named CLARITY on trial data.

Blood measurements came from 125 people in a bariatric surgery trial, sampled before and after a weight management intervention. Standard mixed models first flagged molecules whose levels changed. CLARITY then separated those with changed relationships to other molecules from those with level changes only, and it surfaced an extra cluster undergoing purely relational change that traditional methods missed. The authors argue such relational views can sharpen hypotheses about which biological pathways an intervention truly alters.
pmc-13407667:
Sami Rayanne Lewis, Lisa Long, and Karan Sampat describe, in 2026, a pregnancy complicated by a fresh blood clot in the vein draining the gut. The blockage raised pressure in that venous system without liver disease being the cause, and swollen veins in the gullet, a dangerous bleeding risk, developed during the woman's third pregnancy.

Care was shared across centres and specialties throughout the pregnancy, weighing the mother's bleeding and clotting risks against the baby's safety at each step. She ultimately delivered a healthy baby at full term through an induced vaginal birth. Alongside the case, the authors discuss the treatment options available for pregnant women with this form of portal hypertension and how its complications can be managed.
pmc-13407867:
Michael Brazzill and co-authors expand, in 2026, the vocabulary that DNA-targeting strands can read. Triplex-forming strands grip double-stranded DNA at set sequences. They are a tool for medicine and synthetic biology. Natural bases restrict which sequences can be targeted, though. Stable binding usually needs acidic conditions. The team borrowed extra bases from an expanded genetic alphabet.

Testing 120 combinations of three-base recognition units yielded at least twelve building-block units that can be mixed and matched. The expanded strands bound targets containing ordinary, damaged, or synthetic base pairs with nanomolar strength at neutral pH. Tests included detecting oxidative DNA damage and synthetic pairs inside enzyme-built DNA, using strands made chemically or by enzymes. Precision gene targeting and molecular sensing are the intended uses.
pmc-13408067:
Eiichiro So, Chigusa Morizane, and Takuji Okusaka review, in 2026, drug therapy for neuroendocrine neoplasms of the gut and pancreas. These tumours spring from hormone-making cells. Under the 2022 World Health Organization scheme they split into well-differentiated tumours graded one to three and poorly differentiated carcinomas. That distinction now steers treatment selection.

For unresectable well-differentiated tumours, hormone therapy, targeted drugs, chemotherapy, and radioisotope-tagged peptide therapy are standard options, while chemotherapy alone anchors care for the poorly differentiated carcinomas. Outcomes for advanced disease remain unsatisfying, partly because rarity slows trials. The review maps current systemic options and their biological rationales, then surveys recent advances and the field's open challenges, from sequencing treatments to finding better targets.
pmc-13408567:
Shun Ikeda and Arata Momohara re-examine fossil conifers from Miocene Japan in 2026 and conclude that two supposed genera are actually one species. Sequoia leaves were long treated as unchanging through the group's history, yet living coast redwoods carry small scale-like leaves high in the crown beside the usual flat sprays. Fossils named Protosequoia have exactly those scale leaves, hinting at a mix-up.

Re-studying the specimens, the authors found shoots preserved in organic connection that grade from flat leaves to scales along their length, with surface cell patterns and pore orientation shifting gradually to match. Seed cones and pollen structures also agree between the two fossil forms. They therefore propose a single new Sequoia species with densely branched, small-scaled twigs, possibly an adaptation to its local climate, and a caution against splitting fossils by leaf shape alone.
pmc-13408867:
KS Govinder and SD Maharaj study fold bifurcations in the collapse of a radiating star with shear, in relativity. A simple field form for such a star is used. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Surface match rules shrink to a single nonlinear equation of Riccati type, which has exact solutions and suits phase plane study. pmc-13409367:

The authors sketch the research directions most likely to clear those hurdles.
pmc-13411467:

pmc-13411767:

pmc-13414367:

pmc-13415567:

pmc-13415767:

pmc-13415867:

pmc-13416567:

pmc-13417267:

pmc-13417967:

pmc-13418467:

pmc-13419967:
Zhoushan Gu and colleagues review focused radiation as a treatment for rapid heart rhythm that resists drugs and standard ablation. The review covers patient choice, target drawing, motion control, and dose planning in practical detail. Short-term results encourage, yet dose and long-term safety remain open. The paper gives new centers a grounded path into a fast-growing therapy.
pmc-13420667:
Guillaume Serzian, Fiona Ecarnot, and Marc Badoz report a first-of-its-kind defibrillator implant after chest surgery in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. The device sits outside the veins and heart, avoiding lead troubles inside blood vessels. Prior open-chest surgery was thought to bar its use.

Scans showed a clear space behind the breastbone with few adhesions. The lead tunneled in smoothly, shock testing worked, and recovery was uneventful. The authors say careful picks may widen use.
pmc-13421267:
Lea M. Bartsch, Eda Mizrak and Klaus Oberauer investigate, in a 2026 paper, how working memory and long-term memory cooperate during immediate recall. The two systems overlap in practice, and the authors probed their interaction using interference from earlier material and a distracting task during the waiting interval.

In one experiment, volunteers learned word-object pairs; a second used object-colour pairs with a colour reproduction test. Interference hurt performance mainly at larger set sizes, suggesting long-term memory carries more of the load there, while the distracting task hurt most at small set sizes, where working memory dominates. pmc-13421467:
Xiaoyi Wang, Raif Remigio Alves, Qiuyu Hu and Hanlin Chen examine, in a 2026 study, how the framing of AI-written product pitches changes consumer trust. Neural signals diverged by pairing: for pleasure products, promotion framing drew stronger attention-related responses and easier semantic processing. The authors caution that brain signals index attention and processing rather than trust itself, though the pattern in choices was clear.
pmc-13421567:
Muhammad Anwar Ul Hassan and five colleagues map, in a 2026 study, the tiny forces cells use to feel how stiff their surroundings are, and show that oxidative stress scrambles that sense. The authors name mitochondrial integrity as a key control on stiffness sensing under stress.
pmc-13421667:
Erol Keskin and Tevfik Aslanbaş surveyed residents of Isparta, Turkey, about how they use and save water, in this 2026 study. Knowing which habits are common, and which saving steps residents already take, helps target advice where it can change behavior rather than repeat what people already do.
pmc-13422267:
Doyun Ku and co-workers printed a complete genome in 2026 for a mouth germ, Streptococcus strain KHUD_013, taken from human cheek lining. Oral streptococci are diverse, yet high-quality standard genomes for close kin remain scarce, blocking matching and naming.

pmc-13423067:
Lucantonio and colleagues studied in 2026 how a signal protein, IL-27, shapes natural killer cells inside bowel cancers. The tumour setting held these cells in the immature state instead of letting them mature. pmc-13423867:
Marcelo D. T. Torres, Fangping Wan, and Cesar de la Fuente-Nunez use deep learning to mine prion proteins, famous for misfolding and disease, for hidden bacteria-killing peptides. The lab then made 75 of them: 59 killed bacterial pathogens, 53 damaged bacterial membranes, and 2 eased Acinetobacter baumannii infection in mice. pmc-13424167:

Their workflow adds quality checks, terminology control, and name normalisation, with integrity metrics steering each revision. The goal is text that stays searchable across languages and safe for databases.
pmc-13424467:

pmc-13425967:
Yuzhen Ding and colleagues mapped distance-dependent brain connectivity in untreated first-episode depression in a 2026 resting-state MRI study. pmc-13426367:
Jiaqi Chen and colleagues report a giant liver adenoma of unknown cause in a 24-year-old man in a 2026 case study. pmc-13427367:

pmc-13427467:

pmc-13427667:

Findings like these shift attention from lone cells to flexible teams as the unit of auditory memory.
pmc-13427867:

Shellfish gathering added more food from the shore zone. Traces also hint at use of turtles and monk seals at times. The authors link fishing rounds to where settlements sat along the coast. The sea, they argue, anchored Majos life from first settlement to conquest.
pmc-13427967:

Overall survival, time without progression, and response rate were the efficacy outcomes, with treatment-related harms on the safety side. Oncologists get a synthesis of what these drugs do when patients are older, sicker, and less selected than trial volunteers.
pmc-13430167:
Alaa G. Al-Maaitah and co-authors present, in a 2026 case report, a late bleed at a tumor site as a possible herald of returning cancer. Surgery removed the growth fully, and pathology named it rhabdoid meningioma, a rare grade III tumor with a fierce reputation. Radiation followed without major problems.

pmc-13430267:

pmc-13430867:

pmc-13431467:

pmc-13431967:

pmc-13432867:
Pang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how Orf virus causes its crusty skin sores and dodges the immune system. Together these tricks let the virus finish its cycle before immunity clears it, and they help explain repeat infections. The authors argue that decoding this evasion kit is the route to better vaccines and new antiviral drugs for livestock and exposed workers.
pmc-13433267:

pmc-13433667:

pmc-13433767:
Mahnesa Gholamrezaei and colleagues test phosphorus amendments for locking lead in contaminated soil, with and without malic acid, a root-zone organic acid. pmc-13434567:

pmc-13435467:

pmc-13435567:

pmc-13436167:
Ana Luiza Cardoso Pires and five co-authors audit reviews of root canal care for spin and quality, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Spin, a slant that bends the message, showed in nearly all abstracts and most full texts, mainly as misleading readings of results. Most reviews rated low or critically low in quality. pmc-13436567:

pmc-13436667:

pmc-13438567:

pmc-13438767:

Cases from one faulty copy have also been reported with two specific variants.

Their cases presented with scaly spots and plaques with only mild redness, a milder picture than the classic form. One variant case showed symptoms on one side of the body only, which the authors say has not been reported before. They urge doctors to weigh this gene-related disease even when skin signs look atypical.
pmc-13439267:
Jing Liu's team remediated soil co-contaminated with cadmium, lead, and arsenic in 2026, testing both cleanup and reuse of the treated soil. Mixed metal soils threaten health and persist in place, yet pilot-scale proof plus a reuse route was scarce. Batch tests used iron and aluminum oxide agents, with dose tuned for economy, then pilot trials and brick making tested the stabilized soil.

A ten percent agent dose cut leaching sharply for all three metals. Bricks fired at nine hundred degrees leached only tiny cadmium and lead with no arsenic detected, while lead locked into feldspar structure. Engineers get a pilot-backed cleanup plus brick reuse pathway. Long-term field leaching must still be watched.
pmc-13439367:
Hamidreza Aliakbari Liavoli's team tested a cytokinin in 2026 to shield safflower from copper toxicity during germination and growth. Copper excess stunts seeds, pigments, proteins, and enzymes while raising stress chemicals, yet plant hormones may buffer the damage. A factorial trial crossed four copper levels with three doses of 6-benzylaminopurine, tracking germination, growth, pigments, proteins, enzymes, and defense genes.

A mid-high hormone dose under severe copper stress lifted chlorophyll, carotenoids, proteins, and antioxidant enzymes markedly, while cutting phenolics and anthocyanins in shoots. The paper frames the hormone as a tolerance booster through antioxidant and defense regulation. Growers on copper-rich soils get a candidate treatment, still at the pot-trial stage.
pmc-13440567:
An and colleagues built a tumour-based printing ink in 2026 for modelling glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer.  The team grew glioblastoma cells in gels tuned to tumour stiffness and squeezed them to mimic pressure inside the skull. This workout pushed cells to release their own matrix, which was collected as a bioink, a cell-friendly printing material.

The ink carried stronger tumour signals than plain gel controls, including higher levels of GDF15, MMP2, and MMP9, all linked to tumour spread. Printed models made from the ink grew faster and switched on more invasion-related genes. Adding vessel cells or fibroblasts, which are support cells, recreated stromal activation and matrix change seen in real tumours. The authors present the ink as a repeatable platform for glioblastoma-on-chip studies and drug tests.
pmc-13441167:
Silvia Piunno and co-authors follow patients with a puzzling form of lupus: blood tests show active disease, yet they feel clinically well for long periods. Their 2026 longitudinal study asks whether two blood markers, anti-dsDNA antibodies and complement C3, can predict future flares in this group.

Patients who flared were also more often anti-Ro positive. The authors argue this state is rarely benign and needs close clinical and blood monitoring.
pmc-13442867:
Prabakar Vaittinada Ayar and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of how blood-pressure drugs used in septic shock affect Escherichia coli, a gut bacterium often involved in sepsis. The team tested norepinephrine, vasopressin, and angiotensin II on 21 diverse strains plus a urinary sepsis model strain, growing them in fluids meant to mimic serum and urine.

Norepinephrine boosted bacterial fitness across strains, body sites, and virulence backgrounds in both fluids, while the two alternative drugs showed little or no such effect. The pattern matters because the first-line drug may unintentionally aid the very microbe doctors are fighting. The authors call for animal studies next, since dish results alone cannot settle how these drugs behave in patients.
pmc-13443767:
Francis Smit and colleagues argue that specialist training is a national asset for South Africa in a 2026 essay. Training a specialist takes 12 to 15 years of public funds, deep in wards where trainees also carry real patient loads. Universities, provinces, hospitals, and councils share the build.

Since training lives inside care, ward quality and school quality rise or fall together. Staff gaps, broken gear, and weak rule hit both patients and pupils at once. The authors say pass marks on school checks now double as a gauge of system health. A specialist's worth spills past one career into leadership, research, and service reach. They urge leaders to fund and guard training as core national wealth, not a side cost.
pmc-13444267:
Gabriel França Toledo Pinto and colleagues measure food insecurity in children and teens with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 study. The clinic sat at a Rio de Janeiro child institute, and a Brazil food scale graded home food stress. The pool held 130 young patients, most of them girls, with mothers as main carers in most homes.

Food insecurity touched 67.4 percent of the group in the count. Mild stress led at 50.4 percent of cases, while severe stress sat at 5.4 percent of cases. Income, carer schooling, and benefit receipt each tied to food stress in the checks. Most children held healthy weight for age, and height ran on track. The authors call for joint health and social policy, since tight food budgets fight the strict meal plans diabetes demands.
pmc-13444367:
Ting Xie and colleagues link felt stress, symptoms, and hippocampus part sizes in first-episode schizophrenia in a 2026 study. The pool held 97 patients at first break and 47 healthy peers. Stress scales, symptom scales, and 3.0-T MRI scans fed subfield maps of the hippocampus.

Patients felt more stress than peers in the checks. Their fimbria zones ran smaller, while tail zones ran larger, after head size and trait fixes. In healthy peers, many zone sizes rose with felt stress in tidy lines. Those lines broke or vanished in patients. In patients, felt stress rose with positive symptoms and with worry-low mood marks. The authors read the break as a sign that stress wiring itself is off in the illness.
pmc-13445567:
Yoko Akazawa-Ogawa and seven co-authors watch alpaca antibodies evolve in real time and find that getting better at binding often means getting worse at staying folded. Their technique tracks antibody sequences from the same starting genome as somatic mutations accumulate after immunization. Mutation-heavy clusters bound antigen more strongly but lost thermal stability, by up to twenty-one degrees in the extreme.

Binding strength and stability, notably, correlated only weakly. Mutations concentrated in the binding loops and one framework region. Less thermally stable clones paradoxically resisted acid and alkali better. The picture reframes affinity maturation as a trade-off managed by selection, with stability acting as an adjustable dial rather than a fixed virtue.
pmc-13445767:
Jinxin Gao and coauthors uncover a 2026 account of how the RNA helicase Dbp7 loads the centromere mark CENP-A in fission yeast, guarding chromosome splitting. Using a visual genetic screen, the team found Dbp7 prevents harmful R-loop buildup at centromeres and traced its pairing with the RNA exosome part Dis3.

Cutting the Dbp7 gene mislaid CENP-A, broke chromosome splitting, and cut centromere muting, with both the helicase domain and a tail motif needed. Dbp7 and Dis3 jointly bind centromere transcripts and recruit CENP-A through its helper Sim3. The work reveals a new loading route with weight for genome steadiness research.
pmc-13446367:
Murat Ferhat Ferhatoğlu and colleagues compare two cold storage tricks for kidneys from living donors, in a 2026 prospective study at an Istanbul transplant clinic. A graft must stay cold and viable between removal and implant, and plain cold storage still rules in living donation for its ease and low cost. The rivals were a chilled sponge wrap and a bag of ice.

Graft results at six months matched between the two methods. The ice bag showed a modest edge in the first days after surgery, in early lab signs of graft work. The authors count both as sound picks, with the bag a touch kinder at the start. Their data fill a gap on early chemistry reads for living donor grafts.
pmc-13447067:
Zhenyu Lu and colleagues open a journal collection on sensing, learning, and control for robots that work with people, in a 2026 editorial. The field is shifting, they argue, from robots as tools to robots as partners that read people and settings, learn from feedback, and act with care. The collection prizes whole-loop builds over lone clever algorithms.

Four contributions show the range. One has robots ask people smart questions to learn reward from feedback. Others cover long action reading, farm perception, and self-running medical scanning. Shared ground runs through all four: better senses, learning that takes user taste on board, and control that holds safety while work gets done. The editors frame the set as a step toward robots fit for human spaces.
pmc-13447267:
Linlin Fang leads a team mapping new antibody targets on a cattle coronavirus protein in 2026 laboratory work. The virus causes calf diarrhoea, winter gut illness in adults and breathing disease, with heavy farm losses. Its nucleocapsid protein, the most stable viral protein, suits early diagnosis and vaccine design, provided exact binding spots are known.

Lab-made protein was used to immunise mice, yielding two specific antibodies through fused-cell methods. Both reacted only with the target virus in blot and cell tests and shared the same antibody class. Cutting the protein into pieces pinpointed two short stretches that each antibody grasps, both lying on the protein surface and stable across strains. Those mapped spots give concrete starting points for targeted diagnostic tests.
pmc-13447367:
Víctor Carballo-Uicab and colleagues build synthetic gene switches to detect Listeria bacteria in raw milk in 2026 proof-of-concept work. Listeria can cause severe foodborne illness, yet direct detection in complex foods without lab amplification had not been shown. Toehold switches are RNA devices that turn on a signal only when a matching RNA sequence appears.

Analysis of a variable gene region found a short trigger stretch unique to Listeria among related bacteria. Three switch designs were built, and the most stable was tested against synthetic triggers across a wide dose range. RNA extracted from pure cultures and from spiked raw milk both activated the switch, while clean milk gave a clearly different signal. Activation stayed modest, yet detection without amplification in a messy food matrix marks a step toward cheaper food safety tests.
pmc-13447667:
Su and colleagues tackled in 2026 a stubborn flaw in cryo-electron microscopy, where sample particles stick to the grid in one preferred pose, leaving missing views that blur the final structure. Fixes such as detergents or tilted imaging are slow and case-bound. Their approach varies the temperature at which samples are frozen, which shifts how particles settle, then merges data sets taken at different temperatures.

Su merged heat-loving ribosome data from several temperatures and rebalanced the particles using a draft three-dimensional model. The merged set gave smoother quality curves, higher roundness scores, and a narrower blind zone than single-temperature data. They proved the method on a protein complex known for severe posing problems, winning a high-quality reconstruction. The authors offer the recipe as a simple, widely usable cure for a bottleneck that limits high-resolution structure work.
pmc-13447867:
Nicole M. Antczak and coauthors test a 2026 side-by-side study of active-site loops in E. coli DinB and human DNA copier kappa, two damage-bypass enzymes with matching bypass patterns. The team scanned loop spots by alanine gene change, assaying primer growth and thermal steadiness for both proteins.

Most variants matched wild-type work, but a few gene changes caused sharp work and steadiness losses, with notably similar effects at aligned spots across species. Less active variants also gained less steadying from DNA or building blocks. The kept loop governs damage toughness in both enzymes, feeding copier biology and blocker design.
pmc-13449367:
Liang and colleagues study anakinra, an immune calming drug, for the brain toxicity that can follow CAR T cell therapy. That treatment reprograms a patient's immune cells against blood cancer. The syndrome, shortened to ICANS, can be life threatening, and steroids fail many severe cases. Their 2026 study reviews 101 patients treated with anakinra at two centers and asks whether improvement in the first three days forecasts the course.

Early response was far from assured. Only about 43 percent reached neurologic improvement by seventy two hours. The median time to resolution ran eight days. Treatment related death at twenty eight days touched about one in eight. Yet the seventy two hour mark proved decisive. Patients who hit it cleared the syndrome faster, needed less steroid exposure, and died less often. The authors propose that checkpoint as the moment to judge whether anakinra suffices or escalation must begin.
pmc-13449567:
Shanshan Xu and colleagues built a deep-learning tool in 2026 to stage cervical cancer from MRI scans automatically. Staging guides treatment, but radiologists now rely heavily on personal experience, which can lead to errors. The team wanted a system that outlines tumors and nearby structures and then assigns a T stage.

A dataset of 17,479 MRI scans from 144 patients across stages T1 to T4 was hand-outlined to train the system. A new segmentation network called CPANet beat UNet, UNet++, DeepLabv3+, and UperNet-Swin on overlap scores for tumor and nearby tissues. Staging models built on those outlines were then compared, with the best chosen by accuracy. Clinics gain a faster, more consistent staging aid.
pmc-13449967:
Fu and colleagues presented in 2026 a step-by-step protocol for mapping where long non-coding RNAs bind, with fine spatial detail. These RNAs guide gene control by gripping chromatin, the packaged DNA in the cell. The classic mapping method needs huge cell numbers, suffers noisy background, and shreds the RNA it hunts during preparation. Their variant, ChIRP-Tag, swaps the shredding step for an enzyme that tags DNA in place.

Antibodies then fetch a cutting enzyme that builds the sequencing library at the binding sites. The swap cuts the needed cell input sharply, spares the target RNA, and speeds library preparation. Sensitivity and spatial detail stay high across cell types, the authors report. The protocol aims to serve studies of rare samples the older method could not handle.
pmc-13450567:
Alvaro Andres Saavedra and co-authors relate a 2026 case where lasting clots in the penis hid a rare cancer for two years. Their patient, a man aged 36, had clots on both sides of the erection chambers with steady pelvic pain. Scans at the time found no tumor, and his care stayed cautious and drug based.

Later a fast-growing mass appeared with spread to groin nodes, and surgery plus tissue tests named it synovial sarcoma, a cancer almost never seen in the penis. The disease came back soon after surgery, and he died eight months later. The team urges doctors to suspect hidden cancer when such clots persist with no clear cause.
pmc-13451867:
Kelsey McAlister and co-authors review in 2026 outcomes for adults who got online therapy for gambling disorder through one provider. Few people with the disorder seek care, and real-world proof for virtual care is thin. Records covered 1,305 adults treated between mid 2024 and spring 2026, with weekly scores of gambling symptom weight.

Patients arrived with mid-level symptoms, and over half carried another mental health condition, most often anxiety. The study tracks how scores moved over the first twelve weeks and which starting traits tied to faster gains. It also times when a gain large enough to matter in daily life first shows. The authors frame the cohort as a base for judging virtual gambling care at scale.
pmc-13452767:
Luka Flegar and five co-authors reflect on their nationwide study of surgery for urachal cancer, a rare cancer of a leftover bladder cord. Their 2026 piece sums up German hospital billing records from 2006 to 2022, covering 2,593 cases. Care for this cancer usually removes part or all of the bladder along with the cord and navel.

The share of cases treated by removing only part of the bladder rose over time and reached 74 percent in 2022. Stays after that smaller operation fell from 14 days in 2006 to just 9 days in 2022, and robot help shortened them further. The piece flags uneven care coverage across the country as a worry. Since the cancer is rare and harsh, the authors call for joint work across centers and countries to test whether the smaller operation stays as safe.
pmc-13453467:
Kaveh Ebrahimzadeh, Mohammad Mirahmadi Eraghi, and Farahnaz Bidari Zerehpoosh report a rare spine tumor that crushed a vertebra in a young man. The tumor, called pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma, grows from blood vessel tissue and sits between benign and cancerous. Their 2026 report covers a 24 year old with a burst fracture at the T12 vertebra, growing back pain, tingling legs, and weakness.

Surgeons removed the whole T12 vertebra from behind, freed the spinal cord, and rebuilt the front column with an expanding cage and screws. Lab checks on the removed tissue confirmed the rare tumor type. Two years on, the patient had no return of the tumor or new problems. The authors stress that this tumor can mimic other bone tumors on scans, so tissue proof and full removal matter.
pmc-13453567:
Xu Xiaomin and five co-authors report a prostate cancer first read as an abscess in a 36 year old man with a transplanted kidney. Transplant patients face a two to four fold higher cancer risk from drugs that mute the immune system. Their 2026 case report follows a man 16 years past his transplant who came in with pelvic pain, fever, and a rising PSA level.

A needle draw from the prostate pulled bloody fluid instead of pus, which pushed the team to biopsy at once. The tissue showed a poorly formed prostate cancer with changes in three DNA repair genes, among them BRCA2. Surgeons removed the prostate with a reshaped laparoscopic plan that kept clear of the graft kidney. One year on, his PSA was undetectable and the kidney worked steadily. The authors urge fast biopsy when a presumed abscess bleeds.
pmc-13453667:
Ryoma Oda, Takeshi Kinoshita, Nobuo Tomizawa, and Minoru Tabata report a case where a moving CT scan exposed silent poor blood flow to the brain. Their 2026 report follows a 72 year old woman with a chronic tear in her aorta, the body's main artery, forming a 53 millimetre bulge found by chance. The tear squeezed the true channel of two neck bound arteries, starving the right side of her brain.

The four dimensional scan, which shows flow over time, caught a delayed peak on the right side that plain scans would miss. Guided by that map, surgeons rebuilt the brachiocephalic and right carotid arteries, the vessels feeding that side. Scans after surgery showed the flow delay had eased. The authors present the moving scan as a planning tool for tears that quietly threaten the brain.
pmc-13454067:
Ghina Fakhri and nine co-authors chart childhood heart muscle disease at a single major center in a resource limited setting over twenty years. Their 2026 review covers 244 children diagnosed before age 18, with an average age of 5.9 years. Dilated cardiomyopathy, where the heart stretches weak, led at 62.7 percent, ahead of the thickened form at 30.3 percent.

Half the children had no symptoms and were found by chance. Suspected inflammation drove most of the stretched cases, while inherited causes led the thickened ones. Five year mortality reached 13.1 percent, concentrated in the stretched group. Two signs at diagnosis predicted death on their own: badly reduced pumping power and high pressure in the lung arteries. Subtype, age, and sex did not. The authors stress early pumping and lung pressure checks.
pmc-13455267:
Yin and co-authors profiled the immune checkpoint TIM-3 in tumors from 117 patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, an aggressive bile duct cancer usually found too late for surgery. pmc-13455367:

Median progression-free survival came to 3.75 months on the standard 200 milligram, three-weekly dosing schedule used. Median overall survival was 7.3 months across the full cohort, and the objective response rate was 13.5 percent, with disease control in 33.9 percent of patients treated. The authors present the figures as a realistic benchmark for counseling patients outside trials.
pmc-13457067:
Hee-Jung Hong and Ju-Dong Jang analyze, in a 2026 national study, how daily habits line up with how older Koreans rate their own mouth health. The data came from a community health survey of 210,212 adults aged sixty and over, gathered across 2022 and 2023. Self-rated mouth health is a practical stand-in for pain, chewing trouble, and unmet care in this age group.

Schooling showed the steepest gradient: college graduates had more than double the odds of rating their oral health well. Brushing after dinner or before bed lifted the odds by about half. Low stress and regular walking also helped. Smoking, low income, and above all unmet dental needs dragged ratings down; unmet need cut the odds to under a quarter. The authors argue that mouth health in old age mirrors social position as much as toothpaste.
pmc-13458267:

That design delivers the poison mainly to cancer cells, sparing healthy tissue better than standard chemo.

Three such drugs are in active trials for advanced breast cancer, including the hardest triple-negative form. One has shown strong results against standard chemo, with tolerable side effects. The review covers pairing these drugs with immune therapy and other targeted drugs. It also covers use when cancer has spread to the brain. Hurdles remain, the authors note, despite clear progress.
pmc-13458567:
Wanli Zhu and colleagues let algorithms pick a biomarker for prostate cancer, and the machines chose HOXC4, a developmental gene better known for body patterning. Ten diagnostic models compete, interpreted with SHAP values showing each gene's push.

A partial least squares model won with an accuracy area of 0.977. Tumors high in HOXC4 leaned on energy metabolism and protein-processing pathways, hosted a suppressive immune mix of regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages, and tied to checkpoints such as CD40 and SIGLEC-15. Expression varied across cancers in a pan-cancer scan. The authors offer HOXC4 as a diagnostic and prognostic candidate wired into immune escape.
pmc-13458667:

Hormone therapy exacts a toll: hot flashes, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, and low mood.
