After 26 weeks, the pill cut the hourly count of breathing pauses and shallow breaths by roughly 44 to 47 percent more than placebo, and night oxygen levels improved. Side effects were mostly dry mouth, poor sleep, nausea, and hesitant urination, with no serious treatment-linked events. Longer data and direct comparison with masks are still needed.
pmc-13511767:
Mirella Vinci and ten co-authors report a gene finding in a boy with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and oppositional defiant disorder, in 2026 work. Both parents were healthy and unrelated. The team read the protein-coding genes of the child and both parents, sorting the found change by standard medical genetics rules and checking it with prediction tools and protein structure models.

The child carried two copies of a rare change in a gene called LNX2, which is active during brain development and helps guide nerve cell growth and connection. The change sits in a region that handles protein partnerships. It was classed as a variant of uncertain significance, since population records list it without any tied condition and the doubled state has been seen only once before. Structure models predicted a local reshaping of chemical bonds. The authors offer the gene as a candidate needing far more proof.
pmc-13513167:
Yazan Omari and co-authors published this liver study in 2026. People with cirrhosis who await a transplant often run low blood pressure, and rules of thumb urge keeping the mean arterial pressure at sixty-five or above. The team asked whether that pressure at listing foretells death on the waitlist. They read records of 103 adults at one center from 2019 to 2023, all with mid-range severity scores.

Survivors had come in with clearly higher pressure than the nine who died. Each extra point of pressure cut the odds of waitlist death a touch. Low pressure also tied to a grave kidney syndrome of liver failure. It did not tie to confusion, fluid build-up, or bleeding. With so few deaths, the authors urge care in reading the result and call for larger cohorts to test it.
pmc-13514367:
Shun-Xin Deng and six co-authors set out in 2026 to build a quality-checking framework for Wolfiporia extensa, a fungus long used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its underground mass yields four drug parts, each prescribed for different purposes, yet makers have lacked clear markers to tell them apart. The team measured seven triterpenoid compounds, mapped sugar profiles, and recorded colour values for each part.

Distinct chemical fingerprints emerged: one acid peaked in the outer skin part, another in the red part, and a third in the inner white part, which also carried the most sugars. Simple ratios between two compounds, paired with lightness readings, separated the parts reliably. Extracts behaved differently in cell tests, with the white part shielding nerve-like cells from peroxide damage and the skin part protecting a second cell line. Readers gain a practical grading scheme for a classic remedy.
pmc-13514767:
Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 survey of Microbispora, a little studied genus of rare actinomycetes, bacteria famed for making useful natural products. These microbes live in soils, seas, plants, and insects, yet drug hunters have largely passed them by. The survey lists every compound reported from the genus so far.

Eighty-one compounds are now known, spanning quinones, chromones, macrolides, alkaloids, peptides, and other groups of molecules. Chen notes effects ranging from killing microbes and cancer cells to guarding nerves and boosting plant growth. Gene studies predict many more chemical factories in Microbispora genomes that remain untested. The authors argue the genus is a rich, little explored source for new drug hunting.
pmc-13515067:
Nina Dimitrijevic Jovanovic leads a twelve-author team documenting oral health among hospitalised patients treated for heroin-related opioid use disorder in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Ninety-seven inpatients received structured interviews and dental examinations, including standard counts of decayed, missing, and filled teeth plus a hygiene index. They also rated how mouth problems affected daily life on a fourteen-item questionnaire.

The average tooth index showed extensive lifetime decay experience, hygiene scores pointed to poor cleanliness, and quality-of-life scores were markedly impaired, worst in psychological and social domains. Worse mouths meant worse lives in the data: quality-of-life scores climbed steeply alongside tooth damage and with poorer hygiene. Longer heroin use tracked more damage on all fronts. Regression pinned poorer quality of life on accumulated tooth damage, hygiene, and unstable housing.
pmc-13515567:
Ionel-Daniel Nati leads a twelve-author team exploring why HPV vaccination lags in Romania in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Cervical cancer is largely preventable, yet Romania records the European Union's highest death rates from it, and vaccination runs on a passive opt-in basis. The team surveyed adult women at four clinics between December 2025 and March 2026, asking about HPV knowledge, trust in health authorities, vaccine views, and exposure to online falsehoods.

Only about twenty-nine percent of the women were vaccinated. Knowledge about HPV and trust in health authorities each tracked a stronger intention to vaccinate. Leaning on official sources went with seeing the vaccine as safer. Negative online content linked weakly to lower knowledge but did not directly move vaccination intent. Nati's team argues that health literacy and institutional trust are the pillars of acceptance.
pmc-13515767:
Yaqian Liang and seven colleagues characterise three bacteria-eating viruses, called phages, that attack Staphylococcus aureus, in a 2026 study. This germ threatens people, food safety, and livestock, and phages are candidate weapons against drug-resistant strains. The team isolated three phages from sewage and profiled them with electron microscopy, killing assays, and full genome sequencing.

Two phages showed the long-tailed siphovirus shape and one the contractile myovirus shape. The myovirus-like phage killed the widest range of strains and kept killing longest, and it also weathered heat and ultraviolet light best. All three stayed infectious across a broad span of acidity and cool-to-room temperatures. Their genomes ran to roughly forty-four thousand letters, with no antibiotic resistance genes found. Some genes hinted at a dormant lifestyle, though, so the authors say safety checks must go further before any farm or clinic use.
pmc-13516367:
Petar Vasilev and co-authors present two case reports, published in 2026. Both infants came from the same family. Each developed severe hepatitis. The cause was linked to hepatitis B virus. Liver infection from this virus is rare in infancy. It is usually mild there. The siblings fell ill two years apart. Their outcomes differed sharply.

The first infant was a five-month-old girl. She suffered fulminant liver failure. She died before full testing could confirm the cause. Her brother fell ill at four months old. His acute infection was confirmed. Other possible infections were present too. He needed prolonged hospital care. He recovered, and the virus later cleared. Testing relatives found chronic hepatitis B in the mother and grandmother. Hepatitis D virus was also present.
pmc-13517167:
Monica-Daniela Padurariu-Covit and five colleagues track blood counts and survival in people newly diagnosed with HIV in a 2026 cohort study. Low blood counts are common at diagnosis, but their warning value is fuzzy. The team reviewed patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2024 at one centre, comparing blood, immune, viral, and inflammation measures at entry and after twelve months of therapy.

Most arrived with advanced disease and deep immune suppression. Anaemia was the commonest problem and travelled with lower defender-cell counts, higher virus levels, and worse survival. High inflammation readings and shortages across several blood lines also spelled trouble. Patients short in two or more lines died significantly more often, a pattern the authors read as a marker of body-wide decline. Counts and immunity recovered markedly after a year of treatment. The team proposes multi-line shortages as a cheap early risk flag.
pmc-13518867:
Shuyi Sun and a large team report in 2026 an optical sensor method that adds up wireless data without demanding tight timing between senders. Internet of Things networks drown in data, and over-the-air computation normally requires signals to arrive in lockstep, which costs overhead. Their sensors trap light-generated charges in defects, holding a fading memory of incoming pulses.

Within one communication window, the system merged signals offset by up to 120 percent of the pulse length, with errors below 1.5 percent on a normalized measure. Pulsed low-frequency readout kept energy use low. A distributed temperature prediction test converged faster with a simpler setup, hinting at practical edge sensing networks.
pmc-13518967:
Burke J Minsley leads a nine-author team mapping salty groundwater hidden beneath coastal Louisiana in 2026 with airborne electromagnetic surveys. Managers usually blame modern seawater creeping inland, yet geology can strand ancient salt underground. Their surveys reveal a buried pattern spanning more than 10,000 square kilometers.

The three-dimensional salinity pattern mirrors aquifers around modern Delaware Bay, fingerprinting a drowned river valley from the last ice age. As post-glacial seas rose, the Mississippi's incised valley flooded into a paleo-estuary, trapping seawater that still lingers under the delta plain. Minsley and colleagues offer the finding as a framework for spotting legacy salt along other coastlines, where it can threaten wells.
pmc-13519867:
Pavithra R and co-authors recount in this 2026 case a painless tearing of the aorta in a thirty-four year old man, a presentation that hides a deadly emergency. Aortic dissection usually announces itself with severe tearing chest pain, but about one case in ten has none.

The man arrived with sudden weakness on his left side, slurred speech, and fading consciousness, looking like a stroke. Scans revealed a dissection running from the top of the aorta down into the abdomen and into a neck artery, which had caused his stroke. Clot-busting treatment was withheld because it is forbidden in dissection. The authors urge doctors to consider this diagnosis in young stroke patients, since fast imaging decides the outcome.
pmc-13520167:
Zhu and colleagues listen to dialysis patients themselves describe the ethical knots of life on a blood-filtering machine, a perspective research usually takes from clinicians instead. Their 2026 study interviewed 35 haemodialysis patients at four hospitals of traditional Chinese medicine in Shandong Province. It organised the dilemmas using ecological systems theory, which sorts influences from the personal up to the societal.

Three levels of dilemma emerged, broken into twelve subthemes. Personal struggles sat at the centre. Clashes and obligations among family, fellow patients, and care providers formed the middle ring. Policy, cultural, and community pressures formed the outer ring. Crucially, the levels feed each other, so a funding policy can become a family argument that becomes a patient's private guilt. The resulting layered model is the paper's contribution: a map showing ethics committees and managers where an intervention at one level might relieve pressure at another.
pmc-13520367:
Juanjuan Guo and colleagues study in 2026 how heat harms flower bud formation in red raspberry and whether spraying salicylic acid can ease the damage. The double-season variety Polka was tracked through eight bud stages lasting about 28 days.

Heat at the pollen mother cell stage disrupted the nourishing tapetum layer, leading to faulty pollen and malformed male flower parts. Growth hormones fell while a stress hormone rose, upsetting balance. Salicylic acid at the tested dose eased anther damage and steadied hormone levels, according to the opening summary. Growers facing hotter summers gain a candidate spray treatment with a stated dose and timing logic.
pmc-13521467:
Ana G. Del Hierro and colleagues build in 2026 software sensors that infer yeast biomass in real time during dense fermentations, where lab weighing and diluted optical checks are too slow for control. Online near-infrared probes give continuous signals, yet scattering bends those signals at high density.

Nineteen fed-batch runs across three industrial yeast species trained fourteen candidate conversion models. Careful leave-one-batch-out checking prevented leakage between related runs. Chosen simple models predicted dry weight well across species, with noisier results for the diluted optical target. Paired full and pocket-calculator versions suit both automated plants and manual operations.
pmc-13522567:
Giorgia Del Missier, Kiyan Shabestary, and Rodrigo Ledesma-Amaro present a tool paper, published in 2026. It introduces WASP, a pipeline for working out protein functions. WASP uses computed three-dimensional shapes. It does not rely on gene sequences alone. AlphaFold now supplies shapes for most proteins. Comparing shapes can fill label gaps. Matching sequences leaves those gaps even in well-studied species.

In tests, known labels were hidden on purpose. WASP recovered them better than leading sequence-based tools. It labelled a fifth to a third of proteins with no known function. This held across twenty species of practical interest. The authors show its use in curating genome-scale metabolic models for biotechnology.
pmc-13522867:
Ameena M Khan Sullivan and colleagues test how simulated night shifts alter responses to meals in a 2026 laboratory study. Nine healthy young adults who did not normally work shifts completed one day shift and then two night shifts, with sleep and meals delayed by ten hours. Four identical meals were eaten per shift, and blood glucose, insulin, and fats were measured hourly alongside hunger ratings.

Lipid rhythms shifted with the new schedule and flattened noticeably. Night shifts raised glucose and insulin responses after meals, while insulin failed to fully compensate, signaling lower glucose tolerance. Time of day mattered in both schedules, with early evening meals producing the highest glucose responses. The authors propose mistimed eating as one route by which shift work raises metabolic disease risk.
pmc-13523267:
Yujie Shi, Ye Jin, and Hui Yu investigate a small RNA as a marker for newborn breathing disease in a 2026 study. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a major cause of illness and death, especially in preterm infants. Blood and amniotic fluid from thirty-five affected newborns and thirty-five healthy controls were compared for levels of one microRNA, and cell experiments tested its effect on lung surface cells.

The microRNA was elevated in both blood and amniotic fluid of affected newborns, and each fluid distinguished cases from controls with good accuracy. Blocking the microRNA in lung cells improved cell survival and raised output of a key surfactant protein, whose gene it directly regulates. The authors suggest the molecule participates in fetal lung development and could serve as a biomarker for the syndrome.
pmc-13523367:
Patricia González-Berdullas leads a team validating a drug measurement method using saliva and finger-prick blood in a 2026 study. Monitoring the antibiotic linezolid helps balance benefit against toxicity, yet standard monitoring needs venous blood. The new laboratory method measured the drug and its two main breakdown products in oral fluid and in capillary blood collected by a volumetric microsampling device, following international validation guidelines.

The assay performed within accepted accuracy and precision limits across all sample types. In paired specimens from thirty-five treated patients, drug levels in both new sample types tracked plasma levels strongly. Breakdown products behaved less cleanly: they were biased in capillary blood, needing correction factors, and rarely detectable in oral fluid. The authors support the new sampling routes for the parent drug.
pmc-13523467:
Muhammed M. Faiz and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two drugs added to a scalp nerve block for awake brain surgery. Blocking scalp nerves eases pain during awake craniotomy, a procedure where the patient stays conscious, yet a local anesthetic alone wears off quickly. Dexmedetomidine and ketamine were tested as additives to ropivacaine.

Forty-six adults were randomized evenly between the two mixtures. Patients given ketamine waited longer before asking for rescue pain relief, roughly 18.7 hours against 14.7 hours, and reported lower pain scores at several later time points. They also used less rescue medicine. Breathing depression was more common with dexmedetomidine, while that drug better blunted heart rate and blood pressure responses during surgery. The authors call for larger multicenter trials to settle the best choice.
pmc-13524967:
Vishesh Jain, Matthew Kwan, and Marcus Michelen published a 2026 mathematics paper on quantum entanglement. Two partners, Alice and Bob, share one quantum state between them. By acting only on their own parts and talking freely, they may turn that state into a new one.

A famous result, Nielsen's theorem, gives an exact rule for when such a change can happen. Nielsen also guessed that in large systems, almost all pairs of states cannot be changed into each other at all. The authors take up that guess in their title's claim: entangled states are typically incomparable. Their work uses the natural measure on states to say what typical means. The result shapes how scientists think about handling quantum states.
pmc-13525167:
Ong and colleagues tested in 2026 whether swinging reduces academic stress in nursing students. Swinging stimulates the vestibular system, the inner-ear balance sense, and is linked to relaxation. The quasi-experimental study enrolled seventy-eight student nurses in Baguio City, split into swinging and control groups. Stress was measured with a standard academic stress scale, and the team varied swinging duration and body position.

The swinging group showed a significant drop in academic stress compared with controls. How long students swung, and in what position, changed how much stress fell. They recommend building vestibular stimulation into nursing education. That includes campus spaces designed for swinging breaks. The study adds a low-cost, non-drug option to the student stress toolkit, tested across year levels of the nursing programme.
pmc-13525667:
Shiqiong Huang and colleagues run a 2026 retrospective study of adverse drug reactions among hospitalized patients with HIV and AIDS in China, using a variable-selection regression method to hunt for risk factors. Such reactions add heavily to hospital burden in this population. Suspected reactions were judged for causality with an international monitoring system.

Among 918 patients, 210 experienced a reaction, an incidence of 22.88 percent. Blood and lymphatic disorders were the commonest manifestation class. Antibacterial drugs caused the largest share, followed closely by antivirals. The selection model singled out one clear factor, the number of medications given during hospitalization, which raised the odds of a reaction substantially. The authors propose the count as a simple flag for closer monitoring and regimen review.
pmc-13525967:
Salvatore Alessio Angileri leads a large team in a 2026 review of interventional radiology for slipped discs, a common cause of spinal pain and nerve pain. Most patients recover with rest and basic care, yet lasting cases need options between drugs and open surgery. Needle techniques guided by imaging fill that middle step.

A structured search of PubMed and Scopus covered mechanical, thermal, chemical, and healing methods for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar slipped discs. Noted results included pain relief, recovery, complications, and repeat procedures. Findings suggest needle procedures can give real short- and medium-term gains in chosen patients whose symptoms match imaging, with less cutting and faster recovery in skilled hands. The authors note the findings are mostly observational and call for trials across many centers with uniform reporting.
pmc-13528067:
Yongyi Pan and eleven colleagues test a plant compound against obesity-linked male infertility in a 2026 mouse study. Puerarin comes from the kudzu plant root. Mice on a high-fat diet gained weight and made less testosterone. Their sperm counts and movement fell. The team combined gene scans with protein hunting to find the compound's target.

Puerarin trimmed weight gain and fat, and it cleaned up blood lipids. Testes kept a healthier shape, and testosterone, count, and motility rose. The compound latched onto a helper protein called GRP78. That grip steadied StAR, a protein that starts testosterone making. Blocking GRP78 in cells undid the benefit. The authors name the GRP78 to StAR route as the mechanism. Human testing would be a distant next step.
pmc-13528167:
Csilla Kurdi and nine colleagues compare amino acid patterns in egg follicle fluid across three infertility-linked conditions in a 2026 study. The fluid bathes the egg and mirrors body metabolism. Samples totaled 171 from IVF patients. Groups covered insulin resistance, endometriosis, and thyroid trouble. Twenty amino acids were measured with precise lab methods.

Overall patterns looked alike across groups. Disease still left a modest but real fingerprint. Insulin resistance came with lower glycine and arginine. Thyroid trouble came with lower histidine, tryptophan, and lysine. Endometriosis stood out for higher histidine. The shifts held after accounting for body weight. Single amino acids sorted the groups poorly. The authors favor whole-pattern readouts. They say the follicle senses whole-body metabolic health in a quiet, spread-out way.
pmc-13528867:
Lucy Hughes and five co-authors tested what adds value to story based word teaching for children with language disorder. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with developmental language disorder and like states. Such children find word learning hard. Word programs often mix three parts: words in a story, clear direct teaching, and sign or gesture with speech. Which parts carry the gains was not known.

Eighteen children took part in a design where each child met each mix. All had a language disorder, most of the set kind. The team gauged the boost from clear teaching, from signing, and from both at once. Readers who treat child language get facts to build leaner, stronger word programs.
pmc-13529267:
Yuichiro Hara and seven co-authors hunt for an HIV cure compound in a 2026 paper. Modern therapy controls the virus but cannot clear hidden reservoirs of infected cells. A shock-and-kill strategy wakes the virus so the cells can be destroyed. Most known waking agents only shock, without the kill. Screening a small-molecule library turned up a compound that seems to do both.

The compound reactivated hidden virus and selectively harmed the reservoir cell lines. At single-cell level the two effects looked independent, so one did not simply cause the other. It also switched on viral activity in cells taken from treated patients. More validation in primary cells is urged.
pmc-13529867:
Shimosato and Goyama review a rare but instructive form of acute myeloid leukaemia driven by rearrangements of the NPM1 gene. The common NPM1 story is a small mutation found in up to two fifths of adult cases, with well-mapped behaviour. Rearrangements, where NPM1 fuses with partners such as MLF1 or RARA, are far rarer and were long neglected. Their 2026 synthesis gathers the emerging evidence on how these fusions look clinically and how they cause disease.

Reassuringly for drug developers, the fusions work through the same machinery as the common mutation. The NPM1 protein ends up stranded in the cytoplasm, partners with the export protein XPO1, and holds developmental HOX genes switched on, driving the leukaemia. Clinically, rearranged cases skew younger and may carry a worse outlook, though the authors flag the small numbers behind that claim.
pmc-13530267:
Mohammad Khorsandi and colleagues test in 2026 green solvents that could dissolve a poorly soluble drug ingredient called 4-hydroxycoumarin. Three acidic deep eutectic solvents, each built from choline chloride plus a simple acid, competed against plain water. Standard shaking-flask measurements spanned a small temperature range.

The propionic acid version lifted solubility more than five hundredfold over water, beating the acetic and lactic versions. Math models fit the data closely, and heating analysis showed dissolving absorbs heat. Cell tests on colon cancer cells found moderate killing power that varied with solvent mix, supporting early drug formulation work.
pmc-13531667:
Silva-Ramos and co-authors combed fleas from rural dogs across 24 municipalities of Cundinamarca, Colombia. They checked them for two bacterial genera that fleas carry to people: Rickettsia, which causes spotted fevers, and Bartonella, behind cat-scratch disease and other illnesses. Colombian data on dog fleas were thin. Their 2026 field study examined 116 dogs in 2019 and 2020, identified the fleas, pooled them, and screened the pools with sensitive DNA tests, following up positives for species identification.

About two fifths of dogs carried fleas, and nearly all the fleas were the cat flea species that happily bites dogs and humans alike. Rickettsia turned up in the large majority of pools, mostly Rickettsia asembonensis with some Rickettsia felis. Bartonella appeared in over a quarter of pools, though sequencing could not pin its species down.
pmc-13531867:
Hongchun Li and colleagues show in 2026 that silencing the Tau protein protects young mice from lasting thinking damage after newborn sepsis. Infection in the first month of life often leaves survivors with cognitive harm into adolescence. Tau, a nerve fiber protein, was the suspect mediator in this mouse work.

Turning Tau down softened memory loss after early inflammation. Brain checks showed reshaped branching in a memory region and renewed birth of nerve cells there in adulthood. The authors nominate Tau as a treatment target for sepsis-related brain injury, with structure and cell renewal as the routes.
pmc-13531967:
Jiangyuan Liu, Johan H Gibcus, and Job Dekker present in 2026 a workflow that calls DNA loops jointly across related chromosome-folding datasets. Loop calls from Hi-C maps vary wildly between similar samples, muddying comparisons. Their tool, UnionLoops, first builds one shared candidate set, then applies uniform filtering and scores support sample by sample.

Joint calling found more shared loops, trimmed spurious one-off calls, and matched independent protein occupancy evidence better than single-sample routes. Cleaner loop maps sharpen reading of how genome folding shifts across conditions, a basic need for studies of development and disease across sample groups.
pmc-13532267:
Yuyuan Xue and a team of co-authors tune a rapid PCR test for skin and nail fungal infections. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Microscopy misses cases, culture takes weeks, and patients wait in limbo.

One hundred thirteen suspected cases ran through all three methods plus the new multiplex assay. A receiver-operating analysis set the positivity cutoff at a cycle threshold near thirty-two point seven. Resampling a thousand times confirmed the cutoff was no fluke. The assay read two major fungus genera with strong accuracy. Pairing microscopy with the rapid test caught sixty-six percent of cases, beating microscopy alone, and answers landed within three hours instead of weeks.
pmc-13532367:
Caroline Cushman and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a usually harmless kidney tumor that invaded the heart of a thirty-six-year-old woman. Such tumors rarely grow into veins, and reaching the heart's right side without the linked genetic syndrome is rarer still. She arrived with belly and back pain plus nausea.

Scans showed a huge left kidney mass with a tumor cord running up the great vein into the heart, dipping through a valve with each beat. Gene tests ruled out the syndrome. A multi-team operation removed kidney and cord together and rebuilt the vein. Final checks confirmed full removal with clean margins.
pmc-13532867:
Yanqiu Wang and colleagues tested what happens while focused ultrasound is beamed at the brain's movement area, rather than after it ends. They measured how strongly one side of the brain reins in the other, a balance key to smooth movement.

Fifteen healthy volunteers received ultrasound to one movement area while magnetic pulses measured the cross-brain braking at two time gaps. Ultrasound weakened the long-gap braking from the treated side to the opposite side during the beaming. The short-gap braking stayed unchanged, and the opposite side's own excitability did not shift either. Wang reads this as ultrasound tuning a complex circuit, and offers it as a probe of how the two brain halves interact.
pmc-13534667:
Mengyue Wei and colleagues optimise in 2026 an ethanol extract of Litsea cubeba fruit and probe how it kills Staphylococcus aureus. The plant has a long history as a spice and folk remedy, and natural germ killers are sought for food and drug use. Response surface methods tuned heat, time, and liquid ratio for the best yield.

Best settings gave a high antibacterial rate, and chemical scans found 20 compounds led by fatty acids. The extract killed germs at low doses and broke their walls and membranes, leaking cell contents. The work supports the fruit as a natural antibacterial source.
pmc-13534767:
Mónika Koós and a large global team develop in 2026 the Paraphilic Disorders Short Screen, a brief tool aligned with current ICD-11 rules. No reliable screen existed for these disorders under the new guidance. Data came from 82,243 adults across 42 countries in 26 languages, with expert-led item design.

The screen covers seven paraphilias in 21 items, with cut scores set per guidance. Voyeuristic interest was most common, and groups meeting disorder cut-offs showed worse depression and anxiety than others. Clinicians and researchers gain a validated way to flag at-risk people across cultures.
pmc-13536267:
Michael Rouse, Yumna Kaleem, and Justin M Yeung discuss in 2026 how artificial intelligence can lower barriers to research for surgical trainees. Research is now core to training, yet cost, time, thin mentoring, and ethics delays block many juniors. Their view maps AI help across each research stage.

Tools can aid idea shaping, literature search, protocol drafting, ethics forms in plain language, data extraction, and analysis code. The authors stress that AI should support, not replace, core skills like design judgement and critical reading. Risks and limits must stay in view for safe trainee use.
pmc-13536767:
Laura Barberán-Bernardos, Miguel Ángel Ariza-Gracia, and David P Piñero compare two eye imaging devices in a 2026 agreement study. Both devices measure front eye shape, corneal thickness, and chamber size used in diagnosis and surgical planning. Fifty-five healthy eyes were measured with each device by the same examiner. Paired tests and agreement plots assessed whether readings could be swapped in practice.

Front corneal curvature agreed well enough for shared use, with no clear average gap. Other measures differed clearly, including back curvature, chamber depth, thickness, and chamber angle, with one device tending toward deeper chambers and narrower angles. Thickness agreement ranges were wide. The authors warn against swapping devices freely for thickness checks before lens surgery or for chamber measures guiding implant choices.
pmc-13536867:
Zichun Wang and colleagues track care delays for migrant tuberculosis patients in suburban Shanghai in a 2026 review of cases from 2015 to 2024. Two delays matter, the wait before a patient first seeks care and the wait before the system confirms diagnosis. Records held 3,178 lung tuberculosis cases, split almost evenly between locals and migrants in Fengxian District. Trends and risk factors for each delay were compared.

Migrants waited fewer days before seeking care than locals, yet waited longer for confirmed diagnosis. The first wait among migrants rose steadily from 2017 onward. Female sex, middle age, and first seeking care outside the district raised the first wait, while test results and care location shaped the second wait. The authors urge better cross-district coordination and stronger local lab testing.
pmc-13538167:
Roberta Borg-Bartolo, Maurus Jaeggi, Martin Schimmel, and Hendrik Meyer-Lueckel review oral health in older adults in Switzerland in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The review spans studies from nineteen seventy onward, for people aged sixty-five and up. It tracks tooth loss, gum disease, false teeth, and chewing function over time.

Toothlessness fell sharply, from near half of older adults in the nineteen eighties to a small share in recent years. The mean count of missing teeth fell by more than half across the same span. People living at home had better mouth health and chewing than those in care homes. Mouth cleanliness stayed middling to poor in all settings, and data on life quality tied to oral health were scarce.
pmc-13538567:
Abdalla Elbialy presents a framework that sharpens spot-based tissue gene maps to single-cell detail without outside references in a 2026 study. Spot platforms average several cells per reading, while rival sharpening tools need reference data or fresh training per dataset. The morphology-guided system works training-free, validated on one colon cancer sample measured across four platforms, including a true single-cell reference.

On the finest spot input, the system matched the single-cell reference more closely than any rival tested. Across six distribution checks on a shared gene panel, its variants led most metrics with no rival winning any. Trained rivals merely tracked raw readings on matched regions. The authors highlight per-cell records with coordinates as output no raw spot reading can supply.
pmc-13539467:
Stéphane Gooré and co-authors profile trunk bark oil from an Ivorian tree across fifty trees in eight places, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Three lab methods split the oils into eighty-three parts. Scent oils of this species are reported here for the first time.

Pine-type scents rule the oils, led by one form that swings from near a third to three quarters. Cluster math split the oils into two groups, one with a split pair of subgroups. Mixes differ by which pine forms lead and which side notes join. Place and tree both seem to shape the oil. Readers get a first chemical map of a little-known bark oil.
pmc-13540867:
Weishan Lin leads a 2026 study explaining part of the bone fragility seen in spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that wastes muscle and leaves many patients with osteoporosis. Muscle talks to bone partly through tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, and patient muscle samples hinted that this traffic was disturbed.

Patients and model mice both showed muscle releasing far fewer vesicles. Those vesicles, when supplied in adequate doses, encouraged bone-forming cells and restrained bone-eating cells just as well as vesicles from healthy muscle, and replenishing them rescued bone in the mice. The chain ran from the missing SMN protein down to a release protein, SNAP23, whose fall throttled vesicle secretion.
pmc-13540967:
Laura L Jelliffe-Pawlowski leads a 2026 California study building an index of preterm birth risk that only counts risk factors medicine can actually act on. Preterm birth is the leading killer of young children, and proven interventions for many maternal conditions reach fewer than half of eligible women.

Linked records for 1.9 million singleton births between 2016 and 2020 were split into training and testing sets. Eighteen candidate risks with evidence-based responses, spanning clinical, behavioural, and social domains, fed the index. Conditions such as chronic hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, asthma, and mental illness anchor the list. The study examines how well the index flags risk through pregnancy and which factors combine most dangerously.
pmc-13542067:
Hilal Kalkan and seven colleagues monitor, in a 2026 field study, whether pole vaulters keep their run-up speed across repeated attempts as effort builds inside the body. Approach speed in the final metres is the main mechanical driver of jump height, so any fade matters to coaches.

Eleven competitive vaulters, four women and seven men, made four jumps twenty centimetres below their personal bests with short rests. Blood lactate and heart rate stayed statistically flat between attempts, while felt exertion rose only late in the set. Run-up speed and every step measure held steady throughout. The authors conclude that this submaximal protocol preserves speed even as internal signals climb unevenly.
pmc-13543167:
Yunxiao Ji and five co-authors asked if salt intake drives bone loss risk. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, pairs two kinds of proof. Osteoporosis is a world health load, most for older adults. Salt is a diet trait that could be changed, but past finds clash. The team used a big United States health survey with just over three thousand adults across three wave spans.

Survey math weighed the salt and bone link with other traits held in check. A gene based method then tested if the link could be causal, through variants tied to salt handling. Readers who guide diet learn if the salt and bone tale holds past plain links. Two proof paths make the read stronger than one.
pmc-13543367:

Sounira Mehri and Josef Finsterer wrote this 2026 letter responding to a study by Oh and colleagues. That study used exome sequencing and mitochondrial DNA analysis in 77 children with blood or protein in the urine and a family history of kidney disease. It reported a yield of 55 percent, with COL4A-related kidney disease the commonest finding. Mehri and Finsterer welcome it but challenge how gene variants were judged harmful.

They argue that prediction tools alone cannot prove a variant causes disease: tools disagree, and their accuracy is low for several variant types. Proof needs patient features, population frequencies, family segregation or lab function tests. They fault the handling of a symptom-free carrier of a mitochondrial variant known for multi-system disease. Such carriers need brain, eye, ear and heart screening, they write. Low mutation levels in blood do not rule out illness, so follow-up is essential.
pmc-13577567:
Lijun Zhang and colleagues classify lung nodules from three viewing angles at once. Their deep learning study from twenty twenty-six targets early lung cancer detection. A single scan slice shows too little of a nodule shape. Multi-view methods help, but they often merge views clumsily.

The system reads axial, coronal, and sagittal slices together. A lesion-guided attention step sharpens features near the nodule. A weighted fusion step then learns each view value per case. Tests used a public lung image collection with hundreds of nodules. Accuracy and related scores beat standard comparison methods. Balanced benign and malignant cases make the test fair. Radiologists gain a second reader tuned to nodule shape.
pmc-13578167:
Elizabeth Dudnik leads a 2026 phase II trial of first-line chemo-immunotherapy for advanced large-cell neuroendocrine lung carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer with little trial data. Patients received durvalumab, an immune therapy, plus platinum and etoposide chemotherapy for four cycles, then durvalumab alone on a monthly schedule. The main goal was the share of patients free of progression at twelve months.

The trial closed early for slow recruitment after twelve of twenty-two planned patients joined. Median time without progression was 4.4 months, while the twelve-month progression-free share reached 25.0 percent, above the bar the design set. Half the patients' tumours shrank measurably, and all three patients with untreated brain spread saw it clear completely inside the skull. Side effects were mostly mild, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results consistent with their hopes, while stressing the small numbers.
pmc-13578267:
Wonyong Kwun and co-authors describe a 2026 rapid test for scabies, the itchy skin disease caused by a tiny mite. Standard checks rely on scraping skin and hunting for mites under a lens, a method that misses many cases. Their test copies mite DNA at one steady heat, so it needs little gear and no full lab.

A quick lysis step frees DNA straight from scrapings, skipping the usual extraction work. Two mite gene targets each lit up within about half an hour, and neither fired on human DNA or on dust mite DNA. Scrapings from patients with classic and crusted forms tested positive, while control skin stayed negative through many repeat runs. The team pitches the kit for clinics and field care.
pmc-13579667:
Irene Kindole and co-authors published this study in 2026 from a large teaching hospital in Tanzania. They asked how well two tools flag sick children who may get worse in the emergency ward. One tool is PEWS, a score built from a child's vital signs. The other is a doctor's gut call, given as a percent chance on arrival.

The team tracked 250 children classed as top urgency, and 48 of them had a bad event, such as a move to high care or death. The gut call proved the sharper tool, sorting cases with more accuracy than the score. Both tools rarely missed a child who stayed safe. The authors back gut calls as a triage aid in low-resource wards, but they warn that a single training hospital may not speak for all settings.
pmc-13579767:
Luyao Ma, Tongxi Hu, and Jinjuan Huang report gut bacteria carrying a plasmid with a potent drug breaking gene, found in a patient with a torn intestine, in a 2026 study. Three strains of an environmental species, Comamonas thiooxydans, grew from diarrheal samples on plates laced with a last line antibiotic. Gene checks confirmed each strain carried a metal based enzyme that disarms that drug class.

Full genome reads placed the gene on a movable plasmid, not the main chromosome. One early strain also held an extra DNA insert with a regulator gene. Set against 481 related genomes, the isolates proved distinct from one another yet closest to a strain from the environment. The authors warn this species may warehouse and shuttle resistance genes inside the human gut, and they urge watch lists to include it.
pmc-13580967:
Claire Birkenheuer, Terri Edwards, David Bloom, and Joel Baines used a human nerve cell model to track how herpes simplex virus 1 changes gene activity, in a study from 2026. They grew LUHMES cells, which can be turned into mature neurons, and compared healthy cells with infected ones. Two lab methods let them separate brand-new RNA from the total RNA already present in the cell.

Infected neurons turned on viral genes far more slowly than other cell types do. During the quiet latent phase, the virus kept starting new RNA copies on all its genes, yet almost none of that RNA built up. Healthy neuron genes also kept a pause in their reading that the virus removes in skin-type cells. The contrast shows that neurons handle this virus in their own distinct way.
pmc-13581467:
Louiza Papantonatou and colleagues compare two gum thickening methods placed with dental implants in the smile zone, in a 2026 trial. Twenty five patients were assigned by chance to a collagen matrix, a graft of their own connective tissue, or no thickening. Ultrasound tracked gum thickness and cone beam scans tracked the bone plate, at placement and six months on, with tissue samples and patient reports added.

Both graft types thickened the gum clearly over doing nothing, with the matrix slightly ahead on paper. The bone plate thinned over time in every group, so thickening the gum did not save bone. Patients rated both routes much alike, though the own tissue graft stung a bit more. Lab views showed both materials settling in well. The authors call for bigger trials to settle the pairing.
pmc-13582767:
Shir Ginosar Yaari, Noa Boker Segal, and Maya Tamir test whether feeling worse makes a person worse at cheering someone else, in a 2026 study. Two experiments paired a helper with a person facing an upsetting stimulus. In one, sixty four pairs of strangers took part; in the other, one hundred ten pairs of closer partners. Helpers rated their own feelings, then tried to lift the other person's mood.

The pattern held in both rounds. Helpers who reacted more strongly left their partners feeling worse than calmer helpers did. Strong reactors also reached for fewer tactics, a sign of lower effort. The authors borrow the airplane rule for their advice: settle your own feelings first, then turn to the other person's. The finding matters for support work, care roles, and close bonds alike.
pmc-13583067:
Donna Ruth, Margaret Hammersla, and Andrea Tanner report a 2026 quality project from a rural elementary school in Montana. Children with anxiety often show up at the school health office with aches that have no clear cause. The school nurse began watching for pupils who came in three or more times in six weeks with such complaints. Those pupils were then offered a standard anxiety check, filled in by both the child and a parent.

Of 430 pupils, eight met the visit rule, six finished the check, and five screened positive for anxiety. Each of those five got a short talk with the nurse and a referral for counseling. The authors present the plan as a workable way for school nurses to spot anxiety early where mental health care is scarce.
pmc-13583867:
Andrea Bernasconi and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on how WhatsApp quietly became a channel for children's health advice in Pakistan. Parents and doctors increasingly consult by instant message, outside any formal system. Little was known about how that practice works day to day. The team interviewed nineteen parents and twelve health providers across Punjab who already used the app this way.

Access ran on social ties and provider goodwill, filling gaps the formal system leaves. Consultations worked by what the team calls digital auscultation: photos, voice notes, and video standing in for the exam room. Parents and providers jointly weighed uncertain calls and informal thresholds for escalating care. The channel clearly widened access and convenience. It also traded away privacy, blurred safety lines, and loaded providers with unpaid, always-on work. The team urges guidelines and training shaped to this grassroots reality.
pmc-13583967:
Navyte, Gillmeister, and Kumari link partner touch to later health in older adults. Touch is a form of social support tied to stress control. Data came from a U.S. aging study with 787 adults. The mean age was 73.34 years. Health was read at two points five years apart.

Health load was split into metabolic, heart, and hormone domains. Frequent partner touch tied to a better metabolic score over time. The link held after adjusting for other factors. Touch from other close adults showed weaker ties. The authors say daily touch may leave a long mark on body systems in old age.
pmc-13585667: Rieza Soelaeman and five co-authors surveyed United States adults in August 2025 about wastewater surveillance, the practice of testing sewage to track viruses in a community. About half of those surveyed had heard of the practice. Nearly four in five said that information about viruses from such testing was important. The authors argue that health agencies should engage communities more about how the testing works and why it matters, so the data are understood and trusted.
pmc-13586667:
Simon Ntumi surveyed more than a thousand Ghanaian senior high school teachers in 2026 about the psychology behind fair grading. A teacher who is exhausted or distressed may mark differently from one who is settled, and fairness in assessment decides students' futures. The study, correlational in design, recruited teachers from public and private schools by stratified random sampling. It measured them with checked instruments. These covered mindfulness, psychological distress, general mental health, and emotional exhaustion. They also covered job satisfaction. And their own perceptions of grading bias and fairness.

Mindfulness emerged as the hub factor. Teachers scoring higher on mindfulness also noted better mental health, greater job satisfaction. And a stronger sense that their assessment was fair. While scoring lower on distress, emotional exhaustion, and grading bias. The pattern suggests teacher well-being is not a private matter but an input into the justice of the grades students receive.
pmc-13587567:
Yong Feng and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 comparing two strains of the monkeypox virus in mice and testing antiviral drugs against both. The newer strain spreading in Africa seems harsher than the one that circled the globe from 2022. The team built a nose-infection mouse model to compare them fairly.

The newer strain killed at about a tenth of the dose the older one needed. It also advanced faster, loaded the lungs more heavily late on, and damaged them worse. Single-cell reads showed unlike immune landscapes in the lungs. Both standard antivirals worked, though one needed a higher dose against the new strain.
pmc-13589367:
Le Liu and five co-authors test a tweaked fat-burn diet plus drills gainst drills lone in young kids with autism. Their chance trial appeared in twenty twenty-six. Sixty-two kids at a Hefei mother-child ward in twenty twenty-four to twenty twenty-five were split to two packs of thirty-one. Both had ward drills on week days and home drills on rest days for two months.

The diet pack also ate a set fat-burn plan with a food powder. Both packs eased on two set sign forms. The diet pack eased more on both. The team call the diet fit in the short run.
pmc-13589967:
Haotian Zhang and five co-authors published a cohort study in twenty twenty-six on how depression shapes frailty over time in older Chinese adults living with chronic pain. Pain and low mood often arrive together, and frailty raises the risk of falls, disability, and death. The team wanted to find who slides fastest.

Using eight years of a national aging survey, they followed four thousand seven hundred seventy-eight people aged forty-five and older. Three frailty paths emerged: low, moderate, and high. Over sixty percent had depressive symptoms, and those symptoms raised the odds of landing in worse trajectories. The results argue for treating mood as part of frailty prevention in people with pain.
pmc-13591167:
Sara Penrod, Zoe Samson, and Stephanie C Chan describe, in 2026, how 68 adults with disorders of consciousness fared in acute care after severe brain injury. Such patients range from coma to near wakefulness, and most prior work looks at later rehab stages. At a major trauma hospital the team tracked awareness with a standard recovery scale. They also tracked breathing, throat tube care, and swallowing.

On arrival most patients were in unresponsive wakefulness, yet by discharge none stayed in coma and many had emerged. Most patients with breathing tubes tried speaking valves, and over two thirds had the tube removed. Penrod and the team argue that structured checks and rehab should start in the first days, not weeks later.
pmc-13591767:
Israa Ismael, Xin Luo, and Sen Li study a 2026 program that pairs new English teachers in Egypt with online mentors, with help from an AI tool. The study asks whether this kind of support can raise the trainees' belief in their own skill and their grasp of feelings in the classroom. Fifty trainees took part in the work.

Half of the group got structured mentoring, shared online tools, and feedback from the Gemini AI system. The other half followed the normal training routine. The first group showed large gains in both self-belief and emotional skill. Their own accounts also showed a shift toward teaching that puts students at the center and gives more room for thought and change.
pmc-13592667:
Serena Kao and three colleagues gather what remote care did for women's mental health during and after the pandemic. Phone and video therapy spread fast, yet results for women stayed scattered across small studies. Their review searched five databases through March 2026 and kept 57 studies with 13,457 women in 24 countries. Trials were pooled for depression, anxiety, and stress outcomes, while other designs fed summaries of acceptability and satisfaction.

Remote care beat waiting lists and usual care on all three outcomes. Depression improved most, with a moderate effect, anxiety close behind, and stress gains modest. Results swung widely between settings, so certainty stayed moderate. Benefits held in women only samples. Kao and the team call telehealth a scalable route to care while demanding stronger trials.
pmc-13595267:
Faraz Pathan and Kathryn Williams review how obesity tangles with heart failure in mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. The two conditions now overlap so often that each complicates the other.

Fresh definitions of obesity open the discussion. Direct and indirect paths from excess weight to heart failure are laid out. Obesity also distorts the usual tests, clouding both scan images and the standard blood marker. Treatment evidence is weighed for both heart failure types, weak and preserved pumping. New gut-hormone-based weight drugs get a safety review. The paper gives clinicians one map of a double burden.
pmc-13597267:
Ke Liu and seven co-authors study leadership and innovation among intensive care nurses in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Responsible leadership may spur nurses to innovate, but the path was unclear. The team tested whether feeling like an insider and speaking up carry that effect.

They surveyed three hundred seventy-two nurses in three large hospitals in northern China in early two thousand twenty-five. All four traits were positively linked. Responsible leadership raised innovation both directly and through the two middle steps, each carrying about a fifth of the total effect. The two steps also chained together for a smaller share. The authors advise leaders to build belonging and open communication so nurses share ideas.
pmc-13597467:
Marina Ritchie and eight co-authors ask trial volunteers how satisfied they feel about taking part. Their 2026 study draws on a preclinical Alzheimer's trial. Participants had no symptoms yet faced years of study visits. Their experience data can shape how future trials are run.

A satisfaction survey ran from the first week to week two hundred forty. Over ninety percent answered every item positively. Helping others was the motive most often affirmed. Design features drew the most complaints. Social motives grew warmer over time. Those lukewarm about joining at the start were likelier to quit. Early satisfaction checks may flag who needs support to stay.
pmc-13598567:
Maitikuerban and colleagues build and validate a questionnaire that measures how people with chronic disease look for health information, a habit that shapes daily self care. Existing tools cover only active searching, missing the passive ways information reaches patients through feeds and pushes. Their 2026 study, published in Chinese, grounds the design in Wilson's model of information behavior. Items are drafted from literature and team debate, refined through expert consultation, and fielded with 368 patients across six Zhejiang cities.

The instrument holds thirty items in four dimensions: information needs, channels used, searching and obtaining, and judging what was found. Reliability ran high, and experts backed nearly every item. Factor analysis pulled out three shared factors covering three quarters of the variation, and a confirmatory model fit well. Nurses and doctors, the authors argue, now have a sound tool for spotting where a patient's information habits need coaching.
pmc-13600767:
Ghari and four co-authors report a 2026 study of how udder infection changes the trace elements in goat milk. The team infected one udder half in nine healthy goats with one of two strains of the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. One strain forms biofilms, sticky layers that help germs persist, and the other does not. Milk was sampled many times over hours and days, before and after antibiotic treatment.

Eight elements were measured in the milk, including calcium, selenium, zinc, and potassium. Goats given the biofilm-forming strain released more calcium and selenium into their milk at several time points. Their milk also held more potassium and phosphorus just before treatment. The authors link the pattern to stronger gland damage from biofilm strains.
pmc-13601367:
Katharina Platzgummer and fifteen co-authors present a 2026 study of two sand fly borne infections in dogs in Austria and Germany. The parasite behind one disease is common around the Mediterranean, where dogs serve as its main reservoir. The second group, a set of viruses, matters mostly for human health, but dogs make good sentinels for its spread.

Neither country is thought to have local spread of these agents. The team tested blood from 1,520 dogs, split evenly between the two countries. They looked for antibodies that mark past exposure to each agent. The results gauge how far the risk has crept into central Europe.
pmc-13602467:
Ting Pan and three colleagues check in 2026 whether two questionnaires measure self-directed weight stigma in women after childbirth. New mothers face intense pressure to lose pregnancy weight quickly, and turning society's weight bias inward can harm mental health. Two scales exist for this, the Weight Self-Stigma Questionnaire and the Weight Bias Internalization Scale, but neither had been validated in postpartum women. The team gave both to 476 Chinese mothers averaging about 31 years old.

Both scales proved internally consistent and tracked with body mass index, felt stigma, worse psychological outcomes, and restrained or emotional eating. Their structures differed: the self-stigma questionnaire's two-factor structure held up, while the bias scale's single-factor structure did not. The authors recommend the self-stigma questionnaire for postpartum use now. The bias scale needs revision and fresh validation before it can be trusted with new mothers.
pmc-13602767:
Qiong Wu and co-authors build food-grade nanoparticles from black fungus extract in a 2026 paper. They first compared two ways to extract the fungus polysaccharide: ultra-high pressure and hot water. The pressure method gave better emulsifying power and stronger anti-inflammatory action in lab tests.

They then paired the extract with soy protein to form composite nanoparticles using ultrasound. The best recipe used equal parts, mid-level power, and ten minutes of treatment. The particles were small, stable, and evenly dispersed. Bonds of several kinds held the network together. The authors propose the particles as carriers for functional foods.
pmc-13602967:
Shroog M Al-Shahrani, Abdulaziz A Al-Askar, Kevin D Hyde, and Fatimah Al-Otibi study, in a 2026 paper, friendly fungi that may protect coffee roots from a damaging rival. Root disease caused by Fusarium fungi is spreading on Saudi coffee farms. The team collected Trichoderma fungi from coffee root zones and tested how they fight two Fusarium strains, probing three suspected weapons at once.

In paired cultures, the Trichoderma isolates grew about three times faster than their rivals, crowding them for space. Two strains blocked the worst Fusarium by over seventy-seven percent. Chemical analysis found sixty-nine scent compounds released by the defenders, some with known antifungal action. Math modeling split the credit among fast growth, scent diversity, and single key compounds. The authors frame the native fungi as a greener shield for coffee roots.
pmc-13603267:
John Dangerfield and two co-authors describe two hard cases of chronic wounds in a 2026 case report. Both patients were older adults whose wounds had failed to heal despite standard care and advanced products. The team treated them with a gel-like carrier holding the secretome, the mix of signals released by stem cells from Wharton's jelly.

One patient was a 95-year-old woman with poor blood flow and a two-year ankle ulcer. The other was a 69-year-old man with a foot ulcer that had lasted a year. Both wounds closed fully after about 27 and 28 weeks of care. The authors note that two cases cannot prove the treatment works.
pmc-13604467:
Shuo Ding and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-six, acupuncture as a precise treatment for nerve damage caused by chemotherapy. That damage causes pain and numbness, and can force doctors to cut drug doses. It affects a wide share of cancer patients, and no treatment yet reverses it. Lab studies suggest electric acupuncture can calm nerve swelling and stress pathways. Trials with fake-needle controls suggest real acupuncture may ease pain, sensory symptoms, and quality of life.

The review is frank about gaps. A high success rate for ear acupuncture comes from an uncontrolled case series. Studies vary much in method, and the key needle sensation is judged by feel. The authors call for trials that sort patients better and track lab markers and costs.
pmc-13605067:
Marina Conesa-Molina and three co-authors gather parent views on sports for autistic boys in a 2026 study. The boys had finished a twelve-week activity program in Valencia, Spain. Children at this support level face barriers to sport that research has barely mapped.

Interviews with seventeen parents of boys aged eight to twelve fed a thematic analysis. Seven themes captured both barriers and helpers. Parents described their own fears and past bad experiences with programs. Bullying and exclusion pushed many boys away from activity. Non-adapted teaching and staff without autism training added further blocks. Few programs exist for this group at all. The findings point to design changes that could open sport to these children.
pmc-13606767:
Han Yang and four co-authors build a soy glue with a salt web and clay to gain both fire block and shear hold. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Soy glues are green but weak in wet and hold. An epoxy in water fixes those flaws, yet fire rules for plywood grow strict. A web of chitosan and a P-N-S salt was dried and set in the glue with clay.

Plywood with the new glue hit a high fire mark and shed far less heat in cone tests. Dry and wet shear holds both met the state rule for in-room plywood. The team offers the mix as a green high-force glue path.
pmc-13607567:
Rosa Gemma Viterbo and five colleagues review how the immune system may shape autism's wide variety. Autistic people differ greatly in language, attention, thinking skills, and long-term outcomes, and genetics alone does not explain the spread. Their review gathers the molecular and cellular routes by which immune disturbance and autoimmunity could modify development.

Topics range over immune activation in mothers during pregnancy, maternal antibodies reacting with the fetal brain, cytokine signaling, and brain immune cells, microglia and astrocytes. Complement-driven pruning of synapses and gut-immune-brain pathways also feature. The authors are careful: immune dysfunction looks like a modifier of autism's shape in some people, not a universal cause. Direct long-term studies tying immune profiles to thinking trajectories remain scarce, above all in adults. Joining molecular, immune, and psychological data, they argue, could define subgroups and guide biomarker work.
pmc-13609067:
Junaid Saleem, Zubair Moghal, and Gordon McKay published an environmental assessment in two thousand twenty-six on a sorbent made from electronic waste. The non-metal part of old circuit boards can be activated to soak up heavy metals from water. The team measured the production footprint of making it.

Making one kilogram of the sorbent caused about five point eight kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent and a set energy demand. They then divided those burdens by how much lead, copper, or zinc the material can hold. Per kilogram of metal captured, lead looked cheapest environmentally. Shop-bought activated carbon had slightly lower production impacts but held far less lead, so its per-capture burden ran higher. Use and disposal stages were left out.
pmc-13611367:
Prachid Saramolee and co-authors published this wearable technology study in 2026. It presents a smart insole made largely of natural rubber, designed to measure body load remotely and cheaply. Each insole carries four load sensors under high-pressure spots of the foot. A small chip streams left and right loads over Wi-Fi to a cloud service. The team tested the insole against reference weights, then compared walking in thirty adults, half with flexible flatfoot and half with normal arches.

Body weight came out with an average error under three percent, and the small bias left over could be removed by one calibration factor. While wearing the insoles, the flatfoot group walked with a wider base but matched the other group in step length and speed. At fast walking, only a drop in cadence survived strict statistical correction. The authors see the insole as fit for remote monitoring.
pmc-13611767:
Zhiwei Si and colleagues design a training scheme for sensor networks that learns together without leaking data or trusting the server, in this computing paper from twenty twenty-six. In federated learning, devices train a shared model locally and send only updates. But updates can leak private facts, and a dishonest server can fake the combined result.

Their scheme, VCFedAdam, compresses each update into a small masked sketch, so little travels and little can leak. A commitment check then lets devices verify the server's combined answer rather than take it on faith. At a quarter of the original size, computing cost fell by about ninety percent and traffic by about three quarters, against standard secure methods. Accuracy on two standard image tests dipped by about one percent. The authors aim the design at the small, battery-bound sensors that need such thrift most.
pmc-13611967:
Philip Buck and co-authors measure what congenital cytomegalovirus costs US families in this 2026 paper. The virus can damage hearing, vision, and development before birth. Care burdens fall heavily on households, not just insurers. Web surveys ran from August 2024 to April 2025.

Respondents included 227 caregivers, 211 affected children, and 173 siblings. Total yearly family costs averaged about 83,140 dollars, counting care spending and lost work. Lifetime home adaptation and special schooling added about 4,713 dollars out of pocket. Caregiver quality of life scores matched general population norms. Scores for affected children varied widely by severity. Sibling scores were near normal on average. Family level data completes the case for prevention and early support.
pmc-13612467:
Yang argues in twenty twenty-six that weaving AI into company decision-making quietly drains the raw material of innovation. Efficiency rises, he grants, but the odd, hard-to-measure ideas that seed new products get filtered out. His lens is the institutional interface: the joint effect of AI design choices, human-AI routines, and company norms on what the organisation notices.

He names a failure mode of automatic execution that runs unseen, strips human agency, and dulls self-questioning. Leftovers that defy the statistical mainstream, called residuals, get dropped at the thinking, acting, and valuing stages alike. Guards like non-optimised zones and outlier paths can help, but each carries stubborn dilemmas of isolation, authority, and judgement. The piece offers testable claims for governing AI-fed firms.
pmc-13613567:
Garnett and a large team asked in twenty twenty-six how species name work is used in the Red List of species at risk. Names set the units that care work tries to save, and name shifts can shake those plans. No broad view yet showed how risk judges use names in their work.

They asked the heads of expert groups that run risk checks for each life group. Ways of work varied a lot, from one judge to full boards that set all name calls. Lists used in Red List work can clash with lists used by other care pacts. More shared rules could help, but may curb the flex that judges need.
pmc-13614067:
Sucheta Kundu and coauthors published a 2026 chemistry study of a flexible two-unit dye molecule, built from two linked porphyrin rings. It serves as a small model for how plants harvest light. The pair can twist around the link between its units. The team asked how that twisting shapes the way absorbed light energy moves and fades. They tracked the molecule with ultrafast laser methods that watch energy states rise and fall in trillionths of a second.

At low light levels the pair behaved much like the single unit. Stronger pulses revealed fading steps lasting about one picosecond and eighteen to twenty-eight picoseconds. Calculations showed that the link between the units depends on the twist angle. The pair sits in a weak-coupling regime. The extra fading fits a process in which two excited states meet and one is lost, driven by overlap between emitted and absorbed light.
pmc-13614167:
Renato D. dos Santos, Guilherme Colherinhas, and Wesley B. Cardoso test in 2026 whether HIV drugs could be reused against West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne virus that can attack the brain and has no approved drug treatment. Working fully on computers, they docked ten HIV protease blockers into the virus's own protease, an enzyme it needs to copy itself, then ran motion simulations to see which drugs stayed bound.

Two drugs, indinavir and atazanavir, held on firmly, with steady contact, lasting hydrogen bonds, and favourable binding energy. Several others scored well in the still docking test yet drifted loose once the simulation moved. The lesson for drug hunting is plain: a good first fit means little until the pairing survives motion. The two winners now merit testing in real lab experiments.
pmc-13615067:
Bingjie Li leads a team on how drive to work hard adapts. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses a new task called CoMET. It varies how much control folks have and how rich rewards are.

Folks were more keen to work hard when they had control. They also tuned effort fast as control changed in the task. Rich reward settings drew more effort as well. The team held mean reward rate fixed while control varied. Poor tuning of effort shows in many mind disorders. The task helps map how that tuning works.
pmc-13617267:
Sebastian Ullrich and co-authors tested whether practicing with virtual patients improves nurses' professional language skills in a 2026 study. Nurses recruited from abroad must pass a demanding German exam to work in Germany. Talking with patients is the hardest part to practice in a classroom.

Twenty-five international nursing staff took part at one language school. Thirteen gained access to a digital tool with interactive patient and colleague scenarios, on top of the same 600 hours of standard training the control group received. The main measure was the fail rate at the first exam attempt. Supervisors were also interviewed a year later about workplace integration.
pmc-13617367:
Paoletti and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a review of allergy treatment given under the tongue. Sublingual immunotherapy slowly trains the immune system to tolerate allergens. It is the only treatment that can change the course of allergic disease. Tablets for grass and dust mite allergy have strong trial support. They cut symptoms and medicine use, with benefits lasting after treatment ends.

Real-world studies agree and add lower risk of new asthma. Effects on day-to-day asthma control are less steady across trials. Children's results mostly mirror those in adults, with good safety. Reviews confirm overall benefit but note wide differences between products. The authors stress standardized doses and at least three years of adherence. Better product-specific trials remain a priority.
pmc-13617767:
Yongbin Xu and seven colleagues describe a pectin-like polysaccharide from the pollen of Typha angustifolia, a cattail plant used in traditional medicine, and test how it steers immune cells. Plant pectins are promising immune modulators, yet their tangled makeup has hidden which parts do the work. The team mapped the molecule's size, sugar building blocks, and branching with chemical analysis and magnetic resonance methods, then exposed mouse dendritic cells to it.

The polysaccharide, about ten kilodaltons in size, mixes smooth pectin regions with richly branched side chains and rare structural motifs. It matured dendritic cells without poisoning them, raising surface activation markers and inflammatory signals while reducing their appetite for swallowing particles. Treated cells then activated antigen-specific killer T cells more strongly, boosting their growth and interferon output. Tests against clipped versions suggest the intact, complex branching underlies the activity, though molecule size may also play a part.
pmc-13618067:
Mansoore Shahabi and two colleagues build a magnetic nanocatalyst pairing nickel and copper for two jobs: converting toxic nitroaromatic compounds into useful amines, and forming carbon-nitrogen bonds in a single pot. Industrial nitro compounds pollute water and resist breakdown, while their amine products feed dyes, drugs, and polymers. The catalyst sits on silica-coated magnetite particles, so a magnet can fish it out afterward.

A battery of imaging and analysis methods confirmed the layered structure. Reactions ran in water, a green solvent, finished within about two hours, and gave high yields. The nickel-copper pairing outperformed what either metal suggests alone, a synergy the authors credit for the activity. Most importantly for practical use, the catalyst survived seven consecutive runs of nitro reduction without significant loss of activity, supporting the design as a cost-effective, environmentally friendlier route to amine chemistry.
pmc-13618267:
Nicole Lardini Freitas and eight colleagues profile spinal fluid proteins in COVID-19 patients with acute neurological problems, hunting for the biology behind them. They compared patients grouped as stubborn headache alone, encephalopathy, or inflammatory brain disease, against controls with non-inflammatory conditions. Protein patterns were read for the processes they reveal.

Altered proteins clustered around the complement system, an immune attack cascade, plus microglia and macrophage activity, inflammation, and nerve-cell housekeeping. Complement and clotting cascades were switched on, with raised levels of two complement products backing the signal. Synaptic pruning pathways appeared in the encephalopathy and inflammatory groups. The inflammatory group also showed glial activation and immune cells moving into the brain, plus more microglia-related proteins. The authors propose that complement-driven inflammation, driven by glial cells, disrupts the blood-brain barrier and produces these distinct syndromes.
pmc-13618767:
Xunzhuo Dong and seven colleagues separate the effect of soil acidity itself from everything else that changes when farmers swap some synthetic fertilizer for organic amendments. Using two complementary global field datasets, they partitioned how much soil carbon gain and yield gain trace specifically to pH moving toward neutral, rather than to the added carbon or other shifts.

Organic substitution consistently nudged pH toward neutrality in acidic, neutral, and alkaline soils alike. The pH improvement alone explained fifteen percent of carbon accrual in acidic soils, about nine percent in neutral soils, and about four percent in alkaline soils, working mainly by boosting microbial biomass. That pH-linked carbon gain underpinned yield rises of roughly five to nine percent across soil types, strongest and most durable in acidic soils and peaking regionally in Africa. The authors urge pairing organic substitution with deliberate pH management.
pmc-13618967:
Dayou Cui and five colleagues build a lightweight neural network that diagnoses bearing faults in rotating machinery under noise and changing speeds. Bearings account for roughly half of rotating machinery failures, yet harsh conditions defeat many models. Their design, MDW-Mamba, decouples noise from fault features in stages. A three-channel input, a multi-scale convolution backbone, and a dual-scale wavelet module model long-range patterns efficiently.

Across three public variable-speed datasets, the network beat current best methods and kept average accuracy above eighty-seven percent even when noise exceeded signal. It does this with about a quarter-million parameters and answers in about a millisecond. That is small and fast enough for real-time diagnosis on small edge devices mounted on the machines. The authors position it for wind turbines, aerospace propulsion, and heavy manufacturing, where catching a failing bearing early prevents downtime and loss.
pmc-13619067:
Andrew J. Webb and seven colleagues show that chewing sugary gum can amplify beetroot juice's blood-pressure benefit, in a 2026 crossover experiment. Dietary nitrate is concentrated in saliva, where tongue bacteria convert it to nitrite, the step to vessel-relaxing nitric oxide. Fourteen volunteers drank a beetroot shot on two visits, chewing either sugary acidic bubble gum or sugar-free gum, and were tracked for seven hours.

The sugary gum dropped salivary acidity, by one and a half pH units. Nitrate delivery did not change, yet salivary nitrite production jumped forty-five percent and plasma nitrite rose a quarter, showing mouth bacteria work faster in acid conditions. Blood pressure followed: systolic fell nearly three points and diastolic nearly two, both significant. The authors note the trick could potentiate other nitrate benefits, such as exercise performance. It reframes an everyday habit, gum choice, as a lever on a body pathway.
pmc-13619467:
Wenming Shao and a team of co-authors report a pilot study of a robot surgery training system in China, in two thousand twenty-six. Robot systems give surgeons three-dimensional views, force feedback, and precise control. Yet few Chinese medical colleges build them into training so far.

Students at one medical college trained on a home-grown multi-port robot for belly surgery tasks. They rated the system's usability highly on a standard scale. Questionnaires showed good acceptance and a sense that learning felt faster and more fun. Male students rated ease of use higher than female students did. The authors note that felt gains are not proof of real skill gains.
pmc-13619567:
Hannah Meinert led a large team searching for a brain wiring pattern tied to social anxiety across diagnoses. Social anxiety runs on a spectrum, from mild shyness in healthy people to a full disorder. The researchers scanned 160 participants across that spectrum and rebuilt each person's structural connectome, the map of white-matter links between brain regions.
